en: *An Analytical Commentary on the Essential Meaning of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* Composed by the later student of the Xianzong lineage,
Tongli; Revised by his dharma-descendant, Xinxing.
First, there is a general exposition of the great meaning.

It is fully endowed with the Great, the Square, and the Vast; it encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena, and is thus termed "Perfect" (*yuan*). It penetrates and unifies the wondrous nature of both the fundamental and the initial.
To illuminate thoroughly through both the mundane and the supramundane mind is what is termed "Awakening" (*jue*).
It cannot be colored by names or forms, nor can it be sounded by voices or sounds. Yet, the compilers had no choice but to give voice to it, forcefully saying, "Thus have I heard.
Furthermore, having no choice but to give form to it, they forcefully say, "At one time, the Bhagavān entered the Great Treasury of Supernatural Radiance. 3.

To be oblivious to right concentration (*samādhi*)—to be enlightened regarding this—means that perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is not separate from one's present location, and the fruit of Buddhahood admits of no seeking outside.

Yet, as for ordinary beings and outsiders who dream themselves lost in the long night, they dream within dreams, and thus have no means to awaken. Furthermore, the provisional and limited teachings (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) arise like flowers that obscure the eye.

As the flowers bloom again and again, the pure eyes no longer appear. Therefore, the Bhagavat manifests various pure lands within the non-dual realm, bringing together the assembly of the Dharma-body;
relying upon the Heaven of Pure Enlightenment, they give rise to clouds of great compassion, with lords and attendants arrayed in infinite layers.

We dwell together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma. The ancients identified this as the sixfold accomplishment (*ṣaḍ-vidha-sampad*), which serves as the introduction for the certification of faith (*śraddhā-pratītya*).
Some claim that the introductory section (*nidāna*) is missing from this sutra; I say this is not so.
Observe how Mañjuśrī first asks the Tathāgata about the original ground of his awakening (*mūla-bhūmi*), and subsequently requests that the Bodhisattvas give rise to the pure mind.
Furthermore, regarding practice in future末代 (final) times so as not to fall into false views, the Buddha also treated this capacity with gravity, delineating two distinct meanings:

first, a general presentation of the True Doctrine (zhēnzōng), and second, a specific response to the preceding question. As for the general presentation of the True Doctrine, it serves as the overarching heading for the subsequent sections on faith, understanding, cultivation, and realization;
none of these depart from this True Doctrine. First, he demonstrates its essence, stating that the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great...

The gateway of dhāraṇī is named Perfect Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*). Next, to manifest its function, it is said that "it flows forth all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, the pāramitās, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "answering the previous question individually": the following sections provide individual answers to each of the questions previously posed by Mañjuśrī.
As for the answer to the first question, it states: "the original cause of all Tathāgatas."

All stages [of the path] depend upon the aspect of perfectly illuminating pure awakening; only by eternally severing ignorance can one achieve the Buddha-way. Next, the text interrogates and explains what is meant by "ignorance":

it refers to all sentient beings who, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions, falsely identifying the four great elements as their own physical form and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as their own mental consciousness. It is like that person with diseased eyes who sees [floating hairs] in the air.
Flowers. And during the second month, because of this, there is the false existence of revolving through birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
One who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment knows these to be empty flowers, and thus there is no revolving, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death therein.

At the end, the summary states: "This is what is called the practice of the Dharma on the ground of causes. Following this, in response to the next two questions, it says: "The Bodhisattva’s cause..."
This is the arousal of the pure mind; in the final age, by relying on this practice, one shall not fall into false views.

Based on this, the ten chapters beginning with Samantabhadra are all initiated according to this chapter on Mañjuśrī. Having concluded the introductory section, the main body of the teaching (*saddharma*) shall now be presented.

Following the precedent of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* commentaries, the major sections are divided into four parts. The first is the "Section on Generating Faith through Three Questions and Three Answers."
The second part consists of two questions and two answers for the purpose of opening understanding; the third part consists of four questions and four answers for the purpose of teaching practice;

and the fourth part consists of one question and one answer for the purpose of indicating the fruit. Within the section on generating faith, there are three questions and three answers. The first is the chapter on Samantabhadra.
According to the *Samantabhadra* [chapter], there is a brief inquiry, a detailed interrogation, and a concluding request. Regarding the brief inquiry, it proceeds from what precedes...
The Buddha replied to Mañjuśrī: "Regarding the initial stage of the causal ground, it is entirely through the aspect of perfectly illuminating pure awakening that one proceeds.
The intention of Samantabhadra is that the realm of perfect awakening and purity cannot be entered except through cultivation; however, he did not know how to cultivate so as to be able to enter it.
As for the detailed inquiry: following the previous chapter, one knows that these are like flowers in the sky, and thus there is no cyclic existence.
The principle of equality arises. Empty flowers are themselves illusions; therefore it is said: "If one knows that all is like an illusion, then body and mind are also illusory.

If one further employs body and mind to engage in affairs and advance in cultivation, this is using illusion to cultivate illusion. How, then, can one cultivate that which is both illusory and illusory?

Moreover, since one already knows all is like an illusion, if one proceeds to engage in affairs and practice with the intent that all illusions must be utterly extinguished—if one is thus insistent...
If all is extinguished, then there is no mind; upon whom could one rely for future cultivation? Why, then, do you further say that cultivation is like an illusion?

Moreover, if one already knows it is like an illusion, then fundamentally there is no need for practice. If one does not practice, then one will perpetually dwell within the midst of birth and death as a mere phantom.
Since there would be no contemplative practice, one would never understand the illusory nature of reality; furthermore, there would be nothing to cultivate.

"How can the mind of discursive thought be liberated? In this request for instruction, following the previous point regarding the faults of not practicing, it is clearly shown that one must certainly practice;
however, it is not known by what means or through what gradual stages of cultivation one may forever transcend all illusions.
In the response, it first states: "The various illusory transformations arise within the awakened mind as their fundamental basis. Next...

It says: "The illusory mind of sentient beings returns to and is extinguished by means of illusion; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind is unmoving. This correctly resolves the preceding doubt. At the end, it says:
"To know illusion is itself to be free from it; no expedient means need be employed. Once one is awakened and free from illusion, there is also no gradual progression.
This responds to the request. It further concludes: "By practicing in accordance with this, one can forever leave behind all illusions. This is also an answer.
[The text] begins: "What is the question concerning the practice of cultivation? According to the *Puyan* (Universal Eye), there are three requests and four meanings.

Following the previous chapter where the Buddha answered the *Puxian* (Samantabhadra) regarding the Dharma-gate of Detachment from Illusion, he taught that "knowing illusion is itself detachment; no expedient means need be employed. Detachment from illusion is itself awakening;
there is also no gradual progression. The intention of *Puyan* was that for those who possess correct expedient means and cultivate through contemplation, it might be possible...
To enter into awakening. Without this, one cannot avoid confusion and distress; therefore, he makes three successive requests. The first, the formal request, contains four points:
first, an inquiry regarding the stages of practice; second, an inquiry as to how one should contemplate; third, an inquiry as to how one should maintain [the practice];

and fourth, an inquiry as to what skillful means should be employed. Second is the indirect request: "If those sentient beings lack the correct skillful means for contemplation, and hear from the Buddha..."
Upon hearing this samādhi, their minds became bewildered and distressed, and they were unable to realize or enter into Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti). They requested three times, saying:
"We pray that out of your compassion, you will provide us—and all sentient beings of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age—with provisional skillful means.

In the response, [the Buddha] first clarifies the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) to eliminate all illusions, thereby facilitating further cultivation. Within the formal answer to the request, he first explains the three preceding meanings and subsequently demonstrates...
The Contemplation of the Dharma Realm causes one to awaken and enter it, proceeding further into its profound mystery. This answers the latter of the two points requested in the formal inquiry.

If one were truly able to awaken and enter from this point, abiding in and maintaining the Great Perfect Enlightenment Site (Mahābodhimaṇḍa) to partake in the same enjoyment as the Buddha, there would have been no need for further requests.
Yet, because their doubts remained unresolved, they again troubled Vajragarbha to rise from his seat. According to the preceding chapter, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva...
Regarding the statement that "sentient beings are originally enlightened Buddhas," there are three challenges raised on their behalf. First, it is asked:

"If sentient beings are originally enlightened Buddhas, why is there still the existence of all ignorance? This uses the truth to challenge the delusion; [the delusion] ought not to exist further. Second, it is asked:
"If ignorance and sentient beings are inherently present, why is it further said that they are originally enlightened Buddhas? This uses the delusion to challenge the truth.
It should not be said that [the Buddha] is accomplished [through practice]. Third, it is said: "Ordinary beings originally accomplish the path of Buddhahood, yet later give rise to ignorance.

When will all Tathāgatas ever again give rise to afflictions? This uses *mūla-awakening* (*mūla-awakening*) to challenge *wondrous awakening* (*prakarṣa-awakening*), implying that one would still have to give rise to delusions for the sake of sentient beings.
The initial challenge reveals a contradiction in one's own words, for it is your own statement that "sentient beings are originally accomplished as Buddhas. Furthermore, there is...
First, [the objection] regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) contradicts one's own words. Second, the objection clarifies the contradiction with worldly consensus:

since it is universally reckoned in the world that ignorance is primordially present, to further state that it is "originally established" contradicts worldly understanding. Third, the objection clarifies that [your position] generally fails to constitute valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

because the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of ordinary beings cannot logically ever become initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), and once the Tathāgata’s wondrous awakening is already accomplished, there can be no further delusion.

Because your three types of inquiry lack clarity, they constitute non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). When you reach the Tathāgata’s establishment of principles and analogies, you should fully comprehend and understand them.
Yet, in the end, you again disparage them as being based on a deluded and frivolous mind, full of various clever views. To engage in such discrimination is not a correct inquiry.
Upon hearing this, new students should naturally give rise to resolute faith in the Great Nirvāṇa.
This concludes the section on generating faith through three questions and three answers, ending with Maitreya’s expression of gratitude at the beginning of the next chapter.

Within the second section, which consists of two questions and two answers for the purpose of opening understanding, the first is the Chapter of Maitreya. This follows from the Buddha’s response to Vajra in the preceding chapter.
The *Zangyun* states: "Desiring to enter the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction... [it continues] up to 'first severing the root of beginningless saṃsāra,' and so forth.

Maitreya’s intention is that since saṃsāra arises from craving and desire, and craving and desire arise from the six consciousnesses—which are subject to arising and ceasing and are impermanent—how could these possibly serve as the root?
Therefore, he first asks: "How should one sever the root of saṃsāra? His intention is thus.
Since its severance must arise from the side of the *ālayavijñāna*, and since the fundamental [nature] resides in the *ālayavijñāna*, the lineage (*gotra*) should also encompass the supramundane.

Therefore, the next question concerns how many types of lineages exist within the various cycles of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). If the cycle of rebirth were restricted solely to the "segmented" (*paricchinna*), then the "transformative" (*pariṇāmika*) would be termed "non-cycling";
as non-cycling naturally leads to higher cultivation, the third question asks: how many [types of beings] cultivate the Buddha-bodhi?

Regarding these distinctions: even if such distinctions exist, they encompass both the heterodox and the orthodox; thus, it is extremely difficult to teach those who abandon the heterodox to return to the orthodox.
Therefore, regarding the four questions on turning the mind away from worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), how many kinds of skillful means (*upāya*) for teaching should be established?

Upon reaching the contemplation of the Tathāgata, one should answer according to the inquiry, providing a thorough and comprehensive explanation. When those newly initiated in the study hear this, there will surely be some slight understanding; how much more so for the Tathāgata himself!

Out of particular compassion for the sentient beings of the final age, I instruct them regarding Great Perfect Enlightenment so that they may give rise to a superior resolve and should formulate the pure, great vows of a Bodhisattva.
May you not encounter those of external paths or the two vehicles. Those who have newly begun their studies here and now should likewise be moved to inspiration.
As for why the section on "Resolution" is not concluded here: it is because the formal conclusion of the section on Resolution must await the clarification provided below.

This is the chapter of Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom. Following the previous chapter, sentient beings in the final age of the Buddha’s teaching give rise to a superior resolve (*adhimukti*) toward Great Perfect Enlightenment.
The intention of Pure Wisdom is that those who give rise to such a superior resolve must necessarily seek what the Buddha has realized.

If this is so, then it is only logical that the assembled assembly of Dharma-sons should hear it first; therefore, he requests that the King of Dharma once again proclaim the Perfection for the sake of the gathered assembly of Dharma-sons.

"Perfecting the nature of awakening. Regarding the phrase "reiterating," this indicates that it was not previously unproclaimed; rather, it is now taught for the sake of sentient beings in the final age, so that they may transmit it in succession.
However, since the perfect fulfillment of the nature of awakening cannot be attained abruptly, he therefore again questions the sentient beings, the bodhisattvas, and the World-Honored One.
Regarding what is realized and attained, how are they distinguished? Up to the contemplation of the Tathāgata, the answer to the initial inquiry has three parts:

first, by means of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), it reveals the equality of self-nature; second, by means of non-enlightenment and initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*), it clarifies how the grasping of illusions results in differentiation.

Third, regarding the wondrous awakening, it further reveals ultimate equality. Thus, the various assemblies of dharma-attendants have also roughly grasped the general outline of the Dharma King’s perfect enlightened nature.
The answer to the subsequent question has four parts. First: the perpetual severance of toil and anxiety leads to the attainment of the nature of the dharma-realm;
yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstacle to itself—this is called the ordinary person’s conformity [to delusion].

Regarding the nature of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*): The second refers to all bodhisattvas who perceive views as an obstruction. Although they have severed the obstruction of views, they still abide in the awakening of views;

these are called bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*), yet who accord with the nature of awakening. The third refers to those for whom there is both illumination and awakening, both of which are termed obstructions.
Therefore, the bodhisattva constantly awakens without abiding; these are called bodhisattvas who have already entered the stages and who accord with [the nature of awakening].
The nature of awakening. Fourth, all obstacles are themselves ultimate awakening; it continues until it says:

"The ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm illuminates and comprehends all phenomena as being identical to empty space; this is called the Tathāgata’s accordant nature of awakening. However, those in the final age who hear this...
Although one may practice in accordance [with the teachings], it will spontaneously become an obstacle; if one is unaware, it is difficult to enter the Buddha-vehicle.

If one is indeed a person of sudden and perfect capacity, they need only abide at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts. Regarding these various deluded minds, they do not even attempt to extinguish them.
They dwell within the realm of false imagination without seeking to understand it; in this state of non-understanding, they do not discriminate what is real. Upon hearing this—
That one does not give rise to alarm or fear in this regard is precisely what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening.

How much more so for those present before the assembly of the Dharma, who personally witness the excellence of the Tathāgata’s three karmas, receiving direct instruction from his own lips and being guided by his personal presence regarding the perfect nature of awakening of the King of All Dharmas.
There has never been anyone who observes fire at night without seeing it as dark, or views a mountain during the day [without seeing its true form].

This concludes the section on "Resolution through Two Questions and Two Answers. Within the third section, "Instruction on Practice through Four Questions and Four Answers," the first is the chapter on "Majestic Virtue and Sovereign Freedom.
According to the preceding two sections on Faith and Understanding, although both reveal the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), they have not yet pointed it out directly.

This demonstrates the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). It is because practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) path possess such sharp and keen faculties that they perceive the Truth with every word and clarify the essential principle with every sentence.

If one were to insist on categorizing them according to the divisions of contemplation, it would instead result in their being rendered dull and obstructed. Therefore, before [the disciples] had yet attained realization, the World-Honored One—

Previously, [the teaching] was merely presented in a general and diffuse manner. Now, after awakening has been attained, when great functions arise in abundance, there are briefly two faults if one does not rely on principle-contemplation (*yuanli guan*):
first, relying on one's own innate capacity, one uses deluded wisdom to illuminate [phenomena] and mistakenly falls into the conditioned;

second, failing to remember one’s own nobility, one easily becomes discouraged when encountering hardships and calamities. Possessing great majestic power and knowing the proper time and the opportune occasion, [the Buddha] speaks through parables.
The request to speak of "a great city" is a metaphor for the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), for it is that upon which the pure *dharmakāya* relies.

The presence of four gates outside represents the various Bodhisattvas; wishing to realize Perfect Enlightenment, they divide the teachings according to the capacities of beings, as all four *dharmadhātus* can be cultivated.
These four *dharmadhātus*, moreover, are the objects illuminated by the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). For this reason—
Therefore, the Tathāgata accords with their requests and reveals to them three gates of contemplation.

Regarding these three gates of contemplation, the fact that each begins by stating "awakening to pure, perfect *bodhi* (*vimala-pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)" makes it clear that these refer to matters subsequent to awakening. Furthermore, within the *śamatha* (calm abiding) contemplation, it says:
"With a mind of pure awakening, take stillness as one's practice. This clarifies that this refers to the realm of the *dharmadhātu* (the dharma-realm). As for *samādhi* (contemplative absorption)...

In the contemplation of the Middle Way, it is said that "by means of the pure awakened mind, one gives rise to all illusory transformations," clarifying that this refers to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
In the contemplation of *dhyāna*, it is said that "by means of the pure awakened mind, one does not grasp at illusory transformations nor at various signs of stillness," and so on,

up to "one forever transcends the realms of the obstructed and the unobstructed, and enjoys the world, as well as body and mind," clarifying that this refers to the non-duality of principle and phenomena.

Obstruction. Non-obstruction in all things. Regarding the second realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the conclusion summarizes: "These three dharma-gates are all Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
By drawing near to and following them, one fully realizes everything and thereby becomes Perfect Enlightenment. Based on this, from beginning to end, there is only the single Perfect Enlightenment.

This clarifies the characteristics of the practice of the three contemplations; below, it clarifies their cultivation, both individually and in combination. In the "Chapter on Bhadrapāla," the Bodhisattva...

The one named Sa (Sa-po) is called Bianyin (Discriminating Sound). He must have, in former lives as a causal practitioner, cultivated the contemplation of the wheel (*cakra*), thereby accomplishing unimpeded wisdom and giving rise to unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Having now come to assist the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of sentient beings], he was given the name Bianyin.

Hearing the preceding chapter on the Buddha’s response regarding the majestic power and the characteristics of the three contemplations, he found them most rare; for although the gates of contemplation are the same, [the manifestations differ].
Because root-natures are not uniform, when all Bodhisattvas hear these various skillful means, there are several ways of practicing within the gateway of Perfect Enlightenment.
Upon reaching the point where the Tathāgata provides his answer, there are three modes of cultivation: single cultivation, comprehensive cultivation, and complete cultivation.

In single cultivation, one is able to bring all three contemplations to ultimate completion. Within comprehensive cultivation, those contemplations that are integrated each further have three aspects. First, the layered...

There are three modes of cultivation: first, repeated cultivation; second, complete cultivation; and third, simultaneous and gradual cultivation. In repeated cultivation, the preceding and succeeding stages do not contradict one another.

In complete cultivation, with the exception of the capacity that governs the whole, the middle and subsequent stages may proceed as appropriate. In simultaneous and gradual cultivation, by unifying the subject and object, both methods may be employed according to convenience.
When it comes to perfect cultivation, one employs the wisdom of perfect enlightenment to perfectly integrate all things, never departing from that awakening.

The nature [of these practices] consists of twenty-four wheels, all of which converge within the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). By practicing them with a single power in a complete manner, they collectively form twenty-five types.
Finally, one is taught to establish markers for each; by binding them according to the hand, one may verify one's innate faculties (*gotra*) and enter through one gate, whether earlier or later.
However, since these are called "wheel-contemplations" (*cakravipaśyanā*), one should still practice them by rotating through this single gate until they are mastered throughout. Thus it is.
Thus, there would be no hindrances that could not be dissolved, and no practices that could not be perfected. Within the section on cultivation, two further chapters remain;

for now, let us discuss them based on the chapter on Pure Practice (*śuddha-karma*). According to the Bodhisattva of Pure Practice, because the preceding chapter stated that "the perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas is pure," he raises this question:
"If the fundamental nature of this awakened mind is inherently pure, by what cause is it defiled, such that all sentient beings..."

He was born, yet he was bewildered and did not enter [the womb]. Upon reaching the place where the Tathāgata gave his response, he distinguished between the four marks of deluded consciousness and the four marks of deluded wisdom.
Regarding the four marks of deluded consciousness: since beginningless time, all sentient beings have falsely imagined and clung to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
From this, the two objects of aversion and attraction arise; based upon this aversion and attraction, they create various [karmic seeds].
The various karmas arise from deluded karma; because of this deluded karma, one undergoes deluded transmigration, namely through the human and celestial realms.
Those who weary of transmigration perceive a deluded nirvana, namely as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because of this, they cannot enter pure awakening.

This refers to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who are deluded by consciousness; whether their thoughts are active or stilled, they all return to a state of bewildered confusion—the four marks of the delusion of wisdom.
This is because, due to the beginningless, primordial ignorance (*avidyā*), it transforms into the *ālayavijñāna* and takes itself as its sovereign.
Consequently, even when continuing in the pursuit of the Way, nothing is accomplished, for one has not yet escaped the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).

Just as those sentient beings have a slight realization but do not forget the wisdom that realizes, they are thereby deluded by that very wisdom; this is called the "mark of selfhood in deluded wisdom. Even if one were to awaken to this...

To take realization as "self," even though one does not explicitly recognize it as such, yet remains unforgetful regarding that which can be awakened to—this is further deluded by wisdom and is called the mark of a person who is deluded regarding wisdom. To counteract that notion of self, it is designated as "person.

Furthermore, to be able to discern that realization and awakening as "self" or "person," while neither grasping at these two, yet still maintaining something that is discerned—this too is [deluded] by wisdom.
Delusion is defined as the delusion regarding the characteristics of sentient beings' wisdom. This refers to the incessant cycle of birth after birth, wherein one cognizes this and cognizes that.

If one can further awaken to both that which cognizes and that which is cognized, yet maintains that only the capacity to awaken is real, one fails to realize that this very awakening is itself all-encompassing karmic wisdom (*karma-jñāna*), which is like the life-force (*jīvitendriya*). This is what is ultimately deluded by wisdom; it is called [delusion].

To be deluded regarding the marks of wisdom and the self (ātmagrāha) constitutes attachment to these four marks. To no longer be deludedly attached to them is to enter pure awakening (*viśuddhabodhi*).
If one were further to give rise to a mind that perceives all who have awakened within this state, it would constitute a dust-like defilement that obstructs pure awakening.

Although these are divided here into four marks, in reality they are nothing other than a single grasping at a self (*ātman*); therefore, throughout the subsequent passages, it is clarified that [all phenomena] do not depart from the self.
Furthermore, because there is a self, all afflictions arise on its account; this is a great calamity that must be urgently severed. As the subsequent verse observes:
"All sentient beings, due to grasping at a self and craving, undergo false transmigration from time immemorial.

Love and hatred arise in their minds, and deceit and crookedness persist in their thoughts. For this reason, they are frequently bewildered and distressed, unable to enter the City of Awakening. Its...
"Observe for yourself. This section below constitutes the "Universal Enlightenment" chapter (*Pǔjué zhāng*). According to this, Universal Enlightenment’s inquiries consist of five parts.

These arise from the text in the preceding chapter which exhorts reliance on correct cultivation, stating: "Sentient beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age who hope to achieve the Way must not seek awakening merely through increasing their learning;
they should instead diligently subdue their afflictions," and so forth, continuing until: "Seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and do not fall [into error]."

Regarding wrong views: because sentient beings in the final age will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, while the worthy and holy ones remain hidden and false teachings flourish, the eyes of the path for those with a beginner's mind will not be clear. Thus, it is difficult to avoid mistaking the true for the semblance.

Therefore, the initial question asks what kind of person sentient beings should seek among the many people—specifically, what kind of person one should seek when seeking the Buddha from within a great multitude.
Good son, furthermore, since one has already sought out that person, one must necessarily rely upon their Dharma; therefore, next he asks, "In reliance upon what Dharma?
This is because he seeks the Buddha’s exposition, and within those teachings spoken by him, he wishes to know which specific Dharma he should rely upon as his standard and support.
Furthermore, since one who relies upon the Dharma must necessarily practice its conduct, he asks a third question regarding what kind of conduct should be practiced;
this seeks the Buddha’s explanation of which specific practices among those to be performed should be taken as the primary object of cultivation.

Moreover, since one who practices that conduct must necessarily attain some realization, he asks a fourth question regarding what kind of afflictions are to be eliminated; this seeks the Buddha’s explanation of that.
Within the midst of what is attained as the true semblance of the Way, one must determine which semblance of illness should be eliminated so that the true medicine may remain.
Furthermore, once the Way has been attained, one must still give rise to the mind to deliver sentient beings; thus, the fifth question asks, "How does one give rise to the mind?

This refers to seeking the Buddha’s teaching on how to give rise to the mind of delivering sentient beings amidst the provisional and the real, the sudden and the gradual, and the partial and the complete. Upon reaching the contemplation of the Tathāgata...

The response: To answer the first question, it is said that one who seeks a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and wishes to practice should seek those who possess right knowledge and vision, who do not dwell in the realms of humans or devas, and who are not attached to what is heard or conditioned. To answer the second question, it is said that the body manifests within the afflictions of the world.

His mind was perpetually pure. He manifested various faults while constantly praising the holy life (*brahmacarya*). When asked three questions, he replied: "One should make offerings without begrudging even body or life.

Seeing him manifest such adversities, [the interlocutor] did not give rise to an evil mind. When asked four questions, he replied: "The wondrous Dharma that has been realized should be free from the four maladies:
first, fabrication; second, indulgence; third, cessation; and fourth, extinction. When asked five questions, he replied: "First..."
"I shall cause all sentient beings to enter ultimate, perfect enlightenment. Within that perfect enlightenment, there is no one who grasps at enlightenment.
The final summary concludes: "If sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age truly give rise to such a resolve, they will not fall into various false views.

Up to this point, the section on the instruction for practice through four questions and four answers is complete. The fourth part consists of one question and one answer, which demonstrates the fruition.

This occurs within the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment" (*Pūrṇabodhi*). The reason the bodhisattva is named Pūrṇabodhi is that he has already realized the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pūrṇabodhi-svabhāva*), yet manifests as dwelling within the stage of causes; he is, therefore, one who has already traversed the path.

Fearing that sentient beings in the final age might confuse the correct with the erroneous at the juncture of cultivating the causes and realizing the fruit, he specifically rose from the assembly to request [the teaching], saying: "We who are here now..."
