This concludes the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching.

Regarding the second section, the classification by the Piṭakas and Vehicles: the holy teachings of the Tathāgata’s single lifetime, when categorized according to their conceptual characteristics and inclusive scope, consist of the Three Piṭakas and the Two Piṭakas.
When categorized according to the provisional and ultimate aspects of cultivation and realization, they consist of the Three Vehicles and the Five Vehicles.

When categorized in detail according to their specific types, they consist of the Nine Divisions and the Twelve Divisions. It should be understood that this sutra [is included] among all those various dharmas.
To clarify their respective categories, they are explained in sequence.
Regarding the "Three Piṭakas": the first is the Sūtra, also called Sūtranta or Sūtrānta; these are variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit language, like different dialects.
This term is translated as "Sūtra" (契經), or alternatively rendered as "Thread" (線). According to the usage in the Five Indias...
The term *sūtra* refers to both "woven mat" and "holy teaching. If that were the case, it should have been translated as "holy teaching.

However, because the ancient masters observed that in this region [of China] the holy teachings are called "jīng" (經), they extracted the character "jīng" from "woven mat" (*xiānjīng*) to represent it; thus, it conforms to the linguistic conventions of this region.

Nor does this lose the meaning of the sacred teaching. As for not including the "seat-thread" (*āsandi-sūtra*) and the "well-rope" (*kūpa-rajjū*), it is because these are not esteemed in this region and are not part of the sacred teaching.
However, the addition of the character "seal" (*qì*) to the title of the sutra is merely borrowing its meaning to assist in naming;

it serves to manifest that this is a sutra that accords with principle and meets the needs of sentient beings. Furthermore, sutras possess multiple meanings, such as the five meanings found in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.

In the *Huayan xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avataṃsaka), it is further stated that although there are many meanings, they do not go beyond "pervading" (*guàn*) and "encompassing" (*shè*). As the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says:
"Because it can pervade and can encompass, it is called a sūtra (*jing*). That is to say, based on the Buddha’s holy teaching, it threads together the meanings that ought to be explained."

Because it encompasses those beings who are to be delivered, it correctly explains the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), which also extends to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The two *vinaya*s are also called *vini*.

This is likely a phonetic variation of the Sanskrit sound. In this language, it is translated as "taming" (*diao-fu*); that is to say, the refining and disciplining of the three modes of action (*trividha-karman*).

Because it subdues transgressions and faults, its training extends to both abstention (*saṃvara*) and performance (*pravṛtti*). "Subduing" (*vinaya*) specifically clarifies abstention and maintenance.

In terms of the conduct it explains, it is designated by this name; alternatively, it is translated as "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*), meaning that by extinguishing afflictions and karma, one attains the fruit of extinction.
It is also called *pratimokṣa*, which translates as "individual liberation. This refers to the three types of action and seven branches [of the path], each separately preventing what is non-virtuous.

It is called "distinct" (*prātimokṣa*) because it is not contradicted when manifest before one, and furthermore, because it distinguishes itself from the precepts shared with non-Buddhists (*itobāhyaka*) and those associated with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*).
Thus, it is named after its cause. It may also be called by way of its fruit, for liberation (*vimukti*) is itself the fruit.

Alternatively, it is translated as "conforming to liberation," meaning that it conforms to the two fruits of liberation—both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, it is named after its fruit.
It may also be called "cause" (*hetu*), as it accords with the cause itself. Alternatively, it is named *śīla*; in its full form, it is *śītalā*, which here means "cooling.
This refers to being free from the causes of feverish affliction and attaining the fruit of coolness; thus, it is named according to both cause and fruit.

While it primarily elucidates the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), it also encompasses concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding the three *Abhidharma*s, they are also called *Abhi-*... [text truncated]
*Tan* is also a variant of the Sanskrit sound *śa*. This is translated as *Abhidharma*. There are two kinds of *dharma*: first, the *paramārtha-dharma* (ultimate reality), which refers to *nirvāṇa*;
because it is wholesome and eternal, it is called ultimate. Second, the *lakṣaṇa-dharma* (phenomenal characteristics), which encompasses the four noble truths;
because they differ in being mundane or supramundane, and in being cause or effect, they are called phenomenal characteristics. *Abhi* also has two meanings: first...

It is directed toward Nirvāṇa. Second, it is directed toward the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. That which is capable of such direction consists of untainted, pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) and its associated mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-saṃskāra*).
These are designated as two types of "direction" based on their respective fruits and objects. In older translations, this is rendered as "the incomparable dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*).
Because it is supreme by virtue of its untainted, pure wisdom, this is clarified as being designated by name solely in dependence upon that which it counteracts;
it is also called *upadeśa*, which translates as "instruction" (*lunyi*), meaning question-and-answer debate, so as to deliberate upon what is heterodox and what is correct.
It is also called *mātṛkā*, which translates as "mother-text" (*benmu*); for the teaching and its meaning serve as the basis and the mother, giving rise to understanding and practice.

Therefore, while it primarily elucidates the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), it also encompasses the other two. Why are these three called "piṭakas" (baskets)? Because they contain and encompass [all teachings].
To which collection does this present sutra belong? It primarily belongs to the Sūtra-piṭaka, as it predominantly discusses meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from beginning to end.

If one considers how this sutra subsumes those [other teachings], it also encompasses the remaining two: for the "Universal Eye" chapter distances one from all illusions, and the "Perfect Enlightenment" chapter [describes] the three months [of practice].
Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), because all [monastics] revere the precepts, the twelve great beings have followed one another in posing questions.

The World-Honored One of the Pure Land answers according to these inquiries, as they constitute a shared discourse. As for the mention of the "two piṭakas," the first is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the second is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
These are the aforementioned three Piṭakas. Because they explain and demonstrate the principles, practices, and fruits of the Śrāvakas, they are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

Because they fully demonstrate the principles, practices, and fruits of the Bodhisattvas, they are called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. The reason the Pratyekabuddhas are not separately established [as a fourth piṭaka] is that Pratyekabuddhas generally do not rely on the teachings;
they appear in worlds where no Buddha exists. When a Buddha does exist in the world, they are subsumed under the Śrāvakas, as their principles are identical to those of the Śrāvakas.
Because the fruits are the same. If one were to distinguish them based on the teachings and practices, one might also hear that the three vehicles constitute the Tripiṭaka;
however, the ancients did not open [the canon] in this way, and it should be understood as such today as well. As for clarifying their classification, this sutra belongs to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
Although the name "śrāvaka" is preserved within the sutra, its principles, practices, and fruits are not adopted; as stated in the Chapter on Maitreya:
"If it is said that all sentient beings in the final age give rise to the superior resolve toward Great Perfect Enlightenment..."
One should give rise to the pure great vows of a bodhisattva and speak these words: "May I now abide in the Perfect Enlightenment of the Buddha;
may I seek out spiritual friends and never encounter non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles. Furthermore, the Chapter on Purifying Karma states:
"All sentient beings mistake the four inversions for their true self-substance," and so forth, continuing: "Because of deluded karma, there is delusion..."
Those who perceive the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and, out of weariness with it, falsely perceive *nirvāṇa*, are unable to enter pure awakening because of this.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Perfect Awakening" states: "If, at the beginning of summer, during the three months of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), one makes this declaration before the Buddha:
'I now respectfully entreat you not to follow the path of the Śrāvakas, but rather to accord with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the Great Bodhisattvas...'"
"Sa. [He] entered the three-month summer retreat for the sake of cultivating the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment of a bodhisattva;

because this was a great causal condition, he did not bind himself to a following of disciples. Such statements as these all intend to exclude and discard the Lesser Vehicle, seeking only the principle, practice, and fruit of the Bodhisattva path.

Regarding the "Three Vehicles": first is the Śrāvaka-yāna. Relying on the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, they apply themselves with diligent vigor, desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek their own nirvāṇa.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "It is like those sons who, seeking the goat-drawn carts, emerged from the burning house.
Second is the Pratyekabuddha-yāna. Relying on the Dharma of Dependent Origination, they apply themselves with diligent vigor, seeking spontaneous wisdom and delighting in [solitary] awakening.
Solitary and serene, he profoundly understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"Just as those children, seeking deer-carts, emerged from the burning house. The three vehicles of the Bodhisattvas, relying on the dharma of the six perfections, diligently cultivate vigor to seek omniscience, benefiting devas and humans and delivering all beings. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Just as those children, seeking..."
The ox-cart [is used] to exit the burning house. Yet, there is the provisional and the real.

If practice abides in marks and cause and effect are distinct and separate, it is called the provisional. If cultivation arises from the nature and cause and effect are all-pervasive and thorough, it is called the real.
As for clarifying its classification, this sutra belongs to the Bodhisattva Vehicle, because in the questions and answers within the sutra, [the focus] is mostly...
It is said for the sake of the bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Worthy and Virtuous Leaders" states:

"If all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this to advance until they reach the stage of Buddhahood, then this is comprised solely of the 'one part of reality' (the ultimate), as it is cultivation after awakening;
cultivation is itself non-cultivation. This is as stated in the "Chapter on Majestic Power" regarding *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and so forth. All say:
Awakening to pure *bodhi* (perfect enlightenment) is because one cultivates it with a mind of pure awakening; thus, it does not belong to the other two [vehicles]. This meaning can be understood.
If one uses this to subsume that, it may also comprehensively include them, for this sutra directly leads to the Perfect [Vehicle] and encompasses immeasurable vehicles.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Worthy and Virtuous Chief" states: "This sutra is named the Sudden Teaching Mahāyāna, for those of sudden capacity."
Birth. From this, one attains awakening; it also encompasses gradual cultivation for all classes of beings. It is like the great ocean, which does not reject even small streams.

Regarding the "five vehicles," the first is the vehicle of humans and devas, which relies on the methods of precepts, wholesome deeds, and meditative concentration to seek the five [desires] of the lower realms.
The pleasures of the desire realm as well as the pure and subtle joys of the two upper realms are compared in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to the smallest vehicle.
The second is the Śrāvaka-yāna, the third is the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the fourth is the Bodhisattva-yāna; these three constitute the aforementioned three vehicles.

The fifth is the Buddha-yāna, which, by means of the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices, adorns the fruit of the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is compared to the great white [ox-cart].
The ox-cart. It is said that even if the elder had not given so much as the smallest single cart, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood;
how much less so when the elder, knowing his own immeasurable wealth and desiring to benefit his sons, gave them all equally the great carts?
Here, the smallest cart is used as a metaphor for the realms of humans and devas, while the equal distribution of the great carts is a metaphor for the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna).
As for its classification, this sutra belongs to the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna). As Mañjuśrī initiated [the discourse], he said:
"I pray that you will, for the sake of all those gathered here in this assembly, expound upon the Tathāgata’s original arising—the pure practice of the Dharma on the ground of the cause."
When the virtuous and wise circulated [this teaching], they said: "This sutra reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata;

thus, the cause is established for the sake of the fruit, while the fruit is established such that the cause is transcended. It does not even pertain to the Bodhisattvas, much less to those of other vehicles.

If one uses this to encompass the other, then even humans and devas are not excluded—just as from a single cloud and a single rain, the three types of grasses and two types of trees receive nourishment according to their respective capacities."
Run: Observe that after the Tathāgata had preached this sutra, the entire great assembly, having heard it, all rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced it.
Thus, the meaning of the universal inclusion of humans and devas can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the "nine divisions" and "twelve divisions": generally speaking, the holy teachings comprise twelve divisions. First is the *sūtra*, here translated as "Scripture" (or "Agreement with the Truth").

This refers to the eleven divisions [of the ninefold teaching], as well as those texts outside the formal canon of the Tripiṭaka that have been handed down through successive generations and which, by way of their structure and meaning, are "punctuated," "interwoven," or "in accord" [with the truth], thus constituting a separate division known as *sūtra*.
Second is the *geya*, here translated as "Repetitive Verse. Third is the *vyākaraṇa*, here translated as "Prophecy. Fourth is the *gāthā*... [here the text continues].
1. Geya (Cloud-like Verses); 2. Udāna (Spontaneous Utterances), here translated as "Self-Explanations"; 3. Nidāna (Causes and Conditions), here translated as "Origins";
4. Avadāna (Parables), here translated as "Similes"; 5. Itivṛttaka (Thus-it-was-said), here translated as "Past Events";
6. Jātaka (Birth Stories), here translated as "Previous Lives"; 7. Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings), here translated as "Universal Expansion. 11.
*Abhūta-dharma*: here translated as "the unprecedented" (*mewei zhengyou*). *Upadeśa*: here translated as "discourse" (*lunyi*).

Guishan said: "The prose sūtras (*qijing*), the verses (*chongsong*), the prophecies (*shouji*), the independent discourses spoken without being questioned (*gusi wuwen er zishuo*), the causal conditions (*yinyuan*), the parables (*poyu*), the past events (*benshi*), the previous births (*benzheng*), the extensive teachings (*fangguang*), the unprecedented (*meweiyou*), and the discourses (*lunyi*) together constitute the twelve [categories]."

Regarding the names, they are as detailed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 33. As for the "ninefold division" (*navāṅga*), this refers to the provisional classification into Great and Small Vehicles;

for example, in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there are only nine divisions. As the verse in the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

An ancient master explained that because the principles discussed in the Lesser Vehicle are narrow and limited, it lacks the "Extensive" (*vaipulya*) division. This does not mean it is entirely absent, but rather that it lacks what is most extensive and vast. Furthermore, because [the Lesser Vehicle] does not speak of attaining Buddhahood, it lacks the "Biography of the Buddha" (*upadeśa*).

*Avadāna* (Accounts). [This does not mean they are entirely non-existent as a category; it simply means there are no predictions of attaining Buddhahood. When asked, one then speaks; therefore, there are no *svayambhū-śāsana* (self-proclamations). [This is not that they are entirely absent; it is simply that they do not consist of direct pointing-out.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Mahāyāna also consists of only nine divisions (*navāṅga*). An ancient master explained this by saying: "The Mahāyāna mostly manifests directly, and thus lacks *nidāna* (causal narratives).

[This is not that they are entirely absent; it is simply that they are not like the establishment of precepts based on specific events. *Aupamya* (Parables). [This is not that they are entirely absent; it is simply that they differ from those that necessarily employ metaphors to guide faith. *Upadeśa* (Expositions).

(3) It is not that they are entirely non-existent; it is simply that one does not go so far as to count grains of sand and thereby exhaust oneself. Furthermore, an ancient master said: "I fear that 'section' (*bu*) might be confused with the rank of a minister, so later it was changed to 'division' (*fen*).
If one clarifies its classification, among the twelve divisions of the canon, this sutra properly belongs to the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings), because its title refers to the *Mahāvaipulya*.
It also concurrently pertains to eight divisions. As the *Great Commentary* states: "The meaning of being pervasive and inclusive applies [to all]. (That is to say, it encompasses...)

Because the *sūtra* (the primary teaching) contains repeated verses for each section, it includes *geya*. Because it records those who have attained peace of mind and achieved Buddha-wisdom, it includes *vyākaraṇa*.
Because it teaches only after being requested, it includes *nidāna*. Because it explains the dharmic practices of the Buddha’s causal ground (*bhūmi*), it includes *itivṛttaka*.
Because the six perfections are not the cause and nirvāṇa is not the fruit, it includes *avadāna*. Because it employs twenty-seven parables, it includes *upadeśa*. Samantabhadra...

There is evidence for this, as there are objections raised by Vajragarbha (which constitute the discussion). It simply does not include the three categories of *gāthā*, *udāna*, and *jātaka*. Question:
Since the majority [of the scriptures] are *sūtras*, why are they not included therein? Answer: Because the *sūtras* within the Piṭakas have already been fully subsumed;
as for the *sūtras* within the divisions (*vibhāga*), these represent only a small portion thereof. This concludes the subsumption according to the divisions of the Piṭakas and Vehicles (*yāna*).
Third, regarding those capable of receiving the teachings: the ocean of doctrine is vast and profound; the clouds of Dharma pervade everywhere; the light of wisdom is boundless;

and its wondrous transformations are inexhaustible. By means of words that transcend speech, it elucidates the principle where speech ceases; through transformations that transcend change, it brings about movement.

One must respond to the shifting mechanisms [of sentient beings]. As these mechanisms differ, the teachings vary; their meanings are divided into many types, yet there are also those that are not so divided.
To gain little while losing much would be a great error; therefore, I shall now distinguish them briefly into three chapters: first, classifying the teachings according to their schools (*zong*);

second, debating the meanings according to the treatises (*lun*); and third, harmonizing the shallow and the deep. Regarding the classification of teachings according to their schools: this refers to how they were propagated and expounded in India and China.
Regarding the flow [of Buddhist teachings] within the holy words of a single lifetime, some condense them into a single teaching, while others expand them into two or three;

further expanding them, they reach four or five. Among both monastics and laypeople, there are altogether eighteen schools. While one may follow another or oppose another, it is difficult to exhaustively critique all other traditions.
In terms of the refinement of facts and the completeness of principle, none surpasses Xianshou (Fazang). Therefore, relying upon the patriarch Xianshou, I shall provide a brief exposition.
The five teachings:
first, the Hīnayāna teaching, also called the "Teaching for the Two Vehicles of Dull Capacity.

It is so named because it differs from the Mahāyāna, because it is established according to the capacities of beings, because it follows the words of others, and because it explains the numerical categories of all phenomena as being exclusively distinct, thereby distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox and defining the noble ones.
Generally speaking, while they clarify cause and effect and distinguish between what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed, the number of dharmas taught therein is only seventy-five.

They speak only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and do not explain the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Even when they do address the emptiness of phenomena, it is rarely clear.

Relying solely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to establish the roots of defilement and purity, they have not exhausted the source of all phenomena; consequently, many disputes arise.
Second is the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, also called the Partial Teaching. It merely clarifies that all phenomena are empty, yet does not fully exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
therefore, it is termed "initial. It only clarifies the characteristics of all phenomena, asserting that some attain Buddhahood while others do not.

Therefore, it is named the *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis). It discusses the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena extensively, while touching upon their nature (*dharmatā*) only briefly. What is called "nature" therein is also merely a category of characteristic.
It teaches that there are one hundred dharmas, which are clearly and decisively determined; thus, there is little room for dispute.

Third is the Final Teaching (Zhòngjiào), also called the True Teaching (Shíjiào). This refers to the clarification that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature and that all things are thusness.

It teaches that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures and icchantikas without the seed of Buddhahood shall all eventually attain Buddhahood; thus, it exhaustively presents the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna.

It is called "Final" because it reaches the culmination [of the teaching], and it is called "True" because it accords with the true principle. It predominantly discusses the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) and only sparingly addresses phenomenal characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
What is called "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) also ultimately converges upon "nature" (dharmatā). This constitutes the entirety of the Mahāyāna teaching; therefore, there is no room for dispute.
Fourth is the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna): it holds that the mere non-arising of a single thought is itself named "Buddha.

It does not rely on stages or positions, nor does it teach through gradual progression. As the *Samparigraha-sūtra* (*Si-yi jing*) states: "One who attains the true nature of all dharmas does not proceed from one stage to another..."
Regarding the single stage, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The first stage is itself the eighth," and so on, up to "there is no sequence whatsoever.
Since this is neither the gradual cultivation described previously nor the perfect integration of virtues described later, it is called "sudden" (*tun*).
It does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) at all, but only discriminates true nature (*bhūtatathatā*). All that exists is merely deluded thought (*parikalpita*).
The entire dharma-realm is solely beyond words. The five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded.
It reviles teaching and exhorts detachment; it destroys appearances and extinguishes the mind. To give rise to the mind is delusion; not giving rise to it is Buddhahood.

Furthermore, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha; neither arising nor non-arising. This is like the silent dwelling of Vimalakīrti and others, intended specifically for a certain class of practitioners whose faculties are free from discursive thought.
It also serves as an antidote for those who cling to the three types of marks—emptiness, existence, and both.

Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This means it universally encompasses the preceding four teachings, being complete and perfect. A single stage is all stages; all stages are a single stage.
The fulfillment of the ten levels of faith (*shixin*) subsumes the five positions (*wwei*), thereby achieving equal and right enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); thus, it is called "Perfect.

What is taught is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein the ocean of nature (*xinghai*) is perfectly interfused and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is unimpeded in its manifestations.
They are thus mutually inclusive, like Indra’s net, with infinite layers upon layers and subtle mutual containment, wherein the principal and its attendants are inexhaustible.
The above provides a brief presentation of their respective meanings to allow for a general understanding of the main points.

If one were to extensively analyze the explained content, as well as the stages of severance and realization, it is fully detailed in works such as the *Huayan xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avataṃsaka) and the *Xianshou jiaoyi* (The Doctrinal System of the First Patriarch).
Regarding the principle that "the words are concise while the treatise clarifies the meaning": the Buddha’s teachings are rooted in the single mind.

When the mind possesses distinctions, the teachings consequently have diverse branches. Thus, when the Tathāgata preached the teachings, he was preaching this mind; when the patriarchs categorized the teachings, they were categorizing this mind.
Now, I shall clarify the fivefold doctrinal meanings by means of the "distinctions within the one mind" from the *Awakening of Faith*.

According to the *Awakening of Faith*, the first [meaning] takes the one mind alone as the source. As the treatise states: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all worlds."
The supramundane dharma (*lokottara-dharma*) constitutes the scope of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Second, based on the one mind, two gates are opened:

first, the gate of the true suchness of the mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*), which is said to be the nature of the mind that is neither born nor extinguished; this constitutes the scope of the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*). The Emptiness School (*kongzong*) of the Initial Teaching (*shijiao*) also implicitly indicates this gate.
Because they do not know that the Tathāgata’s elimination of marks is precisely for the purpose of revealing the nature, this [teaching] is not within their scope.

Second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind (which means that based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind of arising and ceasing; that which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing and yet is in union with arising and ceasing is called the *ālayavijñāna*).

This constitutes the limit of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhānaya*). Although the schools of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*) also secretly indicate this gate, they do not know that the Buddha taught the *ālayavijñāna*.
It penetrates the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it does not belong to that [category]. Third, based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpādavyaya-mukha*), two meanings are clarified.

The first is the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*)—that is, the essence of the mind is free from thought. As for this state of being free from the marks of thought, it is equal to the realm of empty space; it is precisely the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharmakāya. This corresponds to the scope of the Śūnyavāda school within the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

Second is the meaning of non-awakening (meaning that one does not know, as it truly is, that the dharma of *tathatā* is one). Based on this meaning, four [stages] arise, producing the three subtle states:

first, because of non-awakening, the mind moves; this is called the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*). Second, based on movement, there is the capacity for seeing; this is called the "phase of transformation" (*vivartalakṣaṇa*).

Third, based on the capacity for seeing, objects falsely appear; this is called the "phase of manifestation" (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*). Based on these phases, five [stages] arise, producing the six coarse states. First, cognition...

1. The characteristic of appearance (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*). 2. The characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, the arising of mindfulness based on cognition without interruption (namely, the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena). 3. The characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, the false production of grasping (namely, the innate grasping at a self). 4.

The characteristic of calculating names (*nāma-kalpanā-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, the false calculation of names (namely, the conceptualized grasping at a self). These constitute the limits of the Hīnayāna teachings (because they involve severing the grasping at a self and realizing the emptiness of self, which is the meaning of the Hīnayāna).

5. The characteristic of initiating karma (*karma-pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, performing karma by following after names. 6. The characteristic of suffering bound by karma (*karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, receiving retribution according to one's karma. These constitute...

The distinction between humans and devas (furthermore, the karmic retributions of the six realms, which are the expedient means for the contemplations of suffering and emptiness, etc., also constitute the scope of the Hīnayāna).

Regarding the statement on "harmonizing the shallow and the deep": this sutra properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*), while simultaneously encompassing the Small, Initial, and Final [teachings], and directly penetrating to the Perfect [Teaching].
As stated in the Chapter on Bhadrapāla: "This sutra is named the Mahāyāna of the Sudden Teaching; it is for those of sudden capacity."
Sentient beings awaken from this; it can be known that this properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). Furthermore, it says:

"It also encompasses all classes of beings who practice the gradual path (*jian-xiu*). This is like the great ocean, which does not reject small streams; it can be known that this inclusively encompasses the Small Vehicle (*xiao*), the Initial [Vehicle], and the Final [Vehicle] (*san*).
Moreover, it says: "Even down to mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras—anyone who drinks its water shall obtain fulfillment."
It is complete; one may know that its direct penetration reaches the Perfect [Teaching]. This is because, regardless of the amount of water drunk, it possesses the flavor of all hundred rivers.

This is a general synthesis based on the chapter on the Worthy and Virtuous Chief (Xianshou). If one were to synthesize them specifically, each teaching has its own textual passages scattered throughout the eleven chapters;
they are too numerous to be recorded in full here. It is hoped that those who study the Worthy Chief will grasp this principle.

The mind is that which unifies the teachings. By borrowing the teachings to penetrate the sutras, the sutras can be penetrated and the teachings unified. This concludes the exposition on the capacity to convey the meaning of the teachings.

Fourth, regarding the suitability of the recipients: teachings are established because of the capacities [of beings], and capacities are perfected through the teachings. The aforementioned discussion concerned the capacity to convey the teachings.

It has already been understood that [the teaching] can encompass what is vast and profound; now, the appropriate capacities [of sentient beings] are demonstrated to briefly reveal the extensiveness of those who are reached.
Furthermore, two sections are divided to exhaustively distinguish and include [all cases]: first, following the judgments of the ancients; second, relying on what is clarified in the sutras.

Regarding the phrase "following the judgments of the ancients," this refers to the ancient masters who opened up two gates: first, "discriminating" (liao-jian), and second, "universally encompassing" (pu-shou).

As for the five types of those who are not suitable vessels according to the gate of discrimination: the first refers to those who delight in adhering to names and characteristics, taking the literal text as their understanding.

The second refers to those who are stalled in the stage of practice and who loftily dismiss the realm of the sages. The third refers to those whose sentiments are set upon emptiness and who respond to words by treating them as mere non-existence.

The fourth refers to those who rely on their own innate spontaneity and look down with disdain upon diligent cultivation. The fifth refers to those who stubbornly cling to what they have previously heard and who discard the gold while carrying the hemp.
All such individuals are termed "non-vessels. Those who are the opposite of these are all vessels. If one were to universally accept [all beings], [the result would be as follows].
Thus, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; merely hearing of it brings benefit to all without exception.

Those with deep latent capacities awaken and enter [the truth], while those with shallow capacities attain faith and understanding. For those who lack any prior seeds of cultivation, the very act of forming a karmic connection establishes a seed.
This may be illustrated by the analogy of the "eating of the diamond" (vajra).
Regarding what is clarified in the sutras, there are two gates for both analytical discernment and universal inclusion.

As for the analytical discernment, according to the two chapters on "Pure Practice" and "Universal Enlightenment," there are ten types of those who are not suitable vessels: first, those with deluded karmic paths and deluded views who transmigrate;
these are the ordinary beings of the six realms who stubbornly cling to the four marks [of existence]. Second, those who loathe transmigration. Deluded...
They perceive nirvana. This refers to those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) within the Lesser Teaching who, weary of the realms of existence, seek emptiness.

Regarding these two types, the text concludes: "Therefore, both the movement of thought and the cessation of thought alike lead to delusion and confusion. Thus, it is known that they are not the intended audience [for this teaching].

Third, there are those whose minds have attained some realization, thereby manifesting a capacity for realization; these are bodhisattvas abiding in the stages who still possess subtle marks of self (*ātman*). Because...
Fourth, because that which is capable of realization is none other than the self, one awakens to and realizes the existence of a self and no longer validates the conventional notion of a person.

This is because transcending the self is precisely what constitutes the person; such a bodhisattva at this stage still possesses subtle traces of the mark of a person. Fifth, one thoroughly understands that realization.
They do not dwell in the notions of self or person. This refers to the Bodhisattva at the stage of "heading toward" (the first bhūmi), who still possesses subtle signs of arising;
because they maintain a sense of something to be cognized, this is precisely the mark of a sentient being. Sixth is the purity of mental illumination: awakening to that which was cognized.

Although this Bodhisattva at the stage of the [first] ground still possesses subtle signs of a life-span (jīvaka), since their mind is already pure in its illumination, they no longer maintain anything once it has been cognized.

It is right here and now. If you further give rise to a mind that seeks to perceive the reason why that [original state] is able to be realized, this very perception is the "wisdom of karma" (the subtle discrimination within the karmic consciousness).
It cannot see itself (just as the eye cannot see itself), for it is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is the mark of a self (*pudgala*).
Regarding these four marks, the text states: "In the final age, the multitudes..."
"Born [into this state], they do not understand the four marks [of existence]. Though they practice the Way with diligent toil through many kalpas, it is merely called 'conditioned' (*saṃskṛta*);

ultimately, they cannot achieve any of the fruits of sainthood. Therefore, know that they are not of the proper capacity. The above constitutes six types [of practitioners], as seen in detail in the Chapter on Pure Practice.
Seventh: 'I perform various practices within my original mind'—this is called 'the sickness of activity. To distinguish this, [it is said]: 'That Perfect Enlightenment...'"

9. Nature (*dhātu*). Because it is not something attained through effort. (This indicates they are not suitable vessels. Eighth: To leave all things as they are, following the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). (This is called "the illness of complacency. The distinction states:

That nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is not something that exists by mere complacency. (This indicates they are not suitable vessels. Ninth: To cause all thoughts to cease within one's own fundamental mind.

(This is called "the illness of cessation. The distinction states: That nature of perfect enlightenment is not something to be attained through cessation. (This indicates they are not suitable vessels. Tenth: ...
Extinguishing all afflictions, all are eternally stilled (this is called "extinguishing illness"). [The commentary] clarifies:

"That nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a state of stillness" (this reveals that it is not the appropriate capacity). Regarding these four types, they are seen in detail within the "Universal Enlightenment" chapter.

If one were to collect them universally, according to the "Pure Wisdom" chapter, from ordinary beings to sages, all are said to "accord with the nature of enlightenment. However, since all are said to "accord,"...
One should naturally be included among those for whom this teaching is intended; there is no room for selective exclusion.

If one can indeed remain at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts, then both cultivation and effort will naturally dissolve. If one does not even attempt to extinguish the various deluded minds, then both cessation and extinction will come to rest.

If one can further abide within the realm of delusive thought without applying analytical cognition, and within that lack of cognition, does not discriminate between the true and the false—then [the path is complete].
In reality, all obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment; whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation;
whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all termed nirvana; wisdom and folly are both universally the *prajñā*; and bodhisattvas and non-Buddhist practitioners—
The dharmas thus accomplished are all equally Bodhi; ignorance and suchness are not different realms.
All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and delusion, are collectively the Brahma-conduct. Sentient beings and their lands share the same dharma-nature;
the hells and celestial palaces are both pure lands. Those with nature and those without nature alike achieve the Buddha-way; all afflictions are [ultimately]... [exhausted].
Ultimately liberated. Thus, the four marks and the four ailments are entirely gates of the nature of *pariṇispanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment).

The six sense faculties and the six sense objects fully manifest the realm of wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*. These capacities all receive its influence; those with the spiritual nature are all encompassed.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The holy nature has no obstruction; whether following or reversing, all are skillful means. The wondrous mind of *pariṇispanna-bodhi* is likewise so. All things...
There is that which arises; do not let it pass you by. This concludes the section on the appropriate capacities of those to be taught.
Fifth, regarding the depth and shallowness of the essential nature: the words of the Sage are not fixed, encompassing both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; thus, the true teaching is difficult to evaluate.

The various interpretations differ in their depth and substance. Now, following the general purport of the root sūtra and synthesizing the explanations of the ancient masters, I shall briefly present three chapters:

first, opening [the categories] into ten types (as in Chengguan’s *Huayan shuchao*); second, condensing them into four gates (as in Zongmi’s *Yuanjue jing zhujie*); and third, providing a comprehensive synthesis.
Regarding the statement that these are opened up into ten kinds: first, the essence of vocal sound and language; second, the essence of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*);

third, the essence that universally encompasses the four dharmas; fourth, the essence that comprehensively includes the signified objects; fifth, the essence of all phenomena manifesting their meanings; sixth, the essence of the mind that encompasses the nature of objects;

seventh, the essence of entering reality by harmonizing conditions; eighth, the essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; ninth, the essence of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena... [and so forth].
The essence of non-obstruction; the essence of the tenfold brilliant manifestation of the ocean-seal. These ten types range from shallow to deep; they exhaust all words and perfect all principles.
For a detailed explanation, consult the *Huayan xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avataṃsaka).
Regarding the statement that these are combined into four gates: this refers to the ten types mentioned above, which Guifeng has condensed into four.

First, the gate of following phenomena (*suxiangmen*); second, the gate of consciousness-only (*weishimen*); third, the gate of returning to nature (*guixingmen*); and fourth, the gate of non-obstruction (*wunaimen*). Within the gate of following phenomena, there are further subdivisions.
There are two types: first, the essence of sound, name, phrase, and phoneme, which refers to the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

This is because one may take sound as the essence of the teaching, subsuming the provisional under the real; or one may take name, phrase, and phoneme as the essence of the teaching, following the substance through its function.

Here, both are taken together, for the provisional and the real, as well as substance and function, mutually support one another to constitute the essence of the teaching. Second, universal inclusion.
The referent (the *vācya*) consists of the meaning [expressed], while sounds, names, phrases, and syllables belong only to the signifier (*vācaka*).

If there were no referent—the meaning—then it would not constitute the essence of the teaching; therefore, it must necessarily include the referent as well. Thus, the essence of the teaching consists of the mutual concomitance of the words and their meanings.

Regarding the perspective of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*): since both the aforementioned signifiers and signifieds are manifestations of consciousness alone, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "It merely negates external [objects]."
The object [of cognition] manifests the internal mind; apart from consciousness, there are no other dharmas. The *Vyākhyā* (Explanatory Commentary) also states:
"Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the noble Vajragarbha serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the images transformed by consciousness.

These appear as reflections upon the consciousness of the listeners, resembling those dharma-gates. Transmitted through successive generations, they are called 'teaching' (*deśanā*). Thus it is known that [all is one].
All phenomena are merely images transformed by the consciousness-mind; therefore, they take *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as their substance.
Regarding the gate of returning to the nature (*dharmatā*): because the aforementioned consciousness-mind has no substantiality and is solely *tathatā* (suchness), there are two meanings.

First, from the perspective of the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), *tathatā* follows conditions to transform and give rise to the objects of consciousness; all phenomena arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature, thus converging back [to the source].
The single true suchness (*tathatā*). As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Based upon this mind, the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed.

The "Chapter on Holy Conduct" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "To know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind is to accomplish the body of wisdom, which does not depend on another for awakening.
Therefore, taking the return to nature as its essence. Second, regarding the gate of true suchness: it is called "true" because it is unchanging. It is...
"Decay" refers to transformation; only this can serve as the substance of the teaching. That which manifests change and decay is not the substance of the teaching.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All dharmas exist only in dependence upon deluded thought and thus possess distinctions.
If one is separated from deluded thought, then there are no appearances of any objective realms. Therefore, all dharmas, from the very beginning..."
It is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects.

It is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible; it is solely the one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (Suchness). In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, it is said in praise of Vimalakīrti:
"To the extent that there are no written characters or spoken words, this is called the true entry into the non-dual dharma."

Therefore, it takes the return to the nature as its essence. Within these two meanings, the former is the "Mind-Only" of the Final Teaching (Paryantayāna), while the latter is the "Mind-Only" of the Sudden Teaching (Aksobhyayāna);
together they constitute the single Gate of Returning to the Nature. Regarding the Gate of the Fourfold Non-obstruction, there are also two meanings:

first, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; second, the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. Within the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, there are further two meanings.
First, the mutual penetration of the preceding and succeeding; second, the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener. Regarding the mutual penetration of the preceding and succeeding:

among the three gates mentioned above, the first two belong to the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*); they are the phenomenal dharma-realm (*vastu-dharmadhātu*). The latter one refers to the nature to which all returns;
it belongs to the gate of suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) and is the noumenal dharma-realm (*tattva-dharmadhātu*). The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "Based on the single mind-dharma, there are two gates."
However, since both depend upon the one mind, true suchness (*tathatā*) is itself birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha*), and birth-and-death is itself true suchness.

Therefore, subsuming the previous three [aspects], the teaching-body (*śarīra-dharma*) consists of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*). Regarding the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener, there are four propositions:
first, the Buddha completely encompasses sentient beings; this means that outside the Buddha’s true mind, there are no separate sentient beings, and thus he speaks only of non-existence.

First, hearing completely encompasses the Buddha: this means that apart from the true mind of sentient beings, there is no separate Buddha; therefore, there is only hearing and no speaking. Second, sentient beings completely encompass the Buddha:

this means that when the true mind of the Buddha encompasses sentient beings, it does not obstruct sentient beings’ minds from encompassing the Buddha; and when sentient beings’ minds encompass the Buddha, it does not obstruct the true mind of the Buddha from encompassing sentient beings. Third, sentient beings and the Buddha are mutually fused:

this means that when the Buddha’s true mind encompasses sentient beings, it does not hinder sentient beings’ minds from encompassing the Buddha; and when sentient beings’ minds encompass the Buddha, it does not hinder the Buddha’s true mind from encompassing sentient beings.
Thus, both speaking and listening coexist; the two teachings stand side by side; and the four modes of birth and the Buddha are simultaneously subsumed.

This means that when the Buddha’s true mind encompasses sentient beings, beings are identical to the Buddha and are therefore not "beings. When the true mind of sentient beings encompasses the Buddha, the Buddha is identical to beings and is therefore not the "Buddha.
Consequently, speaking and listening mutually negate one another, and the two teachings are equally subsumed. In this way, there is both existence and subsumption.
Freedom. Because principle and phenomena are unimpeded, non-obstruction constitutes its essence. Within the unimpededness of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*), there are also two meanings:
first, the mutual inclusion of successive layers; second, the total inclusion of both speaker and listener. Regarding the mutual inclusion of successive layers:
because principle and phenomena are unimpeded through the three aforementioned gates, it enables each individual phenomenon—such as sounds, names, phrases, and syllables—to...
The Dharma is entirely in accord with principle and unimpeded. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states in the passage on the purity of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*):
"By means of this pure mental faculty, even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings.

Now, the gateway of consciousness (*vijñāna*) being in accord with its nature is likewise so. Furthermore, it says: "Having understood these meanings, one is able to expound upon a single verse or a single phrase."
Regarding periods of one month, four months, or even up to one year, the current meanings of names, phrases, and sentences likewise accord with the nature (*dharmatā*).
As for the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener, there are also four propositions.

First, because the Buddha-fruit accords with the nature and encompasses all phenomena without exception, sentient beings are already contained within the Buddha; how much more so the teachings they hear? Thus, each and every constituent part of the Buddha-fruit...

First, even a single hair-tip and so forth are all that which is heard. Second, this means that sentient beings accord with their true nature (*dharmatā*), encompassing all phenomena without exception.

Since the Buddha himself still dwells within sentient beings, how much more so the teachings he has spoken? Therefore, every individual part of a sentient being’s body, every single hair-tip and so forth, all become the spoken teaching.
Third, because sentient beings and Buddhas mutually interpenetrate while each retaining its own unimpaired characteristics, it follows accordingly for any one [of them].
Voice and teaching are mutually expounded and mutually heard. Therefore, the Buddha within the body of a sentient being preaches the Dharma for the sentient beings within the Buddha’s body;

the sentient beings within the Buddha’s body listen to the Buddha within their own bodies preaching the Dharma. Fourth, because birth is entirely present in the Buddha, it is identical to the Buddha and not birth;
because the Buddha is entirely present in birth, he is identical to birth and not the Buddha. Thus, both positions are equally obliterated.
Since speaking and listening are mutually absent, within the Buddha’s body there are no sentient beings who listen, and within the bodies of sentient beings there is no Buddha who speaks.

Thus, one hearing is all hearing; one speaking is all speaking. Sentient beings and Buddhas exist in mutual interpenetration, yet both are preserved while speaking and listening are mutually absent, such that both are extinguished. Ultimately, even "existence" cannot be spoken of, nor can "extinction" be spoken of.
It is taught that when they are mutually subsumed, they are simultaneously mutually preserved; when they are mutually preserved, they are simultaneously mutually subsumed.

All things are thus perfectly accomplished, without obstruction or hindrance. Therefore, the ultimate teaching-body (*śāstra-śarīra*) is that of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*).

Regarding the statement that [the teachings] are collectively categorized and harmonized: Guifeng’s first gate subsumes the first five of Qingliang’s [classification]; the second part subsumes six (because his "Mind-Only" doctrine is broad in scope;

although Guifeng’s "Consciousness-Only" gate contains the four propositions of original and reflected images, it only implicitly encompasses the Sudden and Complete [teachings], and when strictly discussing Consciousness-Only, it is limited to the Initial [Teaching] divided into two parts;

therefore, they are not fully subsumed together). The third part subsumes six and fully subsumes his seventh (because his explanation of Mind-Only is equivalent to the single source of the One Mind, whereas Guifeng’s third [gate] is limited to being equivalent to the Sudden and Complete; therefore, it only divides [the seventh]).

[Included]. If that seventh [category] meets the conditions for arising and ceasing and enters the reality of True Suchness (*tathatā*), its meaning corresponds to the Sudden Teaching; therefore, it is fully included here. The inclusion of the latter three [categories] among the four can be understood accordingly.

If one correlates this with the root scripture, this sutra properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching; its essence should be taken as the return to the nature (*dharmatā*). It also concurrently includes the Small, Initial, and Final Teachings.

The Small Teaching clearly belongs to the "following characteristics" (*lakṣaṇānuyāyin*); it secretly connects with the Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) school. The Initial Teaching clearly belongs to... [text ends]

Consciousness-only (Vijñaptimātra) darkly penetrates and returns to the nature (dharmatā). As for the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-yāna), it belongs to the same category of returning to the nature as the Sudden Teaching (Aksara-yāna).

Furthermore, this sutra directly penetrates to the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇa-yāna) and also takes non-obstruction as its essence. This concludes the section on the shallowness and depth of the teaching-essence.

Regarding the sixth point, the general and specific characteristics of the tenets (*siddhānta*): that which is esteemed in speech is called a "tenet" (*siddhānta*); that to which a tenet leads is called its "orientation" (*gati*).
These orientations are both general and specific. The general refers to the Buddhist teachings of a single lifetime as a whole;
though the various schools (*nikāya*) have differing views that are each distinct, when these are grouped according to their underlying principles, they can be summarized into six tenets.

First, the school that adheres to the grasping at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-grāha-vāda*). This refers to those who give rise to grasping at existence and non-existence regarding all persons (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

These are the various masters of the Hīnayāna who, relying on sūtras such as the *Āgamas* and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, composed the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and the various treatises of the various schools (*nikāya*).

Within this [school], it is further divided into six: first, the school that asserts the existence of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-astitva-vāda*), namely the Vātsīputrīyas, Dharmottaras, and Bhadantas.

The Vātsīputrīyas, Saṃmitīyas, and the Giriśaila school and others, because they establish a self (*ātman*), are collectively rejected by the masters of the various schools as "outsiders who merely cling to the Buddha-dharma.
Second, the schools that maintain the existence of dharmas but the non-existence of a self include the Sarvāstivādins, Sthaviras, Bahulikas, and others.
They assert that all dharmas are substantially real, yet they do not posit a self, thereby distinguishing themselves from the outsiders.

The *Daogji* (Treatise on the Path’s Calculations) further establishes the principle of correct causes and conditions (*samyag-hetu-pratyaya*) to refute the heterodox views of external paths regarding false causes and the absence of causes.
Regarding the school that maintains the doctrine that the three phenomena have no coming or going—namely, the Mahāsāṃghika, Kaukkuṭika, Caitika, Haimavata, and Dharmaguptaka.
The Kāśyapīya school and others maintain that only present conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas exist;

because past and future dharmas lack both substance (*svabhāva*) and function (*kāritra*), they are not mentioned. Fourth are those schools that distinguish between the provisional and the real regarding the manifest:

namely, the Saṃmitīya school, which asserts within the aforementioned present conditioned dharmas that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are real while the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are provisional. Regarding the *Tattvasiddhi*...

The *Śāstra* states: The Sautrāntika masters of the later period (speaking to the Mūlasarvāstivādins) also maintain this teaching: the five schools that assert the conventional is false while the ultimate is real refer to the Lokottaravādins and others;
they claim that the conventional is merely provisional because it is illusory, whereas the supramundane is the opposite.
The sixth school, which asserts that all phenomena are but names, refers to the Ekavyāvahārikas and others; they maintain that all selves and dharmas exist only as provisional designations.

Because they lack substantial reality, among these six, the first category maintains only existence, the last maintains only non-existence, and the middle one maintains both existence and non-existence;
therefore, collectively, there is only one school of dogmatic attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) according to their characteristics.
Second is the Faxiang school of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra). This school maintains that all phenomena are merely manifestations of consciousness.
Accordingly, Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, relying on such scriptures as the Vaipulya and the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtras, composed works such as the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra and the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra.
Third is the School of Emptiness and Signlessness (*śūnyatā-nimitta-śūnya-vāda*). This asserts that all phenomena are empty and signless.
Thus, Deva and Bhāviveka, relying on sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, composed works such as the *Śata-śāstra* and the *Ratnagotra-vibhāga*.

The fourth is the Mind-Dependent Origination school (Cittapratītyasamutpāda), which asserts that all phenomena are solely True Suchness (tathatā) conforming to conditions and endowed with virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Thus,

Sthiramati and Aśvaghoṣa composed the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and other treatises based on scriptures such as the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The fifth is the school of the quiescent true nature (*tathatā*). This refers to the complete severance of both conceptualization and its characteristics, as it directly reveals the essence of the nature itself.

Thus, Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, relying on such scriptures as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, composed works such as the *Tathatā-samādhi-śāstra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The Sixth is the School of the Perfect Interfusion of the Six Dharma Realms (*ṣaḍ-dharmadhātu-saṃvartana*).

This refers to the inexhaustible dharma realm (*ananta-dharmadhātu*), which, like Indra’s net (*indrajāla*), consists of principal and attendant elements in successive layers, being perfectly interfused and unimpeded. Consequently, Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu, relying on the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras, composed works such as the *Acintyabhūmi-śāstra*.

Regarding these six schools: with the exception of the first [of the first school], which has no destination because it is not accepted by the Buddha’s teaching, the remaining ones each serve as gateways to awakening for specific types of practitioners.
They provide resources for their respective practices so that they may realize the fruits appropriate to their own kind; this constitutes their destination.
If one were to explain the essential purport by addressing this specific sutra individually, there are further general and particular aspects within it.

Generally speaking, the purport of this sutra is based solely upon the Tathāgata’s original ground of practice (*yuanqi yindi*), taking the perfect illumination of the pure aspect of awakening (*juexiang*) as its theme, and the ultimate fruition—the permanent severance of ignorance and the realization of the wondrous, perfect nature of awakening (*miaoyuan juexing*)—as its goal. If we proceed from within that aforementioned general framework:
The primary principle (zōng) is exclusively the fifth [topic], while the destination (qù) encompasses the sixth.
The first, second, third, and fourth may also be understood through lateral connection. Specifically, regarding this sutra alone, they proceed in a sequential cycle, divided into six pairs:

First, the pair of Teaching and Meaning: To seek perfect enlightenment (yuánjué), one must rely on the sacred teaching. Therefore, the teaching that eternally transcends all illusions is first established as the primary principle. As for the teaching...

This is a hollow transmission. The essential point lies in contemplating the meaning according to the teaching; therefore, it is followed by taking the profound contemplation on the meaning of the exhaustion of illusions as its aim.
Second is the pair of doubt and faith: regarding the "exhaustion of illusions and perfection of enlightenment," listeners often harbor doubts.

Thus, one first takes the skillful refutation of the three doubts as the primary theme. Once these deep doubts have been refuted, true faith arises; therefore, this is followed by the generation of decisive faith.
This constitutes the "goal" (*yāna*). Third is the pair of "Awakening" (*bodha*) and "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*): once faith is decisive, awakening must correspond to reality;

therefore, one first takes the mind’s awakening to the true mark (*tathatā*) as the primary principle. Awakening alone is ineffective; it is essential that cultivation necessarily arise from this nature.

Therefore, next, one takes the progressive cultivation of the three concentrations (*samādhi*) as the goal. Fourth is the pair of "Partial" (*prādeśika*) and "Complete" (*pariniṣpanna*): awakening has degrees of depth, and initial cultivation still...

One should act according to the capacity of the individual. Therefore, one first takes the partial cultivation of the three concentrations as the primary principle. As the objects of perception shift between pure and mixed, long-term cultivation will naturally lead to unimpeded mastery;
thus, one next takes the perfect cultivation of the wheel-visualization (*cakravāla*) as the goal. Regarding the five pairs of cause and effect:

this refers to the polishing of the wheel-visualization, whereby the primary cause becomes unimpeded. Thus, one first takes the cessation of hindrances and the perfection of the cause as the primary principle. When the cause has reached fruition...
The *qì* (bond) resides in the subsequent stage; therefore, it follows that taking the attainment of realization within a fixed period as the goal. Sixth is the pair of "end" and "beginning":

this means that once the fruit is accomplished, one returns to the source to honor and propagate the subtle words. Thus, it concludes with the exhortation to manifest [the truth] and the encouragement to uphold and protect it as its core principle.
Regarding what is expected through such upholding and protection, one must still rely on skillful means; therefore, it begins with the perfectly illuminating mark of pure awakening.
The "course" (*gati*). This refers to the sequential progression from the former to the latter, revolving in succession as the specific thematic focus (*mūla-gati*) of this sutra.

By practicing in accordance with it, one naturally attains resonance with it. It may also be said that by knowing what comes first and what comes last, one draws near to the Way. The general and specific aspects of the thematic focus are hereby concluded.

Compiled by Tongli, a later disciple of the Venerable Master, and collated by his dharma-heir Xinxing. △ Ninth:
General Explanation of the Title. This means that a name is the guest of the reality it signifies, and a title is the mainstay of the sutra.

The great meaning of the entire sutra is subsumed within its title; therefore, it is called a "general explanation. This means that the great meaning of the entire sutra is explained in general within the title itself.
This section is divided into four parts: first, a brief explanation of the five names; second, a detailed explanation of the current title.

Third, an appended discussion of ancient methods; fourth, an explanation of the sequence of the fascicles. Regarding the first: according to what the Buddha himself stated within the sutra, there are five types of titles.
The first is called *Mahāvaipulya-pariśuddha-bodhi-dhāraṇī*. This is titled according to both the dharma and its meaning:

"Pariśuddha-bodhi" (Perfect Enlightenment) refers to the dharma; "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Extensiveness) refers to the meaning; and "Dhāraṇī" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "Total Retention. This means that the single dharma of Perfect Enlightenment can encompass all things, while the three meanings of Great Extensiveness can sustain immeasurable meanings; therefore, it is collectively termed "Dhāraṇī."
1) The *dhāraṇī* (named thus). 2) The *sūtra* of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). (This is named after supreme wisdom (*prajñā*). *Sūtra* is the general name for all scriptures.

Scriptures of provisional and gradual teaching are called "indefinitive" (*neyārtha*), while those of perfect and sudden teaching are called "definitive. Because one can cultivate vast and profound wisdom by relying upon them, it is therefore named after supreme wisdom.

3) The King of Secret Samādhis (*guhyarāja-samādhi*). (This is named after supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*). *Samādhi* is the general name for all concentrations. What is cultivated by those of provisional and limited capacity does not merit the name "secret," because it can be fathomed; nor does it merit the name "king," because it lacks sovereignty.)

Therefore, that which is the dwelling place of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is termed the "Secret" and the "King. By practicing in reliance upon it, one attains sovereign spiritual efficacy (*vibhūti*). Because this cannot be fathomed by the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is thus named after its supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Fourth is the "Definitive Realm of the Tathāgata. (This is named after the perfect fruit. It means that the Tathāgata is the already accomplished Buddha-fruit; all who possess a mind will certainly attain it.

This is what is meant by "the fruit thoroughly penetrating the source of the cause. Fifth is the "Self-Nature Differentiation of the Tathāgatagarbha. (This is named after the perfect cause. The Tathāgatagarbha is self-)

"Nature (*prakṛti*) is the cause for the unformed Buddha. The sublime states of the worthies and sages are all distinctions of this self-nature; this is what is meant by 'the cause encompassing the ocean of fruition. The *Great Commentary* states:

"Since phenomena are exhaustive and principles are complete, one must establish five titles [for the text]. This is to enable practitioners to rely on the meaning of the true Dharma, to achieve superior concentration and wisdom, and to cultivate and realize the perfect cause and fruition.

To extract the essentials for titling, two designations are retained. (When lecturing, the full names are cumbersome to pronounce; therefore, for the titles, only the essentials are taken, while the two designations are retained as follows: first, *Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhi*; second, *Sūtra-vyākaraṇa*.)

The meaning: these two names are joined together as a single title; the three characters "dhāraṇī" are omitted, and the final three names are likewise not taken. This is because the causes and fruits of samādhi are all established through the superior wisdom of the dharma-meaning (*dharmārtha*), and thus only these two names are essential.
The brief explanation of the five names is complete. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the present title has two parts:
first, explaining the dharma-meaning that is expressed; second, explaining the names and terms that express it. First:
The Great Commentary on the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-bodhimaṇḍala-pariniṣpanna-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Perfect Enlightenment), Volume One, states:
"Whenever one wishes to understand a sūtra or śāstra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), one must first clarify the interpretation of the dharma and its meaning.

By interpreting the meaning according to the dharma, the meaning becomes distinct; by illuminating the dharma with the meaning, the dharma becomes manifest. Therefore, in the [*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith)], when one..."
This reveals the principles of the profound and hidden nature and characteristics of the Mahāyāna; first, these two are opened up. As the treatise states:
"The Mahāyāna, in brief, is of two kinds: first, the Dharma (the teaching); second, the meaning (the realization). 'Dharma' refers to the One Mind; 'meaning' unfolds the Three Greatnesses."
Now, within this context, the five characters [of the title] and the two characters "Perfect Enlightenment" (yuanjue) are precisely this Dharma.
Because Perfect Enlightenment abiding within the bonds of affliction is itself the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the *Śāstra* states: "That which is called the Dharma is the mind of sentient beings.

This is because, in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna, the Perfect Enlightenment abiding within the bonds is designated as the "mind of sentient beings."

The three characters "Great," "Extensive," and "Vast" (Mahāvaipulya) are themselves the meaning. This is because they correspond, respectively, to the three great meanings of essence, attributes, and function.
The Great Commentary states: "Great" is named according to its own substance; its meaning is constancy and pervasiveness.

"According to its own substance" means that it corresponds to the entire substance of Perfect Enlightenment, which is boundless and transcends all measure; it is forcibly termed "great" to distinguish it from mere dharmic characteristics.
Within our school, "great" is spoken of in contrast to "small. Because "great" is spoken of in contrast to "small," that greatness has limitations;

it is not true greatness. To take "permanence and omnipresence" as its meaning: permanence means vertically penetrating the three periods of time, while omnipresence means horizontally encompassing the ten directions.
Regarding vertical penetration of the three periods of time: the past has no beginning and the future has no end; there is not a single dharma that can...
It precedes and follows all things; because it alone can precede and follow all dharmas, it is called "Great.

As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which is called 'Great' is termed 'Eternal. To "horizontally encompass the ten directions" means that externally it can embrace them and internally it can pervade them.
There is not a single dharma capable of embracing or pervading [it]; only this can embrace and pervade all dharmas. Therefore...
It is called "Great" (mahat). As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "That which is called 'Great' is by nature vast and expansive, like empty space.

"Square" (*caturaśra*) is a name derived from the Dharma (for "square" here means "Dharma"). Its meaning is "providing a standard and maintaining [it]" (*pratiṣṭhāna*). "Standard" (*pratimā*) refers to that which gives rise to understanding in sentient beings.

"Maintaining" means sustaining its own nature. Regarding "providing a standard that gives rise to sentient beings' understanding": it is like sentient beings' awakening and entry into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Although they rely on the instruction of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), their wisdom and understanding arise from the nature of enlightenment itself. It is like the moisture of water and soil that produces grain sprouts and the like;
the sprout arises from the seed, not from the water or soil. Therefore, one should know that awakening and entering Perfect Enlightenment likewise relies upon [the nature of enlightenment].
Perfect Enlightenment serves as the square to guide it. Regarding the maintenance of its own nature:

because all sentient beings possess fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), although they may wander through the six realms of existence, this enlightened nature has never been lost or extinguished.
If one can rely upon this to practice and realize it, then all supreme causes and wondrous fruits will emerge from it. As stated in the Chapter of Mañjuśrī, the World-Honored One said:

The answer to Mañjuśrī states: There is a great *dhāraṇī* named Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), which gives rise to all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās*, and instructs the bodhisattvas.
Thus, one who cultivates and realizes Perfect Enlightenment must rely upon Perfect Enlightenment itself as the method by which to maintain it.
As for its "extensiveness," it derives its name from its function (the vast manifestation of great function is precisely this).

"Extensive" (*guǎng*) means "much" and "vast. As for "much," this nature of Perfect Enlightenment inherently possesses wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, arising secretly and responding subtly without rest or exhaustion. This is why "many" is termed "extensive";
just as in the world, any number that is great is called extensive. As for "vast," it refers to each and every one of these inexhaustible functions.
It is identical to the nature of awakening; it has no boundaries and no limits, as described in the "Universal Eye" chapter. When the World-Honored One replied to Universal Eye, he said:
"The nature of awakening is all-pervading, for it is perfectly circular and without limit. One should know that the six sense faculties likewise pervade the Dharma-realm.
Because the sense faculties (*indriya*) are all-pervading, one should know that the six objects (*viṣaya*) pervade the *dharmadhātu*.

Because the objects are all-pervading, one should know that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) pervade the *dharmadhātu*. In this manner, up to the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates, they pervade the *dharmadhātu*.
This is "broad" by virtue of being extensive; just as in the world, whatever is measured as broad is also called [extensive].
The two characters "Guang" (Vast) and "Yuanjue" (Perfect Enlightenment) directly point to that Dharma. This means: what, after all, is this Dharma referred to above as "Dafangguang" (Great Vastness)?
Therefore, it directly points to Perfect Enlightenment to reveal it, intending to show that it is none other than the nature of Perfect Enlightenment.
To explain its meaning: "Yuan" (Perfect) refers to being complete and all-encompassing; it signifies that beyond this, there is not a single thing...
Because it is the Dharma, that which is empty, luminous, and spiritually illuminating is called "Awakening" (*jue*). This is because within it not a single thought is preserved.
Furthermore, it fully possesses the meaning of "Great, Vast, and Broad," encompassing all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds; therefore, it is called "Perfect" (*yuan*).

It completely traverses the fundamental suchness to its ultimate limit and shines through both the ordinary and the non-ordinary stages; therefore, it is called "Awakening. Prime Minister Pei’s preface states: "It unifies all virtues..."
It is thus fully perfected. It illuminates the masses of darkness while shining alone; therefore it is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*Yuanjue*).
This is what that means. △ Next, the explanation of the designating names: the three characters *xiūduluó* (Sūtra) are the general name for all sutras.
