As for its being called "pure," this refers to the direct mind (ṛjukacitta) that correctly contemplates the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā).

In the final age, by relying on cultivation, one attains correct abiding and maintenance; hence, it is said that one does not fall into false views. The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary has two parts. First:
The Introductory Verse. Second, the Main Verses. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
The Great Commentary states: Generally speaking, there are four types of verses; the first is named *anuṣṭubh*. This...

Whether in prose or verse, when the count reaches exactly thirty-two syllables, it constitutes one stanza (*gāthā*). This second type is called *gāthā*, which here is translated as "recitation" (*fèngsòng*);
in the context of the precepts, it is termed "direct recitation" (*zhí sòng*). This refers to expounding the Dharma using verses, rather than versifying prose.

(Note: Commentators often refer to these as "independent verses. Third is *geya* (祇夜), which means "verses in response" (*ying-song*), so called because they correspond to the preceding prose (*chángxíng*).

Fourth is *gāthā* (蘊陀南), which means "collected giving" (*jíshī*); this refers to the gathering and condensing of many meanings into few words, which are then bestowed upon others for recitation and retention.
Now, among these four types [of prose and verse], this belongs to the *geya* (repeated verse), as it is indicated by the statement:
"To restate this meaning. Furthermore, in Tiantai’s commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *geya* is further divided into two:

first, the "anticipatory verse" (*chao song*), which refers to cases where the prose (*chang xing*) follows later while the verse (*ji song*) precedes it, because the verse anticipates and summarizes the subsequent text; second, the "retrospective verse" (*zhui song*), which refers to cases where the prose...

The prose [sections] come first, and the verses follow later; they are composed in verse to recapitulate what has already been lost [in the prose]. Therefore, in my private commentary *Fahua Zhizhang*, I further divide [the verses] into four types:
first, "extensive verses" (*guǎngsòng*), which mean that what is abbreviated in the prose is expanded upon in the verses;

second, "concise verses" (*lèsòng*), which mean that what is extensive in the prose is condensed in the verses; third, "supplementary verses" (*bùsòng*), which mean that while the meaning accords with the prose, the prose...
Yet there are no prose passages [for these]. This is because the long-form prose was incomplete, and the verses were added as a supplement. Regarding the "Verses on the Four Meanings" (Sicongyi):
their meaning resembles the long-form prose, yet the phrasing does not correspond to it. Since this sutra contains verses at the end of each chapter, they are recorded here in full.
This is to ensure that they may receive instruction whenever an opportunity arises. There are two reasons why the World-Honored One wishes to restate this:

first, because his compassionate instruction is earnest and profound; second, because of the sequence of the assembly (those who gathered earlier have already heard the prose, while those who gathered later still hear the verses).

The main section of the verses is divided into two parts: first, verses replying to the initial request; second, verses replying to the subsequent request. The first part has three sections; the first is a verse on the power of the true cause.
The two verses explain how grasping at delusion forms the cycle of rebirth; the three verses explain how, when delusion is exhausted, one returns to awakening. First, the brief verse:
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that all Tathāgatas, from their original ground of practice, have awakened through wisdom."
Fearing that the preceding prose might not have been fully detailed, [the Buddha] wished to speak in verse; therefore, he taught that one should understand this:

namely, that few words may encompass many meanings, and thus they must not be treated with negligence. All two-line verses are entirely identical to the prose, as each line’s meaning subsumes the prose.

In the three-line verse, the two characters "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refer to the aspect of perfect illumination and pure awakening; the character "awakening" (*bodhi*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the available portion.*

[The character for] "Word" (字). This refers to the permanent severance of ignorance and the attainment of Buddhahood. △ Second, the verse on clinging to delusion as forming the wheel (*saṃsāra*). [This is divided into two parts: (1) a brief verse; (2) two verses.
First, one verse on clinging to what is transformed as forming the wheel; second, two verses on clinging to transformation as forming the wheel. The first [part]:
To thoroughly understand ignorance means to know it to be like flowers in the sky; one can then escape the cycle of transmigration.
To "thoroughly understand ignorance" means to understand fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which gives rise to derivative ignorance (*śākhā-pratāna-avidyā*).

By understanding derivative ignorance, one realizes that within the present body and mind, there is the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena, through which false transmigration occurs. [The phrase] "like flowers in the sky" refers to this.
Following the prose section, it still mentions "the second moon. Those words refer to the present body and mind.

Even if one can understand that this body is a provisional combination of the four great elements and this mind is a shadow conditioned by the six sense objects—both being like flowers in the sky or a second moon—one will naturally no longer grasp at a self or phenomena therein, nor create karma or undergo retribution. Thus, one is able to escape the cycle of transmigration.

This serves as a counter-illumination (pratikṣepa) of what precedes it; there should have been the statement that "the grasping at causes forms the wheel," but because the verse is brief and cannot be exhaustive, I have privately supplemented the explanation regarding the thorough understanding of ignorance (*avidyā*) based on the meaning of the prose commentary. Let the wise examine this.
The section on the verse explaining how the grasping at objects forms the wheel is complete. △ Second, the verse explaining how the grasping at the subject forms the wheel.
Furthermore, it is like a person in a dream who cannot be found upon waking.
The Long Discourse says: "It is like a person in a dream; while dreaming, they are not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found."
The mind arises through the formation of thoughts, appearing as if there were ignorance, like a person in a dream; while dreaming, it is not non-existent.

Yet, if one is free from thought, one awakens, and though one seeks the clarity of ignorance, it cannot be found. Just as when one wakes from a dream, the person in the dream immediately ceases to exist.
Observing it in this way, then cessation is fundamentally without cessation, and arising is likewise without arising. Therefore—
The prose section states: "All sentient beings, within the state of non-arising, falsely perceive arising and ceasing; therefore, it is called 'revolving in birth and death.
This is also an abbreviation following the verse text, which supplements the explanation according to the meaning of the prose to show there is no difference.

The section on the verse concluding the attachment to delusion as forming the cycle is finished. △ Third, the verse on the exhaustion of delusion and the return to awakening. (The preceding prose was not divided; now...)
According to the meaning of the commentary, there are two parts: first, a verse on the ultimate exhaustion of all delusions; second, a verse on not waiting for what is unreal.
Regarding the first: "The Awakened One is like space—equal, unmoving, and unchanging."

The Long Discourse states: "That knower. Here, the term "knower" refers specifically to the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), for it is that which perceives the flowers in the sky [of false appearances].
Since it has realized the delusion, its very substance vanishes and merges with *tathatā*;
therefore, it is like empty space. The Long Discourse says "just as," while the verse retains only "like" (*yathā*), omitting the former for brevity. It is equal.
As for this, once words have ceased and merged with True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is like empty space, then existence cannot exist and non-existence cannot be absent;
arising cannot cause arising and ceasing cannot cause ceasing. This is because existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing are all equal. Regarding "immovable and unchanging":
the nature of True Suchness cannot be shifted by the three periods of time, and no phenomena can transform it. [Thus ends] the long prose section.
This refers to what is called "pure awakening. The verse concludes that all delusions are utterly exhausted. II. Verse on "What Need Is There to Await [the Untrue]?
"Awareness pervades the ten directions; thus one attains the Buddha-way" (up to) "because the fundamental nature is perfectly complete."

The first two lines are a brief verse summarizing the prose. The prose states: "Like the nature of the Dharma-realm, it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
like the nature of the Dharma-realm. The verse omits this for brevity. Its purport is, in essence, to further contemplate pure awakening.

Principle pervades phenomena; therefore, it is said that awakening is pervasive. Once awakening is pervasive, one further examines with discernment and proceeds to contemplate until, after a long time, phenomena are integrated with principle and a thousand lands are subsumed within it; thus, one reaches the worlds of the ten directions.
Now, the text simply says "awakening pervades the worlds of the ten directions," for this single phrase subsumes the meaning of the two phrases from the prose section. Thus, it is attained.
One who attains the Buddha-way does so because of the perfection of awakening. The final three lines of the verse are a supplementary gāthā intended to preempt an objection.

[The objection might run as follows: "It is logically certain that the extinction of delusion results in the realization of truth. Yet, the preceding line stated, 'Furthermore, it is like a person in a dream who cannot be found upon waking,' which seems to imply there is no delusion to be extinguished. Now, however, it says one 'immediately attains the Buddha-way. Does this not mean there is a 'Way' to be realized?"

Therefore, the latter three phrases are used to prevent such misconceptions. The meaning is that the various illusions have been fundamentally non-existent; they are not extinguished within *tathatā* (suchness).

The Buddha-way is inherently accomplished, yet there is no attainment of *tathatā*. This is because the original nature is perfect and complete; it appears deficient only due to the grasping at delusion.

When delusion ceases, it returns to its perfection—this is what is meant by "attaining Buddhahood. How can one raise the objection that there is something "accomplished" [as a new state]? This verse responds to the first [objection].
The response to the initial request is concluded. △ Second, the verse that responds to the subsequent request:
"If Bodhisattvas are able to give rise to the bodhicitta within this [teaching], then sentient beings of the final age who practice it will be spared from false views."
At the beginning of this section, the prose version contains the phrase "concluding the preceding and establishing the cause," which is omitted in the verse.
Regarding the bodhicitta within this context, the prose version refers to it as the "pure mind."
When the mind is thus purified, one is freed from all ailments; by practicing in accordance with this in the final age, one can naturally avoid false views.

△ Second, the Section on the True Teaching (which sets forth the correct meaning of this scripture and clarifies the source of the school’s doctrine). Four parts: First, the Section on Generating Faith through Three Questions and Three Answers;

Second, the Section on Opening Understanding through Two Questions and Two Answers; Third, the Section on Teaching Practice through Four Questions and Four Answers; Fourth, [the Conclusion]. One. [First Part]
The question-and-answer section showing the fruit consists of three parts: first, the Chapter on Samantabhadra; second, the Chapter on Universal Eye; and third, the Chapter on Vajragarbha.

The first of these has three sections: first, the inquiry of Samantabhadra; second, the harmonious union of teacher and disciple; and third, the response to the inquiry and the answering of questions.

The first two [sections]. First, the formal invitation; second, manifesting earnestness. The first three [sub-sections]. First, the general invitation with full ritual decorum; second, holding up difficult points for specific examination;
third, concluding with the skillful means of inquiry. The first [of these].
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, amidst the great assembly... [to] ...how does one practice the pure realm? This chapter takes Samantabhadra as the principal figure.

(In the preceding chapters, Mañjuśrī represented wisdom; in this chapter, Samantabhadra represents conduct. This reveals that wisdom and conduct mutually complete one another, like the eyes and feet supporting each other;

though the destination is far, it can be reached. The remaining members of the assembly are all his companions; hence the phrase "amidst the great assembly. With the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in reverent sincerity, they fully illuminate the text.

The *Shuzhang* (Exegesis on Special Chapters) explains that one must necessarily possess compassion rooted in the same essence (*tongti-bei*) in order to remove the doubts of those present at this assembly and to benefit the practice of those in the末世 (final age).
Thus, it is called the "World of Great Compassion" (*dabei shijie*). The phrase "I pray for this assembly, etc. requests the removal of the doubts of those present at the assembly.

The phrase "as well as for those in the final age, etc. requests the benefit of the practice of those in the final age. Those who practice the Mahāyāna are distinguished from those of inferior capacity; upon hearing this *Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment), they [attain realization].

The "pure realm" (*viśuddha-viṣaya*) is revealed because it is intended for those with the capacity for the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is precisely the single mind.
The "pure realm" specifically points to the gate of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind; this is what is referred to in the Mañjuśrī Chapter as the "perfectly illuminating aspect of pure awakening.
Regarding the question "How does one practice?": this is asked in reference to the cultivation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*). The intention is that the Buddha—
As previously stated, knowing this to be like flowers in the sky means there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death.
This refers to those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence who, through sudden awakening in a single thought-moment, immediately and completely comprehend birth and death.

However, for those of middling or inferior capacities, it is difficult to attain realization and entry without relying on the cultivation of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, he asks in general: "How should one cultivate?"
[The assembly] proceeded. They still hoped for sudden enlightenment. The formal invitation was thus completed. II. Holding Difficulties and Questioning Individually.
"World-Honored One, if those sentient beings were to know that [all things] are like illusions... (up to) ...how could their mind of false discrimination be liberated?"

There are three meanings of "distinct substance" (*biezhi*). First, it means that if those sentient beings know that all ignorance, body, and mind are like flowers in the sky, they are precisely those who know [them] to be like illusions;
that is to say, they are able to know that all ignorance, body, and mind are like illusions.

Because all things are like illusions and lack substantial reality. If this is so, then the body, which is a provisional combination of the four great elements, and the mind, which is a shadow-like reflection conditioned by the six sense objects, are likewise like illusions and lack substantial reality.

How can one use a body and mind that are like illusions and lack substantial reality to further cultivate and treat ignorance—which is itself like an illusion and lacks substantial reality? It would be like using water to wash water; it only increases the amount of water.
Yet, it can never be fully exhausted; on the contrary, it serves only to fuel ignorance—what benefit could there possibly be in that? This is the first point. The second point is as follows:
even if the illusory nature of ignorance were to be completely extinguished, then body and mind would likewise cease to exist, because body and mind originally exist only by virtue of ignorance.
Therefore, the preceding phrase describes ignorance as "illusory nature," for it is capable of producing the body.
Since the mind and all other phenomena are like illusions, there is no such thing as a mind; it follows that there would be neither body nor mind.
Perhaps the character for "body" (身) was mistakenly transcribed as "existence" (有) during the translation and transcription process.

However, since there is neither body nor mind, even if one were to attain sudden enlightenment through principle, who would be the one to practice through successive stages? Why, then, does the Tathāgata habitually speak of practicing through successive stages?
To practice the deeds and purify the illusion-like ignorance in order to achieve the perfect fruit is like joining space with space;
since space provides no benefit and its union yields no merit, such cultivation is merely laborious—what purpose would it serve? These are the two positions.
The third is as follows: if sentient beings, upon hearing that things are like illusions, immediately realize they lack reality and understand from the beginning that they are not needed.
Regarding "cultivation," it refers to cultivation through the observation of phenomena; both types of cultivation are not employed here.
If that were the case, then all sentient beings would be constantly in birth and death. Since they would be constantly in birth and death, they would give rise to delusions and create karma.
One creates karma and receives its retribution: a single thought of goodness leads to the heavens or the human realm; a single thought of evil leads to the hells and the three miserable paths.
Delusions and karma follow one after another, and karmic retributions unfold in succession; through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they can never be halted or severed.

Therefore it is said that one constantly dwells within illusion and transformation. This means that without relying on contemplative practice, one cannot achieve sudden awakening, nor has one ever understood that all phenomena are like illusory realms.
Without passing through the cultivation of practice, ignorance remains vividly present. How can the mind of deluded thought be liberated?
If even the mind cannot be liberated, how much less so the body? It would only serve to further bind one. In this way, the entire world becomes nothing but a dream.
"Who is the Great Awakened One?"—these are the three inquiries. Since these three points of contention have been set forth, the two modes of cultivation are indispensable;

there is nothing that can surpass them in probing the profound and seeking out the hidden. Were it not for Samantabhadra, who else could participate in this? The difficult distinctions regarding the inquiry have concluded.
△ Third, the conclusion of the inquiry into the skillful means.
"I pray that for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age... (omitted)... may all sentient beings forever be free from all illusions.
The preceding general request was made for both the present and the future; this concluding request is specifically for the future.

This is because those in the present assembly may harbor doubts regarding provisional teachings, whereas those in the final age who practice erroneously are truly pitiable. As for "by what skillful means": it refers to observing conduct and practicing cultivation.
All of these are skillful means. Second, because they do not know how to apply them, he asks what should be done. Regarding gradual cultivation:

first one employs contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), and subsequently one practices based on concrete phenomena. Through contemplative practice, one attains sudden awakening in a single thought-moment, immediately and thoroughly understanding that all realms are like illusions.
Through practice based on phenomena, one gradually polishes the mind until the deluded thoughts are eliminated.
The liberation through traversing the stages and the eternal departure from all illusions reside precisely herein. Samantabhadra is one who has already passed through these realms;
yet, out of compassion for sentient beings of the final age, he feigns ignorance and asks questions with complete thoroughness. The formal questioning is concluded.
II. Manifesting Zeal (This section manifests his earnest devotion, showing that he will certainly arrive at the third stage).
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.
The meaning follows the explanation in the "Mañjuśrī Chapter. All ten subsequent chapters are modeled after this. The inquiry of Samantabhadra concludes. II.
The Harmonious Union of Teacher and Disciple. This has two parts: 1. The union of the teacher with the disciple; 2. The union of the disciple with the teacher. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Although he asked this once on the spot, it would not have provided full benefit for both the present and the future; therefore, he spoke again, saying "Excellent," to praise him.

While the various bodhisattvas provisionally manifested doubt, the multitude of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age practice with many errors; all these actions are performed [for their own sake], and it is not Samantabhadra who acts thus.
Because [the original] could not do so, it was therefore able to praise it. The cultivation of the higher meaning is somewhat insufficient;

one should add the four characters "should further inquire of the Tathāgata. This is likely because the translator’s intent reached its goal while the phrasing did not. Upon hearing the teaching that all is like an illusion...
One immediately contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions. When the time comes, one suddenly awakens to their illusory nature;

at that very moment, with not a single thought moving, this is the Illusory Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*). During its cultivation, there are further skillful means and gradual stages upon which sentient beings rely.
One attains liberation from all illusions. This is because the World-Honored One, in response to what was asked, offered this praise.
His exhortation to "listen attentively" is intended to provide a model for others; it is not that Samantabhadra himself fails to listen attentively.

His promise to "speak accordingly" is intended to show that he does not fail the questioner; it simply means that his teaching accords with the capacity of the disciple. Thus, the teacher and the disciple are in accord.
[The preceding section] concludes. △ Second, the union of the disciple with the teacher.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

To receive the instruction with joy and listen is precisely what constitutes the union with the teacher. The section on the convergence of the conditions between teacher and disciple concludes. △ Third, the response to the request.

The response to the questions consists of two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The prose section has three sub-sections: first, the answer to the general question; second, the explanation of specific points;
third, the response to the concluding request. First [the answer to the general question]:
"Good son, although the various illusory transformations of all sentient beings—up to and including illusory flowers—perish, the nature of emptiness is not destroyed.

The previous explanation of Perfect Enlightenment was precisely this One Mind. Now, it is called the 'Wondrous Mind' because it contains both the gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and arising-extinction;
it encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena, which interpenetrate one another without obstruction."
It is because of obstruction. According to what was previously asked by Samantabhadra: "Having heard of this realm of the pure *pariniṣpanna* (perfectly realized) *bodhi*, how should one practice?
Although he mentions *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*, he asks specifically regarding the gate of *tathatā* (suchness).

However, since there is nothing to be practiced within *tathatā*, the World-Honored One provides a comprehensive answer by combining the gate of *utpāda-nirodha* (arising and ceasing) with the fundamental *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*. This is the intended meaning.

This refers to various illusory transformations, such as the body, mind, and ignorance, all of which arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment—namely, what is called the dependent origination of the ocean of nature (*dharmadhātu*). This is illustrated through metaphors, such as flowers in the sky;

the metaphor of flowers in the sky represents these various illusory transformations arising from emptiness, thereby illustrating the dependent origination of the ocean of nature. If this is so, one must directly [realize it] by means of...
Through the power of contemplative practice, one realizes that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature and that the essence of awakening is eternally perfect.

Just as illusory transformations perish while their emptiness remains unimpaired, this initial response—employing the cultivation of contemplative practice—answers the general inquiry of Samantabhadra.
Having concluded the answer to the general inquiry: △ Second, the explanation of the specific substance.
The illusory mind of sentient beings returns to and is extinguished by means of illusion; yet, although all illusions may be exhausted, one does not enter into annihilation.

According to the primary intent of the first question posed by Samantabhadra: "If those sentient beings know that all ignorance, body, and mind are like flowers in the sky, this is to know that which is like an illusion. If this is so, then both body and mind are likewise illusory. Suppose...

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation through successive stages of practice, one asks: how can that which is illusory be used to cultivate back upon the illusory? Therefore, the World-Honored One explained this by saying:
"The illusory mind of sentient beings returns to extinction by relying on the illusory. This illusory mind is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*); it is fundamental ignorance.
"The secondary branches of ignorance are all deluded minds; therefore, they are extinguished by relying on the illusory.

This means that the illusory mind of ignorance belonging to sentient beings is extinguished by relying upon the illusory and deluded body and mind, proceeding through the cultivation of specific practices until it is eradicated.
This explains the first objection. According to the intent of the second objection by Samantabhadra mentioned previously: "Once the contemplative practice has been traversed, furthermore..."
Regarding the cultivation of phenomena: when one naturally cultivates the mind so that ignorance is completely extinguished, if that were the case, there would be no mind;
who then would perform cultivation? Why, then, does the Tathāgata habitually say that while principle is realized through sudden awakening, phenomena must be cultivated gradually?
Therefore, the World-Honored One explains this by saying: "When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoving."
However, this is still awakening spoken of in reliance upon illusion; it is likewise called an illusion. Why is it also called an illusion?
Because if one speaks of the existence of awakening, one has not yet departed from illusion, for it is a phenomenon of relative opposition. Yet, it cannot be said that it does not exist;
for one who speaks of the non-existence of awakening is likewise the same. This is because "non-existence" in relation to "existence" is also a form of relative opposition.
This is the Dharma. For this reason, the extinction of illusion is called "immovability.

Because of this immovability, one is able to enter the realm of entanglements and extend the hand to teach and transform sentient beings, establishing a water-moon *bodhimaṇḍa* and performing great Buddha-works that are like flowers in the sky.
To subdue the demonic armies within the mirror and realize enlightenment within the dream—this is called the profound cultivation of practice that is like an illusion.
This explains the second objection. According to the meaning of the third objection by Samantabhadra mentioned previously:

"If all sentient beings, upon hearing the teaching that things are like illusions, immediately understand they lack reality and thus fundamentally have no need for cultivation—if this were indeed the case," [then what would become of the Bodhisattva path?]

Thus, within the cycle of birth and death, one constantly dwells amidst illusion and transformation. This is because, without relying on contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one has never understood that the realm of experience is like an illusion;
and without undergoing the cultivation of activities, how can the mind of discursive thought (*vikalpa*) be liberated?

Therefore, the World-Honored One explained this by means of "sons of good family" and so forth. Within this, there is the teaching of the principle (*dharma*) and the clarification through analogy (*upamā*). Regarding the teaching of the principle, it says:
"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those present in this assembly who have generated the pure mind; "sentient beings of the final age" refers to those in the future who will generate the pure mind.
The three phrases beginning with "should remain far removed from" provide a general explanation that clearly indicates one must certainly practice [the teachings].

This is because the intention of Samantabhadra was to fear that sentient beings of the final age, upon hearing it said that all things are like illusions, would immediately conclude they do not exist.

Indeed, why must one practice? Therefore, while it was previously stated that one does not originally practice, the World-Honored One now provides the explanation through such terms as "that which should be abandoned.
The intent is to reveal that all illusory and deceptive objects of perception must be diligently practiced for the purpose of abandoning them.
Since illusory and deceptive objects of perception encompass a vast range of phenomena, the term "all" is employed.
It is said: "Just as with that ignorance, so too are the body and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, and the ordinary and the sagely—all are [included].
Regarding such phenomena, one must certainly practice their distancing. This is because distancing is not easy; it requires firmly maintaining the resolve to distance oneself, refusing to let go.
Alternatively, one may use rational contemplation to suddenly dispel them, like a dream of shackles and fetters, which vanish upon waking.
[One] has already become detached. Alternatively, one gradually dispels [delusions] through the practice of the object, like abandoning an enemy, guarding against transgressions from time to time.
Even if one does not engage in formal cultivation, how could [delusions] otherwise be possible? However, this is merely a provisional method of dispelling illusions by means of the mind;

once those illusions are extinguished, this mind is likewise of no further use. Even if this mind were to persist, it would still be like a cataract in a pure eye, and is itself like an illusion. Therefore, one should...
"Furthermore, one is also removed from [this]. A direct explanation states: this dispels the first layer of the mind that performs the act of distancing.

Next, regarding the statement "one is removed from the illusory," it means that since the preceding section already understood the mind to be like an illusion, one again gives rise to the thought of distancing oneself;
however, if the mind itself does not exist, this further distancing is likewise useless. Should one persist in this further distancing, it would be like a coarse cataract having already been removed.
"Detachment. Even though the subtle film over the eye has been removed, it remains an illusion; therefore, one should likewise remain detached from it. A direct explanation states:
this refers to the detachment that dispels the second layer of detachment from the mind.

Below this, it further says "detaching from the detachment from illusion," meaning that since the previous stage took detachment itself as an illusion, one now gives rise to a further detachment to dispel it and cause it to vanish. If...
Having distanced oneself from what has already been transformed, one then distances oneself from that aforementioned "distancing from distancing. This is like the empty light of pure eyes;
it is also called an illusion, and therefore it too must be distanced. A direct explanation states: this dispels the third layer of "distancing from distancing.
To "attain that which is not to be distanced" means there is nothing further to be dispelled. Since there is nothing to be dispelled, it is as follows:

It is like the true essence of the pure eye; therefore, it says, "one immediately eliminates all illusions. This refers precisely to what is called the "aspect of perfectly illuminating, pure awakening" in the Mañjuśrī Chapter.
Furthermore, following this section, each subsequent stage dispels each preceding one; taken collectively, there are four such stages.
That is to say, first, one uses the illusory mind to dispel illusory objects; hence it says, "far removed from all illusions."

One transforms illusory objects by means of a mind that has distanced itself through firm relinquishment; this is called "correct elimination. Second, one eliminates the illusory mind by means of distancing;
thus it is said, "That which is like an illusion (the illusory mind to be eliminated) is also distanced" (by the distancing mind that eliminates it);
this is called "eliminating the correct. Third, one eliminates distancing by means of distancing; thus it is said:

That which is to be eliminated through distancing is itself distant; that which eliminates it is also distant. This is called "successive distancing," the fourth stage, wherein one distances oneself by means of ultimate distancing.
Therefore, it is said: "one distances oneself from the illusion of distancing. That which is to be eliminated through the distancing of distancing is itself distant;
that which eliminates it—the ultimate distancing—is also distant. This is called "distancing again and again. Beyond this, there is nothing further to be eliminated; it is eternally non-existent.

It is an illusion; therefore, it is said that "one attains that which is nothing to be separated from. This means that one immediately eliminates all illusions. The place where all illusions are exhausted is precisely pure awakening, true suchness (*tathatā*).
As the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states: "All things that can be returned [to their source] are naturally not you. That which cannot be returned to you—were it not you, who would it be?
This is precisely the intended meaning. The *Yuyiming* (Metaphor for Clarifying the Meaning) says: "For example, consider one who drills for fire. If we discuss the character 'drill' (*zuan*):"

Just as one uses iron to drill into gold, or drills wood to seek fire—wherein it is said below that two pieces of wood must depend upon each other, both the drill and the object drilled being made of wood—so too, according to the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), wood can produce fire, yet it must necessarily depend on mutual conditions to do so.
This serves as a metaphor for illusory and false realms; just as ignorance gives rise to body and mind, and from body and mind, [delusions] arise.
Ignorance revolves in cycles without end; therefore, it is illustrated by the metaphor of mutual causation.

The emergence of fire and the exhaustion of the wood illustrate the illusory mind dispelling illusory objects—this is what is meant by "correctly dispelling. As for "the ashes flying away": when the wood is exhausted, it becomes charcoal;

as the charcoal matures, the ashes fly away. Yet the charcoal does not mature instantaneously, and the ashes must necessarily fly away gradually. This serves as a metaphor for the mind being like an illusion.
It is likewise removed. That which removes it is itself illusory; that too is removed.

Even the removal of the illusory removal is likewise removed—this is what is meant by "successive negations" (zhengdie). As for the "extinguishing of smoke," it refers to covering [the coals] with ash as described above;
yet the charcoal was not yet fully processed, and there remained a slight trace of smoke. Now that the ash has already flown away and the charcoal is...
When the fuel is completely consumed and the smoke has already vanished, it serves as a metaphor for attaining that which is beyond separation—namely, the elimination of all illusions.

This means that even the act of dispelling reaches a point where there is nothing further to be dispelled; thus, illusions exist eternally no more. The above constitutes the illustration through analogy; what follows is the application of this to the Dharma.
"To cultivate illusion with illusion" encompasses the preceding four stages; that is, to cultivate each preceding illusion by means of each succeeding illusion.
"Though all illusions are exhausted, one does not enter into annihilation" reveals the true suchness of the awakened mind.
This explains the third inquiry. The explanation of the individual inquiries is complete. △ Third, the response that concludes the request:

"Good son, if you know illusion as it is, you are already detached from it; no further expedient means are required" (extending to) "...in this way, you will be able to forever leave all illusions behind."
If it is as I have explained, then one knows that illusion is itself detachment; no further expedient means need be employed.
Detachment from illusion is itself awakening, and there is no gradual progression. To explain this meaning: once one knows it is an illusion, one simply does not cling to it.
Since non-clinging is itself detachment, it is said that "knowing illusion is itself detachment. This means that it is unnecessary to further employ expedient means in order to detach from illusion.

To be free from illusion is itself awakening; furthermore, there is no gradual process. This means that once one has realized that illusion is itself [emptiness], then in being free from it, there is nothing to be removed, for one has already transcended illusion.
Once one is free from illusion, the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment is luminously manifest and never obscured.
Therefore, it is said that "leaving illusion is itself awakening. What need is there for laborious, gradual cultivation and realization? Hence it is said that "there is no gradual sequence.

Nevertheless, this belongs only to the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) and has not yet involved the practice of phenomena (*shi-xiu*). This is what is meant by: "Principle is realized through sudden enlightenment;

riding upon that enlightenment, all is simultaneously dissolved. Only when one again initiates the cultivation of phenomenal characteristics can one thus forever leave behind all illusions. Regarding this...
This means that phenomena are not eliminated instantaneously, but are exhausted through a gradual process. This concludes the prose section. △ Second, the verse commentary has two parts:
first, the introductory summary; second, the actual verses. First [the introductory summary]:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
From here below are eleven chapters of memorial verses; all may be understood by reference to the chapter on Mañjuśrī. Part Two: The Main Verses, in Three Sections: 1.
Verses answering the general question. 2. Verses explaining the specific inquiries. 3. Verses answering the concluding request. First [Section]: Answering the General Question.
Samantabhadra, you should know that from all sentient beings (up to) empty space, there is fundamentally no movement.
That which is the Perfect Enlightenment Mind is precisely the pure, perfect enlightenment mind. This mind is equally received and uniformly bestowed; ordinary beings and sages are one and the same.
As for what is now called "all Tathāgatas," it is because sentient beings are deluded by it, whereas the Buddhas alone are able to realize it.
This is as stated in the Preface by Prime Minister Pei: "One who is perfect in *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment) all day long yet has never experienced *yuanjue* is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
One who seeks to realize *yuanjue* but has not yet reached its ultimate perfection is a bodhisattva.

One who is fully endowed with *yuanjue* and abides in the maintenance of *yuanjue* is a Tathāgata. The remaining meanings are all explained within the prose commentary. △ Second, the verse explanation.
Another substance.
Illusion arises from various cognitions; when illusion ceases, cognition becomes perfected. (Up to: "When the wood is exhausted, the fire returns to extinction.
These first three lines combine the verse to explain the preceding two substances. "Illusion" refers to the two kinds of ignorance, as well as the body and mind.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which gives rise to the deluded mind. As the Extended Discourse states: "It is the illusory mind of sentient beings.
Body and mind are the delusions produced [by ignorance]. However, since both arise from awakening (*bodhi*), they can simultaneously obstruct awakening.

If one wishes to manifest awakening, one must necessarily employ the present body and mind to advance in the practice of deeds, thereby eliminating the ignorance that gives rise to them. As the Extended Discourse states: [and so forth].
It is precisely because of this illusory extinction that it is so. The verse text is somewhat incomplete; I shall now supplement it according to the meaning of the prose commentary.
This is a brief versified explanation of the first substance based on its meaning. Regarding "illusory extinction and the perfection of awakening":

if that illusory extinction is realized, one further transcends all dualistic oppositions (for to speak of "awakening" based on "illusion," or to speak of "non-existence" based on "existence," both constitute dualistic opposition). Thus, the nature of awakening is perfected.
Because it is perfected, there is no void or gap. Since movement reaches nowhere, it is said that the awakened mind is unmoving.

Because it is unmoving, one is able to enter the marketplace and extend a helping hand to teach and transform sentient beings. This is also a brief verse-explanation of the second substance according to its meaning.
As for those two lines, they explain the "seeing" in the prose: "One should always remain far removed from the illusory."
The prose states: "One should remain far removed from all illusory and false realms. This is because one firmly maintains the mind of detachment.
In this verse, the single character "illusion" (māyā) encompasses all "illusory and false realms" mentioned in the prose.
The three characters "should remain far removed" correspond to the prose's "should remain far removed," while "constantly" (chang) corresponds to the prose's "always" (chang).
The single word "one" (eka) encompasses the prose section because it involves remaining far removed from the mind through firm upholding.

This verse, which summarizes the meaning, dispels illusory objects by means of the illusory mind; this is called "correctly dispelling. The single line, "All illusions are entirely abandoned," completely dispels the meaning of correctness.

(The long prose says: "That which is like an illusion in the mind is also further removed. This is a successive removal. (The long prose says: "To remove is itself an illusion; that too is further removed.

This is to remove again and again. (The long prose says: "To be free from the removal of illusions—that too is further removed. Until there is nothing left to remove, and illusions cease to exist forever. (The long prose says:

"When one attains that which is beyond removal, all illusions are eliminated. These are all brief verses based on the underlying meaning. It is like fire produced within wood: when the wood is exhausted, the fire naturally extinguishes. (The long prose says: "For example...")

It is like drilling for fire: when two pieces of wood are brought together, the fire emerges and their original substance is exhausted; the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished. This is also a brief verse. The meaning of the conjunction is not versified here; this is a brief verse on the meaning of illusion.
This concludes the explanation of the third substance. △ Third, the verse answering the request for a conclusion.
Awakening is likewise without gradual expedients. When one awakens, there is no gradual progression;
this verse summarizes the prose that "to transcend illusion is itself awakening," which is also without gradual stages.
Expedients are likewise thus; this verse follows the prose: "To know illusion is itself detachment; no expedients need be applied. This is the single [verse].

The reason the verses praise sudden enlightenment but do not praise the necessity of gradual cultivation is that this sutra is a sudden teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), thereby demonstrating its primary emphasis. This concludes the Chapter on Samantabhadra.
△ Second, the Chapter on the Universal Eye (Puyan), in three parts: 1. The Universal Eye’s request on behalf of others; 2. The harmonious convergence of teacher and disciple; 3.

The response to the request and the answering of questions. The first [part] has three sections: 1. The assembly’s observance of ritual decorum; 2. The full presentation of the words of inquiry; 3. The manifestation of earnestness up to the third [time].
First: At this point, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Puyan), amidst the great assembly... [omitted] ...kneeling with palms joined, addressed the Buddha.

In this context, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye is the principal figure (as his formal observances and questions are fully detailed), while the rest of the assembly are his companions; therefore, it says "amidst the great assembly."
The meaning of the formal ritual within the assembly may be understood according to what precedes. △ Second, the full presentation of the inquiry:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that for the sake of this assembly... [and] for the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age, you will provisionally explain the skillful means."
The initial exposition has been fully set forth. Because there is an urgent desire to seek the Buddha’s compassion, he is addressed as the "World-Honored One of Great Compassion.
The "bodhisattvas in this assembly" refers to those who have newly begun their studies; the "sentient beings of the final age" refers to those with the initial resolve in the future.

The phrases "may [he] act for them" and "for the sake of them" are used because they are intended to reach these specific capacities. Regarding the "gradual stages of bodhisattva practice," this refers to these very bodhisattvas...

[Sa]. What kind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) should one cultivate? Contemplative practice is difficult to cultivate all at once; when first entering the path, there must necessarily be gradual stages that require urgency.
Therefore, I first request that you let [the audience] know. As for "contemplating" (*cintā*), it means investigating with the mind.

Because sentient beings do not know this, he asks on their behalf: "How does one contemplate? As for "abiding and maintaining" (*dhṛti*), it means not being shifted by external objects; sentient beings are unable to do so.

Therefore, he poses a question on their behalf: "How does one abide and maintain [the Dharma] for those sentient beings who have not yet awakened? For those who have not yet attained great awakening, they must surely seek that great awakening;

thus, he asks on their behalf what skillful means should be employed to cause them all to attain great opening and great awakening. This refers, in essence, to the contemplation of the universal interpenetration and harmonious fusion of all phenomena, wherein every single thing is unimpeded.
"World-Honored One," and so forth, serves to clarify the source of the question through a reductio ad absurdum, lest it be thought that [this teaching was only appropriate for] a specific time...
When the occasion arrives, the principle will manifest of itself; why labor to pose questions in advance?

Therefore, when the one who is "appropriately matched" addresses the World-Honored One, he uses the phrase "if those sentient beings," employing this as a *reductio ad absurdum* (prasaṅga) to clarify the point.

Those "sentient beings" still refer to present-day beginners and those with a new resolve in the future. "Correct means" refers precisely to the gradual stages of cultivation, as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

The first two of the three gradual stages of *Śūraṅgama* are essential; otherwise, there will be no gateway for entering [the path]. Contemplation is like the *Śūraṅgama*, which counters one's current karmic activities;
otherwise, the path of awakening will be difficult to traverse. Although one hears that all things are like illusions, one remains unable to escape stubborn attachment;
hence it is said that "the mind gives rise to confusion and distress. This samādhi is precisely the *yathā-māyā-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi), as stated previously in the chapter on Samantabhadra.
All manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment.
It continues, saying that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.
Because they firmly maintain this mind of distancing, even that which is like an illusion within the mind is also distanced. Distancing itself becomes an illusion; it too—

Furthermore, one distances oneself; one distances oneself from distancing itself as an illusion, and again distances oneself until there is nothing further to distance. This constitutes the elimination of all illusions.
Herein, the final two lines refer to the accomplishment of samādhi. If one lacks the correct means and correct reflection, [this cannot be achieved].

Why is this so? Therefore it is said that the mind gives rise to delusion and distress. "Delusion" refers to being deluded regarding the existence of a self, for one is distracted by the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
"Distress" refers to being distressed regarding the existence of phenomena (*dharma*), for one is obscured by the mark of phenomena.

Because one is distracted by the mark of selfhood and obscured by the mark of phenomena, one is unable to awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). Such being the case, this is the correct means and correct reflection.
Regarding these two questions, their momentum is such that they cannot be left unresolved. ○ From "I pray you will arise" (*yuanxing*) onwards, the passage concludes with a general request:

[the Buddha] bestows the joy of awakening through Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and uproots the suffering of delusion and distress through Great Pity (*mahākaruṇā*); thus, the request is made by means of this aspiration for his arising.

As for the phrase "provisionally teaching expedient means" (*jiashuo fangbian*), it does not refer solely to the gradual [teachings]; rather, it generally encompasses the primary [teachings], the maintenance [of the Dharma], and so forth.
All these are merely skillful means. This is because perfect enlightenment is inherently present and the self and dharmas are fundamentally empty; in truth, they do not depend upon skillful means.

However, as the faculties of those gathered here vary between sharp and dull, and the delusions of those in the末代 (final age) vary between thick and thin, those with sharp faculties and thin delusions will already have stirred at the mere shadow of the whip upon hearing this samādhi, whereas those with dull faculties and thick delusions will give rise to confusion and distress. Not...
Entering Perfect Enlightenment. For this reason, Universal Eye requests [the teaching] by means of provisional designations as skillful expedients.

This is because he seeks from the Buddha that which is established through skillful artifice within the absence of expedients—provisionally instituting the names and phrases of expedients so that those present in the assembly, as well as those of the future age, may have their confusion and distress dispelled and awaken to the entry into the nature of Perfect Enlightenment. Having fully set forth the words of his inquiry, [the section] ends. △ Three. To...
Third, manifesting earnestness:
having spoken these words, he prostrates himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he makes this request three times, beginning again from the end.

This may be understood according to what preceded. The Universal Eye has finished making the request on behalf [of others]. △ Second, the harmonious union of teacher and disciple, in two parts: first, the teacher... with [the disciple].
The Convergence of Provisions. Second, the convergence of the provisions with the Teacher. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
First, he praises the question itself; the repeated praise of "Excellent! is because it benefits both the present and the future.
Among the three types of gradual [teaching], the first two constitute the gradual sequence, while the third constitutes reflection. "Abiding and maintaining" refers to providing assurance.

This is the general characterization of the praise for the question. As for "various skillful means," this is a comprehensive praise that incorporates both the general and the specific, as in the case of the gradual sequence.
Because [the stages of] contemplation and so forth each possess all distinct characteristics. ○ From "You now" onwards, he admonishes the listener and grants permission to speak;
this is precisely the union of the teacher and the disciple. Having completed the union of the teacher and the disciple, △ second, the union of the disciple and the teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.

The explanation of the meaning may be understood by analogy with what preceded. The section on the harmonious conditions between teacher and disciple is concluded. Part Three: Responding to the Request and Answering the Questions, in two sections:

1. Prose Exposition. 2. Verses. The first [of the two prose sections] has two parts: 1. Responding to the request by means of the return to awakening through the exhaustion of delusion. 2. Responding by means of cultivation...

Cultivating practice to further respond to inquiries consists of two parts: first, the awakening that returns to purity through the exhaustion of delusion; second, the awakening that returns to perfection through conformity. The former [the first part] consists of two sections:
first, responding to the request concerning the gradual stages of cultivation; second, responding to the request concerning contemplation and maintenance. The first [of these two]: [End of excerpt]
"Good son, that newly initiated bodhisattva (up to) settles his assembly and sits in quietude within a still chamber.
First, in response to the request for practice, he addresses the newly initiated bodhisattvas; 'newly initiated beings of the final age' refers to those of future initial resolve.
Since both of these are newly initiated and of initial resolve, it is said: 'desiring to seek the purity of the Tathāgata.'"
The Perfectly Awakened Mind (Vimalakīrti-nirbhāsa-citta) is the dharma for the original stage of the Tathāgata’s causal ground;

by means of a straightforward mind and right mindfulness of True Suchness (tathatā), one is able to distance oneself from all illusions. If one seeks the pure, perfectly awakened mind, there is nothing other than this.

Therefore, it is necessary to admonish [the practitioner] accordingly. "First, relying on the following... and so forth, answers the request regarding the gradual stages. To travel a long distance, one begins from what is near; to ascend a height, one starts from the base.
O base one, if you wish to seek the pure, perfect, awakened mind (*vimala-pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*), you must likewise have that upon which you first rely:
*śamatha*, here translated as "stopping" (*zhi*). This means stopping all improper actions and all improper mental movements.

The "removal of its auxiliary causes" in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is also subsumed within this. For the Buddha, while on the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), also first relied upon this; therefore, it is said: "As..."
Regarding the practice of śamatha, as for the prohibitions of the precepts, they are categorized and analyzed in such detail that their many varieties cannot be fully exhausted.
If one summarizes those most strictly forbidden, there are ten major categories and four minor ones; the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* extracts their essential nature.
This is also included herein. To "uphold" [the precepts] while being called "firm" means that one cherishes them like a life-preserving float, allowing not even a hair’s breadth of transgression.

As for "retinue," it refers to fellow practitioners who follow one's teachings; to ensure they lack nothing in the four requisites and have no cause for resentment or seeking is called "settling them in peace.
"Settling" (*chu*) is synonymous with "dwelling" (*zhu*). Even if one does not settle others in peace, one cannot avoid [distraction] during one's own time of meditative contemplation.
Because there is that which disturbs. To sit in tranquility (*kṣema*) means to sit in peaceful composure;
that is to say, the body, along with the hands and feet, remains still, at ease, and unmoving. The mind is always serene and calm, never becoming distracted.

Although this is due to dwelling peacefully among a community and being undisturbed by external things, it is fundamentally because one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), remaining unshaken within.
This is merely an exposition based on the principle that concentration arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*), serving as a gateway for entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).
As for "a quiet room": it is a pure and clean chamber. Viewed from below, it is the hall of observation; viewed from above, it is the place for seated meditation (*dhyāna*).

Because it is free from the odors of meat and pungent spices and is secluded from the clamor of the marketplace, it is called "quiet. This concludes the response to the request concerning the gradual stages of practice. △ Second, the response.

Regarding the two aspects of dwelling in contemplation and maintaining [the practice]: first, correct contemplation; second, correct maintenance. The first [section] has two parts: first, contemplating that the body is an illusion;
second, contemplating that the mind is an illusion. The first [of these]:
One constantly maintains this thought: "This body of mine, [up to] being a composite phenomenon, is truly identical to a magical illusion.
The Great Commentary states: "Constantly maintaining this thought" means that during walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—at all times—one always contemplates in this way.
Regarding "this body of mine": because it is firmly grasped and maintained, one contemplates it first. It is a composite of the four great elements.

These—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—combine provisionally to form the body. The fool says this; yet, while this is a general observation, one must then observe the hair, body hair, and so forth in their specific order.
Hair is also a type of body hair, but only that which grows on the head is called "hair";

all the rest are collectively termed "body hair. As for nails, they are the keratinous plates of the fingers. As for teeth, they are the counterparts to the tusks; observing the teeth already includes the tusks. As for skin:
The exterior of the flesh is also the skin that envelops the flesh; the flesh is the lining of the skin, and the skin is the covering of the flesh.
The sinews are the strength of the flesh; the bones are the core of the flesh, and they also support the flesh.
The marrow is the fat within the bones; the brain is the marrow within the crown of the head. Filth is the body’s grime and oiliness; complexion is the body’s color.
All of these possess form and substance; therefore, it is said that they all "return to earth. Here, "return" (*gui*) means to belong to or be subsumed under.
This refers to their conceptual affiliation with the earth element, not to the physical return to earth after death. Saliva is oral fluid; that which drips from the mouth is called saliva.
Mucus is likewise a type of fluid; that which issues from the nose is mucus. Pus, blood, and flesh are the products of decomposition. [This applies to] the entire body.

That which flows and moistens is called blood (*śoṇita*). The essence of blood that circulates internally is called *ting* (chyle); that which exudes externally is called *ye* (fluid). Saliva and froth are both pathological conditions of spittle (*kheṭa*).
That which is viscous, fine, continuous, and dripping is called *xian* (salivary secretion); that which accumulates floating at the corners of the mouth is called *mo* (froth).

That which is expelled from the throat due to coughing is called phlegm (*śleṣman*). That which flows from the eyes due to weeping is called tears (*aśru*). Vital essence (*ojas*) resides in the kidneys (*vṛkkā*).
The essence is powerful. Regarding the feces, one does not take the dregs; they are taken together with the urine, taking only their clarity.

These [substances] above all possess moisture and lubricity; therefore, it is said that they all return to water. As for "warmth," it refers to the warm quality and harmonious energy throughout the entire body.
"Returning to fire" means that [the element] originally comes from the fire-mahābhūta. "Moving and turning" refers to the movement and rotation of the entire body.
"Returning to wind" means that it originally comes from the wind-mahābhūta. "Returning to earth" and "returning to water" can be understood by analogy with this.
As in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the eight returns, all return to their place of origin; likewise, the four returns in the present sutra also return to their place of origin. However...

The former [passage] uses the individual return [of the elements] to manifest the existence of nature, whereas this [passage] uses the individual dissolution [of the elements] to manifest the absence of a body. Therefore, what follows immediately states:
"When the four great elements have each departed, where would this delusory body be? Furthermore, the Great Commentary (*Dà shù*) says:

"Regarding the statement that the four great elements all 'return,' it is because this body was originally formed by the combination of the four great elements. As the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (*Bǎo jī jīng*) states: "When this body is born..."
Of the same nature as the four great elements of their parents, they possess a body of a single type of *kalala*.
If there were only the earth element and no water element, it would be like a person grasping dry flour or ash; it would never cohere.
If there were only the water element and no earth element, it would be like oil or water, which lack solidity and immediately flow away and disperse. If there were only earth and water...
Regarding the absence of the fire element: for example, in the summer months, a mass of flesh in a shaded place will rot and decay if it is not exposed to the light of the sun.
If there were only the elements of earth, water, and fire, but no wind element, then growth would not occur. As for the separation of the four great elements from one another:
At the time of correct contemplation, each has its own point of return; this is precisely what is called "detachment. The fool says: "If there is detachment, then there is no body.
Therefore, the World-Honored One used provisional language to investigate: "Where, then, would this delusory body be? This truly reveals that it has no location.
Since even a location does not exist, how can one speak of a substance? Thus it is said: "One knows that this body ultimately has no substance," for it is a composite.

As for "the four great elements combine to form appearances": these are illusory and false, yet they are called appearances; yet appearances are themselves non-appearance. Therefore it is said that they are truly identical to magical transformations.
The contemplation that the body is an illusion is complete. II. Contemplating that the mind is an illusion.
The six sense organs exist falsely through the provisional combination of four conditions; (up to: ultimately, no mind that takes objects as its condition can be perceived.
Having understood from the preceding [text] that the body is a phantom transformation, one may ask: how can there still be sense organs, objects, and the consciousness-mind?

Therefore, it is said: "through the provisional combination of four conditions" (and so forth). As for the "four conditions," they are seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, because all four natures are present.
Because they are capable of perceiving objects, they are "provisionally combined. This provisional combination refers to the body. Regarding the false existence of the six sense organs:

seeing is the eye organ; hearing is the ear organ; and sensing—wherein all three [organs] function through contact—is collectively termed the nose, tongue, and body organs (the latter three are all known through contact, and are thus generally called "sensing").
Knowing is the mind organ. These are the six organs that existed previously. As for the four great elements of the six organs: because the six organs exist, they further face outward...
The four great elements within are such that the four internal natures can be divided into the six sense organs;

likewise, the four external great elements can be divided into the six sense objects (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena). Thus there are these six sense objects. That which is "middle" is the internal.
When the internal and external combine, it refers to the internal organs and external objects combining to form the twelve bases (*āyatana*). These falsely possess the breath of conditions.

"Those conditions" refers to the breath-energy (*vāyu*) which is precisely the six consciousnesses (for although the six consciousnesses are delusory, they nonetheless possess the functional energy of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing).
"Accumulated therein" means that within the internal sense-faculties and external objects, [the seeds] accumulate and do not disperse; subsequently, the six consciousnesses arise.

"Appearing to have the aspect of conditions" means appearing to have the aspect of an active perceiver. "Provisionally named 'mind'" means that because it appears to exist, it is not [ultimately real].

True. It is for the reason stated above—namely, that there is "delusory existence" through the influence of conditions—that although the three factors of sense organ, object, and consciousness equally belong to delusory existence, it is specifically the power of the six consciousnesses that gives rise to afflictions and creates karma.
Because they are so forceful, [the Buddha] urgently wishes to lead them to contemplate the emptiness and falsity of these consciousnesses;
thus, he repeatedly addresses them as "good sons" to inform them and cause them to pay close attention. This is the false and delusory mind.

This refers to the consciousness of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which appears as if manifest by relying upon sensory objects. Therefore, it is said that if the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) do not exist, [consciousness] cannot exist.

Furthermore, those external six sense objects are themselves a provisional combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). If the four great elements were to disintegrate, no sense object could be found.
Based on this, among the faculties, objects, and consciousness, [one must examine] the faculty that acts as the perceiver and the... [object that is perceived].

Dust particles each return to their dispersion and extinction. (Because when dust is no longer perceived as an object, the sense faculties have nothing with which to pair; since both are equally dispersed and extinguished,) the internal and external are not established.
How, then, could a middle be posited? Therefore it is said: "Ultimately, there is no perceiving mind to be found. "Ultimately" (*atyanta*) means definitively. As the proverb says:
It is indeed so that they ultimately do not exist. In the Mañjuśrī Chapter, the Buddha explains the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) as follows:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions (referring to the two attachments to self and phenomena, each of which has both discriminative and innate forms, all of which are termed 'inversions').

They falsely recognize the four great elements as their own physical body and the reflected images conditioned by the six sense objects as their own mind. Now, since one contemplates the body as being like an illusion..."
Contemplate the mind as being like an illusion. From this point on, one no longer falsely identifies with it; delusions diminish day by day, while right view increases daily.
This concludes the section on Right Contemplation. II. Right Abiding has four parts: 1. The direct explanation; 2. Clarification through analogy.

Three points for the synthesis; four points for the concluding demonstration. First (although it is said that "knowing illusion is itself awakening," there is still apprehension that one may be unable to maintain this realization; therefore, the correct teaching is given first—this refers to the meaning of correctly teaching the principle of maintenance).
"Good son, as for those sentient beings... because illusion is extinguished through extinction, that which is not illusion does not cease.

"Good son" is a term used to address the bodhisattva who is the appropriate recipient of the teaching. "Those sentient beings" refers to those individuals seeking the pure *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) *bodhi* (enlightenment).
To seek the pure *pariniṣpanna* *bodhi*, one must first contemplate the body as being like an illusion. As for this "illusion-like..."
When the objective field can maintain [the body], the illusory body naturally ceases. Because the illusory body has ceased, that which was able to maintain it—the illusory mind—also ceases.
This is because the mind relies upon the body; when the body ceases, the mind has nothing upon which to rely. Because the illusory mind has ceased...
If one is able to maintain [the mind], then illusory objects will also cease. Since objects manifest by relying upon the mind, when the mind ceases, the objects have nothing to rely upon;
thus, because illusory objects cease, that which is able to maintain them—the illusory cessation—also ceases, for it was for the sake of ceasing the objects.
The name "extinction of illusion" is established because once the objects have already ceased, the extinction of illusion has no further function.

Since the extinction of illusion itself ceases, that which can maintain [the state]—namely, these dharmas—is entirely true; therefore, it is called "non-illusion. Because non-illusion is in essence without end or limit, it does not cease.
The formal explanation is concluded. II. Clarification by Analogy.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, its brilliance appears.

In seeking the pure, perfect *bodhi*, one encounters the illusory body, the illusory mind, illusory objects, and illusory cessation—all these layers of obscuration are not the pure, perfect *bodhi*-mind;
they are all like the grime upon a mirror. When the body ceases and the mind ceases...
Dust is extinguished; even the extinction of illusion is extinguished. It is like the tarnish on a mirror being polished away until it is gone;

that which is not illusory does not cease. This is precisely the pure, perfect *bodhicitta*. It is like the original luminosity of the mirror, wherein the whole body [of reality] appears simultaneously.

Based on this, although the illustrative text is brief, its encompassing meaning leaves nothing out. One will know this for oneself by carefully examining the formal exposition. The explanation of the metaphors is concluded. △ Three.
This is the Dharma-consistency.
Good son, you should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements; when the characteristics of these defilements are forever extinguished, the ten directions are pure.
Fearing that he might lose his way upon hearing this extensive teaching, [the Buddha] again calls out "Good son" and instructs him that he must understand this. He does not comprehend the body...
The mind is like an illusion. Grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena obscures the pure and perfect *bodhicitta*. Therefore, it is said that all are illusory defilements.

It must reach the point where the body ceases and the mind ceases, even to the point where the marks of defilement are forever extinguished—this is called the extinction of dust; the extinction itself is also extinguished.
In this way, every phenomenon is truly real; therefore, it is said that the ten directions are pure. This is why it was stated above that "that which is not illusion does not perish.

These points accord with the underlying meaning. Do not be overly rigid or dogmatic in your adherence. The application of the phenomena is concluded. △ Fourth, the summary and demonstration has two parts.
First, it is concluded that attachment to causes constitutes defilement; second, it is concluded that when defilement is exhausted, one returns to purity. Regarding the first:
"Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel... (omitted)... because of this, one cannot remain far removed from illusions."
First, an analogy is presented for illustration. A pure maṇi-jewel is that which exists within the topknot of a nāga-king.
"Pure" refers to its substance, as it is transparent both inside and out and free from defilement. "Maṇi" refers to its function;
translated here as "wishing-fulfilling," it is so called because it can rain down jewels. "Jewel" refers to its characteristic, as it is not an ordinary object but a treasure among jewels. Well—
"A friend enters the sea" refers to that which is taken to save the world. "Reflecting in the five colors": "reflecting" means appearing as a reflection;

it means that in response to the five external colors, they appear as reflections within. This is a metaphor for the pure, perfect *bodhicitta* (awakened mind), which, in response to the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of sentient beings' external bodies and minds, appears as a reflection within the mind, manifesting distinctly according to each direction. As for "in whichever direction there are [colors]," which direction has the five?

Regarding form: in whatever direction the five colors appear as reflections, it serves as a metaphor for how the five aggregates (skandhas) of body and mind manifest within various classes of sentient beings;
that is, according to whichever class one belongs to, one manifests one's own five aggregates of body and mind, just as a reflection resembles its original shape.
Ordinary people of the world who do not recognize these as reflections are called "deluded"; this serves as a metaphor for all sentient beings who do not realize they are like illusions.
They are called "ordinary and small" because ordinary people are deluded regarding the self and followers of the Small Vehicle are deluded regarding phenomena; they are equally ignorant.
A reflection is fundamentally without reality, yet because worldly people do not know it is a reflection, they see the mani-jewel as truly possessing five colors.

This is a metaphor for how illusion is fundamentally not real, yet because ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners do not know it is an illusion, they consequently cling to the notion that Perfect Enlightenment truly possesses the five aggregates (skandhas). Thus they cling.

My adherence to the Dharma is precisely its characteristic. "Good sons" and below: this correlates the Dharma with the analogy. The pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment corresponds to the pure *maṇi* jewel;

its manifestation within body and mind corresponds to its reflection in the five colors; its responding to each type of being corresponds to its appearing in various directions according to the location.
For those who are ignorant, the text of the Dharma and the analogy are identical; the meaning lies in the delusive shadows and illusory transformations.

It is also somewhat similar. Therefore, both are designated by the name "delusion. When explaining the pure *Vimalakīrti* and the perfect *Awakening of Faith*, they truly possess body and mind which combine with their own characteristics;
when seeing that mani-jewel, it truly possesses five colors. The meaning of the dharma is identical to the meaning of the analogy; therefore, it is said, "it is also like this.
By means of this phrase, the manifestation of defilement is concluded. "By means of this" refers to taking up the preceding [notion] of grasping [the jewel] as real.
