To "assert existence" means that by clinging to this [view], one regards body and mind as truly existent. Within this state, people contend with one another over the self, calculating right and wrong;

thus, they are unable to distance themselves from illusionary transformations. Being unable to distance themselves, they naturally remain perpetually within them, giving rise to delusions and creating karma.
Through the creation of karma and the experiencing of its retribution, they cycle back and forth, defiling the pure and perfect *bodhi*.
The mind becomes deeply defiled. This concludes the demonstration that the grasping of causes results in defilement. II. Conclusion demonstrating the return to purity when defilement is exhausted:
"Therefore, I say that the body and mind are illusory defilements" (up to) "...there is then no opposing defilement, nor even one who speaks of it."
"Regarding 'therefore': this refers back to the inability to remain detached. This inability to remain detached arises from ignorance.
For this reason, I say that body and mind are illusory and defiled. By saying they are illusory, I intend to make it known that they are not real and should therefore be abandoned.
By saying they are defiled, I intend to make it known that they pollute pure awakening and should therefore be countered."

Because it serves as an antidote: if those sentient beings, upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, are able to apply the antidote to their defilements and distance themselves from illusions, this constitutes the "antidote for and departure from illusory defilement. Such sentient beings are not ordinary; the Buddha says of such people: [they are extraordinary].

They are called Bodhisattvas because they are able to sever delusions according to their capacity, realize the truth according to their capacity, and establish their stages according to their capacity.
As for "the exhaustion of defilements": they do not settle for minor attainments; they must proceed until even the subtlest defilements are exhausted.
Once the subtle defilements are exhausted, there is no need for further antidotes; therefore, it is called "removal. This is as described above regarding the extinction of illusory objects.
Therefore, it is said that when illusion ceases, that which is extinguished is also extinguished. This means there is no one who opposes defilement;

that is to say, since defilements have already been exhausted and opposition has been eliminated, there is no person who opposes defilement. Since even the "person" does not exist, where could the name "Bodhisattva" be established?
Thus, the phrase "and as for the designation" clarifies that even the name of a Bodhisattva does not exist; there is only pure awakening and reality.
The Mind: As stated above, it is because that which is illusory is extinguished through extinction; that which is not illusory is not extinguished.

Up to this point, it is entirely identical to the meaning of the "Contemplation of True Emptiness Beyond All Characteristics" established by Master Shunzu. This concludes the section on the awakening to the restoration of purity through the exhaustion of delusion.
Part Two: Following and Returning to Perfect Enlightenment. This has two sections: First, the mutual integration of principle and phenomena; Second, the unimpeded inclusion [of all things].
The first two [sections]. First, following up on what preceded to initiate what follows; second, the formal elucidation of principle and phenomena. Regarding the first:
"Good son, this Bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the final age... [up to] ...the boundless empty space manifested by awakening."
These Bodhisattvas, as well as sentient beings of the final age, all refer to those who seek pure, perfect enlightenment.

Regarding the phrase "having realized that all illusions are extinguished as images": because all phenomena fundamentally belong to illusory existence and are originally but images within the pure mind, sentient beings simply do not know this;
even if they did know it, they would be unable to abide therein. Now, by means of right abiding and maintenance...
Therefore, it is attained once and for all; one never again becomes swayed by images. Thus it is said, "realization," and so forth.
"At that time" refers to the very moment of realizing all illusions. Once the images have ceased, pure awakening is fully revealed.
Therefore, it is said that one immediately attains "directionless purity. "Directionless" (wúfāng) carries the meaning of being all-pervasive.

For example, to say that this direction is pure while that direction is impure is called "having directions," which implies a lack of pervasiveness. Thus, we know that "directionless" means being omnipresent.

This is precisely the Pervasive Purity (*viśuddha-vyāpin*). Regarding infinite space: previously, due to the illusory defilements of ignorance, true awakening was obscured and it became a state of inert emptiness.
Now, having realized the extinction of illusion and removed the hindrances, the nature of awakening is manifested;
thus, infinite space is revealed by awakening and becomes the boundless pure nature. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When one person..."
This is what is meant by "truly returning to the source," whereby the empty space of the ten directions is entirely dissolved and extinguished.

What is called "purity without direction" can now be seen. This concludes the section on "taking up what precedes to initiate what follows. **Part Two: Correctly Clarifying Principle and Phenomena (Two Subdivisions)** (1) Establishing Phenomena Based on Principle;

(2) Harmonizing Phenomena with Principle. Regarding "establishing phenomena based on principle": phenomena do not exist as phenomena in themselves; they are established based on principle. Since principle is pure and clear, [phenomena are likewise so].
Thus, the phenomena that constitute the accomplished reality each become pure in accordance with their underlying principle. To clarify this further, let us employ an analogy:
it is like the sunlight, which shines universally upon the void and the worlds; there is no category of thing whatsoever that does not depend on the sun’s radiance for its existence.
Yet, suddenly, it may be obscured by dust and sand, or shrouded in the gloom of clouds and mist.
The sunlight did not appear; all things within that world of empty space were entirely shrouded in darkness, unable to manifest in their purity.

In an instant, the clouds parted and the mist dispersed; the dust subsided and the sands became clear, and the sunlight shone forth with brilliant clarity, illuminating the entire world of empty space so that all things therein were fully revealed.
All appear as pure, analogous to that enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*), which is luminous and clearly aware, perfectly illuminating the *dharmadhātu*.

All phenomena, mundane and supramundane, are established because of it. Yet, when suddenly a single thought moves in delusion, the three subtleties and six coarsenesses arise in succession, and the luminous, clear enlightened nature becomes entirely obscured. Within this *dharmadhātu*, all...
There are mundane and supramundane phenomena that all become obscured and deluded, failing to manifest clearly; they must return to their original purity.
Now, because the Bodhisattva realizes all illusions and extinguishes their reflected images, at that moment they attain directionless purity and boundless space manifested by awakening.
If even empty space is thus, how much more so are all mundane and supramundane phenomena contained within that space?

All phenomena (*dharma*) are manifested by the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) and thereby become pure. The comparison between the phenomena and their metaphors is clearly understood. This is divided into two parts: first, the formation of worldly phenomena;
second, the formation of supramundane phenomena. The first part has two sections: first, a detailed explanation; second, a summary. The first of these has three sections:

first, the formation of the sense bases (*āyatana*); second, the formation of the objective fields (*viṣaya*); third, the formation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). The first [section]: [The text continues with the specific details of the formation of the sense bases.]
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, it reveals the purity of the mind (up to: the nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this).
Building upon the preceding point that even boundless empty space is manifested by awakening, it can be known that the awakened mind is perfect, bright, and pure.
Precisely because it is perfect, bright, and pure, there is no phenomenon that is not revealed. Because there is no phenomenon that is not [revealed]...
When it is manifested, it reveals that the ālayavijñāna-citta, which is formed according to conditions, also becomes pure in nature.
Because the ālayavijñāna-citta is pure, the nature of the perceived objects (viṣaya) distinguished by the ālaya—namely, the nature of seeing (the seeing-nature)—also becomes pure in nature.
Because the seeing-nature is pure, the eye-faculty (indriya) upon which the seeing-nature depends—namely, the two faculties of the fleshly and the subtle—is likewise [pure].
It also achieves the nature of purity. Because the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is pure, the consciousness produced by the eye also achieves the nature of purity.

(This refers to the two elements belonging to the eye, namely the faculty and the consciousness. Although the text mentions "seeing objects" [viṣaya], it does so only in terms of the nature of seeing; as for the element of the object itself, it will be discussed later.
Next, because the consciousness produced by the eye is pure, the nature of the sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*) apportioned by the *ālaya-vijñāna* [also becomes pure].
The nature of hearing also becomes pure. Because the nature of hearing is pure, the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), which is the basis of hearing, also becomes pure in nature.

Because the ear-faculty is pure, the consciousness (*vijñāna*) produced by the ear also becomes pure in nature (this includes the two spheres [dhātu] pertaining to the ear, while the sphere of the object is not included; this may be understood by analogy with what precedes). Furthermore, because the consciousness produced by the ear is pure...

Therefore, the nature of the consciousness that perceives objects, which is differentiated from the ālayavijñāna (i.e., these three natures— since the nose, tongue, and body are all termed "perception"—

also becomes the pure nature). "In this manner, up to and including" means that by omitting the two realms of the nose family, the two realms of the tongue family, and the two realms of the body family,
even the nature of the consciousness that knows objects within the mind family, as well as both the sense organs and their cognitions, all become [pure].
Because their nature is pure, it is said: "it is also thus. This concludes the section on the formation of the sense organs (*indriya*). II. The Formation of the Sense Objects (*viṣaya*).
"Good son, because the sense organs are pure, the sense object of form (*rūpa*) is pure" [up to] "the sense objects of odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are also thus."
Having heard the Dharma for a long time, there is a fear that they may fail to remain attentive; therefore, he again calls out "Good Sons" to admonish them.

Since the six natures and the six consciousnesses all rely upon the faculties (indriyas), he speaks of them collectively as being "pure because the faculties are pure. This refers to the midst of the six faculties.
Each sense faculty, together with its inherent nature and consciousness, all become the nature of purity.
For this reason, even the objects of form encountered by the eye faculty become the nature of purity.

Because the objects of form are pure, the objects of sound encountered by the ear faculty also become the nature of purity. Fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena likewise become pure in succession.
Because their nature is pure, it is said, "it is also thus. This concludes the section on the formation of the sense objects (*viṣaya*). III. The Formation of the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*).
"Good son, because the six sense objects are pure... (up to) "...the fire element and the wind element are also thus."
Regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*): they are the distinct characteristics that confront the sense organs.

Since each one individually constitutes the nature of purity, the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), which is formed by the storehouse nature (*ālaya-svabhāva*) following conditions (*pratyaya*) as something solid and obstructive, also constitutes the nature of purity.

Because the earth element is pure, the water element (*ab-dhātu*), characterized by moisture and wetness, also constitutes the nature of purity. As for the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*)—which possesses the nature of dryness and heat—and the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*)...
Great. (Possessing the nature of movement,) they successively all become the nature of purity; therefore it is said, "it is likewise so.
The detailed explanation is concluded. △ Second, the summary.
Good son, because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are pure, the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), and the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) are pure.

Regarding the purity of the four great elements: as established above, because earth, water, fire, and wind each achieve purity, the phenomena such as the twelve bases that are formed according to conditions likewise each achieve the nature of purity. The twelve bases...

This refers to the aforementioned internal sense bases (*āyatana*) and external object bases. Taking the sense organs as the subjective bases of cognition (*ālambaka-āyatana*) and the objects as the objective bases of cognition (*ālambana-āyatana*), the internal and external are strictly distinguished and must remain fixed without confusion. As for the eighteen elements (*dhātu*):

there are six types each of the internal sense-element (*indriya-dhātu*), the external object-element (*viṣaya-dhātu*), and the intermediate consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which together constitute the eighteen.

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*): the term "nature" (*prakṛti*) has two meanings. As for nature, the faculties are the nature that illuminates, the objects are the nature that is illuminated, and consciousness is the nature of discrimination.
As for the "divisions," there are internal, external, and intermediate divisions, each with its own distinct boundaries, because they can be clearly discerned.
The twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are that upon which sentient beings of the three realms rely and dwell. An ancient master’s verse says:

"The four continents and the four evil destinies, The six heavens of desire together with the Brahma heavens, The four dhyānas and the four formless realms, The realm of non-perception and the *anāgāmin*— These are collectively termed 'existence' (*bhava*), Because within them the causes and effects of birth and death cannot be absent. These three [categories] thus encompass [all of them].
This exhausts all worldly dharmas. Yet, both the sutras and śāstras refer to the four great elements as "seeds" (*bīja*), because they are able to produce all phenomena.
Little do they realize that the capacity to produce these phenomena does not reside in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), but rather in their nature (*dhātu*). Now, this is finally revealed:

[all things] manifest based upon that pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). However, since that which can manifest Perfect Enlightenment is itself without spatial direction (*amūrtatva*), [the nature of the elements is likewise beyond form].
When purified, the dharmas within the manifested spheres (āyatana-dhātu) each and every one become the nature of purity. (Question:

According to the preceding [analysis], the six sense organs and six sense objects all arise in dependence upon the progressively purer natures, manifesting as the subsequent stages. Now, why do the twelve spheres and eighteen elements arise in dependence upon the purity of the four great elements?

Furthermore, are these twelve spheres not simply the aforementioned spheres of the organs and the spheres of the objects? And are these eighteen elements not simply the aforementioned spheres of the objects, the spheres of the organs, and the consciousness-elements contained within those organs? If you say they are not...)

How should this be distinguished? Although the sections are divided into general and specific categories, the general encompasses the specific, and the specific differentiates the general. How can it be said that this is not so? If one says it is so, why is it that previously the four great elements (mahābhūta) arose in accordance with conditions based on the sense organs, their locations, and their objects, whereas now the four great elements and their pure nature arise in accordance with conditions as the locations, realms, and so forth? This appears chaotic and lacks a basis; how can these be reconciled? Answer: Since all phenomena each possess their own pure nature, [the distinctions are established]. When the pure nature of the sense organs is taken as the primary condition, the four great elements arise accordingly. When the pure nature of the four great elements is taken as the primary condition, the locations, realms, and so forth arise accordingly. Thus, there is no contradiction. It is simply that when the pure nature of the sense organs is emphasized, the four great elements manifest; when the pure nature of the four great elements is emphasized, the locations, realms, and so forth manifest. Therefore, they are not confused. This is because all phenomena are fundamentally identical in their pure nature, yet they manifest differently according to the specific conditions encountered. This is called "differentiation. It is not that there is a fixed, separate entity called "differentiation" apart from the phenomena themselves. Because the pure nature of all phenomena is identical, they are "general"; because they manifest differently according to conditions, they are "specific. This is the meaning of the distinction between the general and the specific. There is no need for further deliberation. If one understands this principle, one will see that the various teachings are mutually inclusive and harmonious. At that time, although one possesses diligence (*vīrya*), there may still be intervals; now, having cultivated the exertion within the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), progress is indeed uninterrupted.

Therefore, it is called a faculty (*indriya*; the meaning of "faculty" is as explained above). Third is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*): this means that when cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one is able to bind the mind to its object;
yet, there may still be four distinct objects. Now, having cultivated the desire (*chanda*) within the bases of psychic power, one’s aspiration for bodhicitta is fierce and sharp.

Joyful desire and mindfulness follow their respective origins; therefore, they are called faculties (*indriya*). (The meaning of "faculty" below is as explained above. The fourth is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*):
when practicing the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there is already an element of concentration (as mindfulness has a point of rest), yet it remains relatively slight.

Now, having practiced the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) with the mind focused on a single object, it is therefore called a faculty. The fifth is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*): when practicing the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

This is precisely what constitutes the illumination of wisdom (discerning between good and evil). Now, having cultivated the wisdom within the supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), one uses correct contemplation to destroy Māra;

therefore, it is called a "faculty" (*indriya*). Furthermore, by means of these five, the bodhicitta can be firmly established, just as when a single tree has been planted and its five roots have already emerged.
As for the five powers (*bala*): first is the power of faith, which is the aforementioned faculty of faith, further increased and advanced. The power of mindfulness... [and so forth].
Concentration and wisdom should be understood by analogy with a tree. Once the roots have taken hold, it possesses the power to produce branches and sprout leaves;

thus, the future blossoming of flowers and ripening of fruit can also be anticipated. Regarding the "sevens and eights": these refer to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

As for the seven factors of enlightenment, the first is the factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*). This is the basis upon which the following six depend; that is to say, if the mind becomes sunken...

At that time, one should employ mindfulness, investigation, effort, and joy to arouse it. When the mind is floating, one should employ tranquility, concentration, and equanimity to collect it. (One awakens so that concentration and wisdom are balanced. 2. The awakening factor of investigation (*dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):

When contemplating all phenomena, one is able to discern them well, because one does not erroneously grasp at deceptive phenomena. 3. The awakening factor of effort (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*): When practicing the path of the Dharma, one is able to discern it well, because one does not erroneously engage in useless asceticism. 4. The awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*):

Having attained the joy of the Dharma in the mind, one is able to discern it well, because one does not follow that joy of the Dharma by giving rise to attachment. 5. The awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): [Body and speech...]

The enlightenment factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): skillfully awakening with clear comprehension, because one does not fail to progress by grasping at pliancy. (6) The enlightenment factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): giving rise to all samādhis, skillfully awakening with clear comprehension, because one does not give rise to craving or views. The enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*):

relinquishing the focal object, skillfully awakening with clear comprehension, because one does not give rise to recollection [of past objects]. These are also called the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*). *Bodhi* translates as "awakening" (*jue*); *aṅga* means "factor" (*fen*).

Now, awakening belongs to the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and it is only at the stage of Buddhahood that this fruition is perfected; yet, since they are all currently termed "awakening," [they are so named].
The term "branch" (*aṅga*) clearly indicates that it is not yet complete. Although it is not yet complete, its constituent parts already exist;

however, by practicing this with earnest application, the transformation of afflictions (*kleśa*) into awakening (*bodhi*) will surely be nothing other than this. As for the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*):
first is Right View (because one perceives the principle truly); second is Right Intention (because one intends toward true cultivation); third is Right... [text truncated]

4. Right Speech (speaking the words of the True Dharma so as to inspire genuine faith in others); 5. Right Action (being fully endowed with right conduct by eliminating unwholesome physical actions); 6. Right Livelihood.

(Alms-seeking in accordance with the Dharma, because it is free from the five forms of wrong livelihood) is the sixth, Right Effort. (Because it purifies the fetters of affliction) is the seventh, Right Mindfulness.
(Because it does not forget the unconditioned path) is the eighth, Right Concentration. These are also called the eight factors of the Noble Path.

However, the Noble Path itself is the fruit of cessation; it is also the perfection of the Buddha-fruit. Since these are now all termed "factors of the path," one should practice according to these factors, and thereby generate [the fruit].
To die and realize *nirvāṇa* can hardly be anything other than this. *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*).
This means that it summarizes all phenomena (*dharma*) and retains immeasurable meanings. Because it can summarize all phenomena and retain immeasurable meanings, the term "gate" (*mukha*) is added;
this signifies that all phenomena are born from this, and all meanings find their ultimate convergence herein.
It is said that there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. Regarding this, the ancient masters have two explanations:

first, the "with-syllable" (you-zi), and second, the "without-syllable" (wu-zi). As for the "without-syllable," it is like the Buddha’s response to Mañjuśrī, where he opened his mouth and immediately said:
"The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* called Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), from which all things flow forth."
Pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, as well as the *pāramitās* and so forth—these encompass all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
They bear names that hold immeasurable meanings, and thus one may see their general outline here. As for those with syllables, they are the secret teachings spoken by the Tathāgata;
whether consisting of a single syllable, few syllables, or many syllables, they are all termed *dhāraṇīs*. Now, since they are so called...
It is secret; it admits of no further explanation. Yet, by bringing the three karmas into accord and reciting according to the Dharma, all that is sought shall be fulfilled.
This sufficiently demonstrates that it encompasses all dharmas and sustains immeasurable meanings.
However, this dharma and its meaning can only be known by the Buddha; others are unable to do so. Therefore, it is collectively designated as "secret. If this is so, then [the single]...
It is sufficient; why must it necessarily be eighty-four thousand? The Great Commentary states: "The Dharma gates, when explained extensively, are immeasurable and boundless.
That they are now summarized by this specific number is for the sake of corresponding to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Its meaning is that because the dust-like afflictions and delusions of sentient beings number eighty-four thousand, the Buddha spoke of them in response to these; hence, he says 'eighty-four thousand. One must understand this."

The sequential manifestation (*pindapāta*) does not obstruct the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*); thus, there is no impediment to speaking of the totality of all dharmas and upholding immeasurable meanings.
Perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation; thus, there is no impediment to speaking of the eighty-four thousand [teachings].

However, as for the number eighty-four thousand, only a Buddha can know it as it truly is and speak of it as it truly is. Although the Great Commentary (*Dashi*) cites ancient interpretations, they have not yet...
Having seen the Buddha’s teaching, I did not dare to rely upon it for recording; I await further examination. This concludes the section on "The Integration of Phenomena with Principle.
II. The Fusion of Phenomena with Principle has three parts: 1. The Purity of the Clarification of Principle; 2. The Immovability of Principle; 3. The Pervasive Perfection of Principle.
The first two [sections]. First, the equality of the primary retribution; second, the equality of the secondary retribution. Regarding the first:
"Good son, because the nature of all real marks is pure" (extending to) "the sentient beings of the ten directions are pure in their Perfect Enlightenment."
"All" (sarva) refers to all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. Regarding "true reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇa), the *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary) states:
"All dependently arisen phenomena are false; by integrating with conditions to enter into the real, one attains true reality.

This specifically points to the pure nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which constitutes the true characteristic of all phenomena. The *Anantārthasūtra* says: "The absence of marks and yet not being without marks is called..."

As for the true mark (*dharmatā*), the various phenomena of mundane and supramundane dharmas—the distinctions between defilement and purity—are manifested by the perfect luminosity of the awakened nature (*bodhigotra*).
Thus, they collectively constitute the single true mark, which is the purity of nature.

Because all mundane and supramundane dharmas are identical in this single true mark of the purity of nature, one should, by relying on these dharmas to manifest the self, achieve their harmonious integration.
One's own body and those various phenomena share the same reality-mark of purity. Because one's own body is pure, by means of oneself one encounters others;
furthermore, one should integrate and realize that the bodies of the multitude and one's own body share the same reality-mark of purity.
Because the bodies of the multitude are pure, one expands in this manner...

To fulfill this, one should realize that from the bodies of sentient beings in a single direction, up to the bodies of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, they are all identical in the purity of *pariniṣpanna-avabodha* (perfect enlightenment). Previously, it was only stated that the *dharmatā* (true reality) is pure;

now, it is further stated that *pariniṣpanna-avabodha* is pure because *pariniṣpanna-avabodha* is the very essence (*svabhāva*) of *dharmatā*, and *dharmatā* is the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness).
Regarding "nature": because True Suchness (tathatā) does not abide in its own nature, its darkened essence gives rise to delusory appearances. The ignorant and confused grasp these as a body;

because they grasp at a body, they do not yet perceive their own nature, much less the fundamental essence. Now, one awakens to the fact that the delusory is itself the true, and through the true, perceives the essence;
therefore, it is called the "perfectly enlightened purity. Furthermore, the aforementioned [text] speaks of the "boundless."

Space is manifested by awakening. Now, by bringing forth the purity of Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*), it is shown that the world, space, and so forth should be harmonized as being equally pure;
this will become clear in the following section. This concludes the section on the primary retribution sharing the same principle. △ Second, the secondary retribution shares the same principle.
"Good son, because one world is pure... [up to] all are equally pure and immovable.
Good son, the text below is slightly deficient. According to the preceding section, it should state:

"Because the sentient beings of the ten directions are pure through *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*, by means of the perfect interfusion of the primary and the dependent, one should realize that the world currently inhabited and that [other world] are identical."
The primary retribution is equally pure. Because one currently abiding world is pure, it serves as the condition for many;
furthermore, one should integrate and realize that many worlds are equally pure, just like this one currently abiding world.
By extending and applying this principle, one should likewise integrate and realize that one's own [world] is [equally pure].

Throughout the void of space, all worlds of the three periods of time, even extending to the very limits of the void of space in the ten directions—encompassing all worlds throughout the three periods of time—are of one and the same true mark (*dharmatā*), equal, pure, and immovable.
While the previous passage merely spoke of "purity," this passage further specifies that "all are equally pure and immovable. This is because all...
The world consists of both defilement and purity. To speak of purity in opposition to defilement is not true purity.
Now, whether defiled or pure, all things equally return to the single self-nature of purity; therefore, it is called "equality.

Furthermore, regarding the term "immovable," this is discussed in terms of the three periods of time. If purity were subject to the past, present, or future, it would likewise not be true purity. Now...
Thus, it is perfectly enveloped by the three periods of time, all returning to true permanence and pure clarity; hence it is called "immovable.
Furthermore, as stated above, because one realizes that all illusions are extinguished and their images vanish, at that moment one attains directionless purity.

Now, by bringing forth "equanimity" and "immovability," it is revealed that one should know the nature of awakening is pervasive, pure, and immovable, for it is perfectly encompassing and boundless. In total—
The section on the equality of the nature of bondage and purity is concluded. △ Second, the equality of the nature of immovability:
"Good son, as space is thus equal and immovable... (up to)... you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable."
That which can be identical is the phenomenon (*dharma*); that with which it is identical is the principle (*tattva*). Within phenomena, as previously established, there are two types:
first, worldly phenomena; second, supramundane phenomena. Although worldly phenomena are numerous, here they are subsumed by way of the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*).

Among these five great elements, the element of space (*ākāśa*) comes first; therefore, "empty space" is mentioned first. This means that, by virtue of the preceding integration, one realizes that empty space is thus.
When one perceives that [the mind] is equal and immovable, then at the time of seeing empty space, one should know that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable.
The individual records on earth, water, fire, and wind are omitted here to avoid prolixity; therefore, they are collectively referred to as the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*).

This means that, based on the preceding discussion, one has realized through integration that the four great elements are thus equal and immovable. (Such equality should have been mentioned above by analogy; it is only said here that they are "immovable" because it can be inferred from what precedes. Then one sees...
At the time of the four great elements, one should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.
"In this way, even unto the equals" refers to the five great elements within worldly phenomena, each of which is likewise equal and immovable.
By analogy with this, so it is with the supramundane phenomena, such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and even the eighty-four thousand dharani gates.
When one perceives these phenomena as equal and immovable, one should know that the nature of awareness (*jñatā*) is likewise equal and immovable.
The intent of this section is that, having previously integrated phenomena with principle through reasoning, phenomena now accord with principle and are thus equal and immovable;

therefore, whenever one encounters a single phenomenon, one immediately knows that the nature of awareness is equal and immovable. Thus, while phenomena and principle remain as if they were two distinct things...

As for the essence: when one reaches the subsequent section, principle and phenomena are entirely non-dual. This concludes the section on "The Principle of Non-movement. △ Third, the Principle of Pervasive Perfection:
"Good son, the nature of awakening is all-pervading, pure, and immovable" (extending to) "...the *dhāraṇī* gates pervade the Dharma-realm."
Regarding "the nature of awakening pervades all": this generally refers back to all mundane and supramundane phenomena, which are all manifested by the perfect luminosity of the nature of awakening.
Thus, they constitute purity and immovability; that is, the nature of awakening pervades the *dharmadhātu*.

There is not a single phenomenon it does not encompass, nor a single realm it does not pervade. Therefore, it is said to be "perfectly boundless. This is due to the perfection of the nature of awakening.

Because it is boundless, one should understand that within the *dharmadhātu*, all the six internal sense-faculties are entirely identical with the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) and pervade the *dharmadhātu*.
If they did not pervade, they would possess limits. All phenomena below this [level] are likewise pervasive because of their perfect boundlessness;
the six objects and the four great elements are pervasive accordingly. It should be understood in this manner. Thus, then—
Regarding the phrase "reaching equality" (zhìděng): it means that among all worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), each and every one is thus pervasively filled.

By analogy with this, within supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*), from the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*) up to the gates of dhāraṇī, each and every one is entirely identical to the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*) and pervades the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is because they are all perfect and boundless. This concludes the principle.
The section on the mutual fusion of phenomena concludes. The meaning above is identical to the Patriarch’s Contemplation on the Non-obstruction between Principle and Phenomena.
△ Third, the inclusion within non-obstruction has two parts: first, the mutual inclusion of that which is realized; second, the non-obstruction between the subject and object of realization. First:
"Good son, because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive... (up to) "...its light is perfect, complete, indestructible, and unmixed.
This is the initial explanation by way of the Dharma; that is to say, because that wondrous enlightened nature pervades all mundane and supramundane phenomena.

This follows from the preceding text to explain the reason for their inclusion. Regarding "the nature of the faculties" and "the nature of the objects," these are discussed here by way of worldly phenomena.
This means that because their natures are all-pervasive, the faculties follow their nature and the objects follow their nature; each and every one is neither destroyed nor mixed.
That is to say, when the faculty enters the object, the faculty is not destroyed; when the object encompasses the faculty, the faculty is not mixed. It is as follows:
Just as it is when the faculties enter the objects, so too it is when the objects enter the faculties; therefore, it is said in general that there is neither destruction nor confusion.

Regarding the phrase "the non-destruction of faculties and objects," this cites the preceding [reason] as the cause. The reason it does not explicitly mention "non-confusion" is that it may be understood by analogy.
Thus, it applies to the nature of earth, the nature of water, the nature of fire, the nature of wind, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, up to the *dhāraṇīs*.
The nature of the gates: each and every one is neither destroyed nor mixed. As clarified by the following analogy: a hundred thousand lamps represent mundane and supramundane dharmas;
their light illuminating a single room represents the pervasion according to the nature; that the lights each pervade the space represents their mutual inclusion.
Regarding "neither destroyed nor mixed": when this light enters that light, this light does not undergo destruction.
Regarding their characteristics: that light gathers this light; that light does not perceive any mixed characteristics. This is a metaphor for the mutual inclusion of all phenomena:
this enters that without this being destroyed, and that gathers this without that becoming mixed. The mutual inclusion of what is realized is thus concluded.
△ Second, the non-obstruction between the subject that realizes and the object realized.

"Good son, because they have accomplished awakening (until: because the essence of light is non-dual and free from aversion or attachment, they realize that the nature of awakening pervades all phenomena, being indestructible and unmixed; this is called 'accomplishment.
By virtue of this accomplishment, you should know that these bodhisattvas do not create bondage with respect to any phenomena, nor do they seek after phenomena."
One achieves liberation. Because one has realized that the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) is all-pervasive, all phenomena are awakening;
since bondage and liberation are non-dual, and because one has realized that the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are awakening.

Therefore, one feels no aversion toward saṃsāra and no craving for nirvāṇa. One realizes even the observance of precepts and realizes the violation of prohibitions; thus, regarding the observance of...
One does not revere the precepts, yet one does not loathe the lack of reverence. One awakens through long practice, and one also awakens as a beginner;
therefore, one does not value long practice nor disparage the beginner. Why is this? This is a phrase used to raise a question based on what precedes it, asking:
why is it that what was mentioned above—namely, "not being bound by dharmas" and "not seeking liberation from dharmas," and so forth—is so? It is because of awakening.
The nature is all-pervasive; there is no phenomenon that it does not perceive. Therefore, it is said that "it perceives all. Regarding the analogy below, it is further clarified through a metaphor.
"The light of the eyes" refers to the light of the eye-nature, which serves as a metaphor for the wondrously enlightened luminous nature.

The presence of the root-nature's light within the eyes serves as a metaphor for the presence of the wondrously enlightened luminous nature within all phenomena. "The preceding objects" comprehensively includes everything perceived by the eyes.
"Seeing" serves as a metaphor for all dharmas, because all dharmas are collectively illuminated by the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind.
"Thoroughly understanding" does not rely on discrimination; it serves as a metaphor for the perfect illumination of wondrous enlightenment, which does not involve discursive thought.

Its light is complete and full, serving as a metaphor for the awakening to all things, whereby one attains freedom from both aversion and attachment—this is precisely the metaphor for neither rejecting nor seeking, and neither loathing.
"Not loving, etc. refers to that which is without mutual obstruction between self and other.

In the section of inquiry and explanation, the non-duality of the essence of light serves as a metaphor for the perfection of the nature of awakening (*bodhi*). Because there is neither hatred nor love, it serves as a metaphor for being one in awakening.

Up to this point, it is entirely consistent with the "Universal Containment" contemplation established by Master Shun. In summary, this is based on the principle of returning to awakening through the exhaustion of delusion.

The invitation having been concluded. △ Second, answering the question by explaining the benefits achieved through cultivation, in two parts: first, clarifying the benefits achieved through cultivation;
second, concluding the answer according to the preceding questions. The first part has two sub-sections: first, the benefit of knowing that the assembly has originally attained Buddhahood.
Second is the benefit of realizing the equality of nature without impairment. First:
"Good son, this Bodhisattva and sentient beings of the final age [until] birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday."
Although this section follows the preceding text, it does not refer to those who have already achieved awakening.
According to the "Correct Expedient Means" (Zheng fangbian) above, it refers to beginners present in the assembly, as well as to the multitudes of the末法 (mofa, final dharma age).

It specifically refers to those in the final dharma age who have newly resolved their minds to practice; they cultivate this mind by relying directly upon the wondrous contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue miaoguan).
Contemplating this mind, as the days pass and one's practice becomes pure, the mind suddenly opens up. One immediately perceives this mind as brilliantly clear, empty, and still;
there is no longer seen any practice to be cultivated or any fruit to be attained. Therefore, it is said that there is "no cultivation" and "no achievement.
Only the single nature of universal enlightenment remains—its pervasive illumination, its quiescent extinction, and its non-duality. Within this, for now, we shall briefly rely upon...
To explain: "Within this" refers to within the nature of perfect illumination and quiescence, wherein worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise in accordance with conditions.
Furthermore, these are not merely one set of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
rather, there are unspeakably many such worlds. Moreover, these are not merely unspeakably many; they are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

It cannot be described. It encompasses Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and moreover, not merely one *asaṃkhyeya*, but hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeyas* of unspeakably many Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Great Commentary (*Dàshù*) states: "The intent here is to directly point to all worlds throughout the entirety of empty space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm."

This is not for the purpose of calculating their number; rather, in order to guide those with the appropriate capacity, boundless realms are created, and thus many numbers are provisionally accumulated.
"Like flowers in the sky" is a metaphor for arising in dependence on conditions, as they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

"Arising and ceasing in confusion" is a metaphor for formation, destruction, and transformation, as they possess no fixed essence whatsoever. This collectively demonstrates that flowers in the sky have no reality. Worldly... [text ends]
The realms do not exist; their nature is the single, perfect enlightenment that universally illumines and is quiescently non-dual.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "not identical," it means they are not identical to the realms, because they arise from conditions and lack inherent nature. Regarding "not separate," it means they are not separate from the enlightened nature, because their very substance is itself the truth.

Next, speaking in terms of the primary retribution (the sentient being), following the previous discussion of the environmental retribution (the realm), this should refer to the nature of universal illumination and quiescence.
Within this, ten kinds of dharma-realms manifest. Through the bonds of afflictions, karma, and fetters, the six classes of ordinary beings are formed;

through the conditions of unconditioned liberation, the four types of noble ones are formed. Although bondage and liberation differ, both are devoid of intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions;

they are, in their very essence, the Truth. Therefore, both are absent. "Only then does one know" means that it is by virtue of the absence of bondage and liberation that one finally knows. Since there is none...
Bondage and liberation—these are, in fact, the same Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue) shared by the four classes of noble ones and the six realms of ordinary beings.

Since they share this same Perfect Enlightenment, it follows that sentient beings are fundamentally Perfect Enlightenment, no different from the Buddhas; hence it is said that they have been "originally awakened" (benlai chengfo).
From this perspective, looking back, the previous cycle of birth and death undergone by sentient beings, as well as the realization of nirvana attained by the Buddhas, are all...

This refers to phenomena within the state of delusion, not the realm of Perfect Enlightenment; therefore, it is said to be "like a dream from yesterday," for upon awakening, it is fundamentally empty.
This concludes the benefit of knowing that all beings are originally Buddhas. II. The Benefit of Realizing the Equality of Nature Without Destruction.
"Good son, because it is like a dream from yesterday (up to) the fact that the nature of all phenomena is equal and indestructible.

The phrase 'like a dream from yesterday' subsumes what precedes it. Because of the preceding point—that it is like a dream from yesterday—one first realizes that regarding birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa, while deluded one perceives them as existing, yet after awakening they are fundamentally empty. Since they are fundamentally empty after awakening, then birth-and-death is empty; therefore, there is no arising."
This means that because the afflictions do not arise to constitute birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), *nirvāṇa* is empty; therefore, there is no cessation.

This means that because one does not extinguish birth-and-death to realize *nirvāṇa*, if one realizes *nirvāṇa* without extinguishing birth-and-death, then *nirvāṇa* has no coming and birth-and-death has no going.
If the afflictions do not arise to constitute birth-and-death, then birth-and-death has no coming and *nirvāṇa* has no going. This...
Because it subsumes [all things] like a dream from yesterday, it demonstrates that there are no characteristics of arising or ceasing, nor of going or coming, within both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
That which is realized subsequently subsumes the preceding statement regarding the absence of the characteristics of arising or ceasing, and going or coming, within saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
this realization is itself nirvāṇa. Within it, there are four characteristics: gain and loss, and grasping and abandoning. Regarding the two characteristics of gain and loss...
The Bodhisattva said: "If a bodhisattva progresses in practice, they attain nirvana and lose saṃsāra; if they become indolent or regress, they lose nirvana and gain saṃsāra.
These two aspects of grasping and rejecting are spoken of in reference to ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, who know how to yearn for extinction."
Thus, one grows weary of and abandons birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), while joyfully taking up *nirvāṇa*. Ordinary beings, delighting in the world, cling to birth-and-death and abandon *nirvāṇa*.

This was spoken in reference to the state of delusion within the dream-event. Now, awakening from the dream, one realizes that both birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* are fundamentally empty, devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, or going and coming. From this, one immediately awakens to what has been realized.
The four characteristics within it are also empty. Therefore, it is said that there is no gain, no loss, no grasping, and no relinquishing.

As for the "one who can realize," there are four types of practice by which realization is achieved: first, the practice of action (*kriyā-caryā*), which refers to performing various practices with the desire to seek nirvāṇa;

second, the practice of cessation (*śama-caryā*), which refers to forever stilling all thoughts so that everything is tranquil; third, the practice of spontaneity (*anābhoga-caryā*), which refers to spontaneity...
All of these follow the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Regarding the four modes of cessation—namely, the body, mind, faculties, and objects—all are eternally extinguished.
Since the four characteristics are empty within that which is realized, how could the four modes of realization exist independently?

Therefore, they are also said to be non-existent. The phrase "within this realization" also subsumes what precedes it; furthermore, it refers to the relationship between the subject and object of realization.

To "abide and maintain" in this way refers to abiding and practicing according to what I have taught. As stated previously: because the illusory body of those sentient beings has ceased.

The first challenge reveals a contradiction with one’s own words; for while it is your own statement that sentient beings are fundamentally established as Buddhas, you further claim they possess ignorance, which contradicts your own words.

Please grant an exposition.

Conversely, for those who seek clarification, one speaks immediately upon their request, and because the explanation is clearly manifest, the two treasuries are thus opened.

"For the sake of all sentient beings in the final age. The term *sūtra* is the general designation for the *Sūtra-piṭaka*.
