"Good son, all worlds—from their beginning and end, their arising and ceasing (up to) their various graspings and relinquishings—are all saṃsāra.
"All worlds" refers generally to the phenomena of the three worlds. "Beginning and end, arising and ceasing" specifically pertains to the world of true awakening (*samyaksambuddha-loka*).

"Beginning" means manifesting birth according to conditions; "end" means returning to cessation when conditions are exhausted. "Arising and ceasing" refers to the transformations occurring in the interval.

This is easily understood. "Presence and absence before and after" refers specifically to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*): "before" refers to the prior phase of birth; "after" refers to the subsequent phase of death;

and "presence and absence" refers to the intermediate phases of abiding and change, as well as aggregation and dispersion, arising and ceasing. "Aggregation and dispersion, arising and ceasing" refers specifically to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*):

"aggregation" refers to the gathering of atoms to form the world; "dispersion" refers to the dissolution of the world into atoms; and "arising and ceasing" refers to the intermediate period between these.

Regarding "formation and destruction," "moment-to-moment continuity," and so forth: this means that while the middle [state] consists of moment-to-moment continuity, the two ends consist of cyclic recurrence.

As for "various kinds of grasping and relinquishing": this means that at the two ends there is great grasping and great relinquishing, whereas in the middle there is slight grasping and slight relinquishing.
All of these take the six pairs as their objects and grasping and relinquishing as their mental activity. Since the objects are moment-to-moment...
It continues in succession, circulating and revolving; the mind is likewise thus. Therefore, it is said that all are in saṃsāra—referring to the six consciousnesses of arising and ceasing.
Since one employs this mind, one will inevitably incur the Buddha’s reprimand, as seen at the beginning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* where the Buddha clearly rebukes what is not the true mind.
Ānanda said: "The Tathāgata is now inquiring about the location of the mind, yet I have used my own mind to investigate it."
"Seeking and pursuing"—that which is capable of such investigation, I shall take to be the mind. The Buddha said, "Alas! This is not your mind," and so on, up to:
"This is a false appearance and conceptualization of external objects that deludes your true nature. Now, in this context, Gangotsa (Gang-tsang) sets forth three difficulties;
how is this different from investigating and seeking? It is simply that one does not grasp the investigator as being the mind, but rather [regards it as follows]...

The letter you sent sets forth various instances of grasping and rejecting, all of which belong to saṃsāra. You have fully presented three difficulties to demonstrate that what is being employed is still the mind of arising and ceasing;
thus, it is known that [the teaching] was subsequently rebuked by the Buddha, which is not without reason.
This concludes the detailed exposition of the underlying causes. II. Clarifying why it is subject to rebuke.
"Without having emerged from saṃsāra, one attempts to discern Perfect Enlightenment" (up to) "it is also like this when a boat moves and the shore appears to shift.
This is the initial explanation by means of the Dharma. "Without having emerged from saṃsāra" means that one still employs a mind of arising and ceasing.

Because one employs a mind of arising and ceasing, one seeks to discern and clarify Perfect Enlightenment (referring to the three difficulties set forth by Gaṅgottara). If it were thus, one would speak in vain without clarity; even if one were to achieve clarity, [it would remain so].
No. The nature of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) clarified by them is actually based upon perfect enlightenment;

it arises from the mind of birth-and-death consciousness (*utpāda-vināśa-vijñāna*) as a transformation of false names and phrases, and is not the true nature of perfect enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that they are identical to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
If one relies on this and wishes to escape saṃsāra, it is absolutely impossible;
hence it is said that "there is no such place. The analogy below clarifies this: the frequently moving eye represents the discriminating false mind;
the still water represents the self-nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It is said that the still water is fundamentally unmoving, yet because of the... [frequent movement].

Moving one's eyes depends upon the still water; thus, the illusory appearance of movement arises. This is a metaphor for the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-āśraya*), which is fundamentally not subject to transmigration.
Because of that [movement], the mind of arising and ceasing relies upon Perfect Enlightenment to give rise to illusory names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) in order to define Perfect Enlightenment.
Consequently, the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, following those names and phrases, also becomes subject to transmigration.
It is like the movement of the eyes being able to shake still water; there is no difference.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "as when the steady eye revolves around a fire," the *Lüshū* (Brief Commentary) states: "The visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is dull and sluggish.

When a whirling fire forms a circle, its meaning is that because the visual consciousness is dull and its perception of the fire is not true, one forcibly fixes the gaze and observes it for a long time while revolving it. That fire, in reality..."
"Revolve. Because of long-term contemplation through revolving, the fire also becomes revolving; this is the illustration.

In the Dharma, it is because one's faculties are dull and one’s perception of principle is not true, that one forcibly clarifies and stabilizes the conscious mind to give rise to false names and phrases, repeatedly debating the true principle of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Yet, that Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally not subject to transmigration, nor..."

Regarding names and conventions: because they falsely employ names and conventions to engage in repeated debate, the nature of Perfect Enlightenment likewise follows those names and conventions and becomes subject to transmigration.

It is like clouds flying swiftly; because one perceives the moon as having the appearance of movement, though the moon does not actually move, it appears to move due to the manifestation of the swift-moving clouds.
It is like a boat traveling like an arrow; because one perceives the shore as having the appearance of shifting.

The shore does not actually move; it appears to move because of the movement of the boat. Likewise, when one says that within the Dharma beings have not yet emerged from saṃsāra, this is explained based on the deluded mind.
Based on perfect enlightenment (bodhi), deluded names and phrases manifest;

though perfect enlightenment is fundamentally not names or phrases, it is manifested through the discussion of names and phrases, and thus perfect enlightenment also becomes names and phrases. One comes to know the Dharma by means of these metaphors.
Therefore, it is said, "it is likewise so. This concludes the clarification of what is subject to censure. △ Third, the actual censure of their delusions:
"Good sons, as long as the various revolutions have not ceased... (until) for this reason you give rise to the three delusions."
O you who revolve: the movement of the eyes, the steadiness of the gaze, the swiftness of the clouds, and the motion of the boat—these are moments when they have not yet ceased:

the very moment of moving, the very moment of being steady, the very moment of rushing, and the very moment of traveling. Those objects which previously remained stationary—the water did not first ripple while the eyes were moving;
the fire did not first rotate while the gaze was steady; the moon [did not move] while the clouds were rushing.
First, it does not move. While the boat moves straight ahead, the shore does not move first; that this cannot even be attained is because it contradicts the principle of resonance (ganying).
This takes a present event as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) to reveal the beginningless nature of mind as the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*).
"Whirling" reveals that this is the beginningless deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), which undergoes birth and death and gives rise to delusions.

The creation of karma does not fail to rely upon this; therefore it is said that the defiled mind of birth and death has never been purified, and one remains within the cycle of transmigration, just as those various rotations have not yet ceased.
Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālayavijñāna*) is the true nature without beginning. To contemplate this non-rotating state is to depart from the flow of transmigration;
it is like that object which abides from the outset. This, too, should be understood as being contrary to [the notion of] causal response. That...
Since this cannot be attained, how could it possibly be so? Therefore, the phrase "how much more so" (*he zai*) is placed at the beginning;
that is to say, how could it be possible to manifest such a state through comparison, such that their opposites would become responsive and harmonious? It is absolutely impossible.
Thus, one should know that to discourse upon Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*) while still remaining within saṃsāra—even if one debates it—is not true. Because this is not a true vision, you all...

This gives rise to three types of confusion. First, as previously stated: "Sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning; for what reason, then, do they still possess all-encompassing ignorance?

This confusion arises because it contradicts one's own words. Second, as previously stated: "The ignorance of sentient beings is primordially present; for what reason, then, is it said that they have been Buddhas from the very beginning?
This confusion arises because it contradicts worldly consensus. Third, as previously stated: "Ordinary beings [are primordially... [the text continues].
Having attained the Way of Buddhahood, one subsequently transcends ignorance. Once the Tathāgata has become a Buddha, when could afflictions ever arise again?
These delusions, taken as a whole, constitute invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*). If the fruit were truly a correct knowledge and vision, by what cause could these three kinds of delusion arise?

This concludes the refutation through censure. II. Explaining through analogies to bring about understanding, which is threefold: 1. General explanation through analogies; 2. [The second part]; 3. [The third part]. [Note: The provided text fragment ends with "一泛以喻開。二", indicating the first section on general analogies and the beginning of the second.]
This is truly explained through analogies. Third, the correct view is demonstrated:
"Good son, it is like an illusory cataract that falsely perceives flowers in the sky... [until] it becomes the equal and fundamental nature of empty space."

First, there is a general explanation of the metaphors of illusions and cataracts. Regarding "illusions and cataracts": when a clear eye develops a cataract, it arises without truly arising; therefore, it is called an illusion.

This metaphorizes the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), which are falsely manifested in dependence upon the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*). Since the cataract is itself an illusion, the vision [caused by it] is also not real;
therefore, it is called delusion. This metaphorizes the discrimination of the six consciousnesses. Regarding "flowers in the sky" (*gaganaprasūta-puṣpa*): space originally has no flowers.
Due to false views, signs such as fly-wings and golden stars arise; these are termed "flowers. This is a metaphor for the delusive objects discriminated by the conceptualizing mind.
If the cataracts are removed—meaning one encounters the medicine that dissolves the cataracts—this is a metaphor for encountering the Buddha and hearing the Dharma.
"Instantly realizing that consciousness is empty" means it cannot be said to those who have not yet eliminated their visual impairment:
"This impairment has already been extinguished; when will various impairments arise again? This is a metaphor for worldly ignorance.

It cannot be said to those who have instantaneously realized that consciousness is empty: "This consciousness has already been extinguished; when will various consciousnesses arise again? The Buddha necessarily speaks in general terms.

Regarding this analogy, its intent is as follows: afflictions arise based on the six consciousnesses. I have already realized that these consciousnesses are empty, yet you still ask the Tathāgata when afflictions will arise again.
How does this differ from asking when the consciousnesses themselves will arise again? Indeed, your delusion is extreme. To challenge this with a question:
why not say, "Why do you not speak of flowers in the sky? (i.e., why do you not acknowledge that afflictions are likewise non-existent?).
The commentary explains this by means of the two phenomena of the visual impairment (*taimira*) and the flower. They are not established through mutual dependence.

To say they are not mutually dependent is to reveal that both lack intrinsic substance; they are not established as opposites. When it is simply said that the impairment is removed, it is understood even without mentioning the flower.

It is the same regarding the removal of consciousness within the dharmas. Furthermore, as below, in explaining the metaphor of the "empty-flower" (*ākāśa-puṣpa*), the "empty-flower" refers to the wing of a fly.
The "morning star" and so forth are metaphors for sentient beings, the Buddhas, birth and death, nirvana, and all phenomena.
When these are extinguished within emptiness, it is like having pure eyes free from cataracts; one no longer perceives even the wings of a fly or the morning star.

This is a metaphor for how, once the Tathāgata has realized that consciousness is empty, then because all phenomena—including the arising of Buddhas and sentient beings—are entirely empty, they cannot be described.

As for the statement: one cannot speak to a person with clear vision free from cataracts who does not see floating flowers in the sky, asking, "When will empty space ever again give rise to floating flowers?
This is a metaphor for those in the world who lack knowledge; it is improper to explain this to one who has already realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Within the principle of true emptiness, when could any phenomena ever arise again? Furthermore, the Buddha employed this metaphor because the cataracts have been eliminated.

The cessation of consciousness seems to manifest only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When the flowers are removed and phenomena are extinguished, it further advances to the emptiness of both [persons and phenomena] (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*).
It is certainly appropriate that these are explained as being causally related. Why do you question this with the phrase "how" (*katham*)?

That is to say, why is it that one cannot say that flowers arise again from time to time within empty space? The explanation is that space is fundamentally without flowers, because they are neither produced nor extinguished. Thus, it is empty.

As for "the flowers that were originally non-existent," the pure eye does not see them. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who has already realized that consciousness is empty and thus does not perceive the existence of any phenomena.
Regarding "not because of arising or ceasing": since the flowers are not seen, what could there be to arise or cease?

This is a metaphor for how, within the principle of true emptiness, the Tathāgata does not perceive the arising of even the slightest phenomenon, nor does he perceive the cessation of even the slightest phenomenon. ○ Birth.

The following passage cites the analogy of space. Within it, there are three points. First, it introduces the analogy by means of the Dharma (meaning that it first relies on the preceding explanation of the Dharma to introduce the subsequent analogy of space).
"Birth and death" refers to sentient beings; "nirvāṇa" refers to the Buddhas. "Being identical in arising and ceasing" means being identical to the arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky.
This uses birth and death and nirvāṇa as examples to clarify the mundane and the supramundane.
All phenomena in the world are identical to the arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky. To grasp at them is to create existence; to not grasp at them is to realize non-existence.
One of wondrous awakening has awakened and realized the ultimate. One of perfect illumination has illuminated without obstruction.

When illumination is unobstructed, one realizes that consciousness is empty and phenomena are empty. This is like being free from the cataract that perceives flowers in the sky, revealing that only empty space alone remains.
Based on this, the three difficulties can be resolved; however, this remains a general explanation and not yet definitive. Good son, regarding the correct exposition of the analogy of emptiness:
since it was previously stated that one is "free from flowers and cataracts," revealing that only emptiness remains, this takes empty space itself as the metaphor.

Therefore, the teaching instructs that one should know this is not something that exists only temporarily; it is not something that exists for a time merely because of being free from flowers and cataracts.
"It exists, and it is not merely non-existent for a time" means that it is not the case that this space is temporarily non-existent due to the presence of cataracts.
Here, space is a metaphor for the pure awakening of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the fundamental essence of attaining Buddhahood—namely, the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
It does not exist temporarily because cataracts have been removed; rather, it is revealed to exist even when cataracts are present. Within the Dharma, this refers to the activity of manifestation.
At the time when sentient beings exist, my Dharma is flourishing; they thus possess Buddha-nature, which does not preclude saying they have been enlightened from the beginning.
Furthermore, there is ignorance (*avidyā*), which can generally address the first objection. (The first objection asks: "If they were enlightened from the beginning, why is there still ignorance?

It is not because of the presence of cataracts that space is temporarily non-existent; rather, it reveals that space is inherently present, merely being covered by the cataracts as a provisional condition. Within the Dharma, it is likewise so.

This Buddha-nature is inherently possessed. Although sentient beings are obscured by the afflictions (*kleśa*), this does not preclude saying that ignorance (*avidyā*) is primordially present and that one has been a Buddha from the very beginning.
This can broadly resolve two difficulties (the two difficulties being: "If ignorance and sentient beings are primordially present, for what reason is it further said that they become Buddhas?").

Furthermore, the following section broadly reveals the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): even the nature of emptiness does not exist or cease to exist because of visual distortions such as cataracts; how much less so [in the case of the Buddha-nature].
Furthermore, there are those who transcend even space; thus, all things are equally transcended. It is said that even "birth" and "Buddha" cannot be found.
If one were to further raise doubts or objections regarding birth and Buddha, such a person is either a fool or a madman, and one should no longer speak with them.
"Perfect Enlightenment" (Yuanjue) refers to the perfectly complete enlightened nature. In the treatises on the arising of nature, it is called the "One Mind"; it belongs only to the Buddha.
Because it can realize [this], it is called the Perfect Enlightenment (Pūrṇabodhi) of the Tathāgata.
As for "conforming," it means that by conforming to the two gates of True Suchness (Tathatā)—the gate of arising and the gate of ceasing—it establishes all phenomena, such as space.
Since it can establish space, it is the fundamental nature of space; and since it can establish all phenomena, it is the nature of equality.

For one who realizes this nature, the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the Buddhas, ignorance (*avidyā*), afflictions (*kleśa*), subsequent arisings, and rebirth are all merely illusory transformations.
As the "Chapter on the Universal Eye" states: "Perfect enlightenment shines universally; it is quiescent extinction, non-dual.

This may be used to generally resolve three difficulties (the three difficulties being: "If ordinary beings attain the Buddha-way, they would have subsequent ignorance; since Tathāgatas have already attained perfection, when could they ever give rise to afflictions?"). Generally speaking...

The section on "Opening by Means of Similes" concludes. △ Second, "Applying the Similes to the Reality" (Although the preceding text already contained the meaning sufficient to resolve the difficulties, it was not entirely clear;

the Tathāgata merely spoke similes in a general manner, intending for students to understand them well and realize them for themselves. Therefore, that was categorized as "Opening by Similes in a General Way. This present section, however, specifically targets the root of doubt, providing similes based on actual reality to enable students to sever the root of doubt. Once the root is severed, all difficulties will naturally be resolved).
"Good son, it is like refining gold ore; the gold does not exist because of the refining [itself]. (Up to: The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is also like this.
'Like refining gold ore' means: using the fire of a furnace to melt and refine the ore from which gold is extracted, so as to produce pure gold."
This metaphor refers to practitioners who, by employing the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, eliminate ignorance to manifest the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-gotra*).
"Gold does not exist because of smelting" means that pure gold does not come into being through smelting; rather, it manifests that gold was originally present within the ore.

This metaphor illustrates that the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not attained through the process of grinding away [defilements]; it reveals that even when ignorance has not yet been severed, [the nature is already present].
Because the nature of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) is inherently self-existent. Once it has become gold, it does not return to being ore;
that is to say, once the dross of the ore has been eliminated and pure gold is achieved, it never again becomes dross.

This is a metaphor for severing the delusions of ignorance (avidyā), whereby the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment is fully revealed, such that ignorance never again arises, even throughout infinite time.
The indestructible nature of gold may be fashioned into a vase, a ring, a hairpin, or a bracelet; though many years pass, every such vessel remains gold.
This is a metaphor for the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which engages with the world to practice and transform beings.
Whether one acts as a bodhisattva, as perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), as a śrāvaka, or as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one passes through kalpas delivering sentient beings.

Yet, for the bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and ordinary persons, the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment remains ever-present. One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished;
nor should one say that this golden substance was originally unaccomplished while still in its ore. This is the analogy.

Regarding the discussion of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*), it cannot be said that the essence of this nature of Perfect Enlightenment was not originally complete at the time of ignorance.
This analogy is stated according to the actual reality. If one relies on the actual reality to resolve the preceding difficulty, it is as when it is said that gold is not produced by melting;
rather, it is revealed that gold has always existed within the ore itself. This serves as a metaphor for sentient beings being inherently Buddhas, which does not preclude such an explanation.
"There is ignorance" addresses the first objection. Furthermore, it says: "Once gold has been formed, it does not become ore again. This is a metaphor for severing the delusion of ignorance;
once the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-gotra*) is fully revealed, ignorance will never arise again.

This addresses the third objection. Finally, it states: "One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished. This is a metaphor for those who discuss Perfect Enlightenment in that treatise [and yet claim otherwise].
One should explain that the essence of this nature of Perfect Enlightenment was not originally complete during the state of ignorance;

this is intended to reveal that it was inherently complete even during the state of ignorance. Therefore, although it is said that ignorance is primordially present, there is no contradiction in saying that one has been a Buddha from the beginning.
Thus, both difficulties are resolved. Furthermore, once these two preceding and following difficulties are resolved, the intermediate [difficulties] may likewise be settled.
Consider this: there is no need for further elaboration. If this were the case, one could not speak of "equality" and so forth; rather, this precisely points to the root of doubt.

This is because, based on the Buddha’s answer to Samantabhadra regarding the statement that "sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened from the beginning," Vajragarbha consequently developed three types of difficult questions.
His intention was that fundamental enlightenment was not permitted, yet now it is said to be "impossible."
It is said: "Fundamentally, it is not something to be accomplished. This correct teaching cuts off the root of doubt, whereby all difficulties are naturally resolved.
For this reason, there is no need for further synthesis; it simply states that the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is likewise so. Thus, the explanation through analogy is concluded.

△ Third, the conclusion and demonstration of the correct view has two parts: first, the direct conclusion and demonstration; second, the illustration by way of contrast to reveal its inconceivability. First:
"Good son, the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas... (up to) "...neither delusory saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra.
The former refers to [the state] while still within the bonds [of ignorance], termed the "Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgata"; this refers to the causal mind capable of accomplishing a Tathāgata.
The latter refers to [the state] having emerged from the bonds, termed the "Wondrous, Perfect, and Enlightened Mind of All Tathāgatas"; this refers to that which has already become a Tathāgata.
The essence of the fruition can only be fully exhausted by Buddha after Buddha; thus, it says "all Tathāgatas" to manifest that none other than a Buddha is able to realize it.
Being free from the hindrance of afflictions is termed "wondrous," which manifests that ignorance has already been completely severed.
That which embodies all virtues is called "perfect" (*yuan*); that which never again falls into delusion is called "enlightened" (*jue*). This mind is precisely the absolute, numinous mind;
therefore, it is said that fundamentally there is neither *bodhi* nor *nirvāṇa*. This is because both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* belong to the category of dualistic, relative phenomena.
That *bodhi* belongs to the relative is evidenced by the distinction between attainment and non-attainment: if one attains it, one becomes a Buddha; if not, one does not.
Then one would not become a Buddha. Now, because there is no bodhi, even becoming a Buddha cannot be established; how much less can it be said that one does not become a Buddha?

Therefore, it is said that there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood. As previously stated, to speak of awakening in contrast to illusion is itself called an illusion;
to speak of the absence of awakening is likewise so. Thus, both attainment and non-attainment are not admitted.
Furthermore, nirvana belongs to the realm of relative opposition. There is "wheeling" and "non-wheeling": wheeling is birth and death, while non-wheeling is nirvana.
Now, because there is no nirvana, even "non-wheeling" cannot be found; how much less can one speak of delusory wheeling?
Therefore it is said that there is neither delusion nor saṃsāra, nor non-saṃsāra. As previously stated, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are identical in their arising and ceasing.
When wondrous enlightenment shines perfectly, one is free from conceptual proliferation; thus, both the existence of saṃsāra and the absence of saṃsāra fail to be established.
The Chapter on Samantabhadra. The Buddha replied to Samantabhadra, saying:

"All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should remain far removed from all illusory and false realms. Upon reaching this state, both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are simultaneously transcended.
This is what is meant by 'attaining that which is beyond transcendence,' whereby all illusions are eliminated. One who can contemplate in this manner is called [a true practitioner]."
This constitutes Right View. This concludes the detailed exposition of the fetters. II. Manifesting the Inconceivable by Contrast:
"Good son, the perfected spheres of all Śrāvakas—even those [of the Pratyekabuddhas]—cannot reach the Great Ocean of Perfect Nirvāṇa."

At the outset, the Buddha indicated that the śrāvakas should not come forward, fearing that they might inherit previous doubts and say: "If one has not yet emerged from saṃsāra, then the nature of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) would be identical to the cycle of transmigration;

thus, could it not be that those who have become śrāvakas—having already severed the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāva-kleśa) and having already emerged from saṃsāra—must certainly be able to discern perfect enlightenment and avoid further transmigration? For this reason, the Tathāgata called out to them.
He said to the good man: "The realm perfected by the śrāvakas is vastly different from this. To explain its name:

because they hear the sound-teaching of the Buddha’s Four Noble Truths, sever the delusions of views and thoughts, and realize the principle of the emptiness of persons, they are called 'śrāvakas' (hearers).
As for their 'perfected realm,' it refers to that which is fully realized and grasped by the śrāvaka practitioners."
This is the state of realization. For now, this has been a provisional indication; what follows is the actual accomplishment.

That is to say, by means of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), one completely incinerates and extinguishes the present body, mind, and speech, ensuring they never arise again and that one no longer returns to take birth within the triple world (*tridhātu*).
This is precisely the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) manifested through the principle of the emptiness of persons. This...
If it is already *nirvāṇa*, why is it further said that one ultimately cannot reach it?

Regarding that *nirvāṇa* which is personally realized and manifested, one should know that this *nirvāṇa* is a skillful means (*upāya*) and not the ultimate reality. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The conjured city is not real.
Once one has reached the conjured city, having traversed more than three hundred *yojanas*, one proceeds forward toward the place of jewels; thus, it can also be personally realized.
They arrive there, yet they stop at the conjured city, conceiving the thought that it is secure and no longer proceeding forward for two hundred *yojanas* to personally reach the actual destination.
It is like those śrāvakas who have already realized the emptiness of persons; though they are close to the Buddha’s wisdom, they must advance further in their quest.

The fruit of Buddhahood can also be personally realized. However, because those [beings] cling to the partial truth and sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, they no longer advance to sever the dust-like and river-like ignorance (avidyā) until they reach that fruit of Buddhahood and personally realize the nirvāṇa without remainder that manifests therein.
Therefore, it is said that "they ultimately cannot reach that personal realization," and so forth. Since they ultimately cannot reach this, [how could they attain] the wondrous perfection?
The awakened mind says that it is impossible for such a thing to exist. As for the passage beginning with "How much more so," it means that the state of an ordinary person is inconceivable.
This is explained through both the principle (*dharma*) and illustrated by a metaphor. Regarding the principle: it refers to the śrāvakas, the lesser sages, who have already transcended saṃsāra;
their body, mind, and speech are all completely extinguished. It is said that even for them, the ability to engage in such discrimination does not exist; how much less so for an ordinary person?

Now, those who are inferior to the śrāvakas may engage in such reflections; yet, being inferior even to the portion of wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), they instead wish to fathom and surpass the Tathāgata’s realm of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi), which transcends the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna. This is absolutely impossible.

Therefore, it is next illustrated by means of a metaphor: "The firefly" refers to the light of a firefly insect, which resembles fire but is not fire. This serves as a metaphor for that which exists [only nominally].
One reflects: "This is merely mundane cleverness and eloquence, not the supramundane right wisdom. Since it is not fire, using it to burn things is in vain.
This is a metaphor for ordinary beings who, employing a mind of discursive thought, hope for the blessings and rewards of gods and humans;
in the end, these belong to the realm of delusion. Mount Sumeru stands at the center of the four continents; to burn it requires the conflagration at the end of an eon.
A firefly may wish to burn [the sun], yet it can never achieve it; this is a metaphor for how Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-jñāna) serves as the totality of the four wisdoms.
To realize this, one must rely solely upon Buddha-wisdom; any conceptualization involving effort is worlds apart from it. Those who aspire to Perfect Enlightenment should reflect upon this analogy.
[The passage] "By means of the wheel" below clarifies that raising difficulties is of no benefit. The Buddha’s intention, based on what I have previously explained, is that these various...
Grasping and rejecting are both samsara. Although Vajragarbha is not an ordinary being, according to his objection, he is employing a samsaric mind to give rise to a samsaric view.

When entering the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction (*mahāśānti-nirvāṇa-samudra*), he does not speak of "Perfect Enlightenment" (*pariniṣpanna-avabodhi*) but refers instead to the "great ocean of quiescent extinction.
This is done to avoid redundancy; it is specifically spoken of in terms of the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
To explain the meaning: it is called "Great" because it spans horizontally and exhausts vertically. It is silent and still, beyond the reach of verbal expression;

it is extinguished and formless, beyond the reach of manifest characteristics. Its essence encompasses all virtues, and its function pervades all existence. To use a metaphor: it is like the ocean, vast and boundless.
Since its realm is such as this, how could it be entered with a mind of saṃsāra? Therefore, it is said that one ultimately cannot.

[The Buddha] replied: "If one attempts to discern Perfect Enlightenment while still remaining within the cycle of saṃsāra, then the nature of Perfect Enlightenment will likewise undergo the process of transmigration.
Upon hearing this, Vajragarbha should have realized for himself that his objection was of no benefit. This concludes the section on using analogies to provide clarification.
△ Second, the refutation of the incorrect question.
Therefore, I say that all Bodhisattvas [down to] such conceptual distinctions do not pose the correct question.
Regarding the statement "initially receiving the instruction on the constant teaching to sever consciousness," this refers back to what was said above:
because one uses this mind of saṃsāra to enter the ocean of nirvāṇa, one ultimately cannot reach it. Therefore, regarding me, among all...

Within the sutras, it is constantly stated in this way: "All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age" refers generally to those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta and practice the Mahayana.
The phrase "first to sever" is used because it is the most urgent priority.

Furthermore, knowing what comes first and what follows is to draw near to the Way. The fundamental root of beginningless saṃsāra refers precisely to the six sense bases and the conscious mind, for all sūtras instruct that these must be severed. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have continued in the cycle of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, but instead employ various deluded thoughts."
This perception is not true; therefore, there is cyclic existence. All such things are intended to be severed.
○ Good son, because of the discourse on successive delusions, there arises the act of contemplation. Regarding the functions of the six consciousnesses:
when the eye sees a form, the visual consciousness immediately discriminates what kind of form it is; when the ear hears a sound, the auditory consciousness immediately...
One discriminates what kind of sound [it is], and so on, up to the mind encountering mental objects; thus, the mental consciousness discriminates what kind of phenomenon it is.
That which arises from a mind possessing consciousness proceeds in this way through volitional reflection, all because of the existence of a conscious mind.
It is thus able to arise and act without ceasing; the cycle of birth and death does not fail to proceed from this.
To instruct that one must first sever it is no empty statement. All these phrases reveal that both essence and function are illusory:

namely, the mind that gives rise [to thought] and the volition that is given rise to are both illusory perceptions arising upon the objects of the six sense-fields, together with the subjective faculty that perceives them.
The "vital energy" (*qi*) component refers to the delusory perceptions, which are the consciousnesses of the six sense bases; these are designated as the "essence.

The capacity to take that vital energy as an object is "conditioned conceptualization," which is designated as the "function. Regarding what is not the true essence of mind: there are two aspects to the true essence of mind.
First is the purely true, which is *tathatā* (suchness), like the true moon in the sky. Second is that which is accompanied by delusion.
This refers to the eight consciousnesses. It is like pressing on the eyes so that two moons appear; although two appear when the eyes are pressed, the reality is restored as soon as one lets go.

When it comes to the six sense-consciousnesses, they seem to exist by relying on sensory objects, yet they truly do not exist apart from those objects. Therefore, it is said that they are not the true essence of the mind.
Since the essence is not real, its function can be known; therefore, it is not mentioned separately. Regarding the phrase "already like a flower in the sky":
the sky inherently has no flowers, as they are not seen by pure vision. This metaphor illustrates that both essence and function are illusory.

As for "discerning the Buddha-realm," the Buddha-realm is precisely Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*), because it is the realm realized by the Tathāgata. The three difficulties raised by Vajragarbha all intend—
In order to distinguish this object, one is ultimately unable to do so; therefore, it is likened to "empty flowers.

Furthermore, to "bear empty fruit" means that after the essence and function of the consciousness-mind have already been established as illusory—like empty flowers—one still uses that deluded consciousness to attempt to discern the realm of the Buddha. How could this possibly succeed?

This is unlike expecting empty flowers to bear fruit from the void. As stated previously, if one attempts to discern Perfect Enlightenment while still within saṃsāra, then the nature of Perfect Enlightenment itself becomes saṃsāra; thus it is said that this is a "successive proliferation of deluded thoughts.
If one insists on using this to clarify Perfect Enlightenment, it is absolutely impossible; hence it is said, "There is no such place. According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Ānanda...
That which is difficult to fathom or pursue is the mind. The Tathāgata rebuked it, saying: "This is but a false appearance and conceptualization of external objects that deludes your true nature.
From beginningless time until this present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son, thereby losing your original constancy and undergoing the cycle of transmigration.

The general meaning of this is roughly the same as the preceding. "Good son, [the binding...]"* *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "結" (binding), suggesting the passage continues beyond the excerpt.*
He refutes the question as being incorrect. Being about to conclude this refutation, he calls out to the one who is ready to receive the teaching and addresses him, saying:
"Good son, you must understand that the empty and delusory mind possesses many clever views. This 'empty and delusory mind' refers to the consciousness-mind of the six sense bases;
because it is empty and not substantial, delusory and not real, its superficial floating nature is what is designated as 'mind,' rather than [a mind] that is definitive."
This is a discourse on the essential nature [of practice]. Those with many clever insights engage in various forms of contemplation and skillful analysis to establish their own knowledge and views.
Although they establish such knowledge and views, these remain entirely outside the gateway; thus, they ultimately cannot reach the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Therefore, it is said that they "cannot accomplish the skillful means (*upāya*) for Perfect Enlightenment. The final three phrases serve as the formal conclusion.
[The Buddha] rebuked him. The Buddha’s intention was this: since you now wish to discern Perfect Enlightenment, you have presented three successive difficulties.
Such discrimination is precisely like a deluded and floating mind, abounding in clever views; therefore, he said, "This is not a correct question.
The prose section concludes. (The verse summary states:)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse: [The Main Verses are divided into three parts: 1. One verse on the reason for rebuking the objection; 2.

Two verses explaining through parables to provide clarification; 3. Three verses refuting incorrect questioning. First [a brief verse summarizing the meaning]: The Buddha addressed Mahāmati: "Listen well and reflect deeply. I shall now explain for you the true nature of all dharmas. If one does not understand the meaning of the words, One will fall into the error of grasping at characteristics. If one relies on the literal meaning of the words, One will fail to realize the ultimate truth. Therefore, I have taught the Dharma By means of various provisional names. If one clings to these as being real, One will never attain liberation."
"Vajragarbha, you should know that the nature of the Tathāgata’s quiescence... [cannot enter] the ocean of the Buddhas.
This first verse summarizes the underlying reasons, condensing extensive meaning into few words; for fear that one might lose the intended sense or make an error, [it is thus stated].

Therefore, it is taught that one should know this, so as to cause one to apply one's attention. The Tathāgata’s nature of quiescent extinction refers precisely to the wondrous, perfect nature of awakening (*bodhi*).
Being quiescent, it is without sound and cannot be explained by words; being extinguished, it is without form and cannot be manifested by signs.
It is manifested only through realization, for it alone knows [itself]. That which has never had beginning or end is free from such characteristics as going and coming, arising and ceasing.
It is for this reason that all various acts of grasping and rejecting are nothing but saṃsāra. To clarify what is censurable, it is expressed in two lines of verse.

The Buddha’s intention is that since there is neither beginning nor end, if you now contemplate with a mind of saṃsāra, then the nature of perfect enlightenment will also become subject to flux; hence it is said, "it immediately revolves back. Since it immediately revolves—
Furthermore, how could one possibly escape saṃsāra? It is precisely for this reason that its censurability is clarified. The final two lines of the verse praise the direct censure of that delusion;
the prose section, however, builds upon the preceding to further elucidate it by means of comparison. Therefore, it says: "How much more so [the mind defiled by] saṃsāric birth-and-death?"
It has never been purified. Here, this is stated directly and explicitly; therefore, it says, "merely reaching the limit of saṃsāra.

This correctly shows that the mind defiled by birth and death has never been purified. The long passage states, "One contemplates the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and does not return," which is an analogy intended to reveal their incapacity.
In this context, it is stated directly that they cannot enter the Buddha [nature].

"Ocean. The "Buddha-ocean" refers to the Tathāgata’s wondrous, perfect ocean of *bodhi*. This is intended to reveal that one who is able to enter it does not give rise to the three delusions (*trividha-moha*) within themselves.
The long prose states: "Therefore, you all give rise to the three delusions," which speaks of the inability to enter based on the aforementioned meaning.
Here, however, the inability itself is stated directly; therefore, it is omitted [in the verse]. The verse emerges from the refutation of the objection.

[End of section]. △ Second, the verse on the exposition through parables (the prose commentary is divided into three parts; here, it is briefly generalized by opening with parables). Two [subdivisions]: 1. A verse that establishes the reality through a parable; 2.
A verse that concludes and demonstrates the correct view. First [of these two].
For example, it is like smelting gold ore; it does not exist because it was not previously smelted (up to the point where) it will never again become ore.
The long prose says: "As with smelting gold ore. Here it says: "For example, as with smelting gold ore. The long prose says:
"Gold is not produced by smelting. Here it says: "Gold exists because it was not [previously] smelted. These two sentences are identical to the long prose, except that...

Adding one character to the line completes it as a five-syllable verse. Although there are two lines, they serve as a supplementary verse to preempt a potential objection. (Fearing that the questioner might follow up by saying:

"Since gold exists because it has been melted, this merely reveals that gold was already inherently present within the ore; what need was there to melt it? Therefore, he preempts this with: "Although gold is originally present, it must ultimately be achieved through melting.
This is a metaphor for the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*): although it is inherently present from the beginning, it is nonetheless obstructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).

One must necessarily sever ignorance in order to be able to accomplish the wondrous, perfect nature of enlightenment (*bodhigotra*). The first and second lines are entirely identical to the prose section.
The remaining verses do not eulogize the meaning of the general refutation; all may be understood by referring to the prose.

The eulogizing of the actual illustration through metaphors is concluded. II. Verses on the Conclusion and Demonstration of Right View (The prose is divided into two parts, but the verse only eulogizes the first).
Birth-and-death and nirvana, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are equally like the appearance of flowers in the sky.
The Long Chapter states: "In the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally no bodhi, nor is there nirvana."

There is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood; there is neither deluded saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra. This is because the wondrous, perfect nature of awakening is fundamentally free from all dualistic opposition.

In the prose section, it is said that through wisdom one cuts off [afflictions] and through cultivation one transforms birth into permanence, yet this is described as "originally non-existent" and "non-dual.
In the verse, this sameness is expressed in terms of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as ordinary beings and Buddhas.

Regarding the characteristic of flowers in the sky (*ākāśapuṣpa*), its meaning is largely the same. Because it is identical to flowers in the sky, it merely reveals that [the object] is fundamentally non-existent and equal to nothingness.

It is not praised because its inconceivability is already evident; this can be understood by referring to the prose (*dīrghapaṅkti*). Thus concludes the section on the verses explaining the metaphors.

△ Third, the verses refuting erroneous views and posing the correct question (omitting the section on "permanence, teaching, cessation, and consciousness"; the remainder is also omitted in verse for the sake of brevity according to the meaning).
If even conceptualization is like a magical illusion, how much more so is it to interrogate what is false? If one can thoroughly understand this mind, only then should one seek Perfect Enlightenment.

Regarding the two lines on "conceptualization," the verse explains that they are successively false. The prose commentary states that conceptualization with effort is not the true essence of the mind, being already like flowers in the sky;
here it says conceptualization is "like a magical illusion," for a magical illusion is precisely a flower in the sky.

This is the meaning. The long passage states: "To employ this kind of contemplation to discern the realm of the Buddha is like [seeking] flowers in the sky and then further producing fruit from the sky;
it is a case of successive deluded imaginings, and there is no such possibility. Here it says:

"How much more so to use this to request an elucidation of Perfect Enlightenment—would this not be utterly empty and utterly deluded? It would be akin to expecting flowers in the sky to produce fruit from the sky. If...
The two lines [of the verse] are capable [of conveying the meaning]. Regarding the meaning of the verse, the question posed is not the primary one. The prose states:

"A false and floating mind, full of various clever views, cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment. This intends to clarify that once this mind is severed and understood, one may then seek Perfect Enlightenment;
thus, it is evident that the question asked was not the primary one, as can be known without further words. The meaning of generating faith is found in the Chapter of Maitreya.
The first part, from the initial vision through the three questions and three answers, concluding the section on the arising of faith, is finished.
