proofread by his dharma-heir Xinxing. Part Two:
The Section on Resolving Doubts through Two Questions and Two Answers, divided into two parts: I. The Chapter of Maitreya; II. The Chapter of Viśeṣacintin. First: [The Chapter of Maitreya]

Three [sections]: first, expressing gratitude for what preceded and requesting what follows; second, the harmonious union of teacher and disciple; third, the proper request for instruction. Regarding the first two:

first, expressing gratitude with full ritual decorum for what preceded; second, manifesting earnestness after the request. Regarding the first of these two: first, possessing full ritual decorum within the assembly; second, expressing gratitude for what preceded to establish faith. Regarding the first of these: [End of section]
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, amidst the great assembly, knelt with his right knee on the ground and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha.

This chapter takes Maitreya as its principal subject; because he alone is capable of investigating the source of craving and eradicating subtle delusions—tasks that none other than the Regent (Bodhisattva) could inquire about—the rest of the assembly serves merely as his companions.
Therefore, it says, "in the midst of the great assembly. The rest is all to be understood according to what precedes. △ Second, expressing gratitude for the preceding [teaching] to establish faith:
"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One extensively [taught] for the sake of the Bodhisattvas... up to... arising from the realm of cyclic existence, giving rise to circular views."
In terms of the Dharma, it is extensively manifested for those present; in terms of its benefit, it reaches far into future ages.
Therefore, the World-Honored One is called the Great Compassionate One. Because the Dharma and its metaphors are layered upon one another, it is said to be "extensively manifested.

As for "bodhisattvas," these are the capacities for whom the teaching is intended in the present, such as Vajragarbha and others. Perfect Enlightenment covers over saṃsāra; it is not taught unless there is a suitable capacity, even if it were to be taught.
Furthermore, because it is not clearly revealed, it is called the "Secret Treasury. Previously, when Gaṅgottara raised his difficulties, the Tathāgata explained each point explicitly;

therefore, it is said that he has "opened" [the treasury]. Regarding the phrase "causing the great assembly": this refers, for the time being, to the bodhisattvas present here. Regarding "profoundly awakening to saṃsāra":
this means profoundly awakening to the fact that all various acts of grasping and rejecting are themselves saṃsāra. As previously stated, the empty, false, and floating mind is largely...
All those who possess skillful insight make such distinctions; they do not constitute correct inquiry and so forth, but merely differentiate between the heterodox and the orthodox intent.
The four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) manifest before one, and by means of these, [the teaching] is transmitted successively. Therefore, it can be bestowed upon the final age.

Regarding sentient beings of the final age, this is also spoken in reference to those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta and cultivate *Samantabhadra’s Perfect Enlightenment*. As for "those with the eye of the Way," they are those who discern and identify cultivation.
The eye of the Way is precisely right wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*). This eye was not clear, and for a long time I feared practicing erroneously.
Now, having received the Tathāgata’s discernment of the heterodox and the orthodox, I have distinguished the path I practice and attained the eye of right wisdom;

therefore, I am without fear. *Nirvāṇa* is the fruit of cessation, accomplished by transforming *saṃsāra*. The Buddha has realized it without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), distinguishing it from that of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it is named [the Great Nirvāṇa].
"Great. One who has produced decisive faith possesses profound patience toward and delight in the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because they do not regress.
Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are merely the realm of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), once faith is decisive, there is no longer any returning to follow them.
All conditioned mental constructions are seen as cyclic; since the objective realm no longer follows them, they no longer arise.
This is Maitreya’s expression of gratitude for the benefits received previously; therefore, the preceding chapter is judged to be the section on "Generating Faith.

Having completed the formal ritual of expressing gratitude for the previous [teachings], △ Second, requesting the subsequent [teachings] to manifest earnestness, which has two parts: first, requesting the subsequent [teachings] with a hope for awakening; second, manifesting [that earnestness] through three [stages].

[The Preface] First, the World-Honored One [responds to the request]: "If there are bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age" (up to) "perfectly awaken to the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.

This first section fully sets forth what was requested. The phrase "if there are bodhisattvas and others" identifies the practitioners who are the intended audience. [The goal is] the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction.
The preceding chapter explained this by means of the realm of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Where the former spoke of "entering" (*praveśa*), here it speaks of "wandering" (*vihāra*);

this signifies that understanding and practice mutually reinforce one another, such that one enters spontaneously and effortlessly, much like wandering. According to the preceding chapter, it was said: "by means of the mind of saṃsāra..."
They give rise to views regarding saṃsāra and enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s tranquil extinction, yet they can ultimately never reach it.
For this reason, I say that all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
Although Maitreya heard these words, he still feared that newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age might not yet be able to comprehend them.

[The text is] abbreviated; therefore, [the interlocutor] asks on my behalf. His intention is that, according to the preceding chapter, the root of saṃsāra seems to refer to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).
However, he does not know what fault lies with these six consciousnesses, and thus he inquires: "How should they be severed? According to the World-Honored One’s response below, it is said:
"Because of the existence of various desires, which assist in the arousal of the nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), they are able to cause birth and death to continue in succession. Furthermore...
The preceding chapter stated that there is "volitional thought arising from the mind," which briefly indicates this meaning, though it was not explicitly articulated.
Within this volitional thought, sensual desire alone is preeminent; this is the general presentation of what is requested.
In the specific presentation, three points are briefly set forth: first, regarding the various cycles of saṃsāra, how many types of natures exist? Second...
It is said: "To cultivate the Buddha-bodhi. How many kinds of distinctions are there? Third: "To turn back and enter into the afflictions of the world.
How many kinds of skillful means for teaching and transforming should be established? These will be seen for themselves in the Tathāgata’s response later on.

○ From "I only pray" onwards is the formal request for awakening. "I only pray" (weiyuan) manifests the singularity of the vow; it means that he does not wish for anything else, but wishes solely for this one matter.

Furthermore, having already received those newly initiated students before us, he further delivers sentient beings of the final age, severing the causes of craving and desire and emerging from the suffering of saṃsāra;
this is called "Great Compassion that Saves the World. To "not abandon" means to maintain earnest mindfulness and diligent effort without ceasing.
This enables all practicing bodhisattvas to immediately rescue and receive both the newly initiated students before them and the sentient beings of the final age.
He is born to deliver those of initial resolve in the final age, ensuring they are not obscured by their own greed and attachment; thus, his eye of wisdom is solemnly purified.
Regarding the "eye of wisdom": right wisdom serves as the eye. It is solemn and does not race toward external objects; it is pure and free from internal defilement.
By employing this to form contemplation, one can naturally illuminate the mirror of the mind—meaning that the light of right wisdom acts as the illuminator.
"Radiance" (yào) means that which is illuminated by the mirror of the mind-ground; this is the sense of the mind-ground being opened and unobstructed.
When the mind-ground is opened and unobstructed, it reflects and manifests all phenomena; therefore, the word "mirror" is employed. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:

"Taking the one mind as the source, one illuminates the myriad phenomena like a mirror"—this is precisely that meaning. From this point on, there is nothing not known and nothing not seen. Therefore...
"May I be able to perfectly awaken to the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision. I pray that this may be realized in the future. △ Second to third, manifesting earnestness:
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.

The words of the inquiry having been finished, it says, "Having spoken these words. As for "prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground," this means that after speaking, one bows again and requests the Buddha to certainly preach;
this is also a constant ritual. Regarding "thus making three requests," this refers back to the aforementioned speech and the aforementioned prostration.
That it must reach three times is to manifest the intensity of the devotion. This concludes the section on the request made before and the conclusion following the request. II. Master and Disciple.
The conditions for conjunction are twofold: first, the conjunction between teacher and disciple; second, the conjunction between disciple and teacher. Regarding the first:
at that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
The address to Maitreya is because he is the presiding host. "Excellent" (*sādhu*) is a praise for the excellence of his inquiry.
Since he is able both to rescue and sustain the needs of the present age and to provide far-reaching salvation for the final era, the Buddha spoke these words twice to praise him.
With Maitreya as the leader, all others follow his intent; therefore, the World-Honored One addressed them by saying, "you all. As for "only you," it refers specifically to Maitreya.

Only [Vimalakīrti], Mañjuśrī, and others were able to manifest this; those prior to them were all incapable of doing so. The various bodhisattvas and others manifested the capacity of the audience for whom the teaching was intended;
their inquiries and so forth clarified the Dharma requested. As for the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction, only a Buddha can realize it.

Therefore, it is called the profound mystery of the Tathāgata. Sentient beings have long concealed their emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā-vijñāna*), and the Buddha likewise did not constantly expound it;
hence, it is called secret. Once realized, it illuminates heaven and reflects the earth, becoming equal to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, it is further described as subtle and wondrous.

Those present at the assembly who heard this found that desire and attachment no longer sprouted in their minds; therefore, it is said that the eye of wisdom was cleansed and purified. "Cleansed" (潔).
"Pure" (*qing*) and "thoroughly pure" (*sùqīng*) share the same meaning. In these degenerate times, one's birth and death are no longer bound by the multitude;
hence it is said, "one eternally severs saṃsāra. Right wisdom is clear and distinct, illuminating the mirror of the mind; hence it is said, "the mind awakens to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."

The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the principle of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One who awakens to this principle perceives not even the slightest phenomenon arising or ceasing within the triple world;
hence it is said that they "possess the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). All of this was praised by the World-Honored One according to the meaning requested by Maitreya.
What follows is the admonition to listen and the permission to speak; there is indeed a profound reason for this. [This concludes the section on] the teacher and the student.
The first section concludes. △ Second, the assembly joins with the Teacher.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great multitude, listened in silence.

Having heard the Buddha’s admonition to listen attentively, they revered it and complied accordingly; thus it is said, "having received the instruction. They heard that the Buddha was about to speak...
Granted. Rejoicing and receiving with deep reverence, it is therefore called "joyful. With principal and retinue interpenetrating in layers, all together focus their minds to receive [the teaching];
hence it says, "and the great assembly," who listen in silence. The conditions between teacher and disciple have now been fulfilled. Part Three: Requesting Instruction. This has two sections:
first, the prose; second, the verses. The first section has four parts. First, the instruction on how one should sever the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).

First, the turning back of the root; second, the revelation of how many kinds of natures exist within the various cycles of saṃsāra; third, the revelation of the various distinctions in the cultivation of the Buddha’s bodhi;
and fourth, the revelation of the various skillful means for turning back and entering into worldly toil. Of these, the first three—
First, a brief explanation; second, a detailed demonstration; third, the conclusion. Regarding the first:
"Good son, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past... (up to) because of affectionate craving and desire, there is saṃsāra."
"From the beginningless past" refers to what has been explained regarding the obscured true mind (*tathatā*).
From this obscured true mind, deluded thoughts transform, and through them, affection and craving arise in profusion; therefore, they are described in various ways.
For example, there is the debt of gratitude toward those above and the favor bestowed upon those below. The debt of gratitude toward those above refers to parents, sovereigns, and elders.
The grace bestowed upon subordinates is like that shown toward one's own sons, daughters, and grandchildren. Where there is grace, there is affection;

one may love one’s parents and superiors, or one may love one’s sons, daughters, and grandchildren. Loving one’s parents and superiors, one desires to practice loyalty and filial piety out of a craving for wealth and goods.

Loving one’s sons, daughters, and grandchildren, one desires to provide full protection and nourishment out of a craving for profit and emolument. In all such cases, these [affections] are capable of—
It drags one along through birth and death and brings about coming and going; therefore it is said: "Because there are various forms of affectionate love and greedy desire, there is saṃsāra.
That this love and desire constitute the root of saṃsāra has already been briefly clarified. Having finished the brief clarification:
△ Second, the detailed exposition.
One should know that for all types of beings in all worlds, [up to] saṃsāra, craving is the root.

The word "if" (若) is used here as a particle to introduce the subject; although the meaning was briefly explained above, the phrasing is concise and its full significance may not be understood by the assembly.
Therefore, it is now clearly and in detail demonstrated by saying, "As in all worlds. This first cites the basis (*āśraya*).
This refers to retribution (*vipāka*). Regarding "all types of natures" (*sarva-gotra*), this next passage cites the primary retribution, meaning the self-nature of all categories of beings.
While the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* enumerates twelve classes of living beings, this text clarifies only those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, and transformation.

Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "Those born from eggs arise solely through thought; those from wombs are due to emotional attachment; those from moisture are produced by union; and those by transformation respond to separation. As for eggs—

Regarding the statement that "only those born of thought comprise the twelve classes of beings," the text says: "Because they move through inversion, they combine with vapors to form chaotic thoughts of flying or sinking.
The commentary states: "Thought is the mind's light elevation; this is called 'moving through inversion. Vapors refer to the mutual intercourse of the male and female."
The division of yin and yang energies is likewise illusory. Due to inversion, one clings to it as real and unites with it, thereby giving rise to the confused thoughts of flying and sinking.
Flying, one becomes a bird; sinking, one becomes a fish; possessing both, one becomes a tortoise or a serpent, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "conception through the womb is caused by emotion," the text on the twelve classes of beings says: "Because of the inversion of desire, one unites..."
The union of these results in horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts. The commentary states: "When emotion gives rise to craving, it is called the inversion of desire.
'Nourishment' refers to the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, which mutually nourish one another; this too is illusory and false.

Because of such inversion, one clings to it as real and unites with it, thereby forming horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts. 'Horizontal' refers to the animal realm; 'vertical' refers to the human realm."

Those who possess both [conditions] become dragon-spirits (*nāga*) and the like. Regarding those born through the conjunction of moisture, the *Jātisūtra* states: "Because their destinies are inverted.

It explains that through the union of warmth, they form inverted and chaotic thoughts. The commentary notes: "The 'conjunction' refers to proceeding toward [a destination], hence it is called an 'inverted destiny.'"
Warmth is the accumulation of moist substances; internally, the characteristic of warmth arises. This too is illusory, yet due to inversion, one clings to it as real.
By uniting with it, one subsequently gives rise to inverted and chaotic thoughts. These inverted thoughts then result in the state of being wriggling and crawling.

Because its nature is without cognition, when perception (*saṃjñā*) is inverted, it becomes wriggling movement (*śarīra*). Because its form is not at peace, it transforms through detachment from response. Regarding the phrase "the category of birth," the *Wén* (Text) says:
"It is due to the provisional inversion (*parāvṛtti*). The *Héhé* (Harmony) says: "The formation of novelty through contact is called 'disorderly perception' (*vikalpa*).
The *Zhù* (Commentary) says: "Provisionally abandoning the old for the new is called 'provisional inversion. 'Contact' refers to the new object confronting the old object; therefore, it is so named."
This constitutes contact. The new object is likewise illusory; yet, due to inversion, one grasps it as real and unites with it, thereby giving rise to the deluded thoughts of "new" and "old.
Therefore, when one desires to escape from old thoughts, there is a transformation and shedding; when one desires to attain new thoughts...

This constitutes flight. Furthermore, in the fourth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it explains that when the eight consciousnesses enter the womb, they encounter the parents with whom they have a karmic affinity.
Upon seeing the manifestation of light and form, the perception of clarity arises. (Once the light and form are seen, the desire-thought is already formed.

From divergent perceptions, aversion arises: (if a male sees his father, aversion arises; if a female sees her mother, aversion arises. From concordant thoughts, affection arises: (if a male sees his mother, affection arises; if a female sees her father, affection arises. This flowing affection becomes the seed.

(When the flow of passionate attachment is directed toward one's parents, it becomes the seed for the birth of craving. To harbor conceptualization is to form a womb. (To harbor deluded thoughts within the semen and blood is to form a womb for the nourishment of the physical form.

This is precisely what constitutes harmonious growth. By analogy, the harmony of vital energy (*vāyu*), the harmony of warmth (*uṣman*), and the harmony of contact (*sparśa*) can be understood in this same way.

Thus, all sentient beings who possess a fundamental nature and have physical forms and lives do not fail to take lustful desire as the primary cause for their formation. Therefore it is said: "All are formed through lustful desire. You should know this.

Having already provided this detailed exposition, it serves to startle and awaken one to understanding. Beings of the four modes of birth all dwell within saṃsāra, and there are none for whom sexual desire does not serve as the primary cause of their formation;
therefore, it is said that craving is the root. The detailed exposition is concluded. △ Third, the conclusion.
Because the various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.

Regarding the phrase "it must necessarily form a bond," this is said because there may be doubt; for one might suspect that craving does not arise spontaneously, but rather originates dependent upon form (*rūpa*).
When form flourishes, there is craving; when form declines, there is no craving. Since craving is not constant, how could it be the root of saṃsāra?
Therefore, it is shown that because of the existence of various desires, the nature of craving is stimulated. As for "various desires," this is said in contrast to the aforementioned sexual desire;
it refers to whatever else may be desirable apart from that sexual desire—whether it be desirable forms, desirable sounds, or the like.
Sounds, as well as desirable odors, tastes, and tactile objects, are all sufficient to stimulate and give rise to the nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). This nature of craving is constantly continuous.
For this reason, it is able to cause the succession of birth and death; thus, is it not appropriate to call it the root of saṃsāra?
Having finished explaining how one should sever the root of saṃsāra, [the text proceeds to] the second section: Opening [the Explanation].

Demonstrating how many types of natures exist within the various cycles of saṃsāra, there are three: first, manifesting the continuity of craving; second, the nature according to the divisions of the wheels;
third, that which should be severed first. Regarding the first:
Sensual desire has craving as its cause, and life has sensual desire as its condition. (Up to: Craving and sensual desire are the cause, while craving for life is the fruit.

Regarding what was mentioned above concerning "various desires": these assist in the arousal of the nature of craving and are able to cause the continuity of birth and death, because the nature of craving is never severed.
For example, the single matter of sexual desire arises from mutual affection; without such affection, it does not arise.

Because desire is not established, life cannot exist independently. Life exists because of sexual desire; if there were no desire, the body itself would not even exist, so where could life possibly reside?
Yet, among all sentient beings, there are none who do not cherish their lives. To cherish one's life, one must necessarily preserve the body.
This is returning to rely upon the root of desire; the root of desire is the body, because the body serves as the basis for the practice of desire.
Thus one knows that craving for sensual desires is the cause for future rebirth, and craving for life is the fruit of the formation of a future body.
This is why this craving for existence is not severed, and why birth and death continue in perpetual succession. The explanation of the continuity of craving is concluded.
△ Second, according to the divisions of the wheel, there are three types of nature: 1. The nature of evil seeds; 2. The nature of wholesome seeds; 3. The nature of supreme wholesomeness.
First: [The nature of evil seeds].

Because various agreeable and disagreeable states arise from the objects of desire (up to) "therefore they are reborn again in the hells and as hungry ghosts," the above has revealed the continuity of the nature of craving. This explains how many types of natures there are within saṃsāra;
first, the primary one is clarified, hence it says: "because of the objects of desire. "Objects of desire" refers to the spheres of activity for sexual desire, namely—
A man takes a woman as his object; a woman takes a man as her object. Regarding the arising of various states of aversion and attraction:
there are objects that are agreeable and objects that are disagreeable. That which is disagreeable is called "aversion" because it opposes the nature of self-love;

that which is agreeable is called "attraction" because it accords with the nature of self-love. Furthermore, when it is said that the object opposes the loving mind, this refers specifically to the case of an disagreeable object.
In some cases, their physical form lacks beauty; in others, they refuse to comply with their resolve; in yet others, obstacles arise unexpectedly. When the form lacks beauty, hatred arises instantly.

When there is non-compliance, one’s enthusiasm is shattered and anger is harbored. When obstacles intervene, one’s desires are frustrated and resentment is held. Therefore it is said that hatred and jealousy arise.
Because of this hatred and jealousy, one may either destroy another's physical body or ruin their reputation.
Some devise schemes and recklessly hatch plots; others rely on their power to demand retribution from the victim's fathers and elder brothers.
They even go so far as to secretly take his life and plunder his family estate, implicating his kinsmen and bringing ruin upon his superiors.

The ten wholesome deeds are forever severed, while the ten unwholesome deeds flourish; thus it is said that "various karmas are created. Superior-grade unwholesome karma definitely leads to birth in hell;
inferior-grade unwholesome karma definitely leads to birth as a hungry ghost; and middling-grade [unwholesome karma] leads to birth as an animal—though not explicitly stated, this is understood.
The Great Commentary (*Dàshù*) states: "Hell" is the Sanskrit *naraka*, which here means "vessel of suffering. This refers to...

Because it is a vessel for storing those who undergo suffering, what is now called "hell" (*naraka*) refers to a prison beneath the earth where sinners are bound and made to endure various forms of torment;
it is translated thus to conform to the terminology used for penal institutions in this region.

As for "hungry ghosts" (*preta*), the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that they are so called because they seek from others and are constantly hungry and empty, being timid and full of fear. [As for] "animals" (*tiryagyoni*)...
"Born beings" (*yoni*) refers to the life-sustaining resources of humans, as well as those creatures that are nurtured and raised by humans; thus they are also called "animals" (*tiryañc*).

This term may be applied to both those that are domesticated and those that are not, because they move horizontally. The addition of the word "again" (*punar*) when speaking of birth is used in contrast to the aforementioned cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*);
for while the previous discussion of *saṃsāra* was still considered indeterminate, now one creates evil karma within this [state].
Furthermore, among those in meditative concentration, there are some who, due to that concentration, are reborn in the evil realms. It is not said that one creates karma while in a favorable state;

rather, it is because a favorable condition becomes adverse that one creates extremely grave evil karma, which serves as the cause for the three miserable paths. Merely being in a favorable state is not worth mentioning.
The section on the evil lineage is concluded. △ Second, the virtuous lineage.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, one practices the path of aversion toward it; abandoning evil and delighting in good, one is reborn among gods or humans.

Regarding "knowing that desire is to be loathed": this may be through reading the explicit words of the scriptures and teachings, or hearing the guidance of teachers and friends, whereby one comes to know [the nature of] lust.
Desire is the cause of the evil realms; thus, one should develop deep revulsion toward it.

Even if one has developed revulsion for the path of sexual karma, should one then give rise to a mind of longing and desire to practice it, one thereby abandons the unwholesome karma created by desire through its causes.

One takes pleasure in the wholesome conduct of renouncing desire and guarding against sexual misconduct, transforming the ten unwholesome paths of action into the ten wholesome paths. In the highest grade, this is manifested in the present life.

Those of superior grade are born in the heavens; those of middling grade are born in the human realm in this very life; and those of inferior grade become asuras—this is also known without needing to be stated.
The Great Commentary (*Da shu*) states: Regarding "humans," the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says it is because they possess much reflection (reflecting extensively on their own nature).

The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says it is because their mental faculty is tranquil (appearing tranquil in contrast to others, capable of regulating mental deliberations, and tending toward Bodhi). Regarding "heavens," the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-śāstra* says it is that which is received spontaneously (this refers to...).

[The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "One who thinks of clothing and clothing arrives; one who thinks of food and food comes—this is called a deva. It further says: "Radiant and sovereign. (This refers to the radiance and purity of their physical form, and the sovereignty of their spiritual functions, which define them as devas.
Regarding the term *asura*, the *Mingyi ji* (*Compendium of Names and Meanings*) states: "The Sanskrit term is *asura*; this is translated here as 'non-deva' (*fei tian*).

Because their karmic rewards resemble those of devas, yet their rank and virtue do not equal those of devas, they are called non-devas. It also says: "Lacking in upright beauty" (because while there are beautiful women, there are no handsome men). Furthermore, among these intermediate devas, there are only six types.

Regarding desire: humans inhabit the four continents; for now, let us speak in terms of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). In the text, it is referred to as "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "pleasure" (*sukha*), yet it does not depart from the nature of craving.
This concludes the section on the nature of wholesome seeds. △ Third, the nature of superior goodness.
Furthermore, knowing that all forms of craving are to be loathed, [one realizes] that there even exists the superior wholesome fruit of the conditioned:
the heavens and the human realm. Both arise from craving; in the human realm, one is tormented by the eight sufferings, and in the heavenly realms, the five signs of decline suddenly arrive.
Thus, one knows that all cravings are utterly loathsome. By this means, one abandons the craving for the lower realms and aspires for the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher realms.

Therefore, it is said that one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*). This defines the two aforementioned meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), for in both cases equanimity is the primary factor.

Just as in the four *dhyāna* heavens, one gradually abandons the body from the coarse toward the subtle; and in the four formless (*ārūpya*) heavens, one gradually abandons the mind from the coarse toward the subtle.

As for "returning to nourish the root of craving": pleasure (*sukha*) is also a form of craving; this means that by practicing the concentration of equanimity, one instead nourishes [the very craving] one seeks to abandon.
It is the root from which craving arises. "The root of craving" refers to the body and mind of the upper realms.

This means that when one cultivates the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*), one gradually abandons the increasingly coarse minds and bodies of lower levels and receives increasingly subtle bodies and minds of higher levels.

When one cultivates the meditative absorptions of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu-samādhi*), one likewise gradually abandons the increasingly coarse minds and bodies of lower levels and receives increasingly subtle minds and bodies of higher levels. Since there are thus both body and mind, they are further capable of generating craving; therefore, it is called "craving."

Regarding the statement "it is called thus" and "it then manifests": because taking the cultivation of the concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*) as the cause, there immediately appears the conditioned wholesome fruit.

Although one cultivates the concentration of equanimity, if one has not yet reached the emptiness of the wheel (*cakra-śūnyatā*), it ultimately remains within the conditioned and liberation is not attained.

However, compared to the retributive fruits of the lower realms, it is progressively superior; therefore, it is called a "superior wholesome fruit. This concludes the section on the nature of the divisions of the wheel. △
The severance of the three fetters should come first;
because all [beings] are subject to saṃsāra, they do not achieve the Noble Path. (Up to: relying on various desires, they enter into birth and death.

This is the primary binding. Even if one is born as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, when that retribution is exhausted, one returns and is scattered into the various realms of existence.
How much more so for those below them? Therefore, it is said that they are all subject to saṃsāra. For this reason, they transmigrate through the six destinies;
thus it is said that they do not achieve the Noble Path, meaning they remain constantly within birth and death.

Consequently, for sentient beings of the six destinies who resolve their minds to escape birth and death and ultimately avoid all cycles of transmigration, it is impossible to do so by merely severing desire or severing craving. Therefore, by means of...
First, it is shown by way of a summary that greed and the like must be severed;

for when greed is severed, there is no cause for the lower realms, and when craving-thirst is severed, one’s connection to the higher realms is cut off. As for describing craving as "thirst," it is because the mind of craving approaches its objects.

"Like one thirsting for water": this describes the intensity of his longing. ○ "Good son" and below: this addresses a potential objection. One might fear that Maitreya will raise the following defense:
"When Bodhisattvas engage with the world to deliver sentient beings, they often manifest as having parents, wives, and children; how then can they be said to be free from desire and attachment?"

Therefore, he addresses him as "Good Son" and anticipates this by explaining it for him: that when a Bodhisattva enters the world to deliver sentient beings, it must necessarily be through the manifestation of transformations (*nirmāṇa*), and does not arise from birth by means of parents; hence it is said that these are not rooted in craving.

As for manifesting the possession of a wife and children, it is solely out of great kindness and great compassion, to have pity upon sentient beings who are bound by desire, and to cause them to renounce it.
Through love, he makes use of parents, wives, and children to manifest the presence of desire, thereby entering the cycle of birth and death within the mundane world.

The mundane world is easy to inspire with faith, and those in the cycle of birth and death are easy to transform. This is because, among the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he employs "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*).

That Miaoyan converted [the heretics] from their heterodoxy is precisely the proof of this. The exposition on how many kinds of natures exist within the various cycles of rebirth is hereby concluded. △ Third, the exposition on cultivation.

The second [section] concerns the various distinctions in the Buddha’s bodhi. There are two: first, the transformation from delusion to awakening through severance; second, the manifestation of distinction through the cultivation of causes.
Regarding the first: "If all sentient beings in the final age... shall immediately attain awakening within the pure mind."

The Buddha’s intention was this: if all sentient beings in the final age truly possess desire and attachment—though not to the same degree as bodhisattvas—and yet claim they wish to cultivate the Buddha-bodhi, they must necessarily be able to renounce all desires and eliminate both hatred and attachment.

Since the elimination of attachment must necessarily involve the elimination of hatred, for these are correlative phenomena, once that attachment is eliminated, upon what basis could one speak of hatred? It is simply attachment.

If aversion is removed, hatred is also removed; therefore, there is no impediment to mentioning them together. There are, briefly, two reasons why it is necessary to abandon desire and eliminate craving:
first, in practicing for the Bodhi of the Buddha, one aims for the permanent severance of saṃsāra;

second, in practicing for the Bodhi of the Buddha, one aims for the diligent pursuit of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi). To aim for the permanent severance of saṃsāra, one must necessarily abandon [desire].

The desire to eliminate craving is easy to understand; there is no need for further elaboration. The aim lies in diligently seeking Perfect Enlightenment (Pariniṣpanna-bodhi), which likewise requires the abandonment of desire and the elimination of craving so as to purify the mind. It is within this purified mind that the state of Perfect Enlightenment can be sought.

One then attains awakening. This is because, failing to awaken to Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi), one will ultimately remain stagnant in conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) and be unable to cultivate Bodhi.

Having concluded the section on severing delusion to achieve awakening, [the text proceeds to] Section Two: Revealing the Distinctions through Cultivation, which has two parts: First, the General Statement; Second, the Specific Explanation.
First. "Good son, all sentient beings, due to fundamental greed and desire... (up to) "...they manifest in varying degrees of depth and shallowness based on two kinds of hindrances.
"All sentient beings" refers collectively to those practicing for bodhi; since their specific distinctions have not yet been differentiated, they are referred to collectively as "sentient beings."
It is so named. The *Great Commentary* states: "Merely because they do not realize their fundamental awakening (benjue), they perceive themselves as definitely being sentient beings;

they consequently seek to sever hindrances and pursue the Truth, detesting the ordinary and craving the holy. This refers precisely to the detesting of the ordinary and craving of the holy as that which is fundamentally craved.
From this fundamental craving, [the mind] manifests and exerts itself, desiring to sever ignorance. This is further...
Seeking the Truth by severing hindrances is the fundamental aspiration.

Since these aspirations differ—whether one is at the initial stage of cultivation and has not yet left the rank of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or has entered the Vehicle of the Sages and is distinguished as Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, or whether the distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is indeterminate, or has erroneously entered a heterodox school—it is said that the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) are revealed with their unequal distinctions. This follows from the previous question of Maitreya: "Cultivating Buddhahood..."
Regarding the question, "How many distinctions are there in Bodhi? this is answered by means of the distinctions among the five natures (*pañca-gotra*).

Furthermore, it is said that they are "not equal" because ordinary beings and sages, or the Great and Small Vehicles, cannot be made equivalent. Or, one might ask: "If one awakens to Perfect Enlightenment and cultivates the Buddha-Bodhi, it ought to be equal;
for what reason, then, are there again these distinctions of the five natures? Therefore, the World-Honored One [responded with...]

The two obstacles are explained in terms of their depth and shallowness. This is intended to clarify that while the principle is realized through sudden awakening, the phenomena must necessarily be cultivated gradually.
Because cultivation is gradual, the two types of obstacles manifest as either deep or shallow. This concludes the general summary. II. Specific Explanation (divided into two parts):
1. Specific explanation of the two obstacles. 2. Specific explanation of the five natures. First [the specific explanation of the two obstacles]:

What are the two obstacles? First, the obstacle of principle (*tattvāvaraṇa*), which obstructs right knowledge and vision; second, the obstacle of phenomena (*vastvāvaraṇa*), which continues the cycle of birth and death.

What is the interrogation regarding these terms? The first part provides the explanation. As for the "obstacle of principle": in the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) system, it is termed the "obstacle to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

However, that which is known is not itself an obstacle; rather, attachment to it constitutes the obstacle. Because this prevents knowledge and vision from increasing, it is said to "hinder right knowledge."
"Seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the obstacle to what is known (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Regarding the "obstacle of phenomena" (*vastv-āvaraṇa*):

that which is called the "afflictive obstacle" (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) within the *Vijñaptimātra* [system] is able to obstruct True Suchness (*tathatā*). It gives rise to various afflictions (*kleśa*), causing birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to remain uninterrupted;

hence it is said, "continuing all births and deaths. Here, "the various afflictions" are themselves the "obstacle"; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound. △ Second, the specific explanation of the five natures has three parts. First, the general...
Exegesis. This consists of three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary. First: What are the five natures?

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the five [natures]: first, the nature of ordinary beings; second, the nature of those who hear and take conditions as their object; third, the nature of bodhisattvas; fourth, the nature of... [incomplete].
The nature of fixed determination. Fifth, the nature of icchantika. First:
"Good son, if these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, one is said not to have attained Buddhahood.

This refers to a person who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment]; because they desire to sever the obstacles but have not yet achieved it, it says: "If these two obstacles have not yet..."

They have attained cessation; they possess their own original enlightenment (*prakṛtisthagotra*) and are thus called "not yet having become Buddhas. Among the six stages of Buddhahood in the Tiantai school, this corresponds to the "Buddha in principle" (*li-ji fo*).
Since they have not yet severed the hindrances and do not enter the category of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*), the distinctions between shallow and deep have not yet been made. II.
The Nature of the Conditioned by Hearing (the two natures of *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* are explained together).
If sentient beings have forever abandoned craving (up to: they have not yet been able to manifest and abide in the bodhisattva realm.

If these sentient beings still refer to those who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], who fear the suffering of birth and death and cannot enter the entanglements to extend a helping hand, but merely desire to forever abandon craving—like those in the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle—it is said that they do not enter into form, sound, fragrance, [taste, touch, or phenomena].

If this is so regarding tastes, touches, and mental objects, how much more so for those in the second and third fruits of the path? It should be understood that their fundamental intention is to abandon craving forever.
As for "first removing the obstacle of phenomena": craving is the foremost of the afflictions; when the afflictions are severed, birth and death are also severed. Therefore, one removes it first.
To cling to a partial emptiness is precisely the obstacle of principle (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*); because one no longer advances in seeking [further realization], it is so described.

They have not yet severed [the afflictions]. Consequently, they realize only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), thereby departing from the death and rebirth of the fragmented stages (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*) and attaining entry as Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "They still remain outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut.

Even though they hear that the ground upon which they dwell is near to the Buddha-wisdom, they ultimately lack self-confidence; therefore, it is said that they are unable to manifest and abide in the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "I thought of my own poverty, that I lacked this thing. This section subsumes two of the five natures:
first, the śrāvaka; second, the pratyekabuddha. Because their causes both belong to the Hīnayāna, they are explained together.
△ Third, the bodhisattva nature.
"Good son, as for all sentient beings in the final age [up to] the fulfillment of Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa:
regarding 'all sentient beings in the final age,' although it says 'final age,' it refers universally to those with great roots;

regarding 'all sentient beings,' although it says 'all,' it specifically selects those who have already resolved their minds upon the Great [Vehicle]. Having resolved their minds upon the Great [Vehicle], they seek the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]."
Regarding "bodhi": it is said that one wishes to "float upon the Great Perfect Enlightenment Sea of the Tathāgata. "Floating" refers to a piece of wood drifting along.

The Buddha’s intention is to take perfect enlightenment as being like the ocean, manifesting its capacity to contain and branch out [into various streams]. Thus, the practice of cultivation and entry [into the path] is equivalent to floating upon waves and drifting on ripples.
One must first make vows and so forth, just as the Tathāgata has clearly revealed the methods and tracks, enabling those in the final age [to follow].
Regarding the practice of emulation: those who vow to diligently sever the two hindrances possess the sharp and keen faculties of the Mahāyāna.

They aspire with joyful diligence to simultaneously suppress and sever both the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This is unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles, whose capacities are narrow and inferior;

they merely contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, first severing the hindrance of phenomena and hastening toward liberation from the realm of birth and death by exiting the three realms.

One simply avoids them. Regarding "the two obstacles having already been suppressed": throughout the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Worthies), the manifest, the seeds, and the habitual tendencies are suppressed sequentially and progressively, like grass pressed down by a stone;
as long as the stone does not move, the grass does not sprout, which is termed "having already been suppressed," meaning they have already been successfully treated and subdued.

Since they have been successfully treated and subdued, one advances to achieve the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); therefore, it is said that one awakens to and enters the realm of the Bodhisattva. *Bodhi*...
This is the realm of the Bodhisattva. It is explained in reference to the first stage (*bhūmi*), because the first stage is designated as the position of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).

From the first stage through the tenth stage, one gradually eliminates both the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) regarding both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).

Upon entering the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi-bhūmi*), this is termed "having eternally eliminated," meaning that the manifest, the seeds, and the latencies are all exhausted—just as gold is extracted from ore. Therefore, it is said that one immediately enters the subtle, wondrous, and perfect [state] of the Tathāgata.
"Awakening" (jue) refers to the progressive realization of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), for the Buddha-stage is designated as "Sublime Awakening" (*miao-jue*).

The explanation of the meaning may be understood according to what preceded. The section on "Expressing Thanks for the Previous Request" concludes. △ Second, the harmonious union of teacher and disciple, in two parts. First:
The teacher merges with the disciples; the two disciples merge with the teacher. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying: "Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you."

The address to "Pure Wisdom" (Viśuddhamati) is because he is the host of the assembly. Having already asked about the principle realized, [the Buddha] causes him to attain awakening by following that principle;
furthermore, having asked about the stage attained, he causes him to be able to enter it gradually. Therefore, [the Buddha] spoke "Excellent! twice to praise him.
Although Pure Wisdom is the host, the intent is actually to encompass the minds of the entire assembly; thus, it says "you."
The word "etc. indicates that the assembly also wishes to inquire. Without this [inquiry], it would not be possible; therefore, he praises them so that they may be able to do so.
Regarding the principle realized through the severing of hindrances and the stages attained in accordance with that principle, each has its own gradual sequence.

Without the inquiry of pure wisdom, by what means could sentient beings of the末法 (mofa / final age) realize and enter [the path]? Consequently, he first exhorts them to listen and permits his teaching; this constitutes the conditions for the teacher.
The conditions have converged. II. The conditions converge with the Teacher:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

Out of compassion for sentient beings of the final age, their longing for instruction was urgent. Having heard the admonition and received permission to speak, they joyfully accepted and silently bore it;
thus, the conditions between teacher and disciple were fulfilled. The conclusion of the harmony between teacher and disciple.

III. How to Seek Instruction. This has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first part has two sections: first, the revelation of the perfect enlightened nature; second, the revelation of... [text fragment].

Following this, there is the establishment of distinctions, consisting of three parts: first, original equality; second, differentiation through delusion; and third, ultimate equality. Regarding the first:
"Good son, the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is neither a nature nor a non-nature" (up to) "its nature is inherently equal, yet there is no [subject] that is equal."

In accordance with the previous request of Pure Wisdom (*Viśuddhamati*), he said: "I pray that you will once again proclaim for all the gathered assembly of the Dharma the perfect enlightened nature of the Dharma King.
In response to this request, he called out, "Good son," and addressed him, saying: "The self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment..."

"Neither-nature-nor-nature exists," and so forth. This refers to the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālayavijñāna*). Originally, it is not a nature characterized by differentiation.

That there are now natures with differentiation is entirely due to Perfect Enlightenment not abiding in its own nature, but manifesting various differentiated natures in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*).
These various natures are precisely sentient beings and bodhisattvas; since they are manifested in accordance with conditions, they are differentiated natures.
This is precisely the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Who is there to be the grasper and the grasped? Who is there to be the realizer and the realized?

Therefore, it is said that there is no grasping and no realization. Although it is said that there is no grasping and no realization, there nevertheless appear sentient beings as the graspers and Bodhisattvas as the realizers.
Thus, it is negated by saying: "Within the pure principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), there is in reality no Bodhisattva."

And as for all sentient beings. Next, the inquiry arises: "Why is it that in reality there is nothing? The explanation states: "Because both Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations.
Since they are equally illusory transformations, their very substance is quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*). Who, then, could be the subject who grasps? Who could be the subject who realizes?

Therefore, it is said that "there is no one who grasps or realizes. This is because illusory transformations are extinguished; thus, Bodhisattvas and sentient beings alike return to the same [reality].
Perfect Enlightenment. If one were further to say that there is a person who attains realization, this would mean using Perfect Enlightenment to realize Perfect Enlightenment;
how could such a principle exist? If you do not understand this, let me assist you with a metaphor: it is like the faculty of the eye, which cannot see itself.
In this way, the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally equal; furthermore, who could cause it to act?
This is their equality. Hence it is said that there is no inequality. "Primordial equality is thus concluded. △ Second, delusion and inversion result in differentiation.
Sentient beings are deluded and inverted and have not yet been able to eliminate [this state] (up to: "within the midst of false effort, distinctions are manifested").

The preceding category of sentient beings refers to those who have already resolved their minds and know how to subdue their afflictions. These sentient beings include both those who have not yet resolved their minds and those who do not know how to subdue their afflictions;
these are what Tiantai calls the "inner" and "outer" ordinary persons (*bālai*). Those who have not yet resolved their minds at all are called "deluded.
Although they have already resolved their minds, if they do not realize that afflictions are empty and instead apply effort with the desire to subdue them, this is called "inversion. Even if...
They have already been subdued, yet it is no more than grass being pressed down by a stone; in both cases, they remain unable to be utterly eradicated.

Previously, it was said that "Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations. Here, the term "all illusory transformations" refers not only to Bodhisattvas and sentient beings, but encompasses all causes and effects collectively.
This still takes a partial view of the cause; for when delusion is extinguished, everything [is likewise extinguished].

Because all are extinguished: regarding that which has been extinguished and that which has not yet been extinguished, that which is extinguished is gradually severed and eliminated, while that which has not yet been extinguished is gradually subdued and controlled.
Failing to realize fundamental emptiness, one uniformly applies effort in vain. Within this vain application of effort, there then manifests the distinction between Bodhisattvas and sentient beings;
hence it is called "differentiation. Thus ends the section on how delusion results in differentiation. △ Three.
Ultimate equality.
If one attains the Tathāgata’s quiescence that accords with reality, there is in truth neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent.
When the two obstacles are forever exhausted and the single nature is perfectly luminous, this is the Tathāgata’s quiescence; such is quiescence.
This Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. That which is called the "Dharma King" is the perfection of the awakened nature (*bodhi-dhātu*).
From this point on, wisdom and principle are merged in darkness; there is no principle outside of wisdom that could be realized by wisdom, nor is there any wisdom outside of principle.
One is able to realize the principle and accord with Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), severing all dualistic oppositions.

What was previously stated as "the self-nature is equal, yet there is no equality" is here expressed as "in reality, there is neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent. Although the phrasing differs, the meaning is not distinct.
This concludes the revelation of the perfect enlightened nature. II. Revealing the practice of accord, which consists of two parts.

There are two types of conformity: first, gradual conformity; second, sudden and perfect conformity. Regarding the first, there are four: first, the ordinary person’s conformity to the nature of awakening;

second, the stage-before-entrance (prior to the bhūmis) conformity to the nature of awakening; third, the stage-of-entry (the bhūmis) conformity to the nature of awakening; fourth, the Tathāgata’s conformity to the nature of awakening. First:
"Good son, all sentient beings from time immemorial... [up to] this is called the ordinary person following along with the nature of awakening.
Initially, they became deluded through falsehood. Regarding 'all sentient beings,' the explanation begins first with the ordinary person of the vast ground (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*).
Regarding 'from time immemorial,' it refers to the beginningless state where the darkened true mind has undergone successive transformations to produce the illusory body."
The mind has already arrived. It is due to deluded thoughts such as "self" and so forth; that is to say, based on the deluded mind, various deluded thoughts arise.
Internally, one clings to the five aggregates within the body as being "self," and externally, one clings to those outside the five aggregates who are pleasing to the self.

This refers precisely to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*). "Never having known it for oneself" means that one has never, throughout the course of time, awakened to this for oneself.
"Arising and ceasing moment by moment" means that both the self and what belongs to the self are subject to arising and ceasing in every thought-moment.

They are false and unreal. Because of ignorance, one turns away from what is contrary to one's feelings and thus gives rise to hatred and jealousy; one follows what accords with one's feelings and thus gives rise to attachment and defilement.
For those who harbor hatred and jealousy, desire is extinguished upon seeing it; for those who harbor attachment and defilement, desire increases further upon encountering it;

hence, they are said to be "addicted. "Addiction" refers to the state of mind characterized by deep-seated craving and defilement. As for the "five desires," these are beautiful forms and exquisite sounds, and so forth.
Fragrance, rich flavors, and the touch of smoothness are all objects of desire. ○ "If one encounters" refers to encountering the teaching and thereby attaining awakening;
when the roots of goodness internally perfume the mind, such a meeting occurs unexpectedly, which is called "encountering.

A "good friend" is one who possesses right knowledge and right view, capable of exhorting others toward the good, such as the fifty-three individuals in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the Pure [Bodhisattvas] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Those such as Zangjingyan (Pure Eye) and others are all like this. Out of compassion for those who have long been deluded regarding their own nature and who create karma due to craving and desire, he teaches them to awaken to the pure, perfect, and enlightened nature (*vimala-pariniṣpanna-bodhi-citta*).

Once they have awakened, they will naturally be able to give rise to the light of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which clearly perceives that "self" and "what belongs to self" arise and cease in every thought-moment; thus, they immediately know the sentient beings before them.
All of these are instances of self-exertion and self-concern within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment; yet Perfect Enlightenment has no involvement therein.
"If, moreover," and so forth, refers to how awakening becomes an obstacle due to conditions. "If there should be another person" means: among those sentient beings who have attained awakening.
Furthermore, there are those who are able to subdue the afflictions; this indicates that they have not yet attained the capacity to subdue them completely.

"The toil and anxiety are forever severed" means that one realizes *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (perfect enlightenment) has nothing to do with toil and anxiety, and thus vows to realize it for certain; this refers to the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) to sever [afflictions] forever.

Although one has generated the mind to sever them forever, at the initial stage one employs suppression; therefore, it is said that "one attains the purity of the *dharmadhātu*," meaning within the phenomenal *dharmadhātu*.

One need not exert further effort, for one abides in pure understanding (viśuddha-adhimukti). (Although one has attained awakening above, if one again exerts effort, then pure understanding cannot abide.
That very pure understanding becomes an obstacle to itself means: if one clings to that pure understanding as being final and does not seek further abandonment.
This itself constitutes an obstruction for them; that is to say, it obstructs perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), preventing them from entering it spontaneously.

Therefore, it is said that they lack mastery over perfect enlightenment. The *Tiantai Sijiao song* states: "The distinct teaching’s stage of faith and the five stages of the round teaching together constitute the position of the five ranks.

The initial subduing of the afflictions of views and thought occurs while one still dwells among ordinary beings. Although they dwell among ordinary beings, they do not yet oppose perfect enlightenment. Therefore...

It is said: this is called the ordinary person’s conformity with the nature of awakening (*bodhita*). According to our own school, this constitutes the simultaneous suppression of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

In the stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*); in the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*), it corresponds to the ten abodes (*vihāra*); and in the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*), it corresponds to the ten practices (*caryā*).

Because they have not yet been able to sever the obstacles, this sutra continues to refer to them by the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*). This is the ordinary person’s conformity with the nature of awakening.

[End. △ Second, conforming to the nature of awakening prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) (arising from the first *vihāra* of the Perfect Teaching, the first practice of the Sudden Teaching, and the first stage of the Final Teaching).
"Good son, all Bodhisattvas’ views and understandings constitute an obstruction" [up to] "those who have not yet entered the stages conform to the nature of awakening."

"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those who have previously eliminated the stage of ordinary beings and subsequently eliminated [the stages] prior to entering the grounds—namely, those at the initial stage of perfection, the initial sudden practice, and the initial stage of progression.
"Taking views and understandings as obstacles" means taking that pure understanding of others as an obstacle to oneself.

Yet one wishes to sever it. This means that starting from the first stage (*bhūmi*), one severs it stage by stage. Although the hindrance to liberation has been severed, one still dwells in the perception of awakening;
this refers to taking the perception of pure liberation as a hindrance, which is precisely the nature of partial awakening (*anupūrva-bodha*).
Although one has now severed the obstruction of views, one still dwells in attachment to the nature of awareness that perceives purity as an obstruction.
Clinging to this as being correct, one no longer advances in pursuit [of further realization]; therefore, it is said that "one still dwells in the perception of awareness.

However, since one dwells in this awareness and no longer advances in pursuit, this awareness itself becomes an obstruction; thus, it is called "the obstruction of awareness. Furthermore, it is said to be "an obstruction" because...
Because they constitute an obstacle to Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi), those who lack mastery are unable to enter the nature of Perfect Enlightenment by spontaneous impulse.
These are called "Bodhisattvas" to highlight their superior aspiration for upward-seeking;

because they are still in the stage of ordinary beings, they are called "those who have not yet entered the stages" to highlight their inferiority relative to what follows; because their merit in downward-transforming others does not yet equal that of the noble stages.

However, since one has already transcended the ordinary, although not yet reaching the level of the sages, one still does not act in opposition to perfect enlightenment; hence it is said, "conforming to the nature of enlightenment.
This concludes the section on conforming to the nature of enlightenment prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). △ Third, conforming to the nature of enlightenment upon entering the stages.
Good son, both "illumination" and "awareness" are termed obstructions... (up to) those who have already entered the stages accord with the nature of awakening.

This first section follows the preceding [text] to clarify the point directly. As stated previously, "taking views as an obstruction" refers to illumination, for without illumination there would be no seeing.
Furthermore, as stated previously, "still dwelling in views and awareness" refers to awareness, for without awareness there would be no dwelling.

Therefore, both are termed "obstructions. This means that while the object of illumination is inherently an obstruction, the illuminating awareness is also termed an obstruction because, through dwelling in attachment, it obstructs the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).

For this reason, it is said that "the Bodhisattva always awakens without abiding," meaning that since both having illumination and having awareness are termed obstructions, [one must not abide in them]. Thus...
A Bodhisattva who has entered the stages is constantly awakened throughout the successive positions and does not create obstacles, because they do not give rise to a mind of attachment.
Precisely because no attachment arises, the obstruction that is illuminated and the awakening that illuminates are simultaneously quiescent;
both are inseparable from the nature of Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-gotra*). This meaning is difficult to clarify and must be revealed through analogy; therefore, it is said:
For example, suppose there is a person who intends to die and severs his own head.
This means that the person who intends to die gives rise to the thought of severing his head and dies by cutting off his own head with a blade.

While the head has not yet been severed, the head is the object of the severing (*chedya*) and the person is the agent of the severing (*chettṛ*). Once the head has already been severed, however, that severed head is no longer [the object].
When the one who can sever [delusion] has also perished, it is said that there is no one who can sever.
This metaphor illustrates that both the illumination and the illuminator are simultaneously extinguished; this meaning may thus be understood. To further apply this to the Dharma:

it refers to a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), who, by means of a mind that has extinguished obstructions, personally extinguishes all obstructions. When the obstructions have not yet been extinguished, then the obstructions are what are to be extinguished.

Awakening is that which can extinguish. When the obstacles have reached their end and are extinguished, the obstacles that were extinguished are already empty, and the awakening that extinguished them is also exhausted;

this is because neither departs from the nature of Perfect Awakening. What was said above regarding "illumination" and "the illuminator" being simultaneously quiescent and extinguished refers precisely to this meaning.
[The section] beginning with "Sūtra" below anticipates future inquiries; it considers that there may be someone who asks later on.

It is said: Although there are differences in depth between the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and those within the grounds, both equally belong to the practice of cultivation according to the teachings.
Why, then, is it that one forms attachments while traversing the stages prior to the grounds, whereas within the grounds there is constant awakening without dwelling?

Is it not the case that when the World-Honored One bestowed the teachings, he allowed those prior to the grounds to proceed according to their own convenience, yet privately provided the dissolution of understanding for those on the grounds? If this were so, it would contradict the principle of non-conditionality (*anālambana*).
"O Compassionate One, how could the Buddha's teaching of the Dharma be something that merely accords with worldly conventions?

Therefore, the World-Honored One used this as a safeguard, stating that 'the teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon. The term 'teachings of the Sūtras' refers generally to all the scriptures spoken by the Buddha."
Regarding the phrase "like a finger pointing at the moon," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "It is like a person who points at the moon with their finger to show it to another.
In using the finger to point at the moon, the finger is precisely the pointer for the moon. That sutra uses the finger as a metaphor for the teaching and the moon as a metaphor for the mind;

its intent is to reveal that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the teachings was originally intended to demonstrate the mind. Thus, the finger pointing at the moon serves as a metaphor for this demonstration.
Regarding the teaching on the mind: "If one sees the moon again," as that sutra states in its sequence, "this person, because of the finger, ought to look at the moon.
This is a metaphor for how a student borrows the teaching and ought to contemplate the mind, fully understanding that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
As that sutra further states in its sequence: "If one were to contemplate the finger as being the substance of the moon, would it not be a loss? (Not only a loss...)

The moon also loses its finger. This is intended to show that one should not grasp at the finger, which serves as a metaphor for a student looking at the teachings and immediately claiming to have realized the mind.
Not only would such a person fail to know the mind, they would likewise fail to understand the teachings themselves; this is intended to show that one should not cling to the teachings.

Although the metaphor used here is the same as in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the point being illustrated differs slightly from it. This is because, regarding those prior to the stages of the bodhisattva path (*bhūmi*), the Tathāgata...
The establishment of stages and the manifestation of awakening within the ground are all Sūtra teachings; they are like the finger that points toward something.

However, the establishment of stages and the manifestation of awakening are fundamentally for the purpose of destroying hindrances and accomplishing wisdom; they are like the moon that is pointed out.

Therefore, it is said that Sūtra teachings are like the finger pointing at the moon. If one truly destroys hindrances and accomplishes wisdom, then the establishment of stages and the manifestation of awakening are likewise [not ends in themselves].
One should abide [in this way]. Therefore it is said: "If one again sees the moon, one clearly knows that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon.
However, the two characters "what was pointed out" (*suǎobiāo*) are somewhat obscure; if one says "the finger that points," then the meaning becomes clear and unimpeded.
Not only should one not abide in or cling to what is spoken by a single Buddha, the Tathāgata, but all Buddhas are likewise so. Hence it is said: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions."
It is likewise even unto this. Thus one knows that within the stages prior to and within the [Bodhisattva] grounds, there is a distinction between inferior and superior wisdom.

When wisdom is inferior, one traverses the stages while forming attachments; yet if one can fortunately maintain self-illumination, wisdom becomes superior, resulting in constant awakening without dwelling [on objects]. It is not that the Buddha has any partiality.
Do not intentionally pose such questions, for fear of incurring the fault of slandering the Buddha. Having finished the precautionary inquiry, the text returns to the formal conclusion;

thus it says: "This is called a Bodhisattva," and so forth, up to "entering the stages in accordance with the nature of awakening. [End of section on] Entering the Stages in Accordance with the Nature of Awakening.
4. The Tathāgata’s Accordance with the Nature of Awakening.
"Good son, all obstacles are themselves ultimate awakening" (up to) "this is called the Tathāgata’s accordant nature of awakening.
First, the境 (*viṣaya*, object of realization) is clarified. Prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), one eliminates obstacles and establishes awakening; yet awakening itself becomes an obstacle.

Upon entering the stages, one dwells in constant awakening without abiding. If there were truly such non-abiding, it would also be called an obstacle—meaning it could obstruct the Great [Wisdom] of the Tathāgata.
Perfect enlightenment. Because of its unimpeded nature, it is now clarified that upon reaching the stage of the Tathāgata, all obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment.
Regarding "all obstacles": prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), there are obstacles to enlightenment; during the stages, one constantly abides in enlightenment without dwelling [on them].

Although there is a difference between coarse and subtle [obstacles], they are collectively termed "obstacles. Therefore, they are designated by the term "all," which is itself ultimate [enlightenment].
"Awakening" (jue) refers to the ultimate convergence in the Great Perfect Awakening of the Tathāgata, because its nature is unimpeded.

Furthermore, these two phrases are termed the general heading; for while "awakening" is established by the cessation of impediments prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and one dwells in constant awakening throughout the stages, although all are generally termed "impediments," this merely expresses them in broad outline. The impediments subsumed therein are still many.

The following sections provide a detailed synthesis of these points. For instance, when mindfulness cuts through obstructions and establishes awakening—being able both to sever and to establish—it constitutes the attainment of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
When one cannot sever what should be severed and cannot establish what should be established, it constitutes the loss of mindfulness.
To attain [mindfulness] is to be bound; to lose it is to be fettered. In neither case is there liberation. Now, one understands this in contrast to loss.
They are established as attainments, yet these attainments are not true attainments; they are established as losses, yet these losses are not true losses.

Since both are unestablished, they equally return to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālaya*). Because both arise from Perfect Enlightenment, it is not called "Perfect Enlightenment" but rather "liberation."

Because perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is itself the dharma that is free from fetters. Furthermore, as one practices according to the teachings, diligence is the dharma of accomplishment, while indolence is the dharma of destruction.
When one opposes destruction to establish accomplishment, such accomplishment is not true accomplishment; when one uses accomplishment to reveal destruction, such destruction is not true destruction.
Both are equally non-accomplishments, converging in the same way upon perfect enlightenment. That which is called *nirvāṇa* is [this very state].
Because perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is itself the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished. Furthermore, that which can illuminate all obstructions is wisdom (*prajñā*);
that which cannot illuminate obstructions is ignorance (*moha*). Wisdom is established in opposition to ignorance; thus, such wisdom is not true wisdom. Ignorance is manifested by means of wisdom;
thus, such ignorance is not true ignorance. Since both are found to be non-existent, they equally return to perfect enlightenment. Yet it is called *prajñā*.
This is because Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ābhisaṃbodhi*) has the meaning of being the light of great wisdom.

Furthermore, it is like observing one's fellow practitioners and calling them "Bodhisattvas"—the dharmas they accomplish are the Right Path; yet observing those of different schools and calling them "non-Buddhists" (*tīrthika*)—the dharmas they accomplish are the Deviant Path.
To establish the Right in opposition to the Deviant, that Right is not the True Right, for it arises because of the Right [in contrast to the Deviant].
To manifest what is false is not true falsity; both together constitute non-being, yet they equally return to Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-avabodha).
