Because it is untainted by the various delusions, it is called "pure. Since it is pure, there is no dharma that can be cultivated.

Since there is no dharma to be cultivated, the dharma being cultivated is entirely empty; how then could there be a person who cultivates? Therefore, it is said that fundamentally there is neither cultivation nor a cultivator.
All Bodhisattvas refer to those at the initial stage of the present life, as well as the multitudes of the末代 (final age).

"Born" refers to new students of the future. Based on those who have not yet awakened, it is said that all Tathāgatas of the past have already realized Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) and thus certainly have nothing further to cultivate.

Now, although all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age have resolved their great minds, they still remain in the stage of learning and have not yet realized Perfect Enlightenment. Because they have not yet realized it, they rely upon it...

When one arouses the mind to practice cultivation, one should know that *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (Perfect Enlightenment) is fundamentally without cultivation. That one now arouses the mind to practice cultivation is itself identical to an illusory transformation;
therefore, it is called "cultivation through the power of illusion. At that time, according to individual capacities, the gates are divided into twenty-five types.

They are collectively termed "pure" because each is capable of severing hindrances. They are collectively termed "wheels of concentration" (*samādhi-cakra*) because—three... [text truncated]... [the three wheels of concentration are established].
The contemplations belong to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because they are practiced in alternation. Furthermore, a wheel possesses the functions of crushing, grinding, and movement;

by analogy, practicing in reliance upon these [contemplations] can crush the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and transport one to the realm of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa. This concludes the general enumeration of the number of wheels.

If bodhisattvas grasp only extreme stillness—up to this point, these bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha alone.
Grasping only extreme stillness is precisely what it means to practice śamatha alone; for "stilling the spirit by dissolving signs" is the meaning of "extreme stillness.
The phrase "grasping only" indicates that this is a solitary practice, meaning they do not grasp at the other two [meditations]. Thus, the power of stillness is predominant.
"Victorious. This means one is able to eternally sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). "Ultimately accomplished" means that obstacles have been exhausted and awakening has been perfected.
"Without rising from the seat, one immediately enters *nirvāṇa*" means that one attains Buddhahood in this very moment;

this reveals an immediate entry (*tongju*), because in a single severance everything is severed, and in a single realization everything is realized. From "This Bodhi" onwards, the names of what was cultivated are concluded. Although it is called "single,"...
It can be known that cultivation truly and suddenly encompasses all. △ Second, the single cultivation of samādhi:
"If bodhisattvas contemplate only [all things] as like illusions, by the power of the Buddha... (up to) "...this is called the single cultivation of samāpatti."

One does not grasp at tranquility or meditative absorption; therefore, it is said that one "contemplates only as an illusion. This refers to practicing the samādhi of the illusion-like contemplation alone.

By practicing the illusion-like contemplation exclusively, one contemplates within that very contemplation that all phenomena—such as the worlds and sentient beings—are like magical illusions, just as a person created by magic conjures various objects through illusory arts.
There is no difference. One should know that the contemplation of illusion is the dharma already cultivated and perfected by all Buddhas.
Now, the Bodhisattva precisely relies upon this dharma cultivated and perfected by the Buddhas to cultivate and perfect it; therefore, it is said, "by the power of the Buddha.
Now, desiring to deliver those illusory sentient beings, he again cultivates and perfects the contemplation of illusion through the power of the Buddha.
Thus, one is able to follow those illusory sentient beings, manifesting illusory worlds and various activities.
These manifestations of worlds are like transforming the Sahā world into a pure land, or transforming the hells into celestial palaces and the like.
These various activities are like guiding and instructing according to individual capacities; although one acts in such a manner...
These transformative activities are all identical to illusory transformations; they are entirely devoid of real nature.
Therefore, it is said that one "fully practices the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva. That the conduct is called "wondrous" is because it is free from obstruction.

This is like practicing contemplative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*) alone, yet not losing silent mindfulness and various tranquil wisdoms regarding the *dhāraṇī*. As for *dhāraṇī*, its name appears in the previous Mañjuśrī chapter.
It is for the sake of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). What is now called "within the *dhāraṇī*" refers precisely to the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment.
This is because the twenty-five types of contemplative wheels were all practiced by relying on the illusory power prior to the realization of Perfect Enlightenment.
Now, as the merit of these illusory contemplations has been perfected, the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests in its entirety; therefore, it is said to be "within the *dhāraṇī*."

This clearly demonstrates that the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-citta*) universally sustains the meaning of all dharmas, and thus encompasses the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Since it universally encompasses the three contemplations, although one does not specifically cultivate *śamatha*, one does not lose the state of quiescent mindfulness;

and although one does not specifically cultivate *dhyāna*, one does not lose stillness-wisdom (*śānta-prajñā*). "Stillness-wisdom" carries the sense of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This precisely reveals that the three contemplations are inseparable.

"One mind. This section below concludes the names of the practices cultivated; although it is said that one cultivates samādhi alone, in meaning it actually encompasses all that precedes and follows it.
△ Third, the single cultivation of dhyāna.
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions... [up to] "this bodhisattva" refers to one who practices *dhyāna* alone.
The word "merely" (*wei*) carries the sense of exclusion. Regarding "extinguishing all illusions": this same phrasing also occurs within the context of that [previous] contemplation of illusions;
however, in the present case, it is excluded from that meaning. Here, the bodhisattva uses only the power of quiescent extinction to extinguish all illusions.

The practice of *māyā-dharma* (illusory phenomena) serves as a preliminary skillful means for severing afflictions (*kleśa*) below; furthermore, one does not grasp at the various functions of illusory contemplation.
That [practice] is for the benefit of others, whereas this is for one's own benefit, whereby one alone severs the afflictions.

Regarding the statement that one "severs afflictions alone," it is because afflictions can obstruct the ultimate truth (*tattva*); therefore, it is necessary that the afflictions be completely severed for the truth to manifest.

The principle now manifests; therefore, it is said that one "realizes the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This true mark is precisely the true mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā-citta*).
Because it can serve as the substance of all phenomena, it is named the "true mark. From "This Bodhi... below, the names of the practices cultivated are concluded.

Regarding the single cultivation and mutual inclusion [of the three contemplations], the meaning may be understood by analogy with the previous two cases. The single cultivation of the three contemplations is finished. △ Second, the unified cultivation of the three contemplations has three parts.

First, the cultivation of śamatha; second, the cultivation of samādhi; third, the cultivation of dhyāna. Regarding the first [dhyāna], there are three distinct cultivations of the seven contemplations, all of which take śamatha as their primary basis;
hence they are termed "comprehensive" (tǒng). These three are: first, repeated cultivation; second, complete cultivation; and third, simultaneous cultivation. The first two are as follows:
First, the combination of śamatha and samāpatti; second, the combination of śamatha and dhyāna.
Regarding the first: if bodhisattvas first attain stillness and first cultivate śamatha before subsequently cultivating samāpatti.
"First, taking up the most profound stillness" means that with a mind of pure awakening, one takes stillness as the practice; this is *śamatha*.
When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, wisdom arises; therefore, with a mind of still-wisdom, one illuminates all illusions—meaning one illuminates those multitudes which are like illusions.
"Thereupon, within this" means that once they have been illuminated and known, one then [acts] within these illusion-like multitudes.

In the middle, one initiates the bodhisattva practices; that is to say, through various transformations of worlds and manifold activities, one fully carries out the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva.
This is precisely samādhi. From "This bodhi" below, the names of the practices cultivated are concluded, as can be understood.
△ Second, the compound term *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom... [up to] "is called first practicing *śamatha* and subsequently practicing *dhyāna*.
In the passage beginning with "If bodhisattvas," there should still have been the phrase "first attaining extreme tranquility" to clarify the meaning of *śamatha*.
The compilers omitted it to avoid prolixity, as it can be understood by analogy with what precedes. Since wisdom arises from the culmination of tranquility, it is said:

By means of tranquil wisdom, one realizes the nature of ultimate stillness, which is the nature of *tathatā* (suchness). Once the nature of *tathatā* has been realized, there are no afflictions (*kleśa*) remaining to be severed.

The turning away from discursive thought occurs through sudden awakening; yet, while awakening brings about simultaneous dissolution, phenomena are not eliminated all at once, but are exhausted through a gradual process.
Thereupon, one deeply cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in order to exhaust all afflictions and forever transcend [suffering].
It is merely the ocean of birth and death. From "This Bodhi" [onward], the names of the practices cultivated can also be known. △ Second, the fulfillment of cultivation has two parts:
first, fulfillment through the beginning, middle, and end; second, fulfillment through the beginning, end, and middle. First:
If Bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom (*śamatha*), first cultivate *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivate *dhyāna*:

"tranquility" is called "stillness"; it is the ultimate state of tranquility. Only when tranquility reaches its peak can wisdom arise; this meaning reveals that one first cultivates *śamatha*, because [wisdom] is attained from within *śamatha*.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of illusory power: it means that by means of this very tranquil wisdom, one illuminates all phenomena.
This assembly, which is like an illusion, further manifests the power of illusory transformation within the nature of the awakened mind;
even through various transformations, it brings all illusory beings to liberation. This meaning clarifies the cultivation of samādhi in the Middle Way by means of various transformations.

This is because [the powers] must be attained from within *samādhi*. However, since one manifests various transformations to deliver sentient beings, one cannot avoid remaining with the body in the realm of dust; thus, there is still the fear of being entangled by sentient beings.
Therefore, during the latter stage, one deeply cultivates *dhyāna*, vowing to sever afflictions and enter into *nirvāṇa*, so that the body becomes like the resonance within a musical vessel.

The names of the practices cultivated in conjunction refer to first practicing *śamatha*, then *samādhi*, and finally *dhyāna*. This constitutes a provisional sequential progression within the practice of sudden cultivation;
it is neither identical to the single-practice method mentioned in the preceding section, nor is it the same as the gradual cultivation described in the previous chapter.
△ Second, the completeness within the sequence of before and after.

If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness (*śamatha*), first cultivate *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivate *samāpatti*, the phrase "by means of the power of ultimate stillness" indicates that they have previously cultivated *śamatha*.
It is only when the practice of *śamatha* is perfected that one attains the power of ultimate stillness.
Having attained ultimate stillness, they further employ that power of ultimate stillness to arouse the mind and sever afflictions; this is precisely [the function of] stillness (*śama*).
"Contemplation" (*cintā*) refers to the wisdom that arises as discursive thought within stillness; this is precisely the meaning of practicing *dhyāna* in the middle stage.
Once afflictions have been severed, the contemplation of *dhyāna* is perfected. When the contemplation of *dhyāna* is perfected, one is capable of attaining Buddhahood.
Yet, unable to bear abandoning sentient beings, one subsequently turns back to pilot the "compassionate vessel," manifesting various kinds of spiritual transformations and cultivating *bodhicitta*.

The pure and wondrous conduct of the Bodhisattva delivers all sentient beings who are like illusions; this refers to the subsequent cultivation of the meaning of *samādhi*. The names of the practices performed are to be understood according to the preceding [sections].
Having completed the full cultivation, there are three types of simultaneous and alternating cultivation: first, alternating the middle and the end while performing the beginning simultaneously;
second, performing the middle simultaneously while alternating the beginning and the end; third, performing the beginning and the end simultaneously while alternating the middle. First:

If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, practice samāpatti-dhyāna in equal measure, the meaning of "by means of the power of ultimate stillness" reveals that they have previously practiced śamatha;
through the power of this ultimate stillness, their discursive thoughts from beginningless time [are stilled].
Suddenly it ceases and is extinguished. (Therefore it is said that the mind is severed. The meaning of "afflictions" belongs to *dhyāna*.
First benefiting oneself, and then delivering sentient beings and establishing worlds—this meaning belongs to *samādhi*. This [passage] below concludes the names of what has been cultivated.

If one examines the preceding explanation and the subsequent conclusion, the sequence of *dhyāna* and *samādhi*, or *samādhi* and *dhyāna*, appears inverted. However, if one considers them as being practiced simultaneously, then...
When one is correctly practicing dhyāna, that is precisely when one is practicing samādhi; when one is correctly practicing samādhi, that is precisely when one is practicing dhyāna.
In reality, there is no sequential inversion between them; generally speaking, through the sovereign power of the Buddha’s word, nothing is impossible.
△ Second: First equalizing the middle, then the remainder.

If various bodhisattvas, having used the power of ultimate tranquility (*śamatha*) to stimulate and initiate transformations, subsequently cultivate *dhyāna*, then while practicing *śamatha*, they employ the power of that very tranquility of *śamatha* to assist and give rise to transformative activity.
This brings about the accomplishment of samādhi, which is defined as manifesting various modes of conduct without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
This is illustrated by such accounts as entering right concentration in the worlds of the east and emerging from concentration in the worlds of the west;

these all represent the simultaneous cultivation of the meanings of śamatha and samādhi. However, śamatha tends toward self-benefit, while samādhi tends toward the benefit of others; though the two are practiced together, they have these respective emphases.

Even while practicing, he still feared his cultivation was not yet perfected; therefore, he subsequently practiced *dhyāna* (meditation) deeply to forever sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Thus, benefiting both himself and others, he did not expect perfection, yet there was nothing that was not perfected. △ Third:
The Equalization of Prior and Posterior with the Intermediate.
If Bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness (*tishijing*) to support quiescence (*jimi*), they subsequently cultivate *samāpatti*.
When cultivating *śamatha*, they use the power of the ultimate stillness of *śamatha* to nourish the nature of quiescent extinction (*jimiexing*), thereby accomplishing *dhyāna*.
However, ultimate stillness is simply quiescence and belongs exclusively to concentration (*samādhi*); quiescent extinction, by contrast, involves the extinction of both the quiescent and the active.
This belongs primarily to wisdom (*prajñā*). As for its being called "power" (*bala*) and "provision" (*sambhāra*):

it means that when one is in the state of perfect stillness and quiescence, the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) gives rise to the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), such that even this quiescence does not remain. This is what constitutes self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*).
Yet, the liberation of sentient beings has not yet been accomplished. Therefore, subsequent activities arise to transform the world and deliver all living beings.
By accomplishing samāpatti, one’s benefit for oneself and others is fully perfected without deficiency.
This concludes the general cultivation of śamatha. Next, the general cultivation of samādhi has three parts: first, alternating cultivation; second, integrated cultivation;
third, simultaneous cultivation. Regarding the first two [of these]: first, the alternation of samādhi and śamatha; second, the alternation of samādhi and dhyāna. Regarding the first:

If Bodhisattvas, by means of their power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*), first cultivate *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivate *śamatha*, they then employ the power of transformation within *samādhi* to deliver sentient beings in accordance with their needs.
Regarding the term "various," it refers to the fact that the faculties, natures, inclinations, and desires of sentient beings are diverse and not uniform; such is the Bodhisattva’s [approach].
The same applies to compliance with conditions. As for attaining ultimate stillness, one knows that all things are like illusions and like transformations, and thus the mind remains unmoving.
Although one spontaneously delivers others, the self remains as it truly is (*tathatā*). It is like clouds responding to conditions and reaching everywhere without exception.
And one dwells eternally upon this seat of Bodhi. However, transformation is not achieved through mere samādhi; it must necessarily be perfected through śamatha in ultimate stillness.
This is why the names are joined together: there is a profound reason for practicing first [śamatha] and then [vipaśyanā]. △ Second, the compound term *samādhi-dhyāna*.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*), first cultivate *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivate *dhyāna*, they first cultivate *samādhi*.
By means of the power of transformation within *samādhi*, they manifest various realms to teach and transform sentient beings;
this demonstrates that *samādhi* has been perfected. Once *samādhi* is perfected, great compassion and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) become eternal.

When one reaches the point of sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence, fearing entry into the realm of the Two Vehicles—that is, taking the realization of extinction as the goal—then *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is perfected.

This is designated as the "Middle" [stage]. First one cultivates *samādhi*, and subsequently one cultivates *dhyāna*; the meaning may be inferred accordingly. Having completed the repeated cultivation:
II. The Complete Cultivation of Both. 1. The complete cultivation of both in the order of first and last. 2. The complete cultivation of both in the order of last and first.
Complete. First: If various bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation (from the beginning) up to the middle, cultivate śamatha and subsequently cultivate dhyāna;
by means of the power of transformation, they perform various buddha-activities for the sake of liberating sentient beings, thereby manifesting the perfection of samādhi.
Thus it is. Although various Buddha-activities are performed, their nature remains as-it-is (yathābhūta), abiding in tranquility; this reveals that *śamatha* is immovable.
Although *śamatha* is immovable, it spontaneously eliminates afflictions and realizes the fruit; this reveals that *dhyāna* is self-so.

Within the summary of the names, the sequence of first practicing the middle, then the middle practice, and finally the subsequent practice is likewise orderly and correspondingly aligned. △ Regarding the second [section]: middle.
The former and the latter are fully perfected.

If various bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, first cultivate dhyāna and subsequently cultivate śamatha, these bodhisattvas accord with sentient beings and manifest unimpeded activity through the power of transformation. This is samādhi.
He has attained mastery. Being able to manifest unimpeded functions, he does not regard the salvation of sentient beings as a burden.
He again gives rise to *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and advances in the cultivation of *dhyāna*. All afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed spontaneously.

Whether his merit is perfected or not, whether the Way is accomplished or not, he retreats to maintain *śamatha*; thus it is said that he "dwells securely in ultimate stillness. This section below concludes the practices cultivated.
The names are visible in the text. Having completed the full cultivation (具足修), there are three types of simultaneous and intermittent cultivation (齊零修):

first, intermittent cultivation with both prior and subsequent simultaneity; second, prior simultaneity followed by intermittent cultivation; third, subsequent simultaneity preceded by intermittent cultivation. Regarding the first:
If Bodhisattvas, by means of their power of transformation (nirmāṇa-bala), practice śamatha and dhyāna in unison—
first employing the power of transformation to establish various skillful means and initiate various activities for the sake of delivering sentient beings—
this constitutes benefiting others through samādhi. Even if they encounter followers of the Hīnayāna Śrāvakas or Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, [they act] in the same way.
When the time comes to strike [the gong], both "Ultimate Stillness" (zhìjìng) and "Quiescent Extinction" (jìmíè) are followed accordingly. Now, "Ultimate Stillness" is *śamatha*;

it is practiced as a skillful means to respond to those with the capacities of the Hīnayāna. "Quiescent Extinction" is *dhyāna*; it is practiced as a skillful means to respond to those with the capacities of the Mahāyāna. These names are combined in the middle [of the sequence].
It should be understood that these two practices, "Leveling" (língqí), correspond respectively to the two preceding stages. [End of Section on] The Two Middle [Practices].
First comes concentration, followed by the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

If various bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*), give rise to various functions (up to) subsequently practicing *dhyāna*, they employ the power of transformation to initiate diverse activities according to the various types of sentient beings, universally practicing and teaching them. This clarifies [the process].
To know that this samādhi has already been accomplished, yet say that it relies upon ultimate stillness, means that being able to remain still amidst movement is what is called "ultimate stillness.
All of this arises from the support of samādhi; there is no need to separately cultivate śamatha, for śamatha is already perfected.
This is precisely what is meant by "cultivating both together. However, the arising of its function is solely for the purpose of delivering sentient beings. And...

Even when one reaches the ultimate stillness, there remains the fear of falling into quiescence; therefore, in the later stage, one deeply cultivates *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), severing afflictions to achieve *bodhi* (enlightenment) and departing from birth-and-death to realize *nirvāṇa*.
These matters may be considered together; the names of these practices have already been established and need no further explanation.
△ Regarding the third [section], the latter is simultaneous while the former is gradual.
If bodhisattvas support their quiescence (*śamatha*) with the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*),

[and so on] up to "later cultivating *śamatha*," supporting quiescence with the power of transformation means that the bodhisattva uses the transformative power of *samādhi* to assist the merit of the quiescence of *dhyāna*,
causing the two to mutually perfect one another. This is because, through various transformations...

Transformations are all identical to illusory phenomena; in their very essence, they lack reality and are solely quiescent extinction. Since they are already solely quiescent extinction, there is no need for further extinction.
This is the fulfillment of the merit of *dhyāna*. Once the merit of *dhyāna* is fulfilled, it is sufficient to know that the merit of *samādhi* is likewise fulfilled.
This is what is meant by the mutual fulfillment of these two aspects. Thus, both *samādhi* and *dhyāna* have achieved their respective merits.

This is the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*). From this point onward, one dwells securely in the pure, unconditioned meditative concentration (*anabhisaṃskāra-dhyāna*), which is the meaning of *śamatha*.
Within the contemplation of *śamatha*, there is a single flavor of purity; being unconditioned and uncreated (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) is the dissolution of signs (*nimitta-pralaya*).

The complete stilling of all thoughts and deliberations is the clarification of the spirit (*citta-vyupaśama*). That which is called "the dissolution of signs and the clarification of the spirit" is precisely this.
Thus it is. From "This Bodhi" below, the names of the practices to be cultivated can be understood. The general cultivation of *samādhi* is concluded.

△ Third, the general cultivation of *dhyāna* has three parts: first, repeated cultivation; second, complete cultivation; third, simultaneous cultivation. Regarding the first two: first, the repetition of *dhyāna* and *śamatha*;
second, the repetition of *dhyāna* and *samādhi*. Regarding the first:
If Bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence (from "to" [the end of the previous section]), first cultivate dhyāna and subsequently cultivate śamatha,
such that arising and ceasing are extinguished and quiescent extinction manifests before them, then the supreme cause has been established and the wondrous fruit is about to be realized.
Yet, if they then give rise to a state of ultimate stillness and withdraw to rest in śamatha, this is precisely what is meant by "receiving and enjoying [the fruits] with the Dharma-nature body."
Dharma-joy. Therefore, it is said that one "dwells in purity. The names of the practices cultivated have been concluded; the repetition [of terms] is as can be understood.
△ Second, the compound *dhyāna-samādhi*:
"If all bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence... (up to) "...is called first cultivating *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivating *samāpatti*."

Having already perfected dhyāna, one does not regard the realization of the fruit as urgent. Instead, one retreats to cultivate samādhi in order to develop skillful means for delivering sentient beings.
Thus it is said: "By the power of quiescence, one gives rise to functional activity regarding all objects.
"Regarding all objects" refers to all objects of deliverance, which is to say, sentient beings; for sentient beings are the objects of deliverance for the bodhisattva.
Regarding "the quiescent function that accords with [reality]": because it is characterized by quiescence (*śānti*), it gives rise to functional activity that accords with the liberation [of beings];

thus, the three samādhis are perfected. This concludes the section on the names of the practices cultivated; the repetition of the structure follows the previous pattern. The repeated cultivation is now finished. Part Two:

The Cultivation of Perfection (*paripūri-bhāvanā*). This has two sections: 1. Perfection in terms of the sequence of after, before, and middle. 2. Perfection in terms of the sequence of after, middle, and before. The first section: [Text continues...]
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence, perceive various intrinsic natures (up to) subsequently cultivating samāpatti;

regarding "by means of the power of quiescence, various intrinsic natures," this means that Bodhisattvas do not, like those of the Two Vehicles, become attached to quiescence and fail to contemplate the salvation of sentient beings.
Now, by the power of quiescence, they perceive that sentient beings possess various intrinsic natures.

Regarding those who are to be delivered: although they are among those to be delivered, one must first stabilize the mind through *śamatha*, and only then, relying on *samāpatti*, give rise to various transformations to deliver them in accordance with their own natures.
The names of the practices to be cultivated are to be understood according to the text. △ Second, within the latter [section], first is the "complete" [practice]:
If various bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*śamatha*), [cultivate] *samāpatti* first and cultivate *śamatha* later.
"By the power of quiescence" means that when the merit of *dhyāna* is perfected, there is the functional power of quiescence.
"Unconditioned self-nature" means that this self-nature is inherently possessed and does not depend upon artificial construction.
"Arising in the pure realm of activity" refers to how a Bodhisattva, within meditative contemplation, observes those sentient beings amidst the dust and toil of afflictions.
Within affliction, there is rising and sinking like the head emerging from and submerging in water; not for a single moment is there purity.

Therefore, by the power of cessation (*śānti*), within the unconditioned intrinsic nature (*anabhisaṃskāra-svabhāva*), one relies upon that samādhi to give rise to functional activity. One transforms those defilements (*kleśa*) into pure realms.
Thereby, all deluded thoughts are suddenly stilled, and one returns to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This concludes the name of what has been cultivated.

The meaning can be understood by examining the text. This concludes the section on "Complete Cultivation. △ Third, the three modes of "Simultaneous and Intermittent Cultivation": 1. Intermitting the latter while cultivating the middle and former simultaneously; 2.
Cultivating the latter and former simultaneously while intermitting the middle; 3. Cultivating the latter and middle simultaneously while intermitting the former. First:

If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence (*śamatha*), practice both *śamatha* and *samāpatti* together until they reach the power of total cessation (*nirodha*), this demonstrates that their *dhyāna* has been perfected.
Being "quiescent" (*śama*) means not clinging to existence; being "ceased" (*nirodha*) means not indulging in emptiness.
Since all phenomena do not transcend existence and emptiness, and they neither cling to nor indulge in them, then [the seeds of]... are planted.
All [roots] are pure. Although they are variously pure, they do not make the attainment of the fruit their primary concern;

rather, they contemplate only the provisional reception of the joy of the Dharma to return and deliver sentient beings. Thereby, they retreat to cultivate *śamatha*, relying on *śamatha* to abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and concurrently cultivate *samādhi*.
Relying on *samādhi*, they manifest various transformations, necessarily aiming for deep roots and flourishing branches.
Lush. Its source is distant and its current long; that the lifespan at the time of attaining Buddhahood is vast and enduring, and that the True Dharma abides for a long time, all arise from this.
△ Second, the equality of priority and posteriority within the zero.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence (up to the point of) subsequently cultivating samāpatti,
practice dhyāna, they then employ the power of quiescence within that dhyāna to support ultimate stillness.

What is meant by "provisioning"? Generally, to be detached from existence is called "quiescence" (*śamatha*); thus, it can provision the arising of stillness. To be detached from emptiness is called "cessation" (*nirodha*);
thus, it can provision the arising of ultimate stillness. This is when *śamatha* is perfected at the time of practicing correct meditation.
These two both pertain to self-cultivation, yet the salvation of sentient beings has not yet been achieved. Thereafter, one must further cultivate *samādhi*.
By manifesting transformations to deliver sentient beings, one benefits both self and others; thus, the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected to be established.
The names of the practices cultivated herein can be known from this conclusion. △ Second, within the latter [section], the equalizing follows the preceding dispersal.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence (up to) subsequently cultivate śamatha, and use the power of quiescence to support their transformative manifestations (nirmāṇa):
"quiescence" here refers to meditative concentration (samādhi), which is capable of giving rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā).

Furthermore, because they are in a state of quiescence, they do not become attached to that quiescence; thus, they are able to support their transformative manifestations. This is the third [stage] of the correct cultivation of dhyāna.
Through this, compassion is spontaneously perfected without further cultivation. In such a state, great compassion and pliancy arise, making it easy to awaken others;
yet, fearing that one's own power of self-awakening may still be weak and that great wisdom cannot be swiftly attained, one subsequently cultivates śamatha.
When the state of ultimate stillness is evoked through clear and lucid wisdom, compassion and wisdom mutually support one another; thus, self-awakening and awakening others are both perfected.
This concludes the general cultivation of the three contemplations. △ Third, the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-jñāna*), perfectly cultivate the three kinds of self-nature purity in accordance with reality;

and if Bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly harmonize all things—according to the previous sequence of the three contemplations, it is stated that they all "realize pure perfect enlightenment" and thus practice with the mind of pure awakening. By this, one knows [the twenty].
The four wheels are all likewise so; they all depend upon the true mind of pure awakening (*viśuddha-tathatā-citta*). One practices them in accordance with one's capacities and suitability.
This refers to Bodhisattvas of complete faculties who, having awakened to Great Perfect Awakening (*mahā-viśuddha-bodhi*), employ the wisdom of that Great Perfect Awakening.
One should practice by unifying all [of them] (referring to the twenty-four wheels). This means that practicing one is to practice all.
If one asks how this can be so, the answer is: regarding the various natures and characteristics, there is no departure from the nature of awakening.
Regarding "the various natures and characteristics," the twenty-four wheels all take the pure, awakened true mind as their nature. To practice them individually is to practice them collectively.
Cultivation and its various distinctions are not uniform, yet they constitute its characteristics.

Those who do not depart from the nature of awakening are all inseparable from the nature of Great Perfect Awakening. Therefore, one should simply cultivate by means of the wisdom of perfect awakening;
thus, one perfectly integrates and cultivates everything as a whole, without further doubt. Within the summary of the names, the person who is able to cultivate is still indicated as "perfect."
Regarding the Bodhisattva Root, he is called "One Who Perfectly Cultivates the Threefold" because he cultivates with the perfect fusion of the wisdom of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*.
For instance, when he cultivates *śamatha*, it simultaneously possesses *samādhi* and *dhyāna*; when he cultivates *samādhi*, it simultaneously possesses *śamatha* and *dhyāna*;
and when he cultivates *dhyāna*, it likewise possesses the other two. In this way, the self-nature of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* is pure.
There are no obstacles; the twenty-four wheels are all fulfilled in accordance with [the practice]. This concludes the separate explanation of the sudden and gradual methods.
III. Conclusion and Instruction on the Method of Practice:
"Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the Bodhisattva... (up to)... if one harbors even a single thought of doubt or regret, one will not achieve success."
First, the formal enumeration of the wheels (*cakra*). According to the previous general indication of the wheel enumerations, it was stated:

"Based on the cultivation of the power of illusion while [reality] is not yet realized, there then arise twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This has not yet been explained.
What are these twenty-five wheels? Now, the preceding section categorized them according to single cultivation, collective cultivation, combined cultivation, and perfectly integrated cultivation.
Having completed the detailed explanation of each one individually, he concludes here: "These are called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva.
All bodhisattvas, according to their own inherent faculties and natures, practice by relying upon these wheels; it does not exceed this."
The phrase "if there are those below" indicates that this also shows the method of cultivation. "All bodhisattvas" refers to those currently engaged in new study;

"the multitudes of the末代 (final age)" refers to those with the initial resolve in the future. "Relying on this wheel" means that if one wishes to practice according to this wheel, one must maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
This means that one must first strictly uphold the prohibitive precepts and cultivate pure *brahmacarya*, taking the precepts as the foundation.
Because it is the very foundation of unsurpassed bodhi. "Tranquil" means to withdraw and collect the body and mind, remaining still and unmoving.
"Contemplating" means to contemplate with right mindfulness which of the twenty-five wheels one should rely upon for cultivation.

Fearing further that past obstructions may be deep and heavy, making correct cultivation difficult to achieve, one must still pay homage to the Triple Gem and seek their compassion through repentance. After three...

For seven days, one should personally recognize the mutual resonance between the path and its response, and earnestly seek instruction for correct cultivation. Regarding the placement of markers on each wheel:

the markers are made of paper, upon which the name of the wheel is inscribed. "Placing them individually" means placing them according to their respective wheels in preparation for binding and extracting them.
"Binding and extracting as they come to hand" means that, as they are encountered, one uses the markers to form knots and mixes them together.
He again takes up the knots in his hand and unfolds them for inspection. "Revealing according to the knots" means that as each knot is unfolded, he reveals which *cakra* (wheel) should be practiced.
"Thereby knowing the sudden or gradual" means that one thereby knows whether one's own faculties are sudden or gradual.
As in the twenty-five *cakras*, there are four meanings: sudden, gradual, partial, and complete; that is to say, practicing [a single method] alone is called "partial."
"Sudden" (dùn): because one observes through observation until all are perfected. One who takes this as their affinity knows that their own faculty is sudden;
following its opening, they say "practice," and entry occurs naturally. Repeated cultivation and complete cultivation are called "gradual" (jiān);

yet these are also the gradual within the sudden, meaning that within the sudden, a brief distinction of before and after is made, such that both are accomplished in a short time. One who takes this as their affinity...
One then knows one’s own faculty (*indriya*). Within the sudden [approach], the gradual is fully contained; by practicing according to that which is revealed, one may also naturally enter [the path].

Because the wisdom of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfectly realized awakening) perfectly unifies all things, it is called "round" (*pariniṣpanna*). One who grasps this essential point will know that their own faculty is round;
by practicing according to what is revealed, it will naturally and easily be accomplished. Those who practice piecemeal are called "partial. However...
This is also the partial within the perfect; that is to say, if one practices both simultaneously, they can be mutually inclusive. If not for long, even the fragmented will be included.
One who grasps this point will know that their own root is the partial within the perfect. By practicing according to what is revealed therein, it will likewise be easily accomplished.
The reason the text does not explicitly mention "partial" and "perfect" is that the four characters form a single phrase, following the principle of the Sudden Teaching.

Because it can be gradually understood. [The section] "In a single thought" below refutes the failure to achieve realization due to doubt. Now that you know both the sudden and gradual approaches, if you practice directly, you will surely succeed.
However, if you harbor a single thought of doubt and fail to practice, or if you repent after having already practiced, you will not achieve success in Perfect Enlightenment.
You must take great care to avoid this; do not abandon yourself. The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary.
(The introductory verse says:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

△ (In the main verses, the meaning and application are abbreviated compared to the prose; furthermore, the sections do not correspond exactly, as they are a summary verse based on the meaning. Divided into three parts: 1. A brief verse summarizing the twenty-five wheels.
Second, the display of the persons who should practice; third, the conclusion showing the swift realization through conformity. First:
"Bhāṣita, you should know that all bodhisattvas [up to] have twenty-five wheels."

Fearing that various bodhisattvas might be unable to practice in accordance [with the teaching], he instructs them on what they should know; by addressing those for whom the teaching is appropriate, he serves as a warning to the rest of the assembly.
All bodhisattvas encompass both the sudden and gradual, as well as the partial and perfect. "Perfect" refers to unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*).
This means that because it perfectly integrates all things, it is called "suddenly purified wisdom" (*prajñā-viśuddhi*). It has pure awakening as its intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, it is unimpeded in both the particular and the universal, meaning it is either unimpeded regarding principles (*dharma*) or unimpeded regarding phenomena (*vastu*). Thus, it is also gradually purified.
This means that because the obscurations are gradually severed and purified accordingly, all [attainments] arise based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Regarding "arising based on meditative concentration," *dhyāna* encompasses the three, such as *śamatha*. "Based on arising" indicates that one should follow [the path]; this refers to the two lines [of the verse].

To specify the three names of meditative concentration, it mentions the three dharmas of sudden and gradual cultivation; it does not speak of partiality or completeness because the verse forms its lines with five characters. Furthermore...

The sudden, gradual, and intermediate [teachings] can be understood accordingly. Regarding the "twenty-five wheels," this is an exposition that combines the partial (provisional) and the perfect (ultimate). II.
Revealing the persons who should practice and those who should be excluded:
"From 'All Tathāgatas of the ten directions and practitioners of the three periods of time'... up to 'all such dharmas are not in accordance with [the truth]'."

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are those who have already attained perfect enlightenment; the practitioners of the three periods of time are those who have not yet attained perfect enlightenment.

There is no one who does not rely on this Dharma to achieve Bodhi. This means that those who have already attained it did so first by relying on this, while those who have not yet attained it will do so later by relying on this. It is to be practiced accordingly, as its meaning is self-evident.

Except for two phrases, which exclude those who do not accord [with the teaching]. There are two types of people who achieve sudden awakening: first, those who achieve it upon initial birth, as they do not perceive anything to accord with;
second, those who achieve it through the manifestation of responsive conditions, as there is no room for further accordance. Regarding non-accordance with the Dharma, there are also two types:
first, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), because the dharmas they cultivate do not accord [with reality]; second, the icchantikas, who lack...

Because they do not momentarily follow the Buddha-nature, these [cases] are all spoken of in reference to the present. If one were to trace back to the distant past or look forward to the future, they would likewise be in accord.
Fearing that those lacking knowledge might cling only to the present and erroneously deny this accordance, I have therefore provided this preliminary clarification.
△ Third, the conclusion indicating accordance and swift realization.
"All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age" (up to) "will before long realize nirvana.

The first three phrases point to the persons [to whom this is addressed] and urge them to uphold [the teaching]. "All Bodhisattvas" and "sentient beings of the final age" specify the individuals who should practice.
The phrase beginning with "constantly" urges the upholding of the dharma that should be practiced. The final three phrases concern the benefits received through such practice; that is to say:
By practicing with diligent perseverance in accordance [with the teaching], one will receive the Buddha’s empowerment and before long realize nirvana. The Chapter on Discerning Sound concludes.
*An Analytical Commentary on the Meaning of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Three.
*An Analytical Commentary on the Meaning of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Four.
Composed by Tongli, a junior disciple of the Virtuous Master, and collated by Xinxing, a successor-disciple of the Dharma lineage.

△ Chapter Four: Purifying One’s Karma. 1. Performing the Ritual and Expressing Gratitude to the Predecessor; 2. Requesting the Successor and Manifesting Zeal; 3. The Relationship between Teacher and Disciple.

Regarding the conditions for conjunction: there are four points on which one should seek clarification. The first two concern the initial stage: (1) assuming the proper deportment within the assembly; (2) expressing gratitude for the benefits previously received. Regarding the first:
at that time, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions [from the passage] down to "kneeling with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying: [is described].

This chapter takes the purification of all karmic obstacles as its primary theme. (Regarding the four phases of delusion regarding consciousness and the four phases of delusion regarding wisdom: those who are not skillful at purifying all karmic obstacles cannot inquire about or understand [this matter].
Since the remaining assembly are merely companions, it says "in the midst of the great assembly. The rest is self-evident. △ Second, expressing gratitude for the benefits previously received.
The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes—[up to] we bodhisattvas—feel profound self-congratulation and comfort.
Regarding the "Chapter on Majestic Virtue," there is sequential refinement; regarding the "Chapter on Eloquence of Sound," there is mutual refinement.

This is for the sake of those newly learning in the present and those with initial resolve in the future age; therefore, he is called the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One. The three successive contemplations have already been [established].
We have spoken briefly; even with the mind, one can only approximate it through words. Yet you have further analyzed the twenty-five wheels for us in detail;
this is truly what is called inconceivable. As the verse in the preceding chapter says:

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and those who practice throughout the three periods of time—there are none who do not attain Bodhi by means of this Dharma. Therefore, it is called the Dharma of all Tathāgatas.

The characteristics of the practices on the causal ground were brought forth so that the assembly might hear them together and each desire to follow them; thus it is said, "attaining what was never before attained.
Yet, as soon as the correct practice is cultivated, malevolent spirits and demons compete to arise. As for our Śākyamuni, the Tamer of Men, he traversed kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To diligently cultivate this realm and undergo all the processes of refinement and polishing is truly difficult to fathom; yet now it is beheld.
In the space of a single thought-moment, it appears vividly and simultaneously within the mind. What joy and consolation this brings is beyond description;
thus, I speak of it from the depths of my own being. Having completed the formal ritual of expression of gratitude, △.

Part Two: Requesting the Teaching and Manifesting Zeal. This consists of two sections: first, requesting the teaching to dispel doubts; second, manifesting zeal through the arrival of the two [disciples].
Regarding the first: "World-Honored One, if this enlightened mind is by nature pure... (up to)... may it serve as the eye for future beings in the final age."
According to what was stated in the previous chapter during the general enumeration of the number of wheels: "All Tathāgatas are the pure, perfect enlightenment;

fundamentally, there is no cultivation," and so forth. Since it is said that there is "fundamentally no cultivation," this reveals the original nature (prakṛti) which has been pure from the very beginning.
For this reason, the Bodhisattvas present as the audience took this as the basis for their inquiry, saying: "If this awakening..."
"The nature of the mind is inherently pure. Previously, it was also stated: "All bodhisattvas and others practice based upon the power of illusion that has not yet been awakened.
Now, this "not yet being awakened" is precisely "non-awakening" (a-jñāna). Non-awakening necessarily entails defilement.

Therefore, the bodhisattva who is the primary recipient of the teaching takes this as the basis for raising a doubt, asking: "By what cause is there defilement? [He asks this] so as to lead the assembly...

One gives rise to confusion and fails to enter; "confusion" means a lack of awakening, and "obstruction" means a lack of penetration. "Failing to enter" means being unable to realize and enter [the state].
Compared to those who have attained the fruit, the difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth. Such profound doubt cannot be resolved except by a Buddha.
Therefore, it says: "I only pray that the Tathāgata... and so forth. "Extensively" means praying that he will not decline the labor.
"We" refers collectively to those present at the time. "Opening" means to clear away their delusions; "awakening" means to enlighten them from their stupor.

Once their delusions are cleared and they are awakened from their stupor, the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) manifests before them; without even expecting to enter realization, they are naturally able to enter it. However, as for this *dharma*...
Nature is precisely perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), because it can serve as the nature of all phenomena. The Great Commentary (*Dà shù*) states:

"If one speaks directly of the fundamental substance, it is called the enlightened nature (*jue-xing*); if one investigates all phenomena to their depths, they are found to lack inherent existence and are identical with this single nature."

This is precisely what is called the *dharmatā*. Now, by analytically deconstructing the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and causing all phenomena to dissolve into openness, one brings them into accord with the nature of awakening;

hence it is said, "to awaken to the *dharmatā*. Regarding the phrase "causing this great assembly [to enter]": it means that the sentient beings of this world realize and enter [it], transmitting it successively until the end of the age;
the sentient beings of that final age realize and enter it, transmitting it successively into the future. In this manner, it is transmitted...
It is transmitted from one to another until the very end of time, so that all sentient beings shall never again fall into confusion or fail to enter [the Way];
thus it is said, "He acts as the eye for the future. This concludes the section on dispelling doubts for those who come after. 2. From the second to the third [verse], he manifests his earnestness.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again after each completion.
After the request, he manifested the utmost sincerity. △ Part Three: The Harmonious Union of Teacher and Disciple, in two sections: 1. The Teacher’s union with the Disciple.
2. The Disciple’s union with the Teacher. The first section:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa: "Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.

Because he praised him for his inquiry and commanded him with words of excellence, and because he commended his capability and cautioned him to listen before granting permission to speak, it is due to the convergence of the conditions of the teacher and the conditions of the disciple.
It is called "inquiry" (*paripṛcchā*) because one seeks to enter into awakening. "Inquiry" (*pari*) has the meaning of "to deliberate," signifying that there is something to be deliberated upon.
And he asked. As for "expedient means" (*upāya*), it refers to the skillful method for entering awakening.

If one were not capable of purifying all karmic obstructions, one would not reach this point of inquiry; therefore, the World-Honored One was able to accord with him. △ Second, the disciple unites with the teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa, together with the great assembly, joyfully accepted the instruction and listened in silence.

They were joyful because they knew that by following the teaching to listen attentively, they would enter the stage of awakening; yet they remained silent because they feared that the discourse might overwhelm their ears.
Furthermore, it was because the conditions for the teacher and the disciple had converged; thus, the conditions between teacher and disciple were in perfect harmony.
End. △ Fourth, the request for instruction has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part has two sections:

first, the instruction on the four characteristics that obstruct the Way; second, the censure of delusion as being fruitless and the exhortation to practice. The first section has two parts: first, the instruction on the four characteristics of deluded consciousness;

second, the instruction on the four characteristics of deluded wisdom. The first of these has three parts: first, clinging to characteristics through delusion regarding consciousness; second, specifically establishing the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Small. Third, a general refutation of delusion and confusion. First:
"Good son, all sentient beings from time immemorial [until] self, person, sentient being, and life-span."
"All sentient beings" includes those in the six realms as well as those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

"Since beginningless time" refers back to the distant past of the obscured true mind (*amūrta-tattva-citta*). From this obscured true mind, there have successively arisen the eight, seven, six, and five consciousnesses.
What is now called "delusive thought" (vikalpa) refers, for the time being, to the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna).
This is because ordinary beings and those of the Hīnayāna know only that the sixth consciousness exists, while they are unaware of the eighth, seventh, and fifth [consciousnesses].
Yet, among all the consciousnesses, the sixth consciousness is already the most delusive; how much more so is this delusive thought, which arises upon the basis of that sixth consciousness?

These false and deluded thoughts are truly the most deluded among all delusions. Being deluded by such false imaginings, one stubbornly clings to the notion that there is a self within the body of the five aggregates;
this is called the mark of self (*ātman*). Calculating that this self transmigrates through various realms of existence is called the mark of person (*pudgala*).
Calculating that this self undergoes a continuous succession of various transformations—such as prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure—is called the mark of sentient beings (*sattva*).
To calculate that one’s retributional life-force remains uninterrupted and persists is called the mark of a self-possessor (*ātmagrāha*).

Among these four marks, although the latter three involve calculations that shift according to objects, they all fundamentally take the mark of a self as their basis. In the *Vajraśekhara-śāstra*, this is termed "delusion regarding the objects of consciousness.
This concludes the section on delusion regarding consciousness and the attachment to marks. II. Specifically Establishing the Ordinary and Hinayana [Views].
To recognize the four inversions as the true essence of the self (up to: those who loathe the flow [of saṃsāra] falsely perceive nirvāṇa. "Recognizing" refers to stubborn attachment.
All four characteristics contradict the truth and pursue the false; they are inverted dharmas. Being inverted, they are unreal.
Because of delusion regarding consciousness, one recognizes and stubbornly clings to them, taking them to be the true essence of the self. This, too, is an inversion.

To such an extreme do they go. From this, they conceive of a real self (*ātman*). Toward that which opposes the self, they give rise to hatred; toward that which accords with the self, they give rise to attachment.
Therefore, it is said: "They then give rise to the two objects of aversion and attachment. Yet, the notions of "self" and "person" are fundamentally illusory.
Nevertheless, they further cling to that which opposes the self as being detestable and that which accords with the self as being lovable. Thus, it is said: "Regarding the illusory..."
The substance [of delusion] is to repeatedly cling to what is false; this is the ultimate in falsity. Although it is the ultimate in falsity, it can ultimately not be severed;
therefore, it is said that "the two delusions rely upon one another," meaning the substance of delusion and the objects of delusion abide in mutual dependence.
Thus, one may either be attached to the conditioned and create conditioned karma, or one may incline toward the unconditioned and cultivate the unconditioned.
This is the Way. However, that the paths of karma are collectively termed "delusion" (mṛṣā) is because the conscious mind lacks understanding; thus, even practicing the Way is delusion.
Due to deluded karma, one follows the causes of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and receives retribution among the heavens and the human realm;
hence it is said that "deluded views cause transmigration," meaning transmigration within birth and death (*saṃsāra*). For those who weary of transmigration, [they] accord with...

Although they follow the unconditioned path, they experience its fruit as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; therefore, it is said that they "delusively perceive nirvāṇa," meaning they attain extinction within the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*).
This concludes the section on the distinct formation of ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners. △ Third, a general censure of deluded confusion.
"Because of this, one cannot enter pure awakening" (extending to) "and together with the cessation of thought, all return to delusion and confusion.
By means of these two characters ("because of this"), it refers back to the preceding [passage]: "Because of this false view, one wanders in saṃsāra or falsely views nirvāṇa.
Taking this as an obstruction, one does not see the nature of pure awakening. Because one does not see it, one cannot enter it; hence it is said, "one cannot enter."
"Pure awakening. The two phrases "not awakening" and so forth serve to prevent a question. Fearing that someone might ask:
"If all sentient beings have realized perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), why are they unable to enter it? Is it because this nature of awakening resists those who seek to enter?
Therefore, he provides this precaution: "It is not that awakening resists those who seek to enter. This means it is not the case that the nature of awakening is contrary to or rejects them.

To obstruct them so that they do not enter is neither to oppose nor reject them, nor is it to follow along with them. This is because, although there are various capacities for entry, these are not entries made by the awakened awareness (*buddhi*).

As for those who possess the capacity for entry, it is as stated in the preceding text: when a bodhisattva practices the three kinds of contemplative methods, they are able to realize and enter [the state].
Yet, even though they are able to realize and enter, this is not a matter of following along with the nature of awakening (*buddhatā*). To cause [them] to...

Because they both involve "entering," the general statement regarding "entering" and "not entering" has no bearing on true awakening. For this reason, when ordinary beings stir their thoughts, they give rise to delusion and create karma;
when those of the Two Vehicles stifle their thoughts, they sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence—both of these belong to deluded thinking.

They do not accord with the True Vehicle; therefore, it is said that they all return to delusion and confusion. This means they are deluded and lack awakening, and they are stifled and lack penetration.

The *Great Commentary* states: "This passage precisely answers the preceding question. The previous question asked: 'For what reason are they deluded and confused, failing to enter? Now the answer says:
It is because they recognize the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), whereby errors arise successively. Even if they escape the six realms of existence, they again fall into the two [extremes]."
"Vehicle. For this reason, they do not enter. Next, regarding the statement "it is not due to the obstruction of non-awakening," it is because the preceding question asked:
"For what reason do you cause all sentient beings not to enter? Therefore, this answer states: "It is not that non-awakening obstructs them so that they do not enter;
rather, it is solely because they cling to a self that they do not enter. This concludes the exposition on the four characteristics of deluded consciousness. △ Second, the exposition on delusion.
The four aspects of wisdom consist of three parts: first, the citation of the inquiry; second, the detailed explanation according to sequence; third, the concluding summary. First: "Why is this?
Because from beginningless time there has been fundamental ignorance... [until] ...the continuous pursuit of the Way fails to achieve fulfillment."
The first sentence承接 (takes up) the preceding inquiry. The *Great Commentary* states: "If one allows thoughts to stir, it is permitted that one turns away from awakening;
if one stills the thoughts, one immediately accords with the Truth. For what reason are both stirring and stilling called 'deluded confusion'?

This is because [the text] below explains this by means of the fundamental arising of ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which serves to introduce the repeated explanation of the meaning of the four phases of the delusion of wisdom. The *Direct Explanation* states: "Fundamental arising ignorance refers to..."
The first moment of non-awakening is the ignorance of the arising aspect (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*). The Dharma-body is without self (the Dharma-body refers to True Suchness;

this sutra calls it the "pure awakening true mind"). Due to a single moment of ignorance, one becomes deluded regarding the fundamental Dharma-body, resulting in the *ādāna-vijñāna*, which serves as the root of the mark of self.
From this point onward, all are the functioning of ignorance; therefore, it is said that [the *ādāna-vijñāna*] acts as its own sovereign. This is the intended meaning.

The sovereign is the self (*ātman*); "self" carries the meaning of being the master. "All sentient beings"—this refers generally to the ordinary and Hinayana practitioners within the six realms of existence—"who have been born without the moon of wisdom" means that from the time they were conceived by their parents until now, they have lacked the eye of wisdom and are thus unable to illuminate and shatter ignorance.
They falsely identify the four great elements as the characteristics of their own bodies and perceive the shadows of the six sense-objects as the self.
Because they are the manifestations of one's own mind, it is said that the nature of body and mind and so forth are all ignorance (*avidyā*).
This means they are established based upon ignorance; therefore, from this ignorance, [the delusions] can never be severed. For ignorance cannot sever ignorance itself.
That which is called "stirring thoughts and ceasing thoughts both returning to confusion" is precisely for this reason. I fear...
Still not believing, he therefore clarifies it further through a parable, saying: "For example, suppose there were a person who could not take his own life.
This illustrates that ignorance cannot sever itself; this is intended to make the point credible. "For this reason" means:
because this ignorance is not severed, not only do active thoughts and ceased thoughts alike lead to delusive confusion, but even from...
Even those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta and practice the path of a bodhisattva cannot escape confusion and distress;
therefore, they are taught that they must understand this and personally investigate it for themselves: "Observe those who love me, and see how I comply with them."
Conformity is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). That which is non-conforming and contrary to the self gives rise to hatred and resentment; this hatred and resentment is also ignorance.
Taking as its condition the ignorance that is the branch and offshoot of the mind of loving and hating, it nourishes the fundamental ignorance from beginningless time.
Thus, from the three stages of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) onward, up to the ten stages of the sages and equal enlightenment, such is the characteristic.
Continuing to seek the Way, one cannot yet avoid being deluded by wisdom and consequently falls into the four marks; therefore, it is said that none are accomplished.

Having concluded the citation of the scriptural evidence, the second section—distinguishing the sequence—has four parts: first, the interrogation and explanation of the mark of self (*ātman*); second, the interrogation and explanation of the mark of person (*pudgala*);
third, the interrogation and explanation of the mark of sentient beings (*sattva*); fourth, the interrogation and explanation of the mark of life-span (*jīvita*). First:
"Good son, what is the mark of self (ātman-lakṣaṇa)? [From here until] 'pure nirvāṇa is all the mark of self.
First, this introduces the inquiry and establishes the thesis. The preceding section stated: 'Those who seek the Way through continuous succession do not achieve success.
This implies that they are deluded by wisdom and consequently fall into the four marks. Now, it is inquired: what is called the mark of self that deludes wisdom? This follows upon..."

The first line introduces the inquiry; the second establishes the definition. It means that regarding what all sentient beings realize within their own minds, the "mark of self" (ātman) is subtle and hidden, yet it arises from one's own mind.
When there is something—whether a phenomenon or a principle—that is apprehended and grasped as being realized, its substance then manifests.

"O Good Son. To provide an illustration for the sake of explanation: following the previous statement that what is hidden and subtle is difficult to perceive and only manifests when there is proof, I fear it may not be clear;
therefore, I cite an example to provide proof and explanation. Thus it is said: 'For example, suppose there is a person.
This is not merely a metaphorical reference to a thing, but refers to an actual instance, such as 'suppose there is one matter. As for 'the hundred bones,' this refers to the human body."
"Harmonized": the hundred bones are free from ailment; they are balanced, harmonious, and in accord. "Suddenly forgetting one's body":
when the hundred bones are harmonized, one is unaware of having a self-body, just as Nan-guo Zi-qi was "dumbfounded and lost to himself.
Therefore, it is said he "suddenly forgot. "The four limbs" refers to the two arms and two thighs. "Taut" means straight and unable to bend; "slack" means supple.
They were unable to explain it. All of these cases involved failing to properly protect and nourish [the patient] according to the correct methods.

As for those who applied needles or moxibustion only slightly—whether using needle acupuncture sparingly or applying moxa cauterization briefly—they did so with the intention of definitively proving the existence of a self; however, they immediately realized that there is no such "self."
This single matter can serve as proof. Therefore, it was stated previously that there must be something apprehended and grasped for the substance of the self to manifest.
"Good son," and so forth—this takes up the profound clarity of the principle. It follows from what preceded that it is not merely a matter of objects;

within the mind, there is something apprehended and grasped which constitutes the mark of the self. This mind even extends to apprehending the Tathāgata (referring to the fruit that is realized), ultimately coming to full understanding.
Pure Nirvāṇa (spoken in terms of the principle realized). "Ultimately and thoroughly knowing" means to penetrate and realize it deeply to the very bottom.

"Pure Nirvāṇa" indicates that ignorance has already been shed. However, one must realize that even if one attains the fruit of Tathāgatahood and fully knows Nirvāṇa, there is still something being grasped as an object of realization within the mind;
therefore, it is said that all such states are the mark of self (*ātman*). This explains the nature of the self.
The section on characteristics is concluded. △ Second, the inquiry and explanation of the characteristic of the person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*).
"Good son, what is the characteristic of the person? [This continues] until: "exhaustively exhausting the realization of principle, all are termed the characteristic of the person.

First, this follows the inquiry to establish the definition. Above, regarding the deluded wisdom of the characteristic of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*), it has already been clarified; this inquiry asks: "What is [the characteristic of the person]?"

This is termed "the characteristic of the person who is deluded regarding wisdom. The following section establishes this definitively: it refers to those sentient beings whose minds attain realization.
Since realization arises from the mind, it is called "mental realization. That is to say, awakening arises from the mind, and one realizes that the subject capable of such realization is the self.

When this realization is not forgotten, it constitutes the characteristic of the person who is deluded regarding wisdom; this is because it is spoken of in relation to that [notion of] self. Thus it is named.

"Regarding 'for the person' (wéi rén): ○ 'Good son' and below elaborate upon the preceding point. The two phrases concerning 'awakening' (wù) mean that once one has awakened to the aforementioned capacity for realization as being the self, one no longer recognizes that [realization] as a self; thus, both that [object] and the self are entirely empty.

The two phrases concerning 'that which is awakened to' (suǒ wù) mean that since both that and the self are empty, this refers to the境 (object-sphere) that is awakened to (pointing back to the aforementioned wisdom of realization)."
Since [the object] is already not the self, by this analogy one should know that the wisdom capable of awakening is likewise not the self;

one should forget all emotional attachments. Even if one were to further calculate that the wisdom capable of awakening has already transcended all who can realize it, this remains still being deluded by wisdom regarding the mark of a self; therefore, it is said that all such cases constitute the mark of a person.
However, regarding "realization," it is said to be "all"; regarding "personality mark" (*pudgala-nimitta*), it is said that "all [who] do so" are meant.
This precisely reveals that whatever is realized, as long as one does not forget the wisdom that realizes it, all such cases are termed the "mark of self" (*ātman-nimitta*).

Whatever is awakened to, as long as one does not forget the wisdom that awakens to it, all such cases are termed the "mark of person" (*pudgala-nimitta*). From "Good son" onwards, because the principle is profound and clear, it builds upon the previous point that it is not merely a matter of awakening.
That which realizes is the self; this constitutes the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).
If even the mind that attains full realization of that realized *nirvāṇa* were both considered the self, this would likewise constitute the mark of a person. Such a one is merely a person.

Having thus spoken at length regarding "full realization" above, suppose the mind still harbors even a slight trace of realization or does not forget it, such that one exhaustively masters every principle realized at each successive stage.

All these are called the mark of the person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Because one realizes and attests to this as being the self, the inquiry and explanation regarding the mark of the person are concluded. △ Third, the inquiry and explanation regarding sentient beings (*sattva*).
"Good son, what is the mark of a sentient being? [up to] "that which exists and that which is perceived is called the mark of a sentient being."
First, the definition of the characteristics of sentient beings deluded regarding wisdom was established. The preceding section has already clarified this;
now, the following section defines how these are called the characteristics of sentient beings deluded regarding wisdom.

It states that for all sentient beings, there are things their own mind’s self-realization cannot reach—namely, the failure to give rise to illuminating awareness within one's own mind, thereby failing to clearly comprehend the two aspects of "self" and "other."
Neither [is it] so. This is that which is realized and awakened; it does not reach the mind. Because this mind exists, it is the mark of a sentient being.
This is because, by distinguishing between self and other, the traces of the mind become increasingly manifold. "Good man," and so forth, uses provisional words as an analogy to clarify.
That is, it employs the speech of worldly people as a comparison to reveal the truth. For example, suppose there were a person; taking him as an illustration...

One’s own mind speaks thus: "I am a sentient being. By analogy with that mind, when the cognizant wisdom (*jñāna*) stands forth in solitary independence, one knows that what that person calls a "sentient being" is neither this self nor that other. This is by analogy with that mind's cognizant wisdom.
Standing out in solitary independence, it is naturally not something that can be realized by another, nor can it be awakened to by another.

If that which is capable of being illustrated is not "I," then how can that which is illustrated be anything other than realization? The commentary explains: "I" refers to the sentient being, and thus it is not the true "I.
When the illustration is fully understood, wisdom alone remains, and thus it is beyond the reach of realization; therefore, it is not realization. Within that which is capable of being illustrated...
Why is it not that? Within the analogy provided, why is it not awakening? The explanation is that "I" refers to a sentient being, whereas that [awakening] is not the "I.
When the analogical knowledge (*jñāna*) alone remains, it is beyond the reach of awakening; therefore, it is not awakening.

This employs the terminology of worldly people to establish the logical force of the argument, demonstrating that the third stage of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) stands out preeminently, such that it cannot be equated with realized awakening (*bodhi*).
"And so it is. (The section beginning with) "Good son" concludes this characteristic. Regarding "those who have realized and awakened, all of whom are 'self' and 'person'":
this means that realizing that the mind has something realized is the mark of self (*ātman*), while realizing that the mind has something awakened to is the mark of person (*pudgala*).
