Since there must be a person wherever there is a self, and there must be a self wherever there is a person, these are spoken of collectively.
All are "self" and "person. When it says "those who do not reach the state of self and person," this refers to those whose enlightened wisdom (*jñāna*) is preeminent.
To say that there is something being cognized is to mean that the traces of the mind that has realized and awakened have not yet been forgotten.

Because these mental traces have not been forgotten, there will inevitably be incessant arising and ceasing, which proliferate and multiply. From this, the characteristic of the "aggregate of sentient beings" (*sattva-saṃjñā*) is formed. This explains the term "aggregate" (*saṃgha*).
The section on birth is concluded. △ Fourth, the inquiry and explanation regarding the mark of the life-span.
"Good son, what is the mark of the life-span? [This continues] until: "...that which one cannot see oneself, just like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)."

First, regarding the determination based on the signs of reception: it is said that the mental illumination of all sentient beings is pure. That which is awakened to and understood is the realization attained through the preceding stages;
all these arise as the luminous wisdom-illumination from within the substance of one's own mind, beyond the reach of the notions of "I" and "person.

Thus, the mental illumination is pure. Furthermore, this refers to the mind of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), because the four marks [of birth, abiding, change, and extinction] have not yet been emptied.
Because the mind’s illumination is pure, the marks of sentient beings appear; therefore, one gives rise to awakening-illumination toward these marks of sentient beings.
One awakens to the two marks of "self" and "person" that are perceived, and realizes that all wisdom capable of such perception belongs to self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), which one seeks to sever.
○ From "All... onwards, the text correctly clarifies its characteristics. Yet, one fails to realize that this very...
The awakening of the mind through mindfulness is precisely the wisdom of all karma; this refers to the subtle discrimination upon the eighth consciousness.
As for why "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is used instead of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), it pertains to cultivation and realization:

it is the reversal of delusion to return to the true, transforming the out-flowing consciousness of karma (*sāsrava-karma-vijñāna*) into the non-out-flowing wisdom of karma (*anāsrava-karma-jñāna*). That which one cannot see by oneself refers to this subtle discrimination, which is originally...
It arises from the eight consciousnesses. The eight consciousnesses cannot see themselves; yet, though they do not see themselves, they constantly continue to exist within them in a latent manner.
It is like a person’s life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which constantly continues to sustain life within the body, while the person remains unaware of it.
For this reason, it is called the "mark of the one who lives" (*āyuṣka-dharmatā*). This concludes the sequential summary and the detailed explanation. △

Third, the general summary and demonstration of the two points: first, the summary and demonstration that [the mind] is identical to sensory objects; second, the summary and demonstration that it is not severed.
Regarding the first: "Good son, if the mind perceives all as awakened" (up to) "...if one maintains a self and conceives of a self, it is likewise so."
First is the explanation by way of the Dharma. "If the mind perceives and sees" means that this perception and seeing arises from one's own mind;
this refers to the latter of the three marks. "All awakened ones" refers to the preceding three marks. "All being dust and defilement" collectively belongs to the realm of deluded wisdom;
this is first established as a premise, and what follows is the subsequent explanation. This is because the latter [mark] of the capacity to awaken...
The three stages prior to awakening are all within the pure mind; therein, one distinguishes self from other and establishes the subject of cognition and the object of cognition.

This obstructs superior progress and prevents one from attaining true cultivation; therefore, it is said that "that which awakens to the awakened object" does not depart from sensory dust, and is thus called defilement within the pure mind.
As for the analogy "like hot water," it clarifies this point: "like hot water dissolving ice."
Soup is a metaphor for the illumination of wisdom. Just as water is boiled by fire to become soup, so too does right mindfulness awaken the mind to produce wisdom.
Ice is a metaphor for ego-clinging. Just as water freezes due to cold to become ice, so too does deluded thought confuse the mind to produce clinging.
Using hot water to melt ice is a metaphor for using wisdom to sever grasping. This means that once the ice has melted, there is no longer any separate ice;

likewise, once grasping has been severed, there is no longer any separate grasping. One who knows the ice has melted realizes that the hot water itself no longer exists as such—just as the ice, through the action of the hot water, becomes water, so too the hot water, following the melting of the ice, becomes water. At this point, both the ice and the hot water...
Both are forgotten; there remains only pure water. Who else could know that ice has been melted by hot water?
This is a dissimilar analogy (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) used to conversely clarify the preceding text: that both the perceiver and the perceived are all dust and dross, defiling the pure mind.

Once one realizes that grasping is severed and wisdom is extinguished, such that both subject and object vanish together, there is immediately only the single, pure true mind. Furthermore, who could know this?
Regarding those who hold the view that the self is what is to be abandoned through wisdom: this is explained below by means of an analogy with phenomena.

To maintain the notion of a self and to perceive a self is likewise so. First, to correctly apply the analogy: if the perceiving self and the perceived self both exist in mutual relation, then the defiled and pure minds cannot manifest.
This corresponds to the previous analogy of the melting agent—the hot water—and that which is to be melted.
The ice and the water both exist within one another; thus they obstruct the pure water, preventing it from becoming clear.

Next, when they are reversed and merged—just as when not a single thought arises—the perceiving subject and the perceived object both mutually vanish. Then defilements and impurities are extinguished, leaving only the pure mind.
This corresponds to the previous metaphor of the hot water and ice merging with one another, where all obstructions are completely eliminated, leaving only the clear [water].

Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks [of existence]. For this reason, it is called the "final age of the True Dharma.
Once the True and Semblance Ages have passed, it is termed the Age of the Final Dharma. Sentient beings at this juncture are all the more to be pitied; therefore, I speak of them specifically.
To "not understand the four marks" means to be deluded regarding both consciousness and wisdom; one fails to comprehend both types of the four marks.
This is clear. If one does not understand this, one will not sever [delusion]. If one does not sever it, the grasping at a self remains.

Therefore, even if one practices the Way with diligent effort through many kalpas, it is merely called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). That which is conditioned arises from one's own grasping and personal agency;
this is the cause of the mundane world. As for the result that corresponds to such a cause, it remains within the mundane world, whether in the heavens or elsewhere.

Whether as humans, or as universal monarchs, regional kings, ministers, elders, and so forth—even if one cultivates until reaching the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception—when that retribution is exhausted, one returns once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence. If one wishes to achieve the supramundane fruits of sainthood, [one must practice differently].
Then one will ultimately be unable [to attain it]. Furthermore, there are two types of supramundane noble fruits (*ārya-phala*).

If one fails to understand the four characteristics of deluded wisdom (*jñāna*), one cannot personally achieve the noble fruits of the Mahāyāna (such as the ten stages and the wondrous fruit). Even if one were to fail to understand the four characteristics of deluded consciousness (*vijñāna*), [the same would follow].

Even the noble fruits of the Hīnayāna (the three fruits and the stage of no-more-learning) cannot be accomplished [by such means]. Therefore, this phrase carries the sense of using decline as an analogy for prosperity;

that is to say, because sentient beings of this degenerate age do not understand the four marks [of existence] and thus fail to accomplish the noble fruits, one can know that even when you were born during a time of flourishing, if you did not understand the four marks while cultivating the causes, it may likewise be called [a state of decline].
In the final age of the True Dharma, how can one not be cautious? This concludes the section on "Neither Ceasing Nor Attaining the Holy Fruit. Part Two:

A Successive Investigation and Explanation of the Reasons, in Three Sections: 1. One-sided Misapprehension; 2. Myself Not Being Liberated; 3. The Dharmas Not Being Liberated. The first [section]: One-sided Misapprehension.
Why is this? Because one takes all that constitutes a self to be *nirvāṇa*. [This continues until: "The family's wealth and treasures will ultimately never be accomplished. First, the interrogation:

Why is it that, failing to understand the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), one does not achieve the fruit of sainthood despite long-term cultivation? In the explanation: It is said that the four marks are all "self";
thus they are called "all-selves" (*sarva-ātman*). Failing to understand them means one identifies with them; identifying with them means the mind gives rise to attachment and preservation.

Attachment. To falsely conceptualize nirvāṇa is precisely its characteristic, as it was previously explained regarding the two marks of self and person: that there is realization and awakening, which is termed "attainment.
The fact that it does not explicitly mention "having knowledge" or "having awareness" can be understood by analogy. An illustration follows.

The analogy is not established. The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are all "self," yet they are detrimental to the Path; in meaning, they are like thieves. Nevertheless, one falsely calculates them as the fruits achieved by oneself;
therefore, it is illustrated by the analogy of taking a thief for one's own son. The Great Commentary (*Da shu*) states: "If a thief were outside, he could still be warded off;
but if you raise him as your child, how can you exercise vigilance? Furthermore, one must recognize that the thief is indeed a thief."
The thief can do nothing; raising him as one's own child, how could there not be ruin?
Just as the six sense-faculties perceive their objects and may still be restrained, the deluded self within the *ālayavijñāna* is difficult to discern.

Consequently, the jewels of merit within the *tathāgatagarbha* waste away with every thought-moment. Therefore, it is likened to a family’s wealth and treasures that ultimately fail to be realized. As it is said:

This is why those who have practiced for a long time fail to attain the fruit of sainthood. (Question): According to what has been said above, because one recognizes all "selves" as *nirvāṇa*, and because there is realization and awakening which is termed "attainment," it seems that "all selves" refers to that which is realized and that which is awakened.

Yet, in the previous explanation of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), you instead pointed to the "realizer" and "awakener," the "one who understands" and "the one who perceives. If so, does "all selves" seem to refer to the realizer, the awakener, and so forth?

How can it be that both the realizer and the awakener, etc., are the self, while that which is realized and that which is awakened, etc., are also the self? (Answer): When flowers are made from gold, every flower is gold; when flowers are made from paper, every flower is paper. Since the realizer, the awakener, and so forth are all [of the same nature],...

"How could that which I have realized and awakened to be separate from 'me'? Thus, it is entirely acceptable to say that all 'selves' universally encompass both the subject and the object; what cause for doubt is there?
[This has been] consistently misunderstood. △ Second, "I am not liberated."
Why is this? Those who possess self-love also love *nirvāṇa* (up to: ...), while specifically hating *saṃsāra* is called non-liberation.
This is the initial inquiry. The phrase "why is this? indicates a fundamental misconception. In the explanation, "self-love" refers to one of the four afflictions (*kleśa*).
According to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (*Lakṣaṇayāna*), the seventh consciousness (*manas*) clings to a self in accordance with conditions and is associated with these four afflictions.
First is self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), which refers to being ignorant of the characteristics of a self due to being confused about non-self (*anātman*).

Second is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which refers to falsely perceiving a self within phenomena that are not the self. Third is self-conceit (*ātma-māna*), which refers to the mind becoming haughty by relying upon the self that one clings to.
Fourth is self-love (*ātma-sneha*), which refers to deep attachment toward that which accords with the self. Now, this refers to the seventh consciousness.
Following conditions, one clings to a self, which is constantly associated with the four afflictions (*kleśa*). Consequently, one’s craving for self (*ātmasneha*) should naturally be uninterrupted;
hence it is said that there is "craving for self. Since there is craving for self, one will love whatever accords with the self; therefore, one should also love *nirvāṇa*.
However, this must necessarily subdue my root of craving and serve as the mark of nirvana. Yet, since craving for self currently exists, how could that which is craved truly be nirvana?
To claim it is so would be a mistaken recognition; is it not indeed thus?

Furthermore, regarding those who comply with me, since they have already engendered craving for me, those who oppose me must necessarily engender hatred toward me. Thus, there is also the taking up of hatred toward me.
...is what I loathe. In this way, there is one whom I loathe, and I likewise loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
However, one who loathes birth-and-death must necessarily love *nirvāṇa*. Yet, they do not realize that what they love is truly birth-and-death.
Thus we know that by loving *nirvāṇa* while separately loathing birth-and-death, the *nirvāṇa* one loves is called "non-liberation," because one has not yet departed from [attachment].
"My love" is true birth-and-death; it is precisely because it is a dharma of bondage that I have not yet attained liberation.
△ Third, the dharmas are not liberated.
How should one know that the dharmas are not liberated? (Up to: "One has still not been able to exhaust the root of the mark of self."

The first interrogation differs from the preceding two. In the preceding two cases, because those already explained were not yet fully understood, one simply used "for what reason" (*kena hetunā*) to interrogate them—meaning, "Why is it as stated above?
In this case, however, it is merely an interrogation regarding the reason itself.
This is stated in order to clarify for those who have not yet spoken [of this matter]. Therefore, he interrogates them with "How should one know? and so forth.

The Buddha’s intention is that the previously mentioned practice of the path throughout kalpas of eons could not have brought about the attainment of the holy fruit because, necessarily, both the mark of self (*ātman*) and the mark of phenomena (*dharma*) were not yet liberated. However, as has already been clarified above, I am not liberated. How then...?
Knowing the Dharma yet not attaining liberation, he next addresses the "good man" (kulaputra) to explain and establish this point.
Those who practice for Bodhi in the末法 (mofa / final age) are those who seek to realize the fruit of sainthood.

Their "slight realization" occurs within the mark of self (ātman), their awakening within the mark of person (pudgala), their understanding within the mark of sentient being (sattva), and their enlightenment within the mark of life-span (jīva); all of these possess the characteristics of partial realization.
It is termed "subtle. However, as for realization (*pramāṇa*), one reckons the aggregates (*skandha*—body and mind) to be pure; as for awakening (*bodhi*), one reckons the self (*ātman*) to be pure;

as for comprehension (*avabodha*), one reckons the person (*pudgala*) to be pure; and as for enlightenment (*vibodha*), one reckons birth (*jāti*) to be pure. Therefore, it is said that these are "self-purifications.
What remains, which is realized through enlightenment, is precisely the wisdom of all karma—the very root of the mark of self (*ātman-vikalpa*). Hence, it is said: "still..."
It has not yet been exhausted. Nevertheless, since one uses one’s own slight realization as proof for one’s own purification, this is itself a characteristic of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Although it is a characteristic of dharmas, it does not depart from the root of the characteristic of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), because one says, "This is my dharma.

Since the root of the characteristic of self has still not been exhausted, how could the characteristic of dharmas bring about liberation? This should be used as a point of inquiry; the meaning can be understood through reflection.
He proceeds to investigate and explain the reasons for this in detail. △ Third, verifying that his faculties (*indriya*) are not yet exhausted:
"If there should be another person who praises that Dharma... [until] ...he sports with his faculties without interruption."
Although this serves as proof that my faculties have not yet been exhausted, it is actually used to demonstrate that I have not yet transcended the Dharma.
To praise that Dharma and immediately feel joy is precisely a failure to transcend attachment to the Dharma (*dharmagrāha*).

If one wishes to deliver such a person, one employs skillful means to instruct them, rescuing them from their indolence and leading them toward diligence, desiring that they practice that Dharma and hoping for them to attain [liberation] together.
It is so. If one further slanders what has been attained, anger and resentment arise; this too is because one has not yet escaped the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Because one wishes to reprimand [others] even before they have spoken, it is known that the "mark of self" (*ātman*) is firmly grasped;
this refers to clinging to the dharmas that have been attained so as not to let them be forgotten. The *ālayavijñāna* is precisely the eighth, the *ālaya*.

Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*: according to the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇayāna*), the seventh consciousness internally takes the seeing-division (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, conceiving it as the self.
Since this is the seeing-division of the eighth, it naturally remains latent within the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Furthermore, "latent" is said in contrast to its active engagement with the various sense-faculties (*indriya*); because the sense-faculties are not moving and there is no dharma to grasp, it is called "latent. And as for the various...
As soon as the faculties stir, they spontaneously grasp at a self within the objects of the six sense-fields.
Therefore, it is said that they "sport like worldly thieves": when there is nothing to steal, they remain hidden and latent;
when there is something to steal, they act with spontaneous fearlessness, as if playing or frolicking. This never ceases for even a moment; they constantly and critically deliberate upon the self.

Because they follow one another, the exposition of the four characteristics that obstruct the Path is concluded. △ Second, the censure of delusion as being fruitless and the exhortation to practice, which has two parts:

first, classifying [the faults] for the purpose of censure; second, admonishing for the sake of correct cultivation. The first part has four sections: first, censuring the lack of merit due to having a self; second, censuring the lack of merit due to speaking of one's illnesses;

third, censuring the lack of merit due to misappropriating virtues; fourth, censuring the lack of merit due to increasing pride. The first section: [The text continues with the specific content of the first section.]
Good son, that practitioner who cultivates the Way does not eliminate the mark of self (and so on, up to) sentient beings and life-span; it is likewise thus.

This first section, following the preceding, clearly explains the point: namely, when one contemplates according to what has been stated above, those practitioners of the Dharma in the final age must necessarily sever the mark of self.
If they do not eliminate the mark of self, then realization, awakening, comprehension, and enlightenment will not be attained.
Free from the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span; for this reason, one cannot enter pure awakening. Praising with joy and slandering with anger are precisely the evidence of this.
○ Next, the passage beginning "Good man" and so forth uses reasoning to reveal the opposite. This means it reveals by contrast that one can indeed enter pure awakening;
it is done for fear that one might think that without eliminating the mark of self, one cannot enter pure awakening. This has already been understood.
For one who cultivates the path, there is no achievement through cultivation. Furthermore, how can one ultimately enter [the path]? Therefore it is said: "If one knows that the self is empty.

This means to realize and know the principle of emptiness and non-self. Once one has realized and known the principle of emptiness and non-self, it is natural not to feel anger when hearing disparagement;
hence it is said: "There is no one who disparages me. Since one does not feel anger upon hearing disparagement, then when hearing praise...

Furthermore, what is there to rejoice in? If one feels joy upon hearing praise, and grants permission to deliver teachings for the sake of salvation, this constitutes preaching the Dharma with a self-attachment.
Because such a person has not yet severed the notion of a self, and since the self is not yet severed, the same applies to the notions of "others" and so forth.

Therefore, he intentionally bypasses the term "person" (*pudgala*) and speaks instead of "sentient beings" (*sattva*) and "life-sustainers" (*jīva*). From this, one should understand the mark of self (*ātman*).
Since the mark of a person is empty, and sentient beings and the life-span are likewise entirely empty, one thus realizes awakening and, according to one's capacity, enters pure awareness.
This concludes the refutation of the meritlessness of clinging to a self. △ Third, the refutation of the meritlessness of preaching about illness.
Good son, the sentient beings of the末代 (final age) speak of illness as being the Dharma... for this reason, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
The sentient beings of the末代 do not understand the four marks (*catur-nimitta*). In order to save sentient beings, they preach the Dharma they themselves have attained;

yet they do not realize that preaching what they themselves have realized is precisely the mark of self (*ātman*), and preaching what they themselves have awakened to is precisely the mark of person (*pudgala*). Preaching...
They take what they themselves have understood to be the true characteristic of a sentient being, and they proclaim what they themselves have awakened to as the true characteristic of a life-span.
Therefore, it is said that they preach illness as the Dharma. This is like leading one blind person by another;
thus, they are called those who are to be pitied, for both the speaker and the listener are devoid of merit. Yet, even though the speaker may be diligent in their preaching...

The Dharma is intended to deliver sentient beings by serving as the cause for pure awakening. Yet, although those who hear it may diligently investigate, believe, understand, and practice it in order to attain the fruit of pure awakening, these efforts all serve only to increase their various ailments.
This is because they have not yet severed the mark of self (*ātman*), and thus remain bound by the marks of others and so forth.
For this reason, they are unable to enter into pure awakening. Thus concludes the refutation of the ineffectiveness of their practice regarding these ailments.
△ Third, the refutation of those who steal virtue without merit.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks [of the self] (up to the point where) they practice for themselves and ultimately achieve nothing.

Sentient beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age who do not understand the four marks (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*) are those who have not yet exhausted the root of the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), and thus cannot penetrate the fact that all four marks are empty.

Regarding "the understanding of the Tathāgata and his sphere of practice," this means that while the Tathāgata was on the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), he had long since emptied the four marks; whatever understanding he possessed was entirely pure understanding. Whatever...
All practices are pure practices. Yet sentient beings do not understand the four marks;
they instead seek understanding through the principles taught by the Buddha and cultivate the practices taught by the Buddha, only then grasping them as their own cultivation.
This is called "stealing the virtues of the Tathāgata" and taking them for one's own virtues. Little do they realize that because they fail to understand the four marks, they all fall [into error].
If one’s conditioned, pure practice and understanding ultimately fail to achieve fruition, what benefit is there? This concludes the refutation of those who pilfer virtue without merit.
△ Fourth, the refutation of increasing pride without merit.
There are some sentient beings who, not having attained [realization], claim to have attained it; for this reason, they are unable to enter pure awakening.

"Some sentient beings" refers specifically to those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). "Not having attained, yet claiming to have attained" is said in reference to the fruit of cessation in *nirvāṇa*.
This means that such a person has merely severed the four phases of deluded consciousness and has just barely escaped birth-and-death within fixed limits (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*).
This is a semblance of nirvana; in reality, they have not yet attained pure nirvana, yet they immediately claim to have attained it.

Regarding those who "claim realization when they have not realized," this is said in reference to the fruit of bodhi-wisdom; it refers to a person who has merely temporarily severed the afflictions of self-grasping.
Having merely realized the partial truth of the awakened nature—a semblance of Bodhi—one has not yet actually realized perfect, complete Bodhi, yet one immediately claims to have done so.

(This is merely a slight manifestation of overweening pride; those who rely on themselves and lecture others should certainly not be charged with the offense of a great lie among the four *pārājika* rules.
Should they see someone superior to themselves who aspires to advance further, they give rise to jealousy and say:

Envy arises when one feels unable to do as others can; jealousy arises when others excel where one does not. Both of these depend upon the mark of self (*ātman*)—the mark of self within the realm of deluded cognition—and thus it is said that because those sentient beings have not yet severed their craving for self (the last of the four secondary afflictions associated with ignorance), the four marks arise in competition.
Consequently, how could the mark of pure awakening ever enter? Therefore, by means of this...
[This section] concludes the classification of refutations. △ Second, the exhortation for correct cultivation:
"Good son, if sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age desire to achieve the Way... [they] will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening."
At the outset, there was a warning against mistaking the path for the fruit; yet in this degenerate age, there is hope for the attainment of the Way.
This refers to those who have already resolved their minds on Bodhicitta. Having resolved their minds and aspired to attain the fruit of the Way, they must first awaken to their own mind.

According to this Sūtra, this is precisely the True Mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ālayavijñāna*). To cultivate practice based upon this mind is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood. Now, however—

Do not allow them to seek awakening; this would be to be deluded regarding the True Cause. To speak at random without cultivation, or even if they do practice, will ultimately never lead to accomplishment.
Furthermore, they merely value the benefit of extensive learning, yet still consume the leftover spittle of others, claiming for themselves that they have attained personal realization.
Thus it is said that they increase their view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which conversely becomes a dharma that obstructs the Way. ○ But...
"At that moment, one must apply oneself to urgently severing delusions.

'One should simply be diligent' means that regardless of whether one has attained realization or not, one should simply unify the mind and remain free from other distractions, exerting the body without indolence.
According to the following passage, this means that severing delusions alone is the urgent task. 'Subduing afflictions' refers to first severing [them]."
The four characteristics of deluded consciousness briefly reveal the principle of emptiness and non-self, whereby one attains a semblance of nirvana.

This is because it rescues one from the immediate urgency of a burning brow; yet, even while rescuing one from a burning brow, there remains the concern that the body itself may be consumed by fire. Therefore, one is further exhorted to arouse great courage.
"Courage" means advancing in practice without retreating; "fervor" means remaining unbowed despite facing hardships. Until pure nirvana is attained, one must persevere with diligence.
One must cause [the practitioner] to attain it. One must strive to sever the four marks of deluded cognition that have not yet been severed.
When greed, hatred, craving, pride, and so forth do not arise in response to objects, this is pure nirvana; it is what is called "that which was not yet attained has now been attained.
When self, other, affection, and so forth—all such things—are utterly extinguished, this is the exhaustion of the marks of deluded cognition; it is what is called "that which was not yet..."
"Severed" means already severed. The Great Commentary (*Da shu*) states: Greed (*rāga*) has the nature of being stained by and attached to existence and the instruments of existence;
its function is to obstruct non-greed and to give rise to suffering. Hatred (*dveṣa*) has the nature of malice and resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering;
its function is to obstruct non-hatred and to serve as the basis for conduct lacking forbearance. Pride (*māna*) is the act of exalting oneself in comparison to others based on self-reliance.
Its nature is to obstruct non-pride (*amāna*). Its function is to give rise to suffering. These three are among the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*);

I have cited the *Great Commentary* (*Daishu*) to explain them briefly. As for the remaining three, since they are not fully present in the sutra, there is no room for forced interpretation. Furthermore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is not explained here.
Because craving has no distinct nature of its own and is subsumed under greed (*lobha*). Furthermore, the Great Commentary (*Da shu*) states:
"Deceit (*māyā*), crookedness (*śāṭhya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*) are the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). They are called 'minor' because they arise individually;

they are called 'secondary' because they are specific states of greed and the like, being of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). As for deceit: it is the fabrication of artificial behavior through craftiness in order to delude and deceive others; it is treacherous and crooked.
Its nature is to obstruct non-deceit (*aśāṭhya*). Its function is to hinder instruction. Its essence consists of the two factors of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).

Envy (*īrṣyā*) has the nature of being preoccupied with one’s own fame and profit while being unable to endure the prosperity of others; it functions to obstruct non-envy and results in grief and distress.
Its essence consists of one portion of *dveṣa* (hatred). Although these are four characters, they represent only two of the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Since *śāṭhya* (deceit) inherently includes *māyā* (crookedness), and *īrṣyā* (envy) inherently includes *mātsarya* (jealousy), I have explained them according to the Great Commentary (*Daishu*). As for those not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, I dare not add anything arbitrarily.

As for the statement that "no [affliction] arises in relation to objects," this reveals that both the seeds and the habitual tendencies have been exhausted; were they not exhausted, afflictions would arise immediately upon encountering objects.
To say that one is in the pure nirvana means that hearing praise does not bring joy, nor does one desire to bestow grace or deliverance;
hearing slander does not bring anger, nor does one desire to withdraw grace or reprimand. This is called "the grace of self and others."

Affection (*preman*). (If he praises what I have attained, that is his affection; if I rejoice and desire to deliver him, that is my kindness. Regarding "all things are quiescent" (*sarva-śānta*): quiescence is spoken of in contrast to movement;

this merely eliminates the branches and leaves of the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*). When both [movement and its cessation] are quiescent and extinguished, one then proceeds to eliminate the root of the mark of self.
This is because it is said that the deluded marks of cognition are exhausted. ○ From "The Buddha says" below, he permits a gradual approach.

Next is accomplishment. This means that while principle is realized through sudden enlightenment and is extinguished simultaneously with that realization, phenomena must necessarily be eliminated gradually as they are exhausted through successive stages.
For such a person, one first severs the four phases of deluded consciousness, and subsequently severs the four phases of deluded wisdom; this constitutes gradual accomplishment.
"Seeking the Good" and below teaches that one should draw near to virtuous friends and offer sincere devotion, for even a hair’s breadth of deviation [leads to great error].

Errors spanning a thousand li arise through gradual accumulation; fearing one might fall onto a divergent path, it is necessary to seek out a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for guidance and instruction, so that one may not fall into false views.
Furthermore, in seeking a spiritual friend, one should take their correct knowledge and vision as the primary criterion, regardless of whether their lineage (gotra) is high or low.
If, at the time of seeking, one does not take their knowledge and vision as the standard, [the search will be in vain].
To give rise to hatred or attachment based on the high or low status of one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*) indicates that the mark of self (*ātman*) has not yet been exhausted;

therefore, it is said that such a person cannot enter the ocean of pure awakening (*vimala-bodhi-sāgara*). To describe awakening as an "ocean" is because an ocean gives birth to all streams, and all streams flow back into the ocean;
this serves as a metaphor for the Great Perfectly Round Awakened Mind (*mahā-vartula-bodhicitta*), which gives rise to all phenomena and transforms sentient beings.
One accomplishes the mind of Great Perfect Enlightenment. As stated in the Chapter on Mañjuśrī:
"There is a great *dhāraṇī* named Perfect Enlightenment, from which flow forth all *tathatā*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās*, which instruct the bodhisattvas."
The analogy of the ocean is indeed most appropriate. This concludes the prose section. △ Second, the verse summary (the heading for the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

△ (The main verses are divided into two parts: First, one verse reveals the four characteristics that obstruct the path. Second, two verses condemn delusion regarding the lack of merit and exhort practice.
The first part (a brief verse summarizing the meaning):
"Pure Karma, you should know that all sentient beings [cannot] attain Bodhi.
Since he calls him by name and addresses him as "you," it is to manifest the urgency of his exhortation. "You should know" means that one ought to clearly understand:
"I-love" must be eliminated, and the four marks of selfhood (*catur-viparyāsa*) must be severed. All duality...
This phrase clearly indicates that self-love (*ātmasneha*) must be eliminated. Regarding "the beginningless false transmigration":

from time immemorial, ordinary beings have clung to a self and loved it, thereby giving rise to afflictions and creating karma, and thus transmigrating through the *paricchinna-śarīra-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death).

The followers of the Two Vehicles, weary of this transmigration, cultivate the path and realize cessation, yet they still transmigrate through the *pariṇāma-śarīra-jāti-maraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death). All of these are like flowers in the sky; they are identical [in their lack of inherent existence].

This reverts to falsehood. The two lines [of the verse] have not yet been eliminated; they precisely reveal that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) should be severed. All four characteristics arise from the self (*ātman*). The long prose states:
"Subduing the root of self-love is called the characteristic of nirvāṇa. Now, since the four characteristics have not yet been eliminated, the characteristic of self remains present.
If the fruit of the severance of nirvāṇa is not true, how can the fruit of bodhi-wisdom be accomplished? Therefore, it is not attained. [The] Verse:

The explanation of the four characteristics that obstruct the Path is complete. △ Second, the verse refuting delusion regarding lack of merit and exhorting to practice (summarized in verse according to its meaning), which has two parts:
first, a verse classifying [the types of practitioners] as a refutation; second, a verse of admonition for correct cultivation. First:
"Love and hatred arise in the mind; crookedness dwells within one's thoughts. For this reason, there is much confusion and distress, and one cannot enter the City of Enlightenment.

According to the prose commentary (*dīrgha-pada*), this is divided into four categories of censure: first, the existence of self (*ātman*); second, speaking of illness; third, stealing virtue; and fourth, increasing pride.
Herein, "love and hatred arise in the mind" is a verse summarizing the meaning of the first category, the existence of self; that is to say, [attachment to] those who are favorable to oneself.

Regarding "attachment": because one hates those who oppose one's will, and because crookedness (*śāṭhya*) persists within one's thoughts, these [three] are subsumed under the latter three [afflictions].

This is because there is the sense that the speaker treats the teaching as a mere remedy while the listener acts with flattery; and because there is the sense of secretly appropriating virtues to increase pride while crookedly protecting one's own shortcomings.
All of these obstruct superior progress, and thus lead to much delusion and distress. "Delusion" means not awakening; "distress" means lack of penetration. Since—
Because they were deluded and dazed, they could only enter the City of Tranquil Awakening; therefore, [the text] generally dismisses them by stating that they "could not enter.
The prose section classifies and specifically refutes this, consistently saying they "could not enter the pure awakening. To refer to awakening as a "city" carries two meanings.

The first refers to being frequently lost on the road but regaining one’s bearings upon entering the city; this is a metaphor for having already realized Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), like gold extracted from ore, because its dark nature will never again become ore.
The second refers to a gate with four paths through which one may proceed once outside;

this is a metaphor for having realized Perfect Enlightenment and yet continuing to contemplate the deliverance of sentient beings, as one can reach any direction. These verses are categorized under the section "Concluding the Refutation."
△ Second, the exhortation based on the practice of the support and the supported.
"If one can turn toward awakening and first eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion" (up to) "...ultimately it is not accomplished.

According to the long prose version, this section contains four meanings. First, there is a warning regarding the pursuit of the fruit while remaining deluded about its cause. Now, it says "if... [and so forth].

"One is able to take refuge in the land of awakening. Here, "taking refuge" means to accord with. The "land of awakening" refers to the object of awakening, for it is the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment that serves as the object of awakening.

If one can turn back from that [delusion] and not seek awakening elsewhere, but instead take refuge in and accord with perfect enlightenment to constitute the land of awakening, then the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood is complete. How could there be any delusion? Next, one should urge [the practitioner]:
Regarding the urgent severance of delusions, the instruction to first eliminate greed, hatred, and ignorance is an exhortation to sever the four marks of consciousness regarding delusion.

These four marks all arise from the self. Now, it is said that greed, hatred, and ignorance all belong to the mark of self. "Greed" refers to the arising of a greedy and affectionate mind toward those who accord with one's self;
"hatred" refers to the arising of a mind of anger and resentment toward those who oppose one's affection. Both of these belong to self-love.

This means they arise based on the same substrate of self-love (*ātmasneha*). Ignorance (*moha*) here refers specifically to self-delusion (*ātmamoha*), meaning one is deluded regarding the characteristic of a self and confused about the principle of non-self (*anātman*).

According to the prose commentary (*dīrghapaṅkti*), there should still be the two terms "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "pride" (*māna*). However, "craving" is simply greed (*lobha*), as it is subsumed under greed.
Pride is not mentioned because five terms would be difficult to accommodate, and it can be understood by referring to the prose commentary. Furthermore, the prose commentary...
There are two minor derivative afflictions (*anuparivartin*), yet they are not fully enumerated in the verse.

This is because the two terms "deceit" (*māyā*) and "crookedness" (*śāṭhya*) are subsumed under the two portions of greed (*lobha*), while the two terms "envy" (*īrṣyā*) and "jealousy" (*mātsarya*) are subsumed under one portion of hatred (*dveṣa*). These all arise from delusion regarding consciousness.

The notions of self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), sentient being (*sattva*), and life-span (*jīva*) are likewise established on this basis. For those whose minds do not harbor attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), I exhort them to sever their delusion regarding wisdom.
Regarding the four marks: yet, even the realization, awakening, and clear comprehension [of these] are all forms of attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
If one maintains a deliberate mind, one clings and thus establishes the four marks; if one does not maintain such a mind, one is liberated and enters pure awakening.

While the third [approach] allows for gradual accomplishment, what is meant here by "gradual accomplishment" is that if one merely clings to sudden awakening, one may not necessarily be able to accomplish pure awakening. Now...
Since one can both return to the realm of awakening and gradually eliminate the two kinds of four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), one may enter the ocean of pure awareness;
therefore, it is called "accomplishment. Fourth, the teaching on drawing near to friends with sincerity:

"My body fundamentally does not exist" means that when pure awareness is accomplished, one thoroughly realizes that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty; this is already reaching the emptiness of non-self (*anātman*).
This is the principle. Once one has realized the principle of emptiness and non-self, then that which opposes the self is no longer seen as opposition;
how, then, could hatred arise? That which accords with the self is no longer seen as accord; how, then, could attachment arise? In this way, one seeks instead to befriend the virtuous.
One will certainly be able to offer sincere devotion and, having received from them the instruction in right view, will ultimately not fall into error.

However, if one harbors feelings of attachment or aversion toward those practitioners based on distinctions such as their spiritual lineage or level of attainment, then even if some results are gained, they will ultimately not be true accomplishment.
This is because the presence of attachment and aversion is the very root of the mark of selfhood (*ātman*), and [one has thus] not yet...
Because it is exhausted. The Chapter on Pure Practice is finished.
△ Fourth, the Chapter on Universal Awakening has three parts: 1. Expressing gratitude for the past and requesting for the future; 2. The harmonious union of teacher and disciple;

3. The response to the request for instruction. The first two [parts] have one: 1. Expressing gratitude for the past with full ritual decorum; 2. Requesting for the future to manifest earnestness. The first of these two has one: within the assembly...
The ritual protocol is complete. Second, the expression of gratitude for the benefits previously attained. First:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Awakening), amidst the great assembly... [until] ...kneeling with his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, addressed the Buddha, saying:

This chapter takes the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Enlightenment) as its principal figure. Regarding the four phrases—“acting,” “stopping,” “relying,” and “extinguishing”—medicine and disease are presented as a dual pivot: awakening constitutes the medicine, while attachment constitutes the disease.

Because the Bodhisattva is universally able to awaken to and understand this, he acts on behalf of the assembly to pose questions; the rest of the assembly are his companions, which is why the text says "in the midst of the great assembly. The remainder is self-evident. △ Second, expressing gratitude for the previous attainment of benefit.
"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has skillfully expounded upon the illnesses of dhyāna" (up to) "the mind and will become vast and open, attaining great peace and stability.
Out of compassion for sentient beings of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age, he explains illness as the Dharma. Now, by means of the present assembly, he provides preliminary guidance;

therefore, he is called the "Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One. Regarding the phrase "skillfully expounded upon the illnesses of dhyāna," there should be a pause after the character "快" (kuài). That is to say:

"Qingxing" (慶幸) expresses a sense of joy. If these three characters are taken together, they constitute the words of the Bodhisattva of the Occasion (Dangji Pusa) expressing his joy for the sake of the assembly—much like saying, "How fortunate!
That which the Buddha has taught is truly a disease of Chan, for it is based on [the concepts of] realization, awakening, and understanding.
Awakening is attained entirely through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), yet if one clings to it, it becomes a sickness; one does not realize this for oneself.
Now, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, I have deeply awakened to the four marks of deluded wisdom. How joyful this is! This is something I have never before spoken of.
Now it is finally explained. Therefore, it is said that the great assembly "attains what they have never had before.
The four marks (the four phases of existence) are harmonized within their breast, and thus their minds and intentions become vast and open—meaning they are empty, hollow, and unobstructed.

Pure awakening enters beneath the words, and thus they attain great peace and stability—meaning they are liberated and free from impediment. Having completed the formal expressions of gratitude, [the second part follows: II. Requesting the Subsequent [Teaching].
Manifesting earnestness has two parts: first, the detailed request out of concern for the future; second, manifesting earnestness three times. Regarding the first:
"World-Honored One, in the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha... until now those blind ones have not fallen into false views."
Sentient beings of the final age who have gradually drifted far from the Buddha are still not far from the Buddha during the period when the True Dharma (Saddharma) circulates;
yet by the time of the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma), they are far removed from the Buddha.

If they further pass through the Final Dharma (Paścimakāla), they will move ever further away, descending lower and lower until it finally becomes impossible to return. At such a time, even virtuous friends will flee.
As for their physical forms, the Holy Masters do not manifest them; some remain hidden in mountain valleys, while others lie concealed in the corners of the seas.
Since the True Teaching has declined, false doctrines have naturally flourished, blazing like a raging fire such that few escape being consumed by its flames.
Nevertheless, there are those who, riding upon the power of great vows, come to ferry the lost across the straits of delusion; therefore, the preceding chapter instructs one to seek them.
Good friends do not fall into false views; however, because their practice follows the flow while their transformation works against it, there are many traces of the Path.

Were they not to receive the clear instruction of the Tathāgata, it would be difficult to avoid misrecognition. Therefore, the initial question asks which kind of person all sentient beings should seek.
This is to clearly state that one should seek the Buddha among the many people who practice in accordance with the flow and transform through opposition.
What kind of person should one seek as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? Having sought such a person, one must certainly rely upon their teaching;
yet, there is concern that the teaching they proclaim may not necessarily correspond to what they have realized themselves. Therefore, the next question asks:
"By what teaching should one rely? This means that among the teachings spoken by the Buddha whom one seeks, one should rely upon which specific teaching.

It serves as the instructional manual. Furthermore, since one must necessarily practice the conduct based upon that Dharma, there is concern that because the modes of such conduct are manifold and their cultivation involves both hardships and technical skills, he asked three times what kind of conduct should be practiced.

That is to say, he sought the Buddha’s explanation regarding which specific conduct among those many diverse modes of practice should be undertaken for dedicated cultivation. Moreover, once one has already engaged in that [practice]...

One must practice; there will inevitably be something gained. However, one must consider that within what is gained, the Path may be either true or semblance-like, and medicine and disease may be intertwined.
Therefore, the four questions ask: "What kind of disease should be removed? This refers to seeking the Buddha’s exposition of the Path.

Within those gains—whether they be the true or semblance Path—one must remove whatever semblance-diseases remain, so as to preserve the true medicine that benefits both self and others. Furthermore, since...
Having attained that Way, one must still personally resolve to cultivate it. However, within this resolution there are provisional and real, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect aspects.

Therefore, the subsequent question asks: "How does one resolve the mind? This refers to seeking the Buddha’s instruction on how, among these provisional and real, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect methods, one should resolve the mind of the causal stage so that those blind people do not fall into false views.

This clarifies the intent of the question posed. It states that sentient beings in the final age lack wisdom and rely on their own sophistry, thereby frequently falling into heterodox paths like a herd of blind men;
therefore, he now inquires in detail, hoping to receive the Tathāgata’s instruction so that they themselves may not fall into false views.
This concludes the section on the detailed inquiry. II. From here to the third part, the intensity [of the request] is revealed.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again.

It should be understood that the preceding and succeeding parts are identical. This concludes the section on expressing gratitude for the prior invitation and the subsequent request. II. The Harmonious Union of Teacher and Disciple, in two parts:
1. The Teacher’s Union with the Disciple; 2. The Disciple’s Union with the Teacher. First [The Teacher’s Union with the Disciple]:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Pujue, saying: "Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.

For the great assembly present here, this shall be transmitted face-to-face to open up right knowledge and right view. For the ordinary minds of the末法 (mofa) age, this shall be transmitted through oral tradition so that they may avoid heterodox teachings and heterodox schools.
Excellent is your question! It is fitting to speak of this again. Were it not for [relying on] the Great Vehicle..."
Regarding the power of aspiration: those who have resolved to attain universal awakening (*samantabhadra-citta*) would not be able to pose such questions.
Therefore, it is said: "That you are able to question and consult is because you have a specific purpose in mind. The Buddha already knew this; he subsequently revealed that which they had intended.
Among the five questions, only the practice (*pratipatti*) is mentioned, because the preceding [questions] sought to understand the Dharma according to the [teachings]. Subsequently...
The reason they gave rise to the aspiration for the cessation of illness was entirely to accomplish the task of spiritual practice.

"Able to bestow [benefit] upon those in the final age," and so forth, refers to the World-Honored One manifesting his strategic intent. This is because sentient beings in the final age fail to attain right knowledge and right view;

fearing they will fall into heterodox schools, they do not achieve the Noble Path. Thus, the Bodhisattvas sought out the World-Honored One so that these beings might obtain right knowledge and right view.
One forms the eye of the path of fearlessness; one does not fall into wrong views and may thus accomplish the Noble Path.
For this reason, he poses his question. The World-Honored One, rejoicing in his inquiry, therefore exhorts him: "Now listen attentively," and grants that he shall explain it for him.
It is simply when the true teacher and the student's provisions meet. △ Second, the student's provisions meeting with the teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue, together with the great assembly, joyfully received the instruction and listened in silence.

With the sincerity of those who respectfully listen, they rejoiced at the promise to speak; knowing that the World-Honored One did not withhold his compassion but would universally benefit all beings of the present and the future, the assembly remained silent, listening with tranquil and clear minds. Furthermore, this was because the conditions for the teaching and the teacher were in perfect harmony.

The section on the harmonious conditions between teacher and disciple concludes. △ Third, the section on how to seek instruction has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] has four sections:
first, showing how to seek a person; second, revealing the illness of the Dharma; third, revealing the illness of practice; fourth, revealing the arousal of the bodhicitta.

The first two [sections of the prose] have two parts: first, the primary instruction on seeking a person; second, the ancillary instruction on serving [the teacher]. The first of these two has two parts: first, clarifying the search for a person.
Second, the clarification of the benefits gained. First:
"Good son, when sentient beings in the final age are about to give rise to the Great Mind... [up to] ...they will not be attached to the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."

Regarding those who wish to give rise to the Great Mind: this refers to those who desire to resolve to generate the mind of the Mahāyāna but have not yet dared to do so, fearing that, lacking a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to guide them, they might fall into wrong views.

Such individuals must certainly seek a spiritual friend upon whom they can rely for their practice. As you previously asked what kind of person such a seeker should look for, I shall now show it to you.
One should seek those who possess right knowledge and vision. Such persons of right knowledge and vision should be verified by two criteria:
first, their mind does not dwell on signs and they are not deluded by the karmic rewards of humans or devas;
second, they do not cling to the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas and are not obstructed by the causes and effects of the Hīnayāna. By relying on such a person, one will not be harmed by the heterodox.
The delusions regarding what is perceived are thus explained; this concludes the section on seeking the person. △ Second, the explanation of the benefits obtained:
"Although they manifest amidst worldly afflictions, their minds are constantly pure... [up to] Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

The phrase "though they appear as equals," and so forth, all refers to those whom one seeks out. Confucius said: "When three people walk together, there will surely be someone among them who can be my teacher.
I choose what is good in them and follow it; I take what is not good in them and correct myself.

Whenever I observe students of recent times who associate with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they focus exclusively on criticizing the shortcomings of their friends and fail to adopt their virtues. As soon as...
Abandoning this place to go to that, and then finding fault with that to depart for another—this merely wastes straw sandals and toils one’s physical strength in vain.
I have often cited the words of Qingliang: "To clarify what is correct is to be 'south'; when the direction is fully south, it is simply south.

To increase my virtue is to be a friend; when all people are friends, they are truly friends. Consider what the World-Honored One told Bodhisattva Pujue: "Though he manifests within the dust and toil..."
The mind is constantly pure. "Dust-labor" (*rajas-kleśa*) refers precisely to the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.
This is why it is said that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), in order to deliver sentient beings who are immersed in dust-labor, must first manifest those very afflictions;
by becoming intimate and close with them, one then gathers and transforms them through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Upon reaching the contemplation of the spiritual friend—

The mind is eternally pure, and worldly afflictions do not enter it. Furthermore, it is said that one may manifest various faults and praise pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) so as not to cause sentient beings to fall into non-discipline (*avinaya*). Here, "faults" refers to the acts of non-discipline.
This means that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), in order to deliver sentient beings who possess faults, must first manifest various faults and dwell in mutual reliance with them.

Appendix: He then praised their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and guided them. Having observed that they had relied [upon him] for a long time, he did not allow those beings to fall back into non-discipline (*asaṃvara*). All of this was a manifestation of "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*).
New learners should understand these distinctions. The two lines beginning with "seeking as... are the World-Honored One’s concluding response to Pujue.
Regarding these words: as for your previous question concerning what kind of person you should seek, you must seek one who possesses the roots of the Mahāyāna and is endowed with virtuous conduct;
only such a person is fit to be inspired to arouse the Great Mind and guided toward correct practice. Thus, by means of this right condition, [the goal may be attained].
One attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Viewed from this perspective, spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) provide immense benefit;
indeed, one must certainly seek them out. This concludes the section on seeking spiritual friends. △ Second, the section on serving them concurrently.
Sentient beings of the final age who see such a person (up to: their mental flowers will radiate light, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
This first section clarifies the practice of service. Seeing such a person, one already knows that this is the primary condition for attaining Bodhi; therefore, one should make offerings.
That is to say, one should respectfully cultivate the four requisites of service, not daring to transgress them. Furthermore, by means of all manner of offerings...
Among these, the offering of Dharma is supreme. Thus, by relinquishing both body and mind to practice that Dharma, it is said that one does not begrudge body or life;
this means that even if there should be causes and conditions for losing one's body or forfeiting one's life, one still regards them with no concern.

Because that spiritual friend sees that [the practitioner] is capable of such [devotion], they demonstrate to them the practice of compliance regarding the four postures: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Within the four modes of deportment, he constantly manifests purity, serving as a standard and model for them,
so that those sentient beings may rely upon and practice it. Even toward those sentient beings who have committed various transgressions,
he demonstrates "contrary conduct" by manifesting within the four modes of deportment various faults such as lust, killing, stealing, and lying, thereby urging them [to reform].
They offer praise for their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) while simultaneously subduing them.

Although those sentient beings see such things, their minds remain free from arrogance, for they know that these acts are intended to first draw them in with the hook of desire and later lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom.

Had they not known this, they would certainly have given rise to arrogance; "arrogance" (*māna*) means to boast of one's own superiority over others, while "pride" (*mada*) means to look down upon others.
They are inferior to me; yet if they know [the Dharma], they will certainly be able to emulate my practice and cultivate it both in accordance with and against [circumstances].

If they do not know, they can only cultivate in accordance [with circumstances], and thus they are far inferior to those of harmonious consciousness (*he-shi*). Furthermore, the phrase "even more so" implies a comparison where the heavy case illustrates the light.
It speaks of various faults and afflictions, encompassing matters such as lust, killing, stealing, and lying—these being violations of the precepts (*vinaya*).
Even the Most Victorious One does not give rise to arrogance upon seeing them, much less those who are spiritual friends among the laity, who are greedily attached to morsel food and material wealth;
or those who are spiritual friends among householders, who are stained by love for wives, children, and kinsmen.
Even if they should transgress the rules of discipline, there is still no great fault; upon seeing them, one should not only refrain from giving rise to arrogance, but furthermore—
All evil thoughts will not arise at all. ○ "Good son" and below: next, the benefits obtained are explained. This is also the World-Honored One’s concluding response to Pujue.

"Good son, you should know that regarding the various faults and afflictions pointed out by that virtuous friend, if you do not give rise to arrogance or other evil thoughts, you may see therein that right mindfulness has matured within the ground of the mind."
Pure. Responding to causes and eliciting results, one is able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment and realize the true mind.
From this flower of the wisdom-mind, brilliance unfolds and radiates, universally illuminating the lands of the ten directions to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings.
It is nothing other than this. The instruction on seeking the person is concluded. △ Second, the instruction on the illness of the Dharma, in two parts:
1. The instruction on relying on the Dharma to leave illness behind; 2. The instruction that leaving illness behind is itself the correct state. The first part:
Good son, the wondrous Dharma realized by that spiritual friend should be free from the four illnesses.
Having already explained this based on the preceding discussion of karma, if one does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that virtuous friend, one will immediately attain perfect enlightenment.
Now, once again, he provides instruction: regarding the sublime Dharma realized by that spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one should remain free from the four maladies.
This "sublime Dharma" is *Perfect Enlightenment* (*yuanjue*); because it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and functions without obstruction, it is called the "sublime Dharma.
If one relies upon this Dharma, one will not fall into false views; this is the correct demonstration of which Dharma to rely upon. The four maladies:
This is precisely the practice of "resting in natural cessation. If one can become free from illness, one achieves correct practice;

by cultivating according to this, all may enter the perfect state. This is the direct demonstration of what kind of practice it is. According to the points raised by the Bodhisattva’s questions, these have been categorized and asked separately.

In the World-Honored One’s response, he generally indicates that among the matters of attending a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the sublime Dharma realized by that spiritual friend is itself the Dharma upon which one may rely;
there is no other separate Dharma to rely upon. Apart from the correct practice that cures the illness, this is the practice that should be performed;
there is no other separate practice to be performed. Therefore, he shows and exhorts [the practitioner] regarding what should be abandoned and purified.

It is called "Cloud. This means that one merely eliminates the illness, but does not eliminate the Dharma. Having thus completed the instruction on eliminating illness by relying on the Dharma, [the text proceeds to] △ Second, the instruction that eliminating illness is itself the Correct Path, in two parts:
First, a detailed explanation of the four illnesses; second, a general demonstration of the deviant and the correct.
Regarding the first, there are four: 1. Causing illness; 2. Yielding to illness; 3. Stopping illness; 4. Extirpating illness. First: [The section on] Causing Illness.

What are the four illnesses? First is the illness of action (karma). [This continues until: because it is attained through non-action, it is called an "illness. The initial phrase poses a general inquiry.
Since this belongs to a general inquiry, it applies universally to the following four points; thus, they should be treated as a single section.
It would be inconvenient to divide them separately as isolated phrases, so the inquiry is placed here. First, the sentence establishes the heading: "If, furthermore," and so forth.

Explanation and establishment: Furthermore, if there is another person who, referring to a certain class of practitioners, speaks thus to reveal those who do not practice—saying that these are merely thoughts arising from the mind and utterances of such false conceptualization, "I perform various practices within my original mind"—this is a mistaken interpretation of the meaning within the previous illusory contemplation (*māyā-vipaśyanā*). It arises...
To engage in various practices with the desire to seek Perfect Enlightenment is, in truth, not to have realized that one must first awaken to Pure Enlightenment;

only then, by means of the mind of Pure Enlightenment, can one give rise to illusory wisdom, observe those illusory multitudes, and initiate illusory practices, until even illusory appearances are forever extinguished, whereby one finally fulfills the pure and wondrous conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Now, you are instead engaging in empty and false deliberations, mistakenly imitating that [awakened state].

If one practices with the desire to seek Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodhi*), how could it ever be attained? One should know that Perfect Enlightenment is pure and fundamentally requires no cultivation;

how could it be produced through effort? Therefore it is said: "That nature of Perfect Enlightenment cannot be produced through effort; to speak of it as such is called a sickness. This is indeed appropriate.
This concludes the section on the sickness of effort. II. The Sickness of Indulgence.
Second, the illness of being "unconstrained" (*anupādāna*): If there is another person... [omitted] ...it is called an illness because it does not exist through non-appropriation (*anupādāna*).
Second, the phrase provides the heading; the following section explains and establishes it.

"If there is another person" still refers to a certain class of practitioners, by contrast revealing that those who do not practice lack this false conceptualization. It is also from... [omitted] ...saying such things.
The mind gives rise to a thought, forming such false conceptualizations as these: "We are now falsely presiding over ourselves, having already fixed our destiny within this state.
Speaking thus, they do not sever birth and death, and so the wheel of birth and death turns eternally.
Speaking thus, they do not seek nirvana, and so they are forever turned away from it. In both nirvana and birth and death, there is no thought of arising or ceasing.
This means that regarding *nirvāṇa*, one is eternally estranged from it by others, yet there is no thought of seeking its arising;

regarding *saṃsāra*, one is constantly transmigrating through it by others, yet there is no thought of its cessation. One-tastedly, one leaves everything to them, following the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As for *saṃsāra*, one leaves *saṃsāra* to others; as for *nirvāṇa*, one leaves *nirvāṇa* to others. This is a mistaken interpretation of the "Universal Eye" chapter.
Because awakening is already perfected, one is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from them; one neither loathes birth-and-death (saṃsāra) nor craves nirvāṇa.
To thus engage in such false conceptualizations of "neither this nor that" while seeking to attain perfect awakening—how could that ever be possible?
One should know that although the nature of perfect awakening is fundamentally without cultivation, [it is not something to be attained through effort].
It is not that the power of illusion cannot be cultivated; rather, how could it be something that exists merely by being subject to others?

Therefore, it is said: "That nature of perfect enlightenment does not exist by mere dependence; thus it is called a 'sickness. This concludes the section on the sickness of dependence. △ Third, the cessation of the sickness.
Third, the cessation of illness: "If there is another person... [up to] "...it is called 'illness' because it is not the union of cessation.
Third, the phrase establishes the definition; the following section provides the explanation. "If there is another person" may be understood according to the preceding context.
To speak such words is still to give rise to thoughts from the mind; to utter such words of false conceptualization is entirely delusion.
[He] reflects: "All [mental] activities arise from one's own mind. Now, desiring to bring all thoughts to eternal rest, how could they be summoned from without? Therefore, it is said:
'I shall now, within my own mind, bring all thoughts to eternal rest. The meaning is that because of these various thoughts, one perceives all phenomena."
Regarding the distinction of arousal: if one were to permanently cease all thoughts, one would then attain the quiescent equality of all natures.
This is a mistaken interpretation of the meaning of the "Chapter on Pure Wisdom," which states that throughout all times, one does not give rise to deluded thoughts;
yet you have fabricated this false calculation of "permanently ceasing all thoughts. You do not realize that the more diligently you strive to cease them, the more numerous those thoughts become.
As soon as one gives rise to a single thought of stilling the mind, one merely adds another layer of deluded thought upon the existing delusion.
If this is the case for a single thought, it will be so for every thought that follows. If one seeks perpetual stillness in this manner, how could it ever be attained?
To seek Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue) by such means is truly impossible. One should know that Perfect Enlightenment is pure and inherently free from all delusions.

[The Buddha] said: "What need is there to further employ cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) in order to seek union? Therefore it is said: 'That nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not attained through cessation or union;
to speak of it as such is called a sickness. This concludes the section on the cessation of sickness. △ Fourth, the eradication of sickness.
Fourth is the cessation of illness. If there is another person... [up to] ...it is called "illness" because it is not the mark of tranquility. Fourth is the heading that establishes the topic.
From "If there is another person" onwards is the explanation that accomplishes the meaning. "If there is another person" should also be understood according to the preceding section.
"To speak such words" refers to the false conceptualization arising from the mind; it refers to speaking such words as "permanently severing the afflictions. Its...
The mind and body that receive retribution are all driven by afflictions (*kleśa*). Now, one wishes to sever them so that they do not arise again;
therefore, it is said that "all afflictions are forever severed. Once they are forever severed, there is no delusion (*moha*); with no delusion, there is no karma (*karman*).
If there is no karma, how could there be a body and mind to receive retribution? Thus, it is said that the body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent.

There are. Furthermore, the body and mind constitute the general characteristics of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), while the sense organs and objects constitute the specific characteristics of the body and mind.
Since the body and mind are empty and non-existent, how much more so are the six sense organs, the five sense objects, and the illusory realms of the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*).

Furthermore, what could possibly remain? Therefore, it is said that "all is eternally quiescent. This is a mistaken interpretation of the meaning of severing all afflictions and conforming to cessation within the previously mentioned contemplation of extinction;
in truth, one has not understood it. By cultivating with a mind of pure awakening, there is absolutely no room for such deluded conceptualizations.
Now, to conceptually construct that "all is eternally quiescent" while seeking Perfect Enlightenment is like using a square [tool] to [measure a circle].
It is like a piece of wood that one wishes to insert into a round hole; I certainly know it will not fit.

One should understand that the wondrous, perfect nature of enlightenment (bodhichitta) is fully endowed with virtues and functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, being unimpeded and inconceivable. How could a mind dwelling in quiescence possibly correspond to it? Therefore, it is said:
"That nature of perfect enlightenment is not a mark of quiescence; therefore, it is called a 'sickness. This concludes the detailed explanation of the four sicknesses. Part Two.
This provides a general indication of the heterodox and the orthodox.
One who is free from the four maladies knows [the state of] purity. (Up to: "If one observes otherwise, it is called heterodox observation.
The first two lines conclude by indicating purity; that is to say, if one is able to be free from those four maladies, then one knows that person is [pure].
Pure cultivation: "Acting thus" and below refers to distinguishing between the correct and the deviant according to their respective divisions.

That is to say, one who practices *Perfect Enlightenment* while performing this contemplation and remaining free from the four maladies will enter the true nature of *Perfect Enlightenment*; this is called "correct contemplation."

If one practices the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment through other views and does not necessarily distance oneself from the four maladies, such a person will fail to enter the true nature of Perfect Enlightenment;
this is called "erroneous contemplation. To practice in reliance upon correct contemplation is the level path to Buddhahood;
to practice in reliance upon erroneous contemplation will inevitably lead to sinking into the perilous paths of Māra. Those who are resolved upon Perfect Enlightenment must [not...].

Not yet explained. The exposition on the illnesses of the Dharma is complete. △ Third, the exposition on the illnesses of practice has two parts: first, showing the entry into perfection through cultivation;
second, showing liberation through the removal of illness. First [part].
