"Good son, those sentient beings in the末法 (mofa/declining dharma) age who wish to practice [the path]—[from here until] 'only by practicing in this way will they enter Perfect Enlightenment'—are sentient beings of the末法 age who are far removed from the Buddha. Those who wish to practice encounter many obstacles and conditions;

without relying on virtuous friends to provide guidance and stabilization, it is difficult to avoid entering deviant paths. 'One should devote one's entire life,' etc., are words of correct admonition and exhortation."

"Providing offerings throughout one's life" means to supply the four requisites for as long as one's physical life lasts; do not be diligent in the morning and lax in the evening, nor be close in the day and distant in the month.

Generally, "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra) is termed "knowledgeable friend" (jñānamitra), and "knowledgeable friend" is called "good friend," according to the convenience of the speaker without much distinction. Since both terms are used here in the scriptural text, the commentary should follow suit.
They are distinct. Since they are called "friends" (*mitra*), they should refer to fellow students and companions;
however, because one takes those whose nature is virtuous and dwells with them, gaining the benefit of mutual exhortation between one another, they are termed "virtuous friends."

Regarding the requirement that one must provide offerings for the rest of their life: it is feared that if the four requisites are insufficient, they will be unable to settle their minds and cultivate the Way.
Therefore, we shall mutually exhort, polish, and admonish one another to bring about their benefit.

A true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) should point out the lineage of teachers to be approached—one who possesses right knowledge and right view, is able to discern the Dharma and recognize the capacities of others—and through whom, upon initial intimacy, one may untangle attachments and cast off fetters. Long-term...

Since one will surely extract the nails and pull out the wedges in the near future, it is called "good. Teaching them to observe the etiquette of a disciple and to skillfully attend to the handkerchief and water vessel is therefore termed "service.
For those who wish to seek proximity, the teacher may do so because of their observance of etiquette and skillful service, or because they perceive that the time has come and the capacity is mature;
thus, the teaching comes without waiting for a request. Regarding "one should sever arrogance": *māna* (pride) refers to—
Self-exaltation and arrogance consist of looking down upon others; such ignorant folly occasionally occurs. As it is said:
"If even those I know come near me, why should I go to seek them out? These two sentences alone constitute both pride and arrogance.
Furthermore, as for departing [from a place], it may be for the purpose of subduing this pride and arrogance, or to respond to the karmic resonance of others. Thus one departs.

Because there is benefit in both cases, one should sever resentment. "Anger" (*krodha*) refers to the arising of fury when standing; "resentment" (*upanāha*) refers to harboring a grudge in the heart.
As for "ignorance and lack of knowledge," these also occur occasionally. For example, it is said: "Let him go; I shall not follow after him again.
From this point on, I shall never seek him out. These two phrases alone constitute both anger and resentment. However...
This pride and resentment are both causes and conditions that obstruct the Path; therefore, each is entrusted [to you] as something to be severed.
As for the manifestation of adverse and favorable conditions: the favorable are such as precepts, concentration, and wisdom, while the adverse are such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

These are all skillful manifestations made in accordance with the capacities and needs of sentient beings. The adverse are certainly not adverse, and the favorable are likewise not favorable; thus it is said: "It is just like..."
Space. Since both compliance and resistance are like space, one can naturally understand that the body and mind of the spiritual friend are ultimately equal;
they do not manifest compliance because of a good person, nor do they manifest resistance because of an evil person.
This is because they are identical with all sentient beings. The essence of the enlightened nature has no differentiated views; how, then, could it admit of [such distinctions]?
"Practicing in such a way—alternating between aversion and affection within that interval—one will only then enter Perfect Enlightenment.

This means that as I have explained, by thus making offerings to virtuous friends and serving spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*), and by practicing in reliance upon them, one becomes free from the causes and conditions that obstruct the Path;

therefore, it is said that "one will only then enter Perfect Enlightenment. This concludes the demonstration of the practice for entering Perfect Enlightenment. △ Second, the demonstration [of the result].
Liberation removes illness.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age cannot achieve the Way (up to: "self and others, hatred and love are likewise thus").
The above text concerns making offerings to virtuous friends and serving spiritual mentors; by practicing in reliance upon them, one will finally enter Perfect Enlightenment.
This is because they lack the various obstructive conditions such as enmity, kinship, hatred, and attachment.
By this, one knows that the reason sentient beings in the final age cannot achieve the Way is not without cause; hence it is said, "due to these beginningless [afflictions]," and so forth.
"Beginningless" refers distantly to the obscured true mind, which has no point at which its commencement can be grasped; it is obscured and dark.
The true mind, relying upon ignorance, transforms into the ālayavijñāna, and from this arises the mind that conceives of a self.

Because of this conception of a self, one falsely discriminates between self and other. If there is someone who opposes oneself and accords with another, one immediately gives rise to a mind of hatred;
furthermore, if there is someone who opposes another and accords with oneself, it causes one to give rise to a mind of attachment. This is the case regarding persons; as for dharmas, it is likewise.

It is likewise so. Because of this, one gives rise to aversion and attachment toward humans and dharmas, thereby perfuming and forming all seeds of love and hatred within the field of the eight consciousnesses.
Yet you boastfully claim not to know how to practice; even if you were to practice, [it would be in vain].
Furthermore, this does not go beyond merely eliminating their active manifestation (*samudācāra*). Since the seeds within the field of consciousness (*vijñānabīja*) remain, one is not yet liberated.

How, then, can the Path be accomplished? Because they arise immediately upon encountering conditions and are capable of acting as obstacles to the Path, it is known that to accomplish the fruit of the Path, one must completely liberate the seeds in the field of consciousness. What are the characteristics of attaining such complete liberation? Therefore, it is said:

Furthermore, suppose there is a person who, for the sake of lending something to another and demonstrating its characteristics, considers an enemy—one who harbors a deep-seated resentment in the heart and causes harm upon encountering one—as the most loathsome among men;

and considers a parent—one who is tied to one's body as a closest relative and brings benefit upon relying on them—as the most beloved among men. Yet, it is said that one should contemplate that enemy.
If one regards others as one's own parents, then there is no enmity greater than hatred, nor any kinship greater than love; thus it is said that "the mind has no duality.
This must necessarily mean that both the seeds and the manifestations of hatred and love toward oneself and others have been completely exhausted;
hence it is said, "one immediately eliminates all illnesses," which refers to the total exhaustion of both seeds and manifestations. Furthermore, the four preceding illnesses all arise from hatred.
They arise from craving. If both the seeds and the manifestations of that craving are completely exhausted, then none of these ailments will exist.
However, while the above discussion concerned hatred and craving within the human realm, the four ailments pertain to hatred and craving within the realm of phenomena (*dharma*). One might wonder:

even if the seeds and manifestations of hatred and craving among humans are both exhausted, why would the ailments not likewise all vanish? Anticipating such a doubt, the following section [proceeds].
To provide a clear illustration: among all phenomena, regarding the feelings of aversion and affection toward oneself and others, it is as follows:

if one’s own mind arises while another’s ceases, one will necessarily love the arising and hate the ceasing; if one’s own mind ceases while another’s arises, one will necessarily love the ceasing and hate the arising.
As it is with arising and ceasing, so it is with subsiding and extinguishing. This is what is called "aversion within phenomena."
Regarding "loving-kindness": beyond this, one merely brings the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) to an end.

If one contemplates those afflictions and the cycle of birth and death as being identical to bodhi and nirvāṇa, such that the mind perceives no duality between them, then both the seeds and the manifestations are exhausted; thus it is said, "it is likewise.
This means that it is just like regarding an enemy as one's own parents—the mind perceives no duality between them. Now, as for self and other...
Hatred and attachment are the primary causes for contracting illness and the most potent conditions that obstruct the Path.
Although their arousal stems from self-grasping, their initial origin lies in ignorance. I have already explained this at length previously, fearing it might not have been taken to heart;
now, following the instruction on removing illness, I shall reiterate this as a final exhortation. It is most to be avoided when arising toward those one knows well, and yet one desires—

This causes both the seeds and the manifestations [of afflictions] to be exhausted simultaneously. Having been born in this末法 (mofa) age, I receive the Buddha’s compassion from afar; reciting his sincere words three times, I cannot restrain my tears.

Those with the aspiration for Perfect Enlightenment (Yuánjué) should especially pay close attention. The instruction on the illness of practice is concluded. △ Fourth, the instruction on generating the bodhicitta.
"Good son, if sentient beings in the末法 (mofa/deteriorating age) desire to seek Perfect Enlightenment (*vibhutva*), [they should]—up to—" thus resolve their minds so as not to fall into false views.
This section is largely identical in its textual meaning to the instruction on subduing the mind found in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Both Guifeng Zongmi and Hanshan Deqing have commentaries on this. That sutra says: The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas..."

"One should subdue the mind in this manner. Now, it is said that sentient beings in the末法 (dharma-ending age) who seek Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue) should resolve their minds and speak these words. That sutra teaches the use of four minds to subdue the deluded mind;
this sutra directly teaches the arousal of four kinds of minds. Since the four minds have been aroused, the deluded mind need not be subdued.
Furthermore, that sutra states: "All categories of sentient beings are briefly divided into ten types, such as those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, and transformation;
these are called the sentient beings to be saved. Now, when it says "all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space," this encompasses all ten classes.
To save them universally and impartially, without discriminating between enemies and kin or ease and difficulty, is the vast mind.
Furthermore, that sutra states: "I shall cause all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder). Being without remainder means transcending that which has remainder;
this is the method of reaching the destination. The present sutra states: "I shall cause all to enter ultimate *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfectly complete awakening).

Being ultimate means crossing over both the beginning and the source; this too is the method of reaching the destination, which is the primary mind. Moreover, that sutra says: "Thus, [they] extinguish..."
He delivers immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, yet in reality there are no sentient beings who attain liberation.

Because in reality they do not exist, he does not perceive any sentient beings to be delivered. Although they are immeasurable and boundless, he does not give rise to the thought that they are difficult to deliver.

Now, it is said that within perfect enlightenment there is no one who attains awakening; this too is not seeing any sentient beings to be delivered. It is only in this way that one can [fulfill this task].
"Constantly delivering" (*chang du*) refers to the "constant mind. Furthermore, that sutra says: "For what reason?

If a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self (*ātman*), the mark of a person (*pudgala*), the mark of a sentient being (*sattva*), or the mark of a life-span (*jīvitā*), they are not a bodhisattva. First, the inquiry "for what reason? means:
for what reason must one necessarily not view sentient beings as those to be delivered? In the explanation, [it begins] with "if... and so forth.
If one perceives sentient beings as being capable of being saved, then the four marks arise simultaneously; such a person is not a bodhisattva.
This present sutra contains no qualifying terms, but speaks directly of eliminating all marks—self, other, person, and so forth—which is precisely the non-perverted mind.
Maitreya’s verse summarizes the meaning of that sutra, saying: "Vast, foremost, and eternal; his mind is non-perverted. These are the four.
This is how the mind derives its names. Furthermore, while that scripture speaks of "Nirvana," this scripture is titled "Complete Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*).
According to the preceding passage in the Mañjuśrī Chapter, it states: "There is a great *dhāraṇī* called Complete Enlightenment, from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, and *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, one knows that Complete Enlightenment is precisely the One Mind, and that *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are likewise so designated.
These are all merely different designations according to conditions. Such a resolve for awakening does not fall into false views;

this is because the characteristics of a self, a person, and so forth are all shown to be false views. This concludes the summary that one should seek clear instruction. The prose section is finished.
△ Second, the verse summary (the title of the verses states):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

(The prose version contains five sections; the verse version condenses them into four, being a summary based on their thematic content. Four [sections]: 1. A single verse summarizing the primary instruction on seeking the person;
2. A combined verse on relying on the Dharma to leave illness behind; 3. A combined verse on practice and liberation; 4. A direct verse on revealing the arousal of the bodhicitta. First:
"Universal Awakening, you should know that for all sentient beings in the final age... (up to) those whose minds are far removed from the Two Vehicles.
Since they seek those with correct knowledge and vision, and furthermore remain distant from the Two Vehicles, they should follow and rely upon them.
That this is not versified here is to be understood by reference to the prose section. △ Second, the combined verse on relying on the Dharma to leave behind afflictions.
Within the Dharma, one eliminates the four maladies—namely, striving (*ābhoga*), laxity (*pramāda*), cessation (*nirodha*), and extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
These are the phrases within the Dharma. The verse relies on the Dharma to eliminate the maladies; the phrases on striving and cessation specifically indicate the characteristics of the maladies.

It does not separately verse the elimination of maladies as being "correct," because this meaning is already contained within [the preceding]. △ Third, the combined verse on the practice of liberation.
"Associate with those free from pride and remain far removed from those harboring anger" (up to) "the root of precepts is forever pure.
These two lines briefly summarize the meaning of practicing and entering the Perfect [Teaching]. This refers to being able to rely upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
To be free from pride and resentment is precisely the practice by which one may enter the Perfect [Teaching].

As for "those who are close," this refers to teachers who condescend to suit the capacities of their students; however, students are prone to develop pride, which serves as a condition that obstructs the Way. Therefore, it is said they "lack the precepts.
As for "those who keep their distance," this refers to teachers who must attend to other circumstances; however, students are prone to develop resentment, which likewise obstructs the Way.

Because of these conditions, there is no cessation. The five lines beginning with "seeing various [objects]" (*jñāna*) are a reiteration in verse of the prose section explaining that liberation from hatred and love eliminates all illnesses;
the phrasing is not strictly identical, as it is a versification based on the underlying meaning.

"Seeing various objects" (*nānāvidha-viṣaya*) refers to seeing those spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) manifesting various states, such as appearing hostile or appearing compliant; the mind should then give rise to wonder.

As for those who possess [such a mind]: when they encounter favorable conditions, they do not give rise to excessive attachment; when they encounter adverse conditions, they do not give rise to excessive aversion.

In all cases, they maintain within their minds the thought that this is something rare and difficult to encounter, such that even if there were evil conduct, it would be as if a Buddha had appeared in the world.

This is simply because they have generated a perception of the person as being like a Buddha. Since they perceive them as being like a Buddha, they certainly will not suspect that following [their] conduct constitutes a violation of the Vinaya.
[The ritual procedure. Even when practicing in reverse order, one knows for oneself that the roots of one’s precepts are pure. In this way, one draws near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
For one in whom both seeds and manifestations are entirely exhausted, neither self nor others—nor hatred nor affection—can exert any influence. This concludes the verse on the practice of liberation.
△ Fourth, the verse on the instruction for generating the bodhicitta.
To deliver all sentient beings so that they ultimately enter perfect enlightenment (up to the point of realizing enlightenment and entering parinirvāṇa):
to universally deliver all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space with equanimity is the "vast mind.
To ultimately transcend both the beginning and the source and realize entry into the nature of perfect enlightenment is the "supreme mind. It is free from the distinction of self and other.
A person who has already attained the awakening of non-appropriation possesses a mind that is not inverted, due to its constant nature.

To give rise to these four minds is itself right knowledge and right wisdom. By practicing in reliance upon them, one becomes free from attachment and aversion toward self and others, and thus transcends false views.
When the correct cause is established, the wondrous fruit can be attained; therefore, it is said that one realizes awakening.
Parinirvāṇa refers to the realization and entry into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*); this is parinirvāṇa.

Thus we know that while the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is termed "nirvāṇa without remainder," this present sutra is termed "ultimate perfect enlightenment. There is nothing at all strange about this.
This concludes the fourth section of the major outline: the four questions and four answers on the teaching for cultivation.
△ Section Four: Showing the Fruit through One Question and One Answer, divided into three parts: 1. Expressing gratitude for the previous [teaching] and requesting the subsequent;

2. The convergence of teacher and disciple; 3. The request for an exposition. The first two [parts] consist of: 1. Expressing gratitude for the previous [teaching] with full ritual propriety; 2. Requesting the subsequent [teaching] to manifest earnestness.

The first of these two consists of: 1. Full ritual propriety within the assembly; 2. Expressing gratitude for the benefit received from the previous [teaching]. The first [of these]: [The text continues with the specific liturgical details.]
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, amidst the great assembly (up to the point where he) knelt with his right knee on the ground and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

This chapter takes the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment as the principal figure (to demonstrate the Dharma of the true fruit; for one who has not deeply realized the nature of perfect enlightenment cannot accord with it), while the rest of the assembly are merely companions;
thus it says "amidst the great assembly. The rest may be understood. △ Second, expressing gratitude for the benefits previously received.
The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, for our sake—as well as for the sake of sentient beings in the final age—has brought about great benefit.
He has responded to the immediate request of those present and extended his grace to the capacities of those in the distant future; thus he is called the "Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One.
To say that he "extensively expounded various skillful means of pure awakening for our sake" refers generally to himself.
From the stage of faith (*śraddhāṅga*) onward, through the stage of understanding (*adhimokṣa-aṅga*), one arrives at the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-aṅga*).
The Tathāgata has repeatedly revealed these teachings, all for the purpose of extensively explaining the practice of purification within Perfect Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*).

Through various skillful means—such as the indirect indications of "returning to the source" (*pratīpa-nirdeśa*), "removing illness and departing from marks," and "cultivating contemplation to extinguish illusions"—he ensures that sentient beings of the末法 (final dharma) age may be reached far into the future, not only in the present.

The assembly of Dharma-practitioners shall receive benefit. This Dharma-gate shall be transmitted successively after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, even when the periods of the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma have passed and during the time of the Final Dharma.

It shall cause sentient beings of that final age to rely upon these various skillful means and practice them gradually, so that they may ascend to the most supreme Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that there is great increase [of benefit].

[The Master] further [recites the verses]. Having completed the formal expressions of gratitude before [the assembly], △ Second, requesting [the Dharma] afterwards to manifest one's earnestness, in two parts: First, the preparatory methods for requesting afterwards;
second, manifesting earnestness up to three times. Regarding the first:
“World-Honored One, we have now attained awakening” (up to) “bestowing great benefit upon sentient beings of the final age.
The Bodhisattva responding to the occasion refers to the assembly present before him, hence saying, “We have now attained awakening.
Having received direct instruction from the Buddha’s own lips and face-to-face, he says, “we have now attained awakening. This means: how does one give rise to faith through this awakening? How...
What is the awakening of understanding? How does one initiate cultivation? It is not merely that understanding is designated as "awakening.
Sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age are born after the Buddha’s passing; they have not yet had the opportunity to personally receive his golden words.

Thus, they do not know how to give rise to faith, how to awaken understanding, or how to initiate cultivation. Therefore, it is said that those who have not yet attained awakening—since they have not yet attained awakening—may, according to their respective capacities...
One should reflect upon this. Whether establishing a site or fixing a date, these matters may all be determined according to one's own convenience.

However, if one encounters the beginning of the summer season, one must certainly enter the *varṣā* retreat for practice. Regarding the ritual procedures for entering the retreat, there are distinctions between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna;

therefore, the question is asked: "How [should it be done]? This means that one should seek the definitive ritual procedures from the Buddha, whether by way of the Mahāyāna or the Hīnayāna, before proceeding with confidence.
Practice in accordance with this. Otherwise, one fears that practice will be erroneous and thus useless.

The realm of the pure *Vajracchedikā-pratyutpanna-samādhi* (Perfect Enlightenment) is unmixed with the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) and untainted by the two deaths (*dvi-mṛtyu*). It is all-pervasive and pure, leaving no room for anything else within it.
Therefore, regarding the three kinds of pure contemplations within this Perfect Enlightenment, they refer to the three methods previously explained for practicing Perfect Enlightenment.
“Pure Contemplation” (*śubha-vipaśyanā*) refers entirely to those who have already attained awakening. As that text states:
“If bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect *bodhi* (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they take the mind of pure awakening as their practice, regarding stillness as their conduct,” and so forth.

Now, with reference to those in the末法 (final age) who have not yet awakened, it merely concerns the question of what should be taken as primary within *śamatha*, what should be taken as primary within *samādhi*, and [what should be taken as primary] in *dhyāna*.
Within that [teaching], what serves as the primary principle? Therefore, these questions are asked together.

We pray that the Greatly Compassionate One will seek the Buddha’s pity and, for the sake of the great assembly, provide immediate benefit for those in the present, and for the sake of sentient beings in the final age, provide lasting benefit for those of the future.
Regarding "bestowing great benefit": it causes them to practice in accordance [with the teaching] so that they may advance toward the realization of the fruit of Great Perfect Enlightenment.
This concludes the request for subsequent expedient means. △ Second, from verse three onward, the manifestation of earnestness.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again. It may be understood according to what preceded.

This concludes the section on "Expressing Gratitude for the Prior Request and the Subsequent [Acceptance]. Part Two: The Harmonious Union of Teacher and Disciple. This has two sections: First, the union of the teacher with the disciple;
Second, the union of the disciple with the teacher. Regarding the first:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, saying: “...Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
He spoke these words once more, praising him with the words “Excellent! because this single inquiry would benefit both those present at the assembly and those of the future Dharma-ending age.
He further showed the teaching of the ultimate fruit; for one who does not possess perfect enlightenment cannot pose such a question. Therefore, he said:
"You are indeed capable [of this], whereas others cannot. Regarding such skillful means (*upāya*), there are briefly two types:
first, general skillful means, which refers to the general methods for practicing *圆觉* (Perfect Enlightenment);

second, specific skillful means, which refers to the specific methods of the three kinds of pure contemplation (*śubha-vipaśyanā*). You shall know these from the Buddha’s response; you have now obtained these specific methods."
Thus, the three contemplations can be accomplished; once the skillful means are mastered, Perfect Enlightenment can be realized.

This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s great benefit bestowed upon all sentient beings. Since the teacher and the student have now converged, he instructs them to listen attentively and grants his permission to speak—meaning that he shall speak immediately following this moment. The convergence of teacher and student is complete. II. The Student.
He joined with the Teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, having received the instruction, rejoiced; together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.

"Having received the instruction and rejoicing" means having received the teaching granted by the admonition; he rejoiced because his question was not in vain. Together with the assembly, they listened in silence.
This is because it is rare to hear of these two skillful means, and hearing them brings great benefit. The conclusion of the conditions for the meeting between teacher and disciple.

Part Three: How to Seek Instruction. This has two sections: first, the prose; second, the verses. The first section has three parts. First, the instruction on the general characteristics of skillful means.

Second, the instruction on the methods for specific characteristics; third, the instruction on the cultivation and realization for those of dull faculties. The first [section] has four parts: first, the method of contemplation according to one's capacity;
second, the method of practice with a fixed time limit; third, the method of entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*);
fourth, entering the period to demonstrate the absence of erroneous grasping. First:
"Good son, if all sentient beings [should] while the Buddha dwells in the world... (up to)... contemplate and examine according to their respective capacities as I have explained.
The address "good son" is used to call upon those who are suitable vessels so that they may pay close attention; do not listen superficially. "All sentient beings" refers to—
Regardless of whether a Buddha is present or absent, this encompasses all those who possess the Mahāyāna nature.
"When a Buddha dwells in the world" refers collectively to the period when a Buddha is present; "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" refers collectively to the period when no Buddha is present.

Furthermore, during the time when no Buddha is present, there are three stages in the movement of the Dharma: first, the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), which means not long after the Buddha has departed.
In the time of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), there is the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit. Second is the time of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*);

this refers to when one gradually moves further from the Buddha and only the semblance of the teaching remains. Although there is the teaching, the principle, and the practice, those who realize the fruit are exceedingly rare.

Third is the time of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*); being far removed from the Buddha, empty sophistry and mere semblances proliferate. Though the teaching and the principle exist, both practice and the realm [of realization] have perished.
The present Emperor’s statement, "If after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa," refers collectively to both the *saddharma* (True Dharma) and *pratirūpaka-dharma* (Semblance Dharma) periods.
The subsequent phrase, "If during the time of the *dharmavyaya* (decline of the Dharma)," specifically points to the era when [the teachings] are empty and resemble mere semblances (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

It must be specified separately because, although the teachings and principles still exist at that time, both practice and realization are rare; thus, they are particularly pitiable. The phrase "There are sentient beings" refers to the period when there is a Buddha.
There are many. This is because there are many who develop the bodhicitta through direct instruction and personal admonition.

During times when no Buddha is present, they are also numerous within the True Dharma (Saddharma), for the teaching has not yet approached heterodoxy and those who develop the bodhicitta are likewise many.

During the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma), however, they are not so numerous, for the Semblance Teaching barely remains and those who develop the bodhicitta are few. This continues until the time of the Final Dharma (Mappō).
The empty sky seems to have measure; those who give rise to the bodhicitta are few and far between. To possess this is called being endowed with the nature of the Mahāyāna.
Once one possesses the seed-nature of the Mahāyāna, one will certainly be able to believe in the Perfect Enlightenment realized by the Buddha.
This is because the Great Perfectly Round Enlightened Mind is realized solely by the Buddha, and is thus termed "secret," as other beings are unable to know it. Although other beings...

They do not know. Even those who possess the lineage of the Mahāyāna are able to believe that the Buddha will certainly realize [enlightenment], and they likewise believe that when I attain Buddhahood, I too will certainly realize it;
thus, they resolve their minds and engage in practice. For this reason, they are called "those who desire to practice."
"Vihāra" is an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term; its full form is *saṃghārāma*, which translates here as "Garden of the Harmonious Assembly.

This refers to a pure grove where the monastic community from all directions dwells together in harmony. One who is both virtuous and senior in years (*vaya*) is qualified to preside over it; thus, it is said to be "located" there.
By ensuring that the four matters of administration are not lacking, the assembly of disciples can then dwell in peace. It is thus.
Thus, one has not yet escaped the influence of circumstantial conditions; hence it is said that there are "conditions and affairs.

Because one cannot practice exclusively and single-mindedly, it is said that one "contemplates and examines according to one's capacity," meaning one contemplates and examines portion by portion according to the limits of what is appropriate for one's cultivation.

First, one causes delusions to be exhausted and the distant purity of awakening to emerge; next, one causes [the mind] to accord with and return to perfect awakening. This is as I previously explained to the Bodhisattva Universal Eye.
[Sa]. Having already explained each point in turn, the section on the method of contemplation according to one's capacity is concluded. △ Second, the method of cultivation for a fixed period:
"If there are no other incidental circumstances... [until] after twenty-one days have passed, one should single-mindedly collect the mind."

At the beginning of the practice period at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), since one neither presides over a monastery nor guides a community of disciples, it is said that there are no other incidental circumstances.
As established in the preceding section, presiding over a monastery and guiding a community of disciples are both matters belonging to the category of benefiting others (*parārtha*).
Because such activities for the benefit of others are manifold, one cannot practice exclusively; therefore, [the text] only commands...

Reflecting upon this as best as one can: since there are currently no conditions for engaging in deeds that benefit others, and because one’s own self-benefit is paramount, one should immediately establish a *maṇḍala*. A *maṇḍala* is a field for cultivating the Way. As for "establishing" it:
whether square or circular, large or small, its boundaries are demarcated on all sides, and the site is consecrated by reciting mantras according to the ritual rules.
This is because one must ensure that external affairs do not interfere with the practice. Regarding the establishment of a time limit:
by fixing a deadline, one exerts vigor, and the Way is easily accomplished. If a long period of one hundred and twenty days is established, this is calculated for those of superior capacity;
within this single session, they vow to realize the realization. Taking these periods into account, this amounts to four months. A medium period of one hundred days—

Regarding those of medium capacity, it is feared that if the period is too long, their strength will become exhausted; thus, there is no better way than to combine the middle [periods] and shorten the duration to two weeks.
As for the later period of eighty days, this is for those of inferior capacity; if the goal is not achieved in one session, they are permitted to practice again.
Within that middle period, if two weeks and two days are subtracted, it is already established. However, the Tathāgata’s determination of the three periods was not without purpose;
it was intended so that those of inferior faculties might plant the seeds, those of middling faculties might ripen, and those of superior faculties might attain liberation.
Had it not been so, those of superior faculties would have naturally been able to plan for the distant future, while those of middling faculties might have...
One may strive to achieve this. As for those of inferior capacity, there are few who do not aspire to the rocky crags.
To establish a Pure Abode (śuddhāvāsa), one establishes a dwelling for pure cultivation within the site of practice (dojō). This is like the establishment of a *kṣetrasīmā* (precept field):

the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) serves as the "boundary for not losing one's robes" (*acīvarāpannāsīmā*), while within it, a smaller boundary (*sūkṣmasīmā*) is further established as the place for performing ritual acts (*dharmakarmasthāna*). "If the Buddha [descends]," and so forth—perform prostrations.
The Buddha requested that they perform repentance. "If the Buddha were present" refers to the time when the Tathāgata dwelt in the world.

While the Tathāgata dwelt in the world, if one was unable to go to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to pay homage, one should simply maintain right mindfulness and contemplation—namely, contemplating the Dharma-body of the Buddha as pervading all places, for wherever one pays homage, that very place is the Buddha. "If after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" refers to the time when the Tathāgata has departed from the world.

It is the right time. Since the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, one who wishes to pay homage to the Buddha must establish an image. Establishing an image need not go beyond carving it from wood or molding it from clay;
however, the essential point is that one must maintain the Buddha in the mind and visualize the Buddha with the eyes.

To give rise to right mindfulness means to recollect that the Dharmakāya is eternally abiding and fundamentally without extinction. Thus, even this carved wood or molded clay is identical to the eternal Tathāgata.
On the day of the observance, as for the hanging of banners and flowers: the banners and flowers are placed before [the image];
in the center, they construct a canopy, and the flowers are suspended in the air like those scattered by the gods, fluttering and drifting in the wind.

Just as in the establishment of altars for repentance today, one must strive for the utmost beauty and excellence, exerting all strength and sincerity to constitute true offerings. With careful application of a single mind, [this continues] through three...

For seven days, prostrate before the Buddhas of the ten directions by name, seeking compassion and repenting. "Repentance" (chan) means to repent for and eliminate past transgressions; "regret" (hui) means to regret and resolve not to create them again.
When body and mind are thus purified, the fruits of the Path can be realized. It is like cleansing a vessel to prepare it for holding the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "encountering the good" (遇善): one who encounters a favorable state directly attains efficacy through cultivation. One who encounters a virtuous environment...
Sometimes there may be radiant light as a sign of worship, or auspicious omens in dreams; yet if one does not give rise to thoughts of holiness, these are called "wholesome realms.
One will naturally attain mental and physical pliancy, meaning that one is neither drowsy nor agitated.

Nevertheless, even though it is thus, it will not exceed twenty-one days, for it is only through the mutual resonance of the response and the path that the principle can finally be settled. Thus, single-mindedly...

"Proceeding directly" means to go straight ahead, transcending all deliberation and conjecture, for the purpose of never regressing. "Gathering mindfulness" means to collect deluded thoughts to achieve right contemplation and accord with perfect enlightenment.
This concludes the section on the expedient means for practicing within a fixed period. △ Third, the expedient means for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) consists of three parts:
first, distinguishing the Great [Vehicle] from the Small; second, addressing the Buddha with a formal petition; third, departing according to circumstances if the period expires. First:

If, at the beginning of summer, one enters the three-month *an-guo* (rainy season retreat), and until the mind has become detached from the level of a *śrāvaka* and no longer relies on a following of disciples—according to the *Da shu* (Great Commentary):
"However, when establishing a *mārga-dhāma* (place of practice), whether within a monastery or in another location—if the fixed period has not yet expired..."

If the beginning of summer has already arrived and one enters the communal *varṣā* retreat, it would violate the solemn vow; yet if one completes the period alone, one further commits an offense against the *vinaya*.
Because those within the site of practice harbor doubts on this account, the Tathāgata, mindful from afar, provides this clarification.

If one were to act in accordance with worldly custom while contravening the Vinaya, it would not be a case of abandoning the minor for the sake of the major; thus there would be no fault. Therefore, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"To uphold the śrāvaka precepts is to break the bodhisattva precepts; to uphold the bodhisattva precepts is to break the śrāvaka precepts. Regarding the statement that one "should act":

since the commencement of the summer retreat has already occurred, it is inappropriate to go in and out for the purpose of wandering and teaching; this applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
All should practice the method of *varṣā* (the summer retreat). There are two kinds of purity: first, purity of the nature of mind, which refers to Bodhisattvas;
second, purity of the objective realm, which refers to Śrāvakas. To dwell in stillness is itself the *varṣā*.

However, since one knows that one is fixing a specific period for cultivation in order to seek the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), even while observing the *varṣā*, one should likewise practice the purity of the nature of mind. Bodhisattvas...

The Bodhisattva abides [in this state]. As for "the mind being detached from the Śrāvakas," it is not necessary to again direct the mind toward the sphere of the Śrāvakas, because that is a field of purification.

Furthermore, when a Śrāvaka enters the retreat (varṣā), he must first assemble the community and seek their consent; moreover, the retreat itself must be formally announced to the Saṃgha, as it necessarily requires a following of disciples.
Since [the Bodhisattva] does not enter into such a community, he does not require these formalities. This marks a great distinction.
The Minor Section concludes. △ Second, presenting a petition before the Buddha:
On the day of entering the retreat (until) "for a great reason, he does not bind his followers."
At the beginning of the period, one approaches the Buddha and sits in meditation. Regarding the arrival of the day for entering the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat):

following the Buddha’s regulations and conforming to the customs of this region, the fifteenth day of the fourth month is established as the day for the earlier entry into retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*). Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles enter the retreat on this very day.

That which is performed in the presence of the Buddha clearly indicates the Mahāyāna; that which is carried out by performing monastic affairs according to the Hīnayāna is what constitutes the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to the Saṃgha.
Regarding the phrase "before the Buddha" used here: it refers to performing the work of a Buddha according to the Mahāyāna.
Because one ought to inform the Buddha, one speaks these words by forming a mental recollection directed toward the Buddha; it does not mean uttering them as a vocal proclamation.
The word "I" (aham) indicates a personal statement made by oneself, as it does not concern another. "Bhikṣus" and "bhikṣuṇīs" refer to the two assemblies of those who have left the household life;

"upāsakas" and "upāsikās" refer to the two assemblies of lay followers. According to the *śrāvaka* (Hīnayāna) system of the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*), the retreat is permitted only for these two assemblies of renunciants.
However, this is the Mahāyāna, and here the retreat is based on the nature of the mind (*cittaprakṛti*); it does not depend on physical location and thus applies to both the laity and the ordained.
This is not problematic; therefore, it is stated collectively with reference to the fourfold assembly who have made a formal commitment to practice together.

Those who "dwell in the Bodhisattva Vehicle" are so called because they rely upon the Dharma of the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas to cultivate the practice of *tathatā* (suchness) and cessation (*śānti*).
Now, "cessation" is a name established based on *tathatā*; that is to say, "true" (*tathā*) means being free from delusion and transcending verbal expression.
"Phenomena (lakṣaṇa) are called quiescence; their suchness is unchanging. To be free from mental conditions and characteristics is called cessation (nirodha).

To cultivate the cause in accordance with this principle is termed 'practice' (caryā). [The section] "Together entering below" correctly describes the Bodhisattva’s summer retreat (varṣā). Together they enter into purity.
Regarding "abiding in the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): when one's practice accords with the truth, it is called "entering together.
Regarding "the pure true mark": in this sutra it is called "pure awakening. In terms of the *Awakening of Faith*, this is the gate of the suchness of mind (*cittatathatā-mukha*).
As for "pure," it means not giving rise to a single thought. As for "true mark," it means maintaining its own nature; that is, this very non-arising of a single thought, maintaining its own nature.
The nature itself is the abbot. It is like the arrangement of the Pure Abode within a *maṇḍala*, or the establishment of a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) within a precept field (*śīlakaṇḍa*).
Although the principle and the phenomenon differ, their boundaries are quite similar. To take Great Perfect Enlightenment as one’s monastery (*ārāma*):
the nature of Great Perfect Enlightenment is referred to at the beginning of this sutra as the "Great Dharani. According to the Flower Garland [Sutra]...

"Yan" (the Enclosure) is precisely the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*). To call it "my monastery" (*gālayana*) is because the *dhāraṇī* encompasses all phenomena and sustains immeasurable meanings.

The One True Dharma-realm subsumes both the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) and the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). Cultivating the causes and realizing the fruits are entirely contained within this;
thus, it possesses the meaning of a monastery. It is like the establishment of a site for practice (*maṇḍala*) according to a fixed schedule, analogous to the precepts.
The boundary of the field where robes are not lost is also quite similar in its demarcations. Regarding the "abiding in peace of body and mind":
initially, it is because True Suchness (tathatā) does not maintain its own nature that the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) arises through transformation.
Subsequently, moved by the winds of objective conditions, the preceding seven consciousnesses arise as waves. From these, the first five consciousnesses pursue external objects.
Within the sixth consciousness, one takes as objects the reflected images of phenomena; consequently, this drags along the five aggregates of body and mind so that they cannot abide in peace.
Now that you have together entered the maintenance of the pure true reality (*dharmatā*), the first five consciousnesses no longer pursue external objects.
The sixth consciousness also does not internally take mental images as its object; since its successive states do not reach the aggregates, the body and mind attain stable abiding.
As for the seventh manas-consciousness, it formerly took the six consciousnesses as its function and internally took the eighth consciousness as its essence.
Now that the body and mind are unmoving, the six consciousnesses no longer engage in discrimination; thus, the seventh is without function, as there is nothing external [for it to grasp].
It is that which is taken as an object. Since there is no external object, one does not conceive of the eight consciousnesses as a self, and thus internally, too, there is no object.

When there is no object either internally or externally, the seventh manas-consciousness is immediately the Wisdom of Equality, and the ocean-like mind of the ālayavijñāna returns to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "The True Suchness of the Mind is precisely this One Dharma."
The essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristics of the Dhātus is what is called the nature of the mind, which is neither born nor extinguished.
That which is neither born nor extinguished is the very self-nature of Nirvāṇa; for it is "nir" because it does not arise, and "vāṇa" because it does not perish.
Since it is unborn, it is not bound to existence; since it is unextinguished, it does not belong to emptiness. Therefore, it is said to be without attachment or dependence. Based on this:
Thus, they dwell together in the universally illuminating, quiescent, and non-dual nature of Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi).
Because there is no attachment to spatial directions or boundaries, as stated above, they take Great Perfect Enlightenment as their monastery (ārāma).

The meaning lies herein. "I now," and so forth: I respectfully request that [this case] not be treated like other assemblies. The period for the *śrāvaka* rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*) is also a regulation established by the Buddha;
out of fear of violating it, I would not dare to do so. If permission is granted, then even if I were to violate [the rule], there would be no transgression.

"Not following the *śrāvaka*" means that this is a retreat in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which differs from theirs. It should be equal to that of the ten directions; this refers to the Buddha.

Together with the bodhisattvas, they all abide in the pure true mark (*dharmatā*). Taking perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) as their monastery (*ārāma*), they themselves are likewise identical to it.
Regarding the three-month *varṣā* retreat, it is fixed at a period of exactly three months; this differs from the śrāvakas, who observe two separate retreats, one before and one after the summer.
The reason for not adhering to minor formalities is that they are cultivating the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
For a great reason, he did not bind his followers together; for he feared that if they could not keep pace with the great, they would also lose their way along with the small.
Having finished presenting his words to the Buddha, △ third, he followed after the lapse of the time limit.
Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of the summer retreat (*vassa*), which proceeds without obstruction after the three-month period has passed.
Since the Mahāyāna takes the pure *dharmatā* as its dwelling place and the nature of Great Perfect Enlightenment as its monastery, this itself constitutes the summer retreat;
why then must it necessarily begin at the start of summer? It is merely to spare the world from worldly affairs while manifesting the Dharma, thus demonstrating the commencement of the summer season.
Regarding the summer retreat (*varṣā*): it is also intended to cause those who originally lacked great resolve to feel shame when they see others undertaking the summer retreat at its commencement.
As for the statement that one may travel freely after the three-month period has passed, the *Great Commentary* states:

"When the three-month period at the site of practice is completed, although the summer limit according to the Hīnayāna has not yet ended, because this was originally not a Hīnayāna-style retreat, there is no impediment to traveling as one pleases."

"Good son, if all sentient beings [from this point] until all objective realms can never be grasped, [this] first demonstrates the skillful means.

If there are sentient beings who, still referring to those not yet awakened in the final age, wish to practice *dhyāna*, from where should they first begin? Therefore, he teaches that one should first grasp the count."
This is the "Gate," which refers to the contemplation of counting the breaths. For when practicing *śamatha*, one first takes up ultimate stillness;

yet if one is biased toward stillness, one falls into the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. When practicing *samādhi*, one first takes up recollective thought; yet if one is biased toward thought, one remains close to ordinary people and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Now, by gathering thought and recollection into a single breath, one transcends the ordinary and the non-Buddhist, transforming ultimate stillness.

Regarding the counting [of breaths], one does not fall into the conditions of hearing. When the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the "Chapter on Majestic Power" is accomplished, one transcends the realms of both obstruction and non-obstruction;
this method of counting is merely its preliminary stage. From "Within the mind" downwards, it clarifies the practice of cultivation.
"Thoroughly knowing" means to know with perfect clarity that between each exhalation and inhalation, there are the arising of thought, the abiding of thought, and the cessation of thought.

Because they are not confused. When a thought first arises, it is "arising" (*utpāda*); once the thought has arisen, it is "abiding" (*sthiti*); as the thought is about to end, it is "change" (*anyathātva*);
and once the thought has ended, it is "cessation" (*nirodha*). Now, the reason "change" is not explicitly mentioned here is that it is on the verge of ceasing;
since it is subsumed under cessation, there is no cause for discrepancy among the various sūtras and śāstras when some speak of three characteristics and others speak of four. This is the division.
Regarding the method of counting from one: there is the portion of arising for what arises, the portion of abiding for what abides, and the portion of ceasing for what ceases.
Counting from one up to ten, one must ensure that each is clearly and distinctly understood.
As for the skillful means to gather the scattered mind and enter stillness, and to transform that stillness so it does not remain fixed, nothing surpasses this.
Furthermore, the above refers to the practice of counting the breath during seated meditation for a beginner.

The following passage, beginning with "In this way," refers instead to one who has practiced for a long time until their skill is perfected, such that they do not abandon the practice during the four modes of conduct; hence it says, "pervading the four modes of conduct," and so forth.

Regarding "discriminating the count of thoughts": this means analyzing and discerning. Between one exhalation and one inhalation, there arise thoughts of arising, thoughts of abiding, and thoughts of ceasing.
Furthermore, these segments are combined into a single breath. Thus, counting each breath from the beginning up to ten, there is nothing that is not clearly known.
This is the means by which one gathers the scattered mind to enter stillness, and transforms that stillness so as not to... [become stagnant].
The skill of abiding is even more refined and subtle than before. ○ "Gradually" and so forth below, reveals the benefits:
thus, by gathering the scattered and entering into stillness, one is not obstructed by phenomena; by transforming stillness so as not to dwell therein, one is not obstructed by principle.

In this way, as one gradually progresses, the absolute, numinous mind seeks to emerge. Through the power of its latent arousal and secret operation, one does not merely know the cessation [of the breath].
He knows thoughts; he knows numbers, until there is nothing he does not know, and all phenomena are fully understood by him.
First, let us take one of the most difficult things to know as an example; thus it is said, "thereby knowing hundreds of thousands," and so forth.

The Buddha’s intention is that the hundred thousand worlds are the most distant and thus most difficult to know, and each drop of rain is the most numerous and thus most difficult to know; yet these can now be known. As for the rest...
As for those who are closer and those whose [defilements] have diminished, it goes without saying. It is like seeing with one's own eyes;

the metaphor clarifies that what is known is perceived with utter clarity, as if observing a fruit in the palm of one's hand, rather than seeing it indistinctly. ○ "Not that" and below: this prevents the error of misapprehension; one should still rely on the previous understanding.

It will be abandoned; one cannot achieve success because it is obstructed by past karma. One should diligently seek repentance.

As for ritual repentance (*sāṃvṛtika-pratideśanā*), one should solemnly prepare a flower altar, prostrate before the Buddha, recite sutras, and maintain mantras. As for ultimate repentance (*pāramārthika-pratideśanā*), one should sit peacefully in a quiet room and observe that the nature of sin is ungraspable.
Upon encountering a wholesome state, one attains mental lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*). Thereafter, one should single-mindedly collect the mind.
One constantly gives rise to two kinds of aspirations: first, the aspiration to sever the delusions of aversion and attachment; second, the aspiration to seek the superior mind.

Regarding the severance of the delusions of aversion and attachment: "aversion" refers to the arising of a mind of loathing toward objects that are disagreeable, which is precisely the affliction of *dveṣa* (hatred) among the root afflictions, because aversion necessarily entails hatred. "Attachment" refers to [the mind] toward objects that are agreeable.

To give rise to a mind of passionate attachment (*rāga*) is itself the affliction of greed (*lobha*) among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), because where there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is necessarily greed.

Envy (*īrṣyā*) and deceitfulness (*śāṭhya*) are both minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*); they are called "derivative" (*anu*) because they are of the nature of outflows from the root afflictions.
Although they are called "derivative," they arise individually; therefore, they are called "minor" (*paritta*). Envy (*īrṣyā*) means to be intent upon...
To seek fame and profit for oneself while being unable to endure the prosperity of others, having envy as one's nature, is therefore called *īrṣyā* (envy).

It is subsumed under one portion of *dveṣa* (hatred). *Śāṭhya* (deceit) refers to deceiving others by feigning a different demeanor; it has crookedness as its nature and is therefore called *śāṭhya* (deceit).

It is subsumed under one portion each of *lobha* (greed) and *moha* (delusion). Furthermore, these, together with hatred (*dveṣa*) and attachment (*rāga*), are collectively termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*). This is because an affliction is characterized by a lack of clarity.

Ignorance is precisely delusion (*moha*). Just as when one’s hatred does not cease but is followed by jealousy, or when one’s attachment does not cease but is followed by flattery and crookedness—how great is that delusion!
Therefore, among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), [it is listed first].
To speak only of hatred and love while not manifesting the meaning of delusion (*moha*) is because delusion is inherently present; there is no need to manifest it further.
"Seeking the supreme mind" means that seeking is itself the arousal [of the mind], for seeking necessarily entails arousal.
The "supreme mind" is precisely the unsurpassed bodhicitta. Because this bodhicitta transcends the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle, it is called the "superior mind. All...
Because no mind can surpass it, it is called the "supreme mind. The three kinds of pure contemplation refer to those previously explained;
they are the three contemplations practiced based on awakening. Since these [practitioners] possess dull faculties, there is concern that they may be unable to practice all three simultaneously;

This is because when one focuses exclusively on a single object, success is easily achieved. If this meditation cannot be accomplished, it may be due to past habitual tendencies that do not correspond to the practice;
therefore, one is further instructed to retrain in that specific meditation. In this manner, they should practice them alternately.
The general instruction is that one must not let the mind stray, but should gradually refine it until one inevitably seeks entry into realization.

When the time of fruition arrives and the capacity is matured, one will naturally push open the door and fall into the mortar—as evidenced by the World-Honored One’s six years on the Snowy Mountains, where he waited for the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month to attain enlightenment. This is explained in the "Mañjuśrī Chapter. △ Second, expressing gratitude for the benefits received:

Because he has expounded with utmost effort the stages of faith, understanding, practice, and realization, manifesting them for the sake of the final age so that all may universally receive their benefit, he is called the World-Honored One of Great Compassion.
When he says, "Extensively for us and for the multitudes of the final age," this refers to the teaching as being an extensive exposition on the absence of aggregates (*an-ūna*).
In terms of its capacity to respond to sentient beings, it is universally pervasive without exception; this is precisely why it is called "Great Compassion" and "World-Honored One.

Regarding the phrase "awakening those above," the text is slightly deficient; if the two characters "universally cause" (普令) were added, they would correspond to the two characters "extensively for" (廣為), and the meaning would then be complete.
Such inconceivable matters refer generally to the ten chapters of the main teaching, meaning "thus and thus."
Faith is born. In this way and that way, understanding is developed; in this way and that way, practice is initiated;

in this way and that way, the fruit is realized. Each and every stage can be clearly elucidated; each and every stage can be thoroughly awakened to. The benefit received is truly an inconceivable matter.

"To receive and uphold [the teaching] by imperial command—if the Buddha does not speak it, how shall we receive and uphold it?

Good son, this sutra is the pure eye among hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sands of [sutras] up to the twelve divisions of the canon.
At the outset, it gives rise to joy and delight. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for only one purpose.
If they did not preach this, their appearance in the world would be without purpose. Thus we know that this sutra is indeed [the essence] of all Buddhas.
It is taught collectively that when one speaks of "hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions of Ganges-sands," these are also numbers beyond calculation;
in truth, there is no Buddha who does not preach it. Those who uphold it do not speak at the wrong time, but only when the time has arrived.

Those who protect it do not transmit it to those who lack the capacity, but only when the capacity has matured. Thus we know that the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have diligently upheld and protected this.

It is to cause this Dharma to abide eternally without decay or extinction. The fact that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Amitābha*, and other sutras all state that they are "protected and remembered by all Buddhas" is also for this very purpose.
The reason these words are specifically spoken is to inspire a heart of joy and delight toward this sutra among the bodhisattvas present in the assembly.

It gives rise to all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the pāramitās, thereby instructing bodhisattvas.

Since it is called "instruction for bodhisattvas," it should be the refuge for bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions. Furthermore, since it is called the "Great Dhāraṇī," it encompasses everything.
The Dharma upholds immeasurable meanings; thus, one who attains the realization of Perfect Enlightenment is able to clearly comprehend the meaning of all dharmas.

Therefore, it serves as the pure eye for the twelve divisions of the scriptures. The reason for necessarily speaking of this is to cause sentient beings of the末代 (final age) to give rise to a heart of profound faith in this sutra.

Answer: This sutra is titled *Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhichitta-dhāraṇī* (up to) "you should uphold it.
First, the direct answer regarding the title of the sutra: there are five names for this sutra, but the title takes only two; within those two, three further characters are omitted.
Regarding the title: its general explanation has been detailed in the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*. The meanings of the other three names have also been briefly recounted;
thus, there seems to be no need for further prolixity here. Nevertheless, since the meanings within the sūtra are inexhaustible, what harm is there in explaining the titles once more?
The first name is *Mahāvaipulya-pariśuddha-bodhi-dhāraṇī*. This is a name formed by combining both the general and specific aspects of the dharma’s meaning.

That is to say, "Perfect Enlightenment" (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa) is the *dharma*, and "Great Vaipulya" is its meaning. This *dharma* can encompass all phenomena, and this meaning can sustain immeasurable meanings;
therefore, it is also designated by the term *dhāraṇī*. In the Sanskrit language, *dhāraṇī* [means that which holds].
This is translated as "dhāraṇī" (total retention). This means that it encompasses all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings.

Thus, the first five characters are specific, while the last three characters are general. In the title, the specific is taken and the general is omitted; therefore, the first name retains only these five characters.
The second name is *Sūtra-lakṣaṇārtha* (The Sūtra of Definitive Meaning). This is named according to the relationship between the object and the wisdom. The above...
This sūtra is called the "Pure Eye of the Twelve Divisions of Scripture" (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). The "Twelve Divisions" refers to the twelve *aṅgas*.
As for its current designation as a "sūtra," although each division has its own distinct name, anything that belongs to the Buddha’s teaching may be designated by the term "sūtra.
Thus, it should be understood that the three characters *sūtra* (xiūduluō) refer collectively to all twelve divisions of scripture.
The doctrinal meanings elucidated therein—such as the sudden and gradual, the partial and perfect, and so forth—are all objects of illumination.
The two characters "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*) refer to the wondrous wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*);

it is this wisdom that is able to fully comprehend each and every meaning within the twelve divisions of the scriptures, whether sudden, gradual, partial, or perfect, thereby serving as the illuminating subject. Thus, there is a mutual correspondence between the object and the wisdom.
It is designated by the name "Sūtra of Definitive Meaning. The third is named the "Secret King Samādhi";

it is so named because this meditative concentration is unimpeded in both stillness and movement. As for "samādhi," it is precisely what is called the "illusion-like samādhi" in the Chapter on Samantabhadra.
Contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations. Within all phenomena, when not a single thought arises, one immediately attains samādhi;
this is called "stability" (dhyāna). Having realized they are illusory, one then gives rise to various illusions to eliminate the illusionist.
By manifesting these illusions, one opens the way for the illusory multitudes and attains great mastery, which is metaphorically likened to a king; this is called "movement" (samāpatti). However...
This movement does not exist apart from concentration; rather, it is movement within concentration itself. This concentration does not exist apart from movement;
rather, it is concentration within movement itself. There may be sentient beings who see only concentration and do not see movement, whereby movement becomes a secret.
There may be sentient beings who see only movement and do not see concentration, whereby concentration becomes a secret. Its...

It is truly unimpeded; therefore, it is named the "Secret King Samādhi. The fourth is named the "Tathāgata’s Decisive Realm," which is designated by the name of the unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*).
A "Tathāgata" is one who is able to realize Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Being able to realize Perfect Enlightenment, they directly use Perfect Enlightenment to deliver sentient beings; yet, because sentient beings are largely deluded and distressed, [the teaching proceeds] by means of the Gate of True Suchness.
And one provides relief for them, as explained in the Mañjuśrī Chapter: "extinguishing delusion and returning to pure awakening. This definitive realm is precisely *tathatā* (suchness).
In this fundamental scripture, it is termed "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*). Because it is unchanging, it is called "definitive";
because it manifests through the extinction of delusion, it is called a "realm. If one practices in accordance with this in a compliant manner, then—
Returning to Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*): the essential function of this single scripture does not exceed these [five names]. Thus, they are so named.
The fifth name, "The Distinctions of the Self-Nature of the Tathāgata-garbha," is a name based on the nature of the *tathāgata-garbha* as it accords with conditions.

The preceding names were established for those of the Sudden Teaching’s One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Regarding those of the Sudden Teaching’s One Vehicle: although they have turned their backs on Perfect Enlightenment, they have not yet wandered far from the path; however, because—

Connecting through the gate of *tathatā* (suchness), with a brief degree of conformity, one immediately reaches perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). This designation is established for those of the Mahayana path, such as those of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*).
It is said that those of the root-nature of the Final Teaching and other Mahayana vehicles have turned their backs on perfect enlightenment and have gradually strayed from the path.

If one were to connect them solely through the gate of *tathatā*, there would likely be some among them who fail to reach the goal. Therefore, one further employs the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

It brings them to completion through its transformative influence. The *tathāgatagarbha* is itself *tathatā*. Because it is fully endowed with the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) within, and because all Buddhas can arise in dependence upon it, it is termed the "Tathāgatagarbha.
As for the designation of its specific distinctions regarding its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*):
The self-nature, following conditions, constitutes the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*). Within this gate of arising and ceasing, there are many varieties of differentiation:

namely, when through the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*), the three subtleties (*tri-sūkṣma*) immediately arise; then, with objective realms as conditions, the six coarsenesses (*ṣaṭ-sthūla*) further develop—this is what is meant by "the path of delusion gradually becoming distant.
It is by means of this gate that the path of delusion is gradually distanced and completed in its curvature.

This is to cause one to know that from the True (zhen) one can give rise to the delusory (wang), yet by reversing the delusory, one immediately returns to the True. Taking this path, one returns home;

there is no further need for the extraordinary or the marvelous. How much more so when returning to the True and attaining full realization—how could the progress toward such certification be difficult?
It is as described in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in the "Maitreya Chapter" regarding the differentiation of the five natures, and in the "Pure Wisdom Chapter" regarding the five kinds [of lineages].

"Conforming to" [the nature of reality] refers entirely to the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), wherein the meaning of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodhi*) is skillfully established;

for this reason, the title was thus set forth. This indeed has its justification. The final phrase also answers the request regarding "receiving and upholding. According to the previous request by the virtuous Śrī-maṇi, he asked:
"What is the name of this Mahāyāna teaching? How should it be received and upheld? Now, since the World-Honored One has already spoken of the five kinds [of teachings], [the response follows].
Regarding the name: at the end, he further instructs, "You should uphold it. "Upholding" (feng) means to uphold it for one's own cultivation;
"upholding" (chi) means to uphold it for the purpose of teaching others. Both self-benefit and benefit for others must involve giving rise to the meaning based on the name.

Therefore, he instructs, "You should," meaning that one ought to give rise to the meaning based on the name and thus uphold it. If one does so, then self-benefit and benefit for others will be nearly perfected.

[The] fruit. All existing objects of experience are revealed within this sutra. To say that it "only reveals" [this] means it does not involve other vehicles, much less heterodox teachings;
thus, one further knows that these have no bearing upon this sutra. Someone may ask:
