Good son, this sutra is titled "The Mahāyāna of Sudden Teaching" (up to: "and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice through gradual cultivation.

This sutra uses words to manifest the principle; once the principle is clarified, words are forgotten. It does not establish written characters; it requires only that for a single thought-moment, non-arising occurs.
This is immediately named "Buddha. It is called the Sudden Teaching because it does not explain according to the gradual sequence of stages and positions.
As for the term "Mahāyāna," it does not accommodate those of small capacity, meaning that it is beyond the reach of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, this is not merely Mahāyāna, but rather Ekayāna (the One Vehicle), because this sutra reveals exclusively the single Buddha-vehicle. That it is now called "Great" is as follows:
It is not that what is called "great" is so merely in contrast to the small; rather, it is named "great" because it transcends all.
It is like the three carts outside the gate in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: compared to the sheep and deer carts, the ox cart is called "great";

yet if compared to the great white ox cart, it is not truly great. This present great white ox cart is indeed the true greatness. As for those sentient beings of sudden capacity, they have accumulated—

The causes of the kalpa have been fulfilled, yet the fruits of realization have not yet been attained. Now, having just emerged from birth, one attains awakening upon hearing [the Dharma] once—realizing a thousand things at once.

Those who practice in accordance [with the path] are like Sudhana; those who practice in reverse are like Aṅgulimāla; both are vehicles for the Sudden Teaching. From this point on, they shall open to enlightenment.

Upon hearing this sutra but once, the ground of the mind is suddenly opened and one realizes and witnesses perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). What is called "necessarily reaching the stage of Buddhahood" refers precisely to this greatness.
However, this is based on the correspondence between the capacity of the practitioner and the teaching; that the accomplishment of awakening is so profound and swift is indeed as it should be.
One must understand that "sudden" (*tun*) implies being close to the ultimate perfection (*pariniṣpanna*), for by following [the path], one can reach the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).

It also encompasses all classes of beings who practice through gradual cultivation, such as the Bodhisattvas of the two initial teachings, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Lesser Vehicle, and the sentient beings of the six realms of the mundane world.
Since there is not one among those who hear the Dharma who does not attain Buddhahood, it is able to include them all.
As stated in the Chapter on Maitreya: "Due to objects of desire, various conditions of opposition and compliance arise... [The text continues: "...objects..."
If one turns one's back on the heart of compassion and gives rise to hatred and envy, thereby creating various karmas, one will consequently be reborn in the realms of hell or hungry ghosts.
However, if upon hearing this one does not give rise to hatred and envy and refrains from creating such manifold karmas, then even those in the three miserable paths can attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, it is said: "Knowing that desire is to be loathed, one loathes the path of karma; abandoning evil and delighting in good, one again appears as a deva or human.
If, upon hearing this, one abandons evil karma and further transcends even good karma, then even devas and humans of the desire realm can attain Buddhahood.

It is also said: "Knowing that craving is to be loathed, one discards craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*). Yet, if one merely nourishes the root of craving, one will continue to manifest within conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*)."

This results in superior wholesome fruits. If, upon hearing this, one has already abandoned all cravings yet does not delight in that abandonment, and thus fails to nourish the root of craving, then even those in the two upper realms can attain Buddhahood. It is further said: "From fundamental greed and desire, ignorance is unleashed."

This reveals the distinctions and inequalities among the five natures (*pañca-gotra*). If, upon hearing this, one abandons fundamental craving and does not give rise to ignorance, then those of all five natures can achieve Buddhahood.

Thus we know that what this sutra refers to as "also encompassing the various classes of beings who practice gradually" is because this sutra universally encompasses all gradual dharma-gates. This is the explanation according to the Dharma.

II. The actual response concerning what should be protected.
"You, son of good family, should protect [beings] in the final age... causing their bodies and minds to be distressed and leading them to fall into despondency.
First, he addresses him as "you," and subsequently refers to him as "son of good family" to manifest that this is a direct exhortation to the specific recipient, causing him to pay close attention.
This is not a casual reply. According to the preceding request from the one suited to the occasion, who asked: "How may I cause those who protect and uphold this sutra to do so?
he was directly seeking to take charge of the matter himself. Therefore, the World-Honored One responded to his request, saying:

Even those who are currently deluded have long served many Buddhas and possess abundant merit and wisdom;

Thus, the Direct Explanation states: "The cultivation of this Dharma depends upon one’s life of wisdom. If one allows evil Māras to disturb and cause regression," [the life of wisdom is lost].
In that case, the life of wisdom would be severed; therefore, one must protect and uphold it.
The direct explanation does not mention "non-Buddhists" because non-Buddhists are the companions of Māra. "Afflicting their body and mind" means to harm the body and to disturb the mind.
"Retreating and yielding" means to lose one's original resolve and to bend one's will to follow others. This concludes the formal answer regarding what should be protected.

At that time, within the assembly was the Vajra Fire-Head (Agnimukha), [and so forth], whose wealth and treasures were abundant and never lacking.
Initially, he presided over the Vajra host with full ritual propriety; this refers to his presiding over his retinue. The meaning of "with full ritual propriety" can be understood accordingly.
The general title "Vajra" is derived from the name manifested by the *vajra* (thunderbolt) held in his hand, for its entire power resides in that *vajra*.
Regarding "Agnimukha-vajra" (Fire-Head Vajra), a direct interpretation states it means one who has flames upon his head;

this refers to what is described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as the transformation of a mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom, which is a manifestation of a Bodhisattva. As for "Cūrṇana-vajra" (Crushing Vajra)...
As for "the firm" (*kāṭhina*), it refers to the vajra held [in hand], which is able to shatter all celestial Māras, non-Buddhist paths, and the like.
Regarding "Nīlambavajra," both Guifeng and Hanshan state that its translation is unknown. As for the "eighty thousand vajras":
All are of their same kind; together with their retinues, they are merely the followers under their command. ○ Below the words "World-Honored One," it refers to the protection of persons and places.
If there are those capable of upholding this—this term specifically refers to the present sutra—then wherever it is manifest, there will certainly be protection.

It is not that Amoghasiddhi’s words are merely empty; they definitively establish the Mahāyāna. Rather than pointing to the scriptural teachings themselves, he points to the person who can uphold them.

Because this refers to those who definitively seek the Mahāyāna, it is like one who protects their eyes, manifesting the most rigorous protection so that not even a single speck of dust or a grain of sand may cause transgression.
This extends even to the *bodhimaṇḍa* and other such sites, as previously established in the path.
"Place" refers to the site where one practices for a fixed period. "Personally leading the assembly" means guarding the perimeter.
"Guarding morning and evening" means patrolling continuously day and night. In this way, demons and outsiders will not dare to commit transgressions, and one will naturally be free from regression.
Regarding the phrase "his home": it also includes protecting his private residence; "his home" refers to his personal dwelling. Forever...
The absence of calamities and obstacles manifests the peace and security of one's person and retinue; the abundance of wealth and treasures manifests the flourishing of the household.
Without the protection of the Vajra-holders, it would not be possible to reach this state. Thus ends the protection by the Vajras. △ Second, the protection by the various devas.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King and the twenty-eight kings of the heavens (up to) "constantly causing them to be peaceful and secure, so that their minds do not regress.
Regarding the initial ritual protocol for the celestial hosts, the direct explanation states: The Great Brahmā King is the sovereign of the First Dhyāna Heaven and the lord of the Sahā World.
Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, this king acts as the host for the invitation. The "twenty-eight heavens" refers collectively to the three [lower] heavens.

The various heavens of the realms refer to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the eighteen heavens of the dhyāna realms (*rūpadhātu*), and the four heavens of the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, Śakra is specifically mentioned as he is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. As for the Heavenly Kings who Protect the Nation, they belong to the Cāturmahārājika Heaven and serve as the lords who guard the boundaries of the realm.
[The commentator] privately notes: Below the Great Brahmā Heaven, the twenty-eight heavens have already been collectively indicated. This is...
Furthermore, Śakra and the Four Kings are specifically mentioned because they possess the majesty to lead assemblies and are capable of providing protection.
[The passage] from "The World-Honored One" downward grants permission for protection so that they may abide in peace; abiding in peace and remaining hidden, their minds should naturally not regress.
The protection by the various devas is concluded. △ Third, the protection by the assembly of spirits.
At that time, there was a great powerful ghost-king named Kumbhāṇḍa... (until)... I shall cause him to be crushed like fine dust.

They consume the vital essence of humans and move as swiftly as the wind. Their transformations are boundless, and they dwell in forests and wilds.

Because they govern the various classes of ghosts, they are titled "Kings. They do not belong to the realms of humans or devas, but reside alone within the *preta* destiny. [The practitioner] rises from their seat, prostrates, and circumambulates.

The direct explanation states: One *yojana* is forty *li*. To say "guarding the quarters" means that within a radius of forty *li*, there shall be no calamities.

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* is the true doctrine of all Buddhas and the ground of awakening for all sentient beings. Those who are deluded regarding it sink and drift through vast eons;

those who awaken to it realize sudden enlightenment in a single moment. From antiquity, there have been several schools of commentary, none of which— [...]* (Note: The source text provided ends abruptly here.)
To propagate the holy teachings and benefit all sentient beings, my teacher—the Elder who expounds the Dharma—has realized the ultimate Way in his mind and feels a profound compassion for others.

He previously composed commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and others; these works have already been carved onto printing blocks and distributed.

In the intervals between his meditative recitations, he happened to reflect upon this present sutra, which had not yet been fully elucidated. Consequently, he has consulted ancient commentaries and further set forth his own insights.

I studied this in sequence, analyzing it chapter by chapter and phrase by phrase, striving to ensure that the meanings were fully elucidated and the text was thoroughly accessible. My aim was to inspire those at the beginning of their spiritual journey;
thus, within less than a year, the work was completed and titled *The Analysis of the Meaning of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué xīyì*).

Its purpose was to make it public throughout the world, so that everyone might rely upon this commentary for practice and together enter the Great Treasury of Radiance (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*), traveling as one through the wondrous field of Perfect Enlightenment.
